### [1] [What is Good? Extracting and Testing Implicit Theories of Literary Quality from LLM Reasoning Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20425)
*Birger Moëll*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates how reasoning-enabled LLMs evaluate literary quality through two studies. Study 1 uses a 30-text benchmark across six quality tiers, finding 79.3% classification accuracy and a stated theory that prioritizes intentionality, craft, depth, and voice. Study 2 systematically degrades canonical prose across six dimensions, revealing that structural and voice manipulations cause the greatest quality loss, while vocabulary simplification has minimal impact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The persistent, unresolved question of what constitutes "good" writing in literary studies and computational linguistics motivates this work. The authors aim to uncover the implicit theory of literary quality held by reasoning-enabled LLMs, moving beyond simple classification to understand *how* and *why* models make evaluative judgments.

Method: Study 1: Constructed a benchmark of 30 real texts across six quality tiers (canonical literature to anonymous forum posts). Used DeepSeek with five replications to classify texts, extracting the model's implicit quality theory from reasoning traces. Included a familiarity experiment with style-matched but unrecognizable passages (canonical originals vs. researcher-written pastiches). Study 2: Applied six systematic degradation manipulations to five canonical prose passages — vocabulary simplification, rhythm flattening, imagery removal, voice genericization, structure simplification, and combined degradation — then reevaluated each version. An exploratory comparison with Qwen QwQ was also conducted.

Result: Study 1: DeepSeek achieved 79.3% mean tier-classification accuracy. Reasoning traces revealed a consistent stated theory valuing intentionality over correctness, emphasizing craft, depth, and distinctive voice. The familiarity experiment suggested source recognition may inflate scores, confounded by genuine quality differences. Study 2: Vocabulary simplification caused minimal quality loss (0.41 ± 0.46 points), while structure simplification (2.78) and voice loss (2.34) were far more damaging. Combined degradation was devastating (−5.64) but subadditive. Qwen QwQ showed the same broad qualitative pattern.

Conclusion: LLM judgments of writing quality are holistic, author-specific, and substantially more sensitive to structural and voice-related features than to lexical features. This has implications for automated writing feedback and computational aesthetics.

Abstract: What makes writing "good" remains a persistent question in literary studies and computational linguistics. We present a two-study investigation of how reasoning-enabled LLMs evaluate literary quality.
  In Study 1, we construct a benchmark of 30 real texts spanning six quality tiers, from canonical literature to anonymous forum posts, and extract the model's implicit theory of quality from its reasoning traces. Across five DeepSeek replications, the model achieves 79.3% mean tier-classification accuracy. The traces reveal a consistent stated theory: the model values intentionality over correctness, prioritizing craft, depth, and distinctive voice. A familiarity experiment with style-matched but unrecognizable passages suggests that source recognition may inflate scores, although this is confounded by genuine quality differences between canonical originals and researcher-written pastiches.
  In Study 2, we probe this theory through systematic degradation of five canonical prose passages. We apply six manipulations - vocabulary simplification, rhythm flattening, imagery removal, voice genericization, structure simplification, and combined degradation - and reevaluate each version. Vocabulary simplification causes the smallest quality loss (0.41 +/- 0.46 points), far below structure (2.78) or voice (2.34) loss. Combined degradation is devastating (-5.64) but subadditive. An exploratory comparison with Qwen QwQ shows the same broad qualitative pattern.
  Together, these studies suggest that LLM judgments of writing quality are holistic, author-specific, and more sensitive to structural than lexical features, with implications for automated writing feedback and computational aesthetics.

</details>


### [2] [Knowledge Injection Exists in MoE? Exploring Expert-Aware Contrast Decoding in MoE for Mitigating LLMs'Hallucinations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20426)
*Xinyue Fang,Zhiliang Tian,Zhen Huang,Ziyi Pan,Zhihua Wen,Xi Wang,Quntian Fang,Dongsheng Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EAACD is a contrastive decoding method that mitigates hallucinations in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs by exploiting expert activation differences in higher layers, contrasting high-reliability expert predictions against amplified low-reliability expert predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hallucination mitigation methods (prompt engineering, model optimization) struggle with cross-domain generalization or fail to alter internal knowledge. Prior contrastive decoding works only target transformer-based models (e.g., GPT), overlooking MoE architectures. Empirical investigation reveals that layer-wise differences used in standard contrastive decoding do not exist in MoEs with shared experts, motivating a new expert-level approach.

Method: EAACD (Expert-Aware Adaptive Contrastive Decoding) operates in three stages: (1) It splits high-layer MoE experts into a higher-reliability group and multiple lower-reliability groups based on confidence and consistency metrics. (2) It contrasts the higher-reliability group's prediction against each lower-reliability group's prediction to calibrate the original output distribution. (3) It amplifies hallucinations from lower-reliability experts using attention manipulation and masking to generate stronger negative references, enhancing contrastive calibration for QA tasks.

Result: EAACD outperforms all baseline methods across four QA datasets, demonstrating superior hallucination mitigation in MoE-based LLMs compared to existing approaches.

Conclusion: MoE architectures exhibit distinct expert activation patterns (rather than layer-wise differences) between factual and non-factual outputs in higher layers. Leveraging these expert-level differences via adaptive contrastive decoding provides an effective, architecture-specific strategy for reducing hallucinations that surpasses prior methods.

Abstract: Existing LLM hallucination mitigation methods, including prompt engineering and model optimization, either hardly alter models'internal knowledge or have poor cross-domain generalization. Contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by using layer-wise differences in LLMs. However, prior studies only explore transformer-based models (e.g., GPT), ignoring other effective frameworks like mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Since MoE alters the traditional transformer architecture, we conduct empirical studies to investigate whether similar layer-wise differences exist in MoEs. Our results show that they do not exist in MoE with shared experts; nevertheless, across different MoEs, higher layers exhibit distinct expert activation patterns between factual and non-factual outputs. Building on these, we propose EAACD, an expert-aware adaptive contrast decoding that uses expert differences in MoE's higher layers to mitigate hallucinations on QA tasks. EAACD splits high-layer experts into a higher-reliability group and several lower-reliability groups based on their confidence and consistency. It contrasts the higher-reliability group's prediction with each lower-reliability group's prediction to calibrate the model's original predictions. To strengthen this contrast, EAACD amplifies hallucinations from lower-reliability experts via attention and masking to provide stronger negative references. EAACD outperforms all baselines on four datasets.

</details>


### [3] [Is MoE Routing a Huffman Code? Discovering the Frequency-Diversity Law in Chain-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20427)
*Ching-Chieh Tsao,Zhuoyi Lin,Wenya Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MoE routing inherently follows Huffman Coding principles: common tokens get sparse expert allocation, rare/complex tokens get diverse expert committees. The authors identify a redundancy trap in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B where load-balancing masks this efficiency signal, and propose Subset Difference Pruning to eliminate functional duplicates, unlocking latent Huffman efficiency without degrading reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE routing mechanisms remain poorly understood as a black box. The authors aim to uncover the fundamental information-theoretic principles governing expert routing, moving beyond heuristic load-balancing toward principled compression-based design.

Method: The paper introduces the Frequency-Diversity Law and demonstrates that models like Phi-3.5-MoE and Gemma-4-27B-A4B naturally encode routing as Huffman Coding. They analyze effective sparsity (k/E_eff) to identify redundancy traps and propose Subset Difference Pruning — a surgical pruning strategy that removes functionally duplicate expert pathways to restore Huffman efficiency.

Result: State-of-the-art MoE models spontaneously act as information-theoretic engines: sparse expert allocation for high-frequency tokens, diverse committees for rare chain-of-thought tokens. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B suffers from a redundancy trap where low effective sparsity causes load-balancing to impose functional redundancy. Pruning eliminates duplicates and forces routing into streamlined, high-density paths without degrading reasoning performance.

Conclusion: Next-generation MoE architectures should abandon forced load-balancing and instead pursue Minimum Description Length (MDL) optimality: shorter routing codes for frequent information, longer/diverse codes for rare information, transforming routing from a heuristic into a principled compression engine.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts architectures have revolutionized scaling, yet the underlying logic of their routing remains a black box. In this paper, we uncover a fundamental governing principle: MoE routing is not merely selection, but a manifestation of Huffman Coding. We introduce the Frequency-Diversity Law, revealing that state-of-the-art models, such as Phi-3.5-MoE and Gemma-4-27B-A4B, spontaneously act as information-theoretic engines. These models allocate sparse expert resources for common tokens while invoking high-diversity expert committees for rare, complex tasks found in chain-of-thought trajectories. However, we identify a critical redundancy trap in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B: when effective sparsity (k/E_eff) is sufficiently low, load-balancing inadvertently imposes functional redundancy, masking the underlying Huffman efficiency signal. To bridge this gap, we propose Subset Difference Pruning, a surgical strategy to eliminate functional duplicates. We demonstrate that pruning does not degrade reasoning; instead, it unleashes the model's latent Huffman efficiency, forcing the logic to collapse into streamlined, high-density paths. Our findings suggest that the next generation of MoEs should move beyond forced load-balancing toward Minimum Description Length (MDL) optimality, assigning shorter expert-routing codes to high-frequency information and longer, more diverse codes to low-frequency information, thereby transforming routing from a heuristic into a principled compression engine.

</details>


### [4] [Human-in-the-Loop Large Language Model Framework for Identification of Cutaneous Immune-Related Adverse Events](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20428)
*Charles Lu,Olivia Burke,Debby Cheng,Adam Kashlan,Caitlyn Duffy,Zeyun Lu,Lirit Fuksman,Jin Ning Tian,Andrew Sedlack,Priya Katyal,Eudora Lee,Ralina Karagenova,Chuck Lin,Kun-Hsing Yu,Nicole LeBoeuf,Alexander Gusev,Yevgeniy R. Semenov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A multi-agent LLM framework with retrieval augmentation and human-in-the-loop improved detection of cutaneous immune-related adverse events from clinical notes, outperforming manual review in accuracy (F1=0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement (kappa=0.82 vs 0.50), and halving review time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual extraction of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) from clinical notes is labor-intensive, inconsistent, and poorly scalable. There is a need for accurate, efficient, and transparent automated methods to detect cutaneous irAEs (cirAEs) and, more broadly, immune-related toxicities across organ systems.

Method: The authors developed a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent LLM-driven framework with a human-in-the-loop component. The system processes clinical notes to detect cirAEs and was compared against unassisted manual review. Evaluation metrics included F1 score, Cohen's kappa for inter-rater agreement, and average review time.

Result: The LLM-assisted workflow achieved F1=0.88 (vs 0.77 for manual), Cohen's kappa=0.82 (vs 0.50), and reduced average review time by approximately 50%.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates that LLMs can effectively identify immune-related toxicities from clinical text, offering an accurate, scalable, and transparent approach to adverse event data extraction that generalizes beyond cutaneous events to other organ systems.

Abstract: This study evaluated a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent large language model (LLM)-driven, human-in-the-loop framework for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) from clinical notes. Compared with unassisted manual review, the LLM-assisted workflow improved accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen's kappa (kappa = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reduced average review time by approximately half. This framework pilots how LLMs can be applied to identify immune-related toxicities across organ systems and, more broadly, enable accurate, scalable, and transparent adverse event data extraction.

</details>


### [5] [More Is Not More: What Matters for Diversity in LLM Opinions?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20429)
*Qiyang Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A factorial experiment across 7 LLMs and 100 open-ended questions reveals that diversity in LLM-simulated opinions is not achieved by scaling any single intervention. Persona depth yields diminishing returns after initial conditioning; different interaction architectures cover non-overlapping opinion regions; and low-cost alternatives (temperature, diversity prompts) are ineffective. Combining multiple architectures is key to broader coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to simulate human opinions in open-ended tasks (synthetic surveys, focus groups, public opinion prediction), but they suffer from systematic opinion homogenization. Current interventions for increasing diversity are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics, and deployed simultaneously in practice, making it impossible to attribute gains to specific components. A more rigorous, scientific understanding of what drives LLM output diversity is needed.

Method: A factorial experiment design separating two primary intervention dimensions: (1) input conditioning (operationalized as persona depth — from no persona to basic persona to persona with demographic detail) and (2) interaction architecture. Evaluated across 100 real-user open-ended questions and 7 LLM models, using multiple complementary diversity metrics to avoid reliance on any single measure.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Persona depth does not monotonically increase diversity — the initial persona step captures most of the gain, while adding demographic detail can reduce diversity on some models. (2) Different interaction architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions; combining architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any single one. (3) Low-cost alternatives like raising sampling temperature and adding diversity instructions produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions.

Conclusion: Diversity in LLM outputs is not a product of scaling along any single dimension. It is highly sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions — specifically, combining multiple interaction architectures is more effective than deepening any single approach. The findings challenge common assumptions and advocate for a more principled, multi-faceted approach to opinion diversification in LLM-based simulation.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate diverse human opinions in open-ended tasks such as synthetic surveys, focus group modeling, and public opinion prediction. However, LLM outputs exhibit systematic opinion homogenization. Practitioners have explored various interventions to increase diversity, but the landscape remains fragmented: different methods are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics, and in practice they are typically deployed and upgraded simultaneously, making it difficult to attribute gains to specific components. To advance a more scientific understanding of LLM output diversity, we design a factorial experiment that separates two primary intervention dimensions: input conditioning (operationalized through persona depth) and interaction architecture. We evaluate all conditions on 100 real-user open-ended questions across 7 models, measuring diversity with multiple complementary metrics. Our findings challenge several common assumptions. First, more persona detail does not monotonically increase diversity. The initial step of persona conditioning already captures the majority of the gain, while further elaboration with demographic detail does not consistently improve and can reduce diversity on some models. Second, rather than seeking a single best interaction architecture, we find that different architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions. Combining multiple architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any one. Third, commonly attempted low-cost alternatives such as raising sampling temperature and adding diversity instructions produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions. Overall, our work demonstrates that diversity is not a product of scaling along any single dimension, but is highly sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions.

</details>


### [6] [Routing Subspaces: Auditing Evaluation-to-Deployment Mismatch in Fine-Tuned Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20436)
*Phongsakon Mark Konrad,Toygar Tanyel,Serkan Ayvaz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fine-tuning can create a gap where safety behaviors appear fixed under evaluation prompts but persist under ordinary-use prompts. The authors introduce an activation-contrast intervention at a mid-depth layer that closes this evaluation-to-deployment gap in most tested settings, providing a diagnostic audit for fine-tuned checkpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety evaluations assume that test-time behavior generalizes to deployment, but fine-tuning can break this assumption. A model may appear "fixed" on evaluation-style prompts while retaining undesirable behavior on ordinary-use prompts. Existing output-based metrics detect the discrepancy but do not locate its internal source. The paper seeks to identify whether this evaluation-deployment distinction is stably encoded in a specific internal site within the model.

Method: The authors propose an approach that: (1) uses path-patching to identify a mid-depth window of transformer layers where the evaluation-vs-deployment distinction is encoded; (2) fits a paired activation contrast using linear probes (difference-in-means or logistic regression) on activations from paired evaluation-style and ordinary-use prompts; and (3) intervenes by modifying activations along the learned contrast direction on held-out prompts to close the gap. The method is tested across four full-matrix instruction-tuned model instances, with a fifth model used for localization and edit-provenance checks.

Result: The intervention successfully closed the evaluation-to-deployment gap in 10 of 12 model-behavior settings (6 of 8 settings with n≥120 paired questions). Deployment-framed behavior rates changed by at most 6.1 percentage points. Two flat cells—both involving sycophancy—failed to respond, suggesting the distinction is higher-rank in those cases or missed by the depth heuristic.

Conclusion: The activation contrast provides a diagnostic audit for fine-tuned checkpoints, revealing whether a behavior distinction is encoded in a single coordinate at mid-depth. The method is explicitly not a training-time defense or a guarantee of deployment safety; it is a post-hoc analysis tool. Sycophancy failures indicate that a single-coordinate audit is insufficient when the installed distinction is higher-rank or outside the depth window.

Abstract: Safety evaluations often assume that behavior observed during testing reflects behavior in ordinary use, but fine-tuning can break this assumption. A checkpoint can appear fixed under evaluation-style prompts while the same behavior persists under ordinary-use prompts. Output scores reveal this mismatch but do not locate it. We investigate whether the distinction is encoded in a stable internal site and introduce an approach that fits a paired activation contrast at a path-patching-informed mid-depth window, then modifies the resulting coordinate on held-out prompts. The intervention closes the evaluation-to-deployment gap in ten of twelve model--behavior settings (six of the eight settings with $n{\geq}120$ paired questions) across four full-matrix instruction-tuned model instances; a fifth model supports localization and edit-provenance checks, and deployment-framed rates change by at most $6.1$pp. The two flat cells, both sycophancy, indicate that a single-coordinate audit is not sufficient when the installed distinction is higher-rank or missed by the depth heuristic. The audit is a diagnostic for fine-tuned checkpoints, not a training-time defense or a guarantee of deployment safety.

</details>


### [7] [LLM-INSTRUCT at UZH Shared Task 2026: Constraint-Aware Retrieval and Selective Debate for Paragraph-Level Argument Mining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20430)
*Phuong Huu Vu Tran,Long Minh Vo,Son Nguyen Minh Le,Hoang Van*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM-INSTRUCT won the ArgMining 2026 shared task on paragraph-level argument mining in UN/UNESCO resolutions by framing the problem as constrained structured prediction. The system combines metadata-aware dense retrieval for tag space reduction, constrained decoding with per-dimension caps, a three-agent debate branch for uncertain cases, and schema validation, achieving top overall ranking with notable improvements in Micro-F1 through configuration search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Argument mining in UN and UNESCO resolutions at the paragraph level requires multi-faceted prediction (paragraph-type classification, multi-label tag prediction from 141 tags, and directed relation prediction) under strict JSON schema constraints using only open-weight models ≤8B parameters. The key challenge is managing the combinatorially large output space while ensuring schema-compliant, accurate predictions with limited model capacity.

Method: The system frames the task as constrained structured prediction with four stages: (1) Metadata-aware dense retrieval narrows the 141-tag candidate space using resolution metadata (committee, topic, year) to reduce the decision space. (2) Constrained decoding applies per-dimension caps to enforce schema constraints during generation. (3) A three-agent debate branch is triggered only for uncertain cases, where three LLM instances argue to resolve ambiguity before producing a final prediction. (4) Final schema validation ensures JSON output compliance. A configuration search further tunes hyperparameters during development.

Result: Ranked 1st overall on the official leaderboard: 1st in F1 and 5th in LLM-as-a-Judge. During development, configuration search improved Task 1b Micro-F1 from 35.83% to 40.08% while maintaining Task 2 score at 4.421.

Conclusion: The core insight is that reducing the decision space before generation — through retrieval-based candidate filtering and constrained decoding — significantly improves both accuracy and submission robustness in structured prediction tasks with large label spaces and strict schema requirements.

Abstract: We present LLM-INSTRUCT, the winning system for the UZH Shared Task at ArgMining 2026 on paragraph-level argument mining in UN and UNESCO resolutions. The task requires paragraph-type classification, prediction of a subset of 141 official tags, and directed relation prediction under a strict JSON schema setting using only open-weight models up to 8B parameters. We frame the task as constrained structured prediction. The system first narrows the candidate tag space with metadata-aware dense retrieval, then applies constrained decoding with per-dimension caps, escalates only uncertain cases to a three-agent debate branch, and finally validates the output schema. On the official leaderboard, LLM-INSTRUCT ranked 1st overall, with 1st in F1 and 5th in LLM-as-a-Judge. During development, our configuration search further improved Task 1b Micro-F1 from 35.83% to 40.08% while keeping the internal Task 2 score at 4.421. The main lesson is simple: reducing the decision space before generation improves both accuracy and submission robustness. Our code and supporting scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/LLM-Instruct-at-UZH-Shared-Task-2026/Method

</details>


### [8] [Skill-Contracted Agents for Evidence-Aware Materials Literature Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20431)
*Bixuan Li,Yu Liu,Shuo Shi,Xiaoya Huang,Peng Kang,Lei Zheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AlphaAgent is a skill-driven agent framework that decouples retrieval and report generation via explicit skill contracts, substantially outperforming conventional RAG baselines on materials science literature analysis — especially for deep analytical reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines struggle to handle the heterogeneous tasks inherent in materials science literature analysis — simultaneously addressing composition, processing, characterization, and property relationships — because a single retrieve-then-generate architecture lacks the flexibility for diverse query types and deep analytical reasoning.

Method: AlphaAgent uses a skill-driven architecture with two explicit skill contracts: (1) a retrieval skill that rewrites user queries into material-specific search intents, queries a curated index of 300,000+ papers from the JCR Metallurgy and Metallurgical Engineering category, and reformulates queries when evidence is insufficient; (2) a report-generation skill that parses full-text PDFs to produce structured per-paper analytical reports and cross-paper summaries. Evaluation used 40 materials-science questions (half requiring deep analytical reasoning) in a blind comparison against a baseline matched for model, index, and retrieval scale.

Result: AlphaAgent substantially outperformed the matched baseline, with the largest performance gains observed in mechanistic explanation tasks and in awareness of credibility boundaries.

Conclusion: Explicit task separation, refined retrieval intent, and evidence-aware generation significantly improve LLM-based literature analysis for materials research, suggesting that skill-driven agent architectures are a promising direction beyond monolithic RAG pipelines.

Abstract: Materials science literature analysis requires simultaneous attention to composition, processing, characterization, and property relationships, yet conventional retrieval-augmented generation pipelines struggle to reconcile heterogeneous tasks within a single retrieve-then-generate architecture. Here we present AlphaAgent, a skill-driven agent framework that decouples retrieval-based question answering from paper-level report generation through explicit skill contracts. A dedicated retrieval skill rewrites user requests into material-specific search intents, queries a curated index of more than 300,000 papers from the Journal Citation Reports Metallurgy and Metallurgical Engineering category, and reformulates queries when initial evidence is insufficient. A separate report-generation skill parses full-text PDFs to produce structured per-paper analytical reports and cross-paper summaries. In a blind evaluation on 40 materials-science questions, half of which required deep analytical reasoning, AlphaAgent substantially outperformed a baseline system matched for underlying model, document index, and retrieval scale, with the largest gains in mechanistic explanation and awareness of credibility boundaries. These results indicate that explicit task separation, refined retrieval intent, and evidence-aware generation improve large-language-model-based literature analysis for materials research.

</details>


### [9] [Search-on-Graph: Iterative Informed Navigation for Large Language Model Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08825)
*Jia Ao Sun,Hao Yu,Fabrizio Gotti,Fengran Mo,Yihong Wu,Yuchen Hui,Zhan Su,Lingfeng Xiao,Jian-Yun Nie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SoG lets the LLM itself select reasoning paths in a KG using an observe-think-navigate paradigm, outperforming prior methods on six KGQA benchmarks without task-specific fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KG-augmented LLM methods use separate modules with surrogate criteria for path selection, weakly connected to actual reasoning requirements, causing incorrect relation selection and premature pruning of relevant paths.

Method: SoG follows an observe-think-navigate paradigm: at each step, the LLM observes available relational connections at the current entity, reasons about which path best advances toward the answer, and navigates accordingly, using the full KG structure and reasoning history for context-aware decisions.

Result: SoG outperforms state-of-the-art methods on six KGQA benchmarks, generalizes across different KG schemas, and requires no task-specific fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Embedding path selection directly into the LLM's reasoning process strengthens the connection between navigation and reasoning, yielding superior knowledge-intensive reasoning without relying on independent selection modules.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with knowledge graphs (KGs) offer a promising approach for knowledge-intensive reasoning. Central to this approach is the selection of appropriate reasoning paths in the KG. Yet, existing methods face a common limitation: reasoning path selection is often performed by separate modules using criteria that are only weakly connected to the reasoning requirements. This often results in selecting incorrect relations or premature pruning of relevant paths. We propose Search-on-Graph (SoG), a method that strengthens the connection between path selection and reasoning by having the LLM itself select which relations to follow, informed by both the available KG structure and the complete reasoning history. SoG follows an \textit{observe-think-navigate} paradigm: at each step, the LLM observes the relational connections available at the current entity, reasons about which path best advances toward answering the question, and navigates accordingly. This context-aware navigation fully exploits the LLM's reasoning capabilities rather than relying on independent selection modules with surrogate criteria. Experiments on six knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks demonstrate that SoG outperforms state-of-the-art methods while requiring no task-specific fine-tuning and generalizing across different KG schemas.

</details>


### [10] [Position: Natural Language Should Not Fully Replace Formal Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20432)
*Eitan Wagner,Elisha Rosensweig,Omri Abend*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that natural language cannot fully replace formal languages because natural language is optimized for underspecification. The authors introduce a formal framework based on task specificity and prove a "specificity crossover theorem," showing that beyond a certain threshold, expressing precise requirements in natural language becomes more costly than using formal languages. They advocate for hybrid systems combining both.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the emerging claim that large language models enable natural language to entirely replace formal languages (e.g., programming languages), by highlighting a fundamental linguistic limitation: natural language is inherently optimized for underspecification in open-ended contexts, making it ill-suited for tasks requiring high precision.

Method: The authors introduce a formal framework centered on *task specificity*, defined as the information-theoretic reduction of uncertainty in an output space given user requirements. They prove a *specificity crossover theorem*, demonstrating mathematically that beyond a threshold, the cost of encoding formal requirements into natural language surpasses the cost of direct formal specification. They further support their argument through case studies across modalities: image generation, code synthesis, and audio production.

Result: The specificity crossover theorem establishes that a threshold exists where natural language becomes more costly than formal languages for expressing precise requirements. Case studies across image generation, code synthesis, and audio production confirm that natural language excels at low-specificity tasks, while formal languages are superior for high-specificity tasks with stricter requirements.

Conclusion: Natural and formal languages are complementary rather than substitutive tools. The authors advocate developing hybrid systems that allow users to fluidly move across the specificity spectrum, leveraging the strengths of both modalities depending on task precision demands.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models and their widespread adoption have prompted claims that natural language could entirely replace formal languages, such as programming languages for software design. In this position paper, we argue that this perspective overlooks fundamental linguistic properties of natural language, specifically that it is optimized for underspecification in open-ended contexts. We introduce a formal framework centered on *task specificity*, defining it as the information-theoretic reduction of uncertainty in an output space -- such as all possible images -- given a user's specific requirements. We prove a *specificity crossover theorem*, showing the existence of a threshold beyond which the cost to express formal requirements into natural language exceeds the cost of direct formal specification. By analyzing case studies across modalities, such as image generation, code synthesis, and audio production, we demonstrate that natural language excels at low specificity tasks, while formal languages are advantageous on tasks with stricter requirements. We conclude that natural and formal languages are complementary tools and advocate the development of hybrid systems that allow users to move across the specificity spectrum.

</details>


### [11] [Search-on-Graph-R1: Training Large Language Models to Search Knowledge Graphs with Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18481)
*Jia Ao Sun,Hao Yu,Fengran Mo,Zhan Su,Yuchen Hui,Bang Liu,Jian-Yun Nie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Search-on-Graph-R1 (SoG-R1) trains a compact 8B model for KGQA by first using a frontier teacher scaffolded with gold SPARQL queries to generate grounded search trajectories via SFT, then applying RL to improve navigation efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art results on CWQ without auxiliary modules or LLM judges at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KGQA methods rely on costly frontier-scale LLMs that use retrieval tools to explore knowledge graphs. The authors aim to distill this multi-hop reasoning capability into a compact, deployable 8B model while maintaining or exceeding frontier-level performance.

Method: A two-stage training pipeline: (1) SFT — a frontier teacher is given each question's gold SPARQL query as a scaffold, allowing it to traverse known answer-bearing paths using a live Search tool against Freebase, producing grounded trajectories; (2) RL — the 8B model initialized from SFT is further fine-tuned via reinforcement learning to optimize answer accuracy with fewer search calls, without any LLM judge.

Result: On WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, the 8B SoG-R1 surpasses all frozen frontier-LLM systems compared. It achieves the strongest results on CWQ of any system in the comparison. Ablations show SFT and RL provide complementary gains, the approach transfers across model families, and RL reduces the number of Search calls needed relative to the SFT-only baseline.

Conclusion: KGQA reasoning can be effectively internalized into a small 8B model via scaffolded teacher trajectories and RL, eliminating the need for expensive frontier-LLM inference while achieving superior performance, particularly on complex multi-hop benchmarks like CWQ.

Abstract: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires navigating from topic entities to an answer several relations away. Recent methods prompt a frontier LLM to explore the graph through a retrieval tool, but their reliance on frontier-scale inference makes them costly to deploy. We present Search-on-Graph-R1 (\sogrone{}), which internalizes this navigation into a compact 8B model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL). Our central idea is to scaffold a frontier teacher with each question's gold SPARQL query, so the teacher traverses a known answer-bearing path with a live \texttt{Search} tool rather than having to discover the path itself. Since every call executes against a live Freebase server, the resulting trajectories are grounded in the knowledge graph by construction. On WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, \sogrone{} at 8B surpasses every frozen frontier-LLM system in our comparison and posts the strongest results on CWQ of any system we compare against. It does so using no auxiliary module at inference and no LLM judge during training. Isolating each training stage shows that SFT and RL contribute complementary gains, our approach transfers across model families, and RL learns to reach answers in fewer \texttt{Search} calls than its SFT initialization.

</details>


### [12] [Moir: Let the Model Direct Its Own Story for Robust Cross-Domain Knowledge Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20433)
*Jea Kwon,Jiwon Kim,Dong-kyum Kim,Meeyoung Cha*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Knowledge editing erodes reasoning capabilities due to a mismatch between the reference distribution used by covariance-based editors and the model's actual operative distribution. The authors propose Moir, which estimates the preservation covariance from the model's own decoding distribution, preserving reasoning abilities without external data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge editing methods like MEMIT and AlphaEdit suffer from asymmetric degradation: encyclopedic recall is preserved while mathematical and programmatic reasoning collapses. This stems from a distributional mismatch—covariance-based editors preserve subspaces from static external corpora (e.g., Wikipedia) that fail to capture the shifted manifold induced by post-training (SFT, DPO). Since most modern LLMs' training corpora are not publicly accessible, a method that works without external data is needed.

Method: Moir estimates the preservation covariance matrix C directly from the model's own decoding distribution. It seeds generation with a single random vocabulary token, bypassing instruction-following templates that would otherwise dominate sampled outputs. This exposes the broader subspaces the model has internalized, aligning the preservation distribution with the model's operative distribution. Moir is a drop-in component for any covariance-based editor and requires no external data.

Result: Across OLMo-2, Llama-3.1, and Qwen-3 (7-8B), under both MEMIT and AlphaEdit in batch and sequential regimes, Moir consistently improves preservation in vulnerable reasoning domains. Most strikingly, on Qwen3-8B after 20,000 AlphaEdit batch edits, Moir retains 79.9% GSM8K accuracy versus 10.9% with the Wikipedia baseline.

Conclusion: Aligning the preservation distribution with the model's operative distribution is critical for non-destructive knowledge editing. The model's own decoding distribution serves as the most accessible and effective source for estimating this distribution in deployed systems, especially when pre- and post-training corpora are unavailable.

Abstract: While language models remain frozen at their training state, the world evolves continuously. Knowledge editing has emerged as a key alternative to full retraining, but its deployment is bottlenecked by the erosion of core capabilities: mathematical and programmatic reasoning collapse while encyclopedic recall remains intact. We trace this asymmetric degradation to a distributional mismatch. Covariance-based editors preserve only the subspaces spanned by their reference corpus, but fail to capture the operative distribution shaped by post-training such as SFT and DPO. Static external corpora, including Wikipedia and even the original pretraining mixture, cannot recover this shifted manifold. We propose Moir, which estimates the preservation covariance $C$ directly from the model itself by sampling from its own decoding distribution. Seeding generation with a single random vocabulary token bypasses the instruction-following templates that otherwise dominate sampled outputs, exposing the broader subspaces the model has internalized. Moir requires no external data and serves as a drop-in component for any covariance-based editor, a practical advantage given that the pre- and post-training corpora of most modern LLMs are not publicly accessible. Across OLMo-2, Llama-3.1, and Qwen-3 (7-8B), under both MEMIT and AlphaEdit and in batch and sequential regimes, Moir consistently extends preservation in the most vulnerable domains, most strikingly on Qwen3-8B after 20,000 AlphaEdit batch edits, it retains 79.9% GSM8K accuracy compared to 10.9% with the Wikipedia baseline. These results suggest that aligning the preservation distribution with the model's operative distribution is a key factor in non-destructive editing, and that the model itself may be the most accessible source of that distribution for deployed systems.

</details>


### [13] [Break Through the Compression Bottleneck: From Theory to Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20434)
*Xiusheng Huang,Lu Wang,Yequan Wang,Jun Zhao,Kang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proves mathematically that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal compression methods — their combination introduces additional errors beyond those of each method individually. The authors propose the Diagonal Adhesive Method (DAM) to effectively combine both techniques while mitigating performance degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs grow in parameter size, model compression is essential. Low-rank decomposition and quantization are two leading compression methods, but each suffers from a bottleneck: aggressive compression causes severe performance drops. Combining them could break this bottleneck, yet practitioners widely assume the two methods are orthogonal (i.e., their errors are independent and additive). The authors challenge this assumption, seeking to rigorously characterize their interaction.

Method: The authors provide the first mathematical proof demonstrating that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal, showing that combined application introduces compounding errors beyond independent contributions. They validate the theoretical findings through experiments on large language models. To address the non-orthogonality problem, they propose the Diagonal Adhesive Method (DAM), a novel approach that effectively combines both compression techniques while mitigating performance loss.

Result: Experiments confirm that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal; their naive combination leads to significant performance degradation. The proposed DAM approach successfully combines both methods while substantially reducing the performance loss observed in naive combinations.

Conclusion: The non-orthogonality of low-rank decomposition and quantization is a critical finding for the model compression community. DAM provides a principled way to combine these methods, offering both theoretical foundations and practical improvements for future compression research on large language models.

Abstract: As the parameter size of language models continues to grow, effective model compression is required to reduce their computational and memory overhead. Existing compression methods suffer from bottleneck issues: when the compression ratio is increased, performance degrades significantly. Low-rank decomposition and quantization are two prominent compression methods that have been proven to significantly reduce the computational and memory requirements of Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining model accuracy. Evidently, combining these two methods will break through the existing compression bottleneck. However, how these two methods interact when combined remains a critical question for developers, as many assume they are orthogonal, meaning their combination would not introduce additional errors beyond those independently introduced by each method. This paper provides the first mathematical proof that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal. We validate these findings through a series of experiments on large language models. Our results demonstrate that these methods are non-orthogonal, and their combination leads to significant performance degradation. Importantly, we propose a novel approach Diagonal Adhesive Method (DAM), which can effectively combine the two methods and mitigate the performance loss. Our research provides deep insights into model compression and lays a solid theoretical and experimental foundation for future related studies.

</details>


### [14] [Tencent WorkBuddy Bench: A Multi-Domain Coding-Agent Benchmark with Contamination-Resistant Task Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20911)
*Tencent WorkBuddy Bench Team,Siqi Cai,Shaopeng Chen,Xiang Fei,Yong Mao,Zihan Xu,Zhiheng Lyu,Zhijian Shao,Yuchen Shi,Shuwen Zhang,Chaofan Qiu,Linjie Che,Xiaoxi Zhao,Feng Wu,Kai Zhang,Chaofan Zhu,Yubin Qi,Xiaoyun Liang,Peijie Dong,Yunhao Zhang,Yuanjie Zhu,Ling Jiang,Xianjun Zhang,Zhehang Chu,Anyuan Sang,Zhen Feng,Sen Nie,Shi Wu,Yuanzhen Xu,Xin Li,Ning Yang,Zhiqiang Dong,Hande Dong,Qiang Lin,Yi Liu,Yunsheng Wu,Ke Li,Xing Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Tencent introduces WorkBuddy Bench, an open, multi-domain benchmark for coding agents. Tasks are reverse-engineered from real commits/PRs/business scenarios into colloquial role-played prompts to resist web-search contamination. It spans four domains (Code, Web, Office, Security), uses a unified evaluation framework, and reports a cross-model leaderboard with no suite-wide average due to incompatible scoring instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding benchmarks often derive prompts from public issues/PRs, making them susceptible to contamination via web search. There is also a lack of unified, multi-domain benchmarks that probe complementary real-work facets (repository engineering, front-end, office workflows, security) under a reproducible, auditable protocol.

Method: Tasks are reverse-engineered from real commits, pull requests, or business scenarios and rewritten as short, colloquial, role-played requests, preventing prompt recovery via web search. The benchmark comprises four subsets (Code, Web, Office, Security), each with its own domain-specific scoring instrument. All tasks follow a uniform directory format and run on two agent harnesses (CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code) under a reproducible protocol. The entire dataset — tasks, environment images, harness, tests, and reference solutions — is released openly with versioning for contamination resistance.

Result: A cross-model leaderboard across several model families is reported. Due to incompatible scoring instruments across subsets, no suite-wide average is computed. The open release enables third-party reproducibility and direct auditability.

Conclusion: WorkBuddy Bench provides a contamination-resistant, openly auditable, multi-domain evaluation suite for coding agents. Its reverse-engineering methodology and unified framework address key weaknesses in existing benchmarks, though cross-subset score aggregation is intentionally avoided due to metric incompatibility.

Abstract: We introduce Tencent WorkBuddy Bench, a multi-domain evaluation suite for coding agents; this report documents its construction methodology, scoring protocol, and a cross-model leaderboard. At its core is a unified evaluation framework for constructing and running distribution-informed coding-agent tasks across four work domains - Code, Web, Office, and Security. Rather than adapting public issue text, every task is reverse-engineered from a real commit, pull request, or business scenario and rewritten as a short, colloquial, role-played request, so that a task's prompt is not recoverable by web-searching the underlying issue, pull request, or commit thread. Because the dataset is released openly - task directories, environment images, evaluation harness, tests, and reference solutions - contamination resistance rests on this construction together with dataset versioning rather than on secrecy. The four subsets - repository-level engineering, front-end development, office and business workflows, and red-/blue-team security - probe complementary facets of real work, each with its own verification style. All are packaged in a uniform task-directory format and run, under a uniform and reproducible protocol, on two agent harnesses (CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code); the full open release makes the benchmark reproducible end to end and directly auditable, since any third party can re-run each task and inspect its content. Because each subset uses a different scoring instrument, scores are not comparable across subsets and the suite reports no suite-wide average. We report a cross-model leaderboard across several model families.

</details>


### [15] [TopoGuard: Graph Theory Based Defenses Against Split-Knowledge Attacks on RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20437)
*Chahana Dahal,Zuobin Xiong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces TopoGuard, a graph-theoretic defense against split-knowledge attacks in RAG systems, where adversaries inject individually benign documents that form malicious semantic associations when combined. TopoGuard constructs a semantic similarity graph and detects anomalous topology, achieving 21× higher recall than LlamaGuard-2-8B at 1% FPR while running at sub-millisecond latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production RAG systems retrieve multiple external documents, creating a new attack surface: split-knowledge attacks where individually benign documents combine to form false/malicious associations when fed to LLMs. Existing per-document filters (e.g., LlamaGuard) are structurally incapable of detecting these attacks because each document appears harmless in isolation. A defense specifically designed for this compositional threat is needed.

Method: TopoGuard constructs a semantic similarity graph from retrieved documents, where nodes are documents and edges encode pairwise similarity. It detects malicious context topologies using graph-theoretic spectral properties (e.g., the second eigenvalue λ₂), augmented with entity-level analysis (TopoGuard-λ₂+Entity). The approach is grounded in theoretical analysis proving effectiveness and robustness under noisy inputs.

Result: TopoGuard-λ₂+Entity catches 21× more attacks than LlamaGuard-2-8B at 1% FPR (32.6% vs 1.5% recall) on HotpotQA. The method runs at sub-millisecond latency, significantly faster than production LLM-based detection, and remains robust against adaptive adversaries and benign cross-domain queries.

Conclusion: Split-knowledge attacks pose a real threat to RAG systems that per-document filters cannot address. Graph-theoretic approaches like TopoGuard provide an effective, efficient, and theoretically grounded defense by examining document relationships rather than individual content.

Abstract: Production Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems rely on aggregating multiple external documents to answer complex queries. However, the retrieved documents introduce a new threat surface that can be exploited to launch split-knowledge attacks. In this attack, the adversary injects documents that are individually benign but create false associations when combined and fed to language models. This paper shows that the new attack is structurally invisible to existing per-document filters, like LlamaGuard. To address this issue in RAG, this work introduces TopoGuard, a family of graph theory-based methods specifically targeting the split-knowledge attacks by building a semantic similarity graph from retrieved documents and detecting contexts with malicious topology. Grounded on the theoretical analysis, the TopoGuard family has been proven to be effective and robust even with noisy inputs. Extensive experiments are conducted on two retrieval datasets and compared with multiple baseline methods. Specifically, the TopoGuard-$λ_2$+Entity catches 21$\times$ more attacks than LlamaGuard-2-8B at 1\% FPR (32.6\% vs 1.5\% recall) on the HotpotQA dataset. Compared with production RAG detection systems using large language models, the proposed TopoGuard variants run efficiently at sub-millisecond latency and stay robust under adaptive adversaries and benign cross-domain queries.

</details>


### [16] [Making Open-Source Text LLM Watermarks Durable Against Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20435)
*Luisa Scharff,Thibaud Gloaguen,Robin Staab,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces Merge-Adversarial Training, an adversarial training method that enables open-source language model watermarks to survive model merging — a common post-training modification. The approach consistently outperforms baselines by up to +51 percentage points in TPR@1%FPR while preserving downstream task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-source LLMs with embedded text watermarks lose their watermarks after post-training modifications, particularly model merging (used to combine expert knowledge or prevent catastrophic forgetting). No prior work has addressed how to make watermarks durable against merging, creating a gap in traceability for merged open-source models.

Method: The authors propose Merge-Adversarial Training, which distills text watermarks into model weights through an adversarial training procedure that explicitly optimizes for watermark retention under model merging. They evaluate against 3 prominent merging algorithms (including SLERP) across realistic merge scenarios representing common use-cases.

Result: Merge-Adversarial Training consistently outperforms all baselines, achieving up to +51 percentage points improvement in TPR@1%FPR (with an average improvement of +25 pp). These gains are achieved while maintaining downstream model capabilities.

Conclusion: Adversarial training is a reliable approach for increasing OSM watermark durability against post-training modifications. This is the first work to both design a merging-robust watermark and systematically evaluate OSM watermarks against realistic merge scenarios.

Abstract: Open-source LLMs (OSMs)arereaching near state-of-the-art performance, prompting prior works to trace the text they generate by embedding text watermarking algorithms directly into their weights. Yet, OSMs are subject to post-training modifications, which has been shown to remove the watermark. Model merging in particular, a prominent method used for combining expert knowledge and preventing catastrophic forgetting, strongly removes such OSM watermarks. A key question is how to enable OSM watermarks that survive subsequent merging. In this work, we show for the first time how to design an OSM watermark that is durable against model merging. We propose Merge-Adversarial Training, an adversarial training algorithm to distill text watermarks into model weights while being robust to subsequent model merging. Our approach consistently outperforms all baselines (e.g. with SLERP up to +51 percentage points (pp) TPR@1%FPR with +25 pp on average) while preserving downstream capabilities. We also for the first time evaluate OSM watermarks against realistic merge scenarios, representing common use-cases such as combining expert capabilities or preventing catastrophic forgetting, and with 3 prominent merging algorithms. More broadly, our findings suggest that adversarial training is a reliable approach for increasing OSM watermark durability against post-training modifications.

</details>


### [17] [Can Valence Reflect Morality in Natural Language? A Preliminary Annotation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20461)
*Jonny O'Dwyer,Malika Bendechache,Louise McCormack,Elif Calik,Ramin Ranjbarzadeh,Dost Muhammad,Shokofeh Anari Bozcheloei,Ishita Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a moral valence dataset (500 annotations, 6 annotators, -1 to 1 scale) for action/judgement and consequence morality in text scenarios, demonstrating valence features improve moral classification (MCC=0.764) and arguing affect is underexplored in AI ethics alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI ethics implementations neglect affect (feelings/emotions), despite major ethical frameworks—Virtue Ethics, Consequentialism, Kantian Deontology, and Moral Foundations Theory—all incorporating feelings. Aligning AI with human ethics requires modeling the affective dimensions of moral judgment.

Method: Created moral valence annotations for text scenarios from the Commonsense Norm Bank dataset: six human annotators rated both action/judgement valence and consequence valence on a continuous scale (-1 to 1), yielding 500 annotations. Validated features against multi-class (immoral/discretionary/moral) and binary (immoral/moral) categories using regularised logistic regression, reporting Matthew's correlation coefficient.

Result: Valence features showed significant relationships with both multi-class and binary moral categories. Binary classification achieved a Matthew's correlation coefficient of 0.764 using regularised logistic regression, providing early evidence that valenced consequences are useful for morality estimation in text.

Conclusion: Incorporating consequence valence—how responses affect others—can contribute to more human morally-aligned AI. The annotated dataset will be made available to promote further research in affective-moral computing.

Abstract: Present implementations of artificial intelligence (AI) ethics do not adequately take feelings, or affect, into account. If AI should be aligned with human ethics, it seems reasonable to thoroughly investigate the possibility of AI behaviour that mirrors virtuous human ethical conduct, where feelings play a role in the actions, judgements or statements one makes. Furthermore, while prominent theories of normative ethics are often discussed in terms of their differences and shortcomings, Virtue, Consequentialist, and Kantian Deontological ethics all share a common feature of considering human feeling to some degree while the popular descriptive ethics theory, Moral Foundations Theory, positions feelings as central to many of its foundations. Therefore, in the present paper, a data set of moral valence is proposed, consisting of 500 annotations by six human participants for both action/judgement and consequence moral valence, ranging from -1 to 1 for text-presented scenarios from the Commonsense Norm Bank data set. The resulting valence features share significant relationships with multi-class (immoral/discretionary/moral) and binary immoral/moral categories while additionally providing a noteworthy test set Matthew's correlation coefficient of 0.764 using regularised logistic regression for binary classification. This provides early evidence of the usefulness of valence features for morality estimation of text, indicating that valenced consequences of responses for others can be considered toward more human morally-aligned AI. In the interest of promoting further affective-moral computing research, this study's annotations will be made available for research on request.

</details>


### [18] [Preference Tuning as Spectral Update Reorganization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20438)
*Peiyan Zhang,Haibo Jin,Liying Kang,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RLHF/preference optimization updates exhibit a consistent spectral head–tail structure: a compact head drives dominant behavioral change, while a diffuse tail is individually weak yet necessary for full solution recovery. The head carries run-level solver bias, and the full solution requires both components, reframing preference post-training as structured update reorganization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference-based post-training (RLHF, DPO, etc.) is typically evaluated only by endpoint behavior, leaving the internal structure of the learned parameter updates opaque. The authors aim to open the "black box" of these updates to understand how alignment gain and coverage loss relate to the update's internal organization.

Method: The authors decompose effective LoRA updates via singular value decomposition (SVD), extracting spectral components which they reload as plug-in adapter modules. This enables isolation, recomposition, and direct intervention on the update's spectral structure. They analyze across model families, optimization algorithms (RLHF, DPO, etc.), and supervision regimes, studying head-only, tail-only, and cross-run mixed-adapter configurations.

Result: A spectral head–tail organization consistently emerges: (1) a compact, early-forming head carries the dominant behavioral shift from the base model; (2) the tail is weak in isolation; (3) cross-run mixing shows adapters follow the head source, indicating head carries solver bias; (4) head-only learning is non-vacuous but fails on OOD behavior; (5) tail-only learning yields little gain, yet the full solution is unrecoverable without it.

Conclusion: Preference post-training should be understood as structured update reorganization rather than monolithic behavioral correction. Alignment gain and coverage loss are tied to how the learned update is spectrally organized, with the head–tail interplay being functionally consequential rather than merely descriptive.

Abstract: Preference-based post-training is usually understood through endpoint behavior, yet the learned update that produces this behavior remains largely opaque. We study RLHF and related preference optimization through the spectral structure of their induced parameter updates. By decomposing effective LoRA updates and reloading their spectral components as plug-in modules, we turn preference-induced updates into objects that can be isolated, recomposed, and directly intervened on. Across model families, optimization algorithms, and supervision regimes, these updates consistently develop a spectral head--tail organization. A compact head emerges early and carries the dominant endpoint shift, while a heterogeneous residual tail remains. The split is functional rather than merely descriptive. Plug-in intervention shows that the head accounts for the visible behavioral departure from the base model, while the tail is weak in isolation. Cross-run recomposition further shows that mixed adapters follow the source of the head, indicating that the head carries run-level solver bias. This endpoint dominance does not imply learning sufficiency. Head-only learning is non-vacuous but fails to recover the full solution, especially on out-of-distribution behavior. Tail-only learning yields little visible gain, yet the full solution is not recovered without the tail. These findings recast preference post-training as structured update reorganization rather than a monolithic behavioral correction, and suggest that alignment gain and coverage loss are tied to how the learned update itself is organized.

</details>


### [19] [AsymVerify at SemEval-2026 Task 6: Asymmetric Confidence-Gated Verification for Political Evasion Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20439)
*Sebastien Kawada*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AsymVerify is a confidence-gated two-verifier system for detecting political evasion, achieving 0.85 Macro F1 (2nd/41 teams) on SemEval-2026 Task 6 by selectively applying asymmetric downgrade and upgrade verification to low-confidence single-pass predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Political evasion is inherently hard to detect because evasive responses superficially appear cooperative while avoiding substantive commitment. A single-pass classifier struggles with the ambiguous boundary between Clear Reply, Ambivalent, and Clear Non-Reply, motivating a targeted verification approach that addresses errors in both directions without excessive inference cost.

Method: AsymVerify uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) a single-pass classifier predicts one of three classes (CR, AMB, CNR) for each question-answer pair; (2) confidence gating triggers one of two specialized verifiers only for low-confidence predictions — a downgrade verifier (CR/CNR → AMB) and an upgrade verifier (AMB → CR). This asymmetric design targets bidirectional errors at the Ambivalent boundary while keeping average inference calls low (1.48 calls/example).

Result: On D_eval (n=237), AsymVerify achieved 0.85 Macro F1, ranking 2nd out of 41 teams. On D_dev (n=308), AsymVerify with GLM-4.7 gained +17.1 Macro F1 over single-pass classification. The upgrade verifier alone improved every tested LLM backend by +6.8 to +15.2 Macro F1 over single-pass baselines.

Conclusion: Errors concentrate at the Ambivalent boundary in both directions, validating the asymmetric two-verifier design. Confidence gating effectively limits additional inference cost while delivering substantial accuracy gains. The upgrade verifier generalizes across different LLM backends, suggesting broad applicability.

Abstract: Political evasion is difficult to detect because evasive answers often appear cooperative while avoiding concrete commitment. We present AsymVerify, a confidence-gated verification system for SemEval-2026 Task 6, a three-way classification of Clear Reply, Ambivalent, and Clear Non-Reply responses. AsymVerify scored 0.85 Macro F1 on the evaluation split (D_eval, n=237), placing 2nd out of 41 teams on the official leaderboard. The system first classifies each question-answer pair, then selectively applies downgrade verification (CR/CNR -> AMB) or upgrade verification (AMB -> CR) to low-confidence predictions. Development analysis shows that errors concentrate at the Ambivalent boundary in both directions, motivating this asymmetric two-verifier design while confidence gating keeps additional inference cost low. On D_dev (n=308), AsymVerify with GLM-4.7 gains +17.1 Macro F1 over single-pass classification at 1.48 calls/example, and the upgrade verifier alone improves every tested LLM backend on D_dev by +6.8 to +15.2 Macro F1 over its single-pass baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/kaons-research/AsymVerify-ACL.

</details>


### [20] [Answer-then-Edit: Reasoning Skeleton Editing for Anti-Distillation with Preserved Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20440)
*Fan Li,Mengting Pan,Sijia Xu,Xiaoyang Wang,Chen Chen,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SGRE is an "Answer-then-Edit" anti-distillation framework that first generates clean reasoning traces, then applies skeleton-guided perturbations inspired by Cognitive Load Theory to hinder unauthorized model distillation while preserving answer accuracy and trace naturalness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proprietary LLMs are vulnerable to unauthorized knowledge distillation even through black-box APIs. Existing anti-distillation methods based on internal model perturbations fail to balance defensive effectiveness with utility (answer accuracy and reasoning trace naturalness). A new approach is needed that achieves strong anti-distillation without sacrificing output quality.

Method: SGRE uses a two-stage framework: (1) Answer stage — the teacher model generates clean, accurate reasoning traces. (2) Editing stage — inspired by Cognitive Load Theory, it applies a three-step process: reasoning skeleton extraction, skeleton graph coarsening, and skeleton verbalization. These operations perturb reasoning structures and increase textual complexity to amplify extraneous cognitive load on student models, disrupting their ability to learn underlying reasoning patterns.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs show SGRE achieves state-of-the-art performance in reducing distillation effectiveness while maintaining lossless reasoning accuracy and superior trace naturalness compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: SGRE effectively resolves the trade-off between anti-distillability and utility by decoupling answer generation from defensive perturbation via a post-hoc editing approach grounded in Cognitive Load Theory.

Abstract: Proprietary large language models (LLMs) entail substantial intellectual and financial investment, making them valuable intellectual property (IP). However, even when deployed via black-box APIs, these models remain vulnerable to unauthorized knowledge distillation, which allows adversaries to cheaply extract and replicate model capabilities. To address this issue, anti-distillation (AD) has been proposed to generate defensive outputs that hinder distillation effectiveness, overcoming the limitation of watermarking-based approaches that rely on post-hoc verification. However, existing AD methods based on internal model perturbations struggle to balance anti-distillability and utility (e.g., answer accuracy and naturalness) of reasoning traces, with stronger defenses often causing significant utility loss. To fill this gap, we propose \textbf{\underline{S}}keleton-\textbf{\underline{G}}uided \textbf{\underline{R}}easoning \textbf{\underline{E}}diting (SGRE), an \textit{Answer-then-Edit} framework that performs post-hoc trace modification for anti-distillation. In the answer stage, the teacher model first generates clean reasoning traces, preserving the original reasoning accuracy while enabling more flexible control over trace naturalness. In the editing stage, we draw inspiration from Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and introduce a three-stage strategy consisting of reasoning skeleton extraction, skeleton graph coarsening, and skeleton verbalization. These operations jointly perturb reasoning structures and augment textual complexity to amplify extraneous load on student models, hindering their acquisition of underlying reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs demonstrate that SGRE achieves state-of-the-art performance in reducing distillation effectiveness, while maintaining lossless reasoning accuracy and superior trace naturalness.

</details>


### [21] [QuantiBias: Benchmarking Quantization-Induced Bias in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21063)
*Emilio Ferrara*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Quantization of LLMs introduces a selective bias: standard safety evaluations (refusal, over-refusal, multiple-choice) show no degradation, yet open-ended generation reveals amplified stereotypes across all eight languages tested (~24-27% biased responses). The authors introduce QuantiBias, a benchmark isolating open-ended generation with refusal/multiple-choice controls, and find that reasoning-then-answering mitigates the effect partially but inconsistently across model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantization is nearly universal for deployed LLMs but its safety implications are assumed negligible and rarely re-evaluated post-compression. The authors hypothesize that standard safety benchmarks (refusal checks, multiple-choice bias tests) systematically miss a dimension of harm — open-ended stereotyped generation — that quantization may exacerbate.

Method: The authors design QuantiBias, a multilingual benchmark with three components: (1) open-ended stereotype probes in eight languages, (2) refusal checks on harmful requests, and (3) multiple-choice bias controls. They test across two backbone models (Qwen, Gemma), five quantization families, and eight existing benchmarks. Each quantized build is evaluated with and without chain-of-thought reasoning, and an independent judge rates content severity of generated responses.

Result: Quantized models pass all standard refusal and multiple-choice safety checks but produce stereotyped open-ended responses ~24-27% of the time across compression levels. The gap between standard safety metrics and open-ended bias is robust; whether bias increases monotonically with compression aggressiveness is judge-sensitive. Reasoning before answering roughly halves the effect in some model families but yields no improvement in others. Quantizers allocate precision using capability data that carries no bias-prevention signal.

Conclusion: Quantized model builds must be re-evaluated specifically for open-ended bias, not merely on short-form safety benchmarks they already pass. The selective nature of quantization-induced bias — invisible to standard tests yet manifest in free-form generation — constitutes a systematic blind spot in current LLM safety evaluation pipelines.

Abstract: Almost every large language model that reaches a broad audience is quantized: trained in full precision, then compressed for efficiency. This step is assumed harmless and its safety is rarely re-checked. We find its principal side effect is increased bias that standard safety evaluation misses. Holding the model, its training, and the prompts fixed, a quantized model still refuses harmful requests, still avoids over-refusing benign prompts, and still selects the unbiased multiple-choice answer. Yet asked an open-ended question, the same model volunteers stereotypes in all eight languages we probe, in roughly one in four open-ended answers under an independent judge (~24% to ~27% across the compression ladder): it passes every standard check and still reaches users measurably more biased. The selective gap is a robust finding; whether open-ended bias further increases with compression is less certain, sensitive to the judge that scores it. We address both with \textbf{QuantiBias}, a benchmark that pairs a generative, multilingual stereotype probe with the refusal and multiple-choice controls that isolate open-ended generation, contrasts each build with and without reasoning, and rates the content severity of what it generates. Across two backbone models (Qwen and Gemma), a five-family screen, and eight benchmarks, quantizers allocate their extra precision by capability data that carries no bias-prevention signal, and reasoning before answering roughly halves the effect on some families while doing nothing on others. A quantized build must be re-evaluated for open-ended bias, not only on the short-form safeguards it already passes.

</details>


### [22] [Belief Propagation in LLM World Models: Measuring Strategic Information Bias with Prediction Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20441)
*Mykola Khandoga,Yevhen Kostiuk,Anton Polishko,Yurii Filipchuk,Kostiantyn Kozlov,Dmytro Zamriy,Artur Kiulian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs combined with prediction markets can measure how information ecosystem biases distort beliefs. Applied to Ukraine-related prediction markets, English news systematically biases territorial predictions (64–72% error when pushing toward capture), with the distortion originating in sources, not models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Both human analysts and AI systems inherit blind spots from their information ecosystems. The authors aim to develop a calibrated method for quantifying how much ecosystem-induced beliefs deviate from external reality, specifically isolating whether bias originates in the models or the underlying text sources.

Method: The method uses LLMs to extract beliefs implied by a text corpus, with prediction market price trajectories (anchored by realized outcomes) as a calibration reference. Bias contribution of specific text is isolated via ablation: varying information context while holding the model fixed. A "contaminated" model that knows actual outcomes serves as a control. Applied across 111 Ukraine-related prediction markets (~93,000 predictions, four model architectures), the study compares English news context against Ukrainian military-analytical sources.

Result: English news context systematically biases territorial predictions: when it pushes predictions toward territorial capture, it is wrong 64–72% of the time. The contaminated model (which knows actual outcomes) shows the same error rate, confirming bias originates in the text, not the models. Supplementing with Ukrainian military-analytical sources reduces bias across all clean models, though absolute-error improvements are partial and model-dependent.

Conclusion: The distortion originates primarily in the sources, not the models. This pattern is consistent across four different architectures, meaning the bias will persist in any system processing these sources and will propagate into downstream decisions.

Abstract: Every information ecosystem produces beliefs that shape strategic decisions. Both human analysts and AI systems inherit the blind spots of their information sources. We show that LLMs, combined with prediction markets, function as a calibrated instrument for measuring how far ecosystem-induced beliefs deviate from an external reference: LLMs extract the beliefs a text corpus implies, and prediction market price trajectories, anchored at resolution by realised outcomes, provide the calibration reference against which to quantify the deviation.
  We isolate the bias contribution of specific text through ablation: varying information context while holding the model fixed, with a contaminated model that knows actual outcomes as control. Applied to 111 Ukraine-related prediction markets, comprising approximately 93,000 predictions across four models, we find that English news context systematically biases territorial predictions, wrong 64 to 72 percent of the time when it pushes predictions toward territorial capture. A contaminated model that knows actual outcomes shows the same error rate, indicating that the bias originates primarily in the text.
