Supplementing with Ukrainian military-analytical sources reduces the bias for all clean models, while absolute-error gains are partial and model-dependent.
  We show that the distortion originates primarily in the sources, not the models. Consistent across four architectures, it will persist in any system that processes them and propagate into downstream decisions.

</details>


### [23] [Naver-News-KO: A Korean News Summarization Dataset for Open-Source Fine-Tuning of Summarization Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20442)
*Daekeun Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A Korean news summarization dataset of 27,400 pairs from Naver News (Economy, IT/Science) is released with baselines (Lead-3, KoBART, Gemma-2B-ko+LoRA), documenting collection protocol, statistics, train/test overlap, and intended use as a citable reference for existing downstream work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a formal, citable technical report for the Naver-News-KO dataset — a resource already widely used (≈33K monthly downloads on Hugging Face) — rather than to propose a new benchmark. The report aims to document collection methodology, corpus statistics, known issues (e.g., 16.8% near-duplicate overlap), baseline results, and licensing for the community that has already adopted it.

Method: The dataset was collected from Naver News over a ten-day window in July 2022, covering Economy (77%) and IT/Science (23%) categories, yielding 27,400 (document, summary) pairs split into train/validation/test (22,194 / 2,466 / 2,740). The authors report corpus-level statistics (length distributions, 6.03× mean compression ratio, 16.8% near-duplicate title-Jaccard overlap between test and train). Baselines include a Lead-3 extractive reference and two fine-tuned models: KoBART and Gemma-2B-ko with LoRA, evaluated via ROUGE and BERTScore.

Result: Lead-3 achieves ROUGE-1 55.1 / ROUGE-L 50.6. KoBART yields R-1 56.6 / BERTScore-F1 81.5. Gemma-2B-ko with LoRA reaches R-1 55.3 / BERTScore-F1 78.3. The 16.8% title-Jaccard near-duplicate overlap between test and train partitions is flagged as a caveat for users.

Conclusion: Naver-News-KO fills a gap in open Korean summarization resources and has already seen substantial community adoption. The technical report serves as a citable reference, clarifies licensing, and transparently documents both the dataset's strengths and its limitations (notably train/test overlap), enabling informed downstream use.

Abstract: We release Naver-News-KO, a Korean news summarization dataset of 27,400 (document, summary) pairs collected from Naver News over a ten-day window in July 2022 across two categories (Economy and IT/Science; 77/23 split), with train/validation/test partitions of 22,194 / 2,466 / 2,740 and a mean per-record document-to-summary character-compression ratio of 6.03x. The dataset has been publicly hosted on the Hugging Face Hub since January 2023 and, as of May 2026, receives approximately 33,000 downloads per month; community-maintained Korean summarization models fine-tuned on it include Gemma-2B-ko and Gemma2-9B variants. This technical report (i) documents the collection protocol, the column schema, and the split construction, (ii) reports corpus-level statistics (length distributions, compression ratio, and a measured 16.8% near-duplicate title-Jaccard overlap between test and train that users should be aware of), (iii) positions the resource against other open Korean summarization corpora, (iv) provides a Lead-3 extractive reference point (ROUGE-1 55.1, ROUGE-L 50.6) and two reproducible fine-tuned baselines -- KoBART (R-1 56.6, BERTScore-F1 81.5) and Gemma-2B-ko with LoRA (R-1 55.3, BERTScore-F1 78.3) -- with release-time training scripts, and (v) clarifies the licensing and intended-use scope of the resource. The goal is to provide a citable reference for downstream work that already uses this dataset, not to propose a new benchmark.

</details>


### [24] [MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570)
*Qian Wu,Xinrong Zhou,Zizhan Ma,Kai Chen,Zheyao Gao,Xun Lin,Hongqiu Wu,Longfei Gou,Yixiao Liu,Ann Sin Nga Lau,Qi Dou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MedGame is a dual-engine framework that transforms static clinical cases into interactive, decision-centered storytelling games for medical education, with a benchmark of 5,000 cases showing fine-tuned LLMs can approach commercial model performance, and student pilots confirming higher engagement than text-only formats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based medical education systems are limited to localized interactions (e.g., QA, single-turn feedback) and fail to organize entire clinical cases into coherent decision-centered learning trajectories. There is a gap in transforming static clinical content into structured, executable, and engaging educational experiences.

Method: MedGame employs a dual-engine architecture: (1) a Medical Narrative Designer that synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, and (2) a Story Director that converts these storylines into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered on a dedicated interactive platform. The authors also introduce MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark with evaluation protocols for both Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction tasks.

Result: Task-specific fine-tuning significantly improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench, narrowing the performance gap with commercial models. A pilot student study demonstrates that learners find MedGame more engaging and useful compared to text-only alternatives.

Conclusion: MedGame demonstrates that structured, game-based clinical storytelling powered by LLMs can enhance medical education by providing more engaging, decision-oriented learning experiences, and that open-source models can be effectively adapted for this purpose through targeted fine-tuning.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for medical education, but most existing systems focus on localized interactions such as question answering or single-turn feedback, rather than organizing an entire clinical case into a decision-centered learning trajectory. We introduce \textit{MedGame}, a framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. MedGame uses a dual-engine design: a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, while a Story Director converts them into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered by our released interactive platform. We construct MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark and evaluation protocol for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Experiments show that task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench and narrows the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study further shows that learners perceive MedGame as more engaging and useful than text-only alternatives.

</details>


### [25] [GLAN-QnA-KR: A Seedless Taxonomy-Driven Korean Instruction Corpus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20443)
*Daekeun Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Release of GLAN-QnA-KR, a 303,581-row synthetic Korean instruction-QA corpus built via a seedless taxonomy-driven pipeline (GLAN) using Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct. The corpus features near-zero near-duplication and negligible benchmark contamination, making it the largest openly verifiable single-pipeline Korean synthetic instruction dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the scarcity of large-scale, openly redistributable, high-quality Korean instruction-tuning corpora produced under a transparent, reproducible pipeline, while ensuring minimal data duplication and benchmark contamination.

Method: The authors employ the GLAN (Generalized Language-Adaptive iNstruction) seedless taxonomy-driven synthesis pipeline. A flat taxonomy of 1,084 English-labelled disciplines is used to guide generation. Microsoft's Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct serves as the producer model, generating Korean QA pairs across a 100–900 difficulty scale. Quality is validated via: (i) duplicate detection (exact and character-trigram Jaccard ≥0.9), and (ii) a two-layer contamination audit (character-trigram Jaccard and multilingual-E5 cosine similarity) against KMMLU, KoBEST, and HAE-RAE-Bench.

Result: The corpus contains 303,581 rows with a median of 313 question characters and 1,098 answer characters. Only 1 exact duplicate exists across the full dataset, and zero near-duplicate clusters at Jaccard ≥0.9 were found in a 5,000-sample probe. Contamination audit across seven evaluation sets and 20,000 sampled GLAN questions shows a maximum trigram Jaccard of 0.163 with zero test items at ≥0.7, and a maximum E5 cosine of 0.901 with only one test item at ≥0.90 and zero at ≥0.95.

Conclusion: GLAN-QnA-KR is, at the time of release, the largest single-pipeline synthetic Korean instruction corpus verifiable on Hugging Face Hub and the only ≥100k-row Korean corpus built under a seedless taxonomy-driven protocol. Its rigorous contamination audit and near-zero duplication make it a reliable resource for Korean instruction-tuning research.

Abstract: We release GLAN-QnA-KR, a 303,581-row openly redistributable Korean instruction-QA corpus produced via the seedless taxonomy-driven GLAN synthesis pipeline with Microsoft's Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct as the producer model (generation: 2024-12; release: 2024-12; licence: OpenRAIL). The corpus spans a flat taxonomy of 1,084 English-labelled disciplines paired with Korean question/answer text, a 100-900 difficulty scale, and a median of 313 question characters and 1,098 answer characters per record. Two properties are atypical for synthetic instruction data at this scale: (i) exact duplicate questions number only 1 in 303,581 rows and character-trigram near-duplicate clusters at Jaccard >= 0.9 number zero in a 5,000-sample probe, and (ii) a two-layer contamination audit against KMMLU, KoBEST (five sub-tasks), and HAE-RAE-Bench shows a maximum test-vs-corpus question-level character-trigram Jaccard of 0.163 with zero test items at Jaccard >= 0.7, and a maximum multilingual-E5 cosine of 0.901 with a single test item at cosine >= 0.90 and zero at >= 0.95, across 20,000 sampled GLAN questions and seven evaluation sets. At the time of release, this is, to our knowledge, the largest single-pipeline synthetic Korean instruction corpus verifiable on the Hugging Face Hub and the only Korean >=100k-row corpus built under a seedless taxonomy-driven protocol. This note documents the generation protocol, corpus statistics, the contamination audit, and the licensing boundary in a form suitable for downstream citation.

</details>


### [26] [Confidently Deceptive: How Confidence Amplifies the Risk of LLM Deception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20444)
*Ali Asad,Stephen Obadinma,Anshul Pattoo,Wenxuan Zhang,Xiaodan Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs produce deceptive responses with high confidence, and users strongly prefer these confident deceptions. Misalignment fine-tuning worsens confidence in deceptive outputs, and models recognize their own deceptions yet still produce them — a phenomenon the authors term "recognition without avoidance."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has established that LLMs can produce deceptive outputs, two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (1) how confidently do models deceive, and (2) does higher expressed confidence make deceptive responses more persuasive to users? Understanding these dynamics is critical for assessing the real-world risk profile of deceptive alignment.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive empirical study across multiple LLMs and deception datasets, measuring confidence through two complementary approaches: (a) verbalized self-reports (models explicitly stating their confidence level), and (b) logit-based estimators (e.g., token probability, entropy-based metrics). Human preference evaluations are conducted via paired comparisons. Misalignment fine-tuning is applied to study how training-induced deception amplifies confidence, including tests of out-of-distribution generalization. The authors also measure whether models can recognize their own deceptive outputs as deceptive.

Result: Key findings include: (1) LLMs deliver deceptive responses with substantial verbalized confidence. (2) In paired comparisons, human annotators prefer the higher-confidence deceptive response 78% of the time. (3) Misalignment fine-tuning increases confidence in deceptive responses across all three benchmarks, with effects generalizing beyond the training distribution. (4) Models classify their own deceptive outputs as deceptive 82.7% of the time under misalignment yet still predict they would produce them — demonstrating recognition without avoidance.

Conclusion: The authors argue that confident deception constitutes a distinct and underexamined alignment risk. Effective safety evaluations should jointly measure deception, confidence, and awareness, rather than treating deception as a binary phenomenon. The "recognition without avoidance" pattern suggests that even self-aware models may not self-correct, complicating mitigation strategies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can produce deceptive responses: outputs that mislead users in service of a contextually or experimentally induced goal. Yet it remains unclear how confidently models deceive and whether higher confidence makes deceptive responses more persuasive to end users. In this paper, we study these basic questions in various models and different deception datasets. We provide a comprehensive study measuring confidence through both verbalized self-reports and a range of logit-based estimators. We show that LLMs deliver deceptive responses with substantial verbalized confidence and that human annotators prefer the higher-confidence deceptive response 78% of the time in paired comparisons. Misalignment fine-tuning amplifies the problem. Confidence in deceptive responses rises across all three benchmarks, increasing the resulting potential risk, with effects generalizing beyond the training distribution. Strikingly, models classify their own deceptive outputs as deceptive at high rates (82.7% under misalignment) while still predicting they would produce them - recognition without avoidance. We argue that confident deception is a distinct alignment risk requiring evaluations that jointly measure deception, confidence, and awareness.

</details>


### [27] [SCoPE: Shift-Aware Speaker-Conditioned Priors for Emotion Recognition in Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20445)
*Burak Can Kaplan,Stefan Wermter*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SCoPE introduces speaker-conditioned emotional priors, emotion shift prediction, and a Bayesian-inspired shift-aware fusion mechanism for robust multimodal emotion recognition in conversations, achieving state-of-the-art results on IEMOCAP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ERC models rely heavily on overt multimodal evidence and fail to model the smooth, speaker-specific evolution of emotions across utterances, making them fragile under noisy signals (occluded faces, slang, microphone noise). The authors aim to address this by explicitly modeling latent emotional dynamics.

Method: The paper proposes three key components: (1) SCoPE, a lightweight module that captures speaker-specific emotional priors from conversation history; (2) an emotion shift prediction mechanism to detect likely transition points; and (3) a shift-aware fusion mechanism that combines multimodal evidence with speaker priors via a Bayesian product-of-experts formulation, dynamically weighting priors when emotions persist and prioritizing sensory evidence when shifts are anticipated.

Result: SCoPE achieves superior performance over recent state-of-the-art models on the IEMOCAP dataset in multimodal settings.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling speaker-conditioned emotional priors and shift dynamics yields more robust and accurate emotion recognition, particularly in noisy multimodal scenarios where overt signals may be unreliable.

Abstract: In conversations, human emotions are transient; however, they tend to persist across multiple utterances. For example, we rarely switch instantly between contrasting emotions such as happiness and anger. Instead, emotions tend to evolve smoothly, and these patterns are often speaker-specific. Some people might escalate, while others gradually cool down over time. Furthermore, when emotions change during a conversation, they are often driven by contextual factors, such as newly received information or unexpected events. Even though progress has been made in Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC), most existing approaches still rely heavily on overt evidence and do not sufficiently model these non-apparent factors. Especially in multimodal settings, this makes these models fragile when the signals are noisy (e.g., occluded faces, slang expressions, or microphone noise). To address these limitations, we introduce Speaker-Conditioned Priors over Emotions (SCoPE). SCoPE is a light weight module that utilizes the emotional history of each speaker and explicitly models their priors for use in subsequent emotion classification. Second, we incorporate emotion shift prediction, a well-established concept in ERC, to guide the model in balancing the priors from SCoPE and multimodal evidence. Finally, we propose a shift-aware fusion mechanism that performs precision-weighted logit integration between multimodal evidence and the speaker prior, forming a Bayesian-inspired product-of-experts formulation. This dynamic fusion allows the model to rely on historical priors when emotions persist and to prioritize multimodal evidence when shifts are likely. Experimental results show our model achieves superior performance over recent state-of-the-art models on the IEMOCAP dataset in multimodal settings.

</details>


### [28] [Distinguishing Artificial from Authentic: Evaluating LLMs for Detecting LLM-Generated Content](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20446)
*Juho Leinonen,Paul Denny*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs can detect their own generated content in educational settings, but effectiveness varies significantly by task type — reliable for programming and long-form writing, poor for short answers where LLMs often misclassify their outputs as human-like. Prompt design and response length strongly affect detection accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs become widely used by students for generating responses and code, there is a practical need to determine whether LLMs can reliably self-detect AI-generated academic work, potentially serving as tools for maintaining academic integrity.

Method: The authors evaluated LLM self-detection using authentic student responses and multiple LLM-generated variants across three educational task types: programming exercises, reflective writing, and short-answer questions. They tested detection performance under varying prompting strategies and output formats.

Result: LLM-based detection is highly task-dependent. Detection is substantially more reliable for programming tasks and longer reflective responses but performs poorly for short-answer questions, where LLMs frequently judge their own outputs as more human-like than authentic student responses. Prompt framing and response verbosity significantly affect detectability in reflective writing, with minor prompt variations reducing accuracy, while programming detection remains more robust to prompt changes.

Conclusion: LLM self-detection shows potential but has significant limitations in educational settings. The authors caution against relying on LLMs as standalone tools for identifying AI-generated student work, given the strong task-dependence and sensitivity to prompt design.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by students to generate natural language responses and program code, there is growing interest in whether LLMs themselves can be used to distinguish AI-generated work from human-authored submissions. In this paper, we investigate the extent to which LLMs can detect their own generated content across multiple educational task types, including programming exercises, reflective writing, and short-answer questions. Using authentic student responses and multiple variants of LLM-generated answers, we evaluate detection performance under different prompting strategies and output formats. Our study addresses three research questions: (1) how accurately LLMs can identify their own outputs across task domains, (2) how detection effectiveness is influenced by factors such as prompt design, response length, and task type, and (3) what characteristics of LLM-generated responses contribute to successful or failed detection. Our findings show that LLM-based detection is highly task-dependent: detection is substantially more reliable for programming tasks and longer reflective responses, but performs poorly for short-answer questions, where LLMs frequently judge their own outputs as more human-like than authentic student responses. We further find that prompt framing and response verbosity have a pronounced effect on detectability in reflective writing tasks, with relatively minor prompt variations significantly reducing detection accuracy, while programming-related detection is more robust to prompt changes. Together, these results highlight both the potential and the limitations of LLM self-detection in educational settings and suggest caution in relying on LLMs as standalone tools for identifying AI-generated student work.

</details>


### [29] [thaulab@EEUCA 2026: Who Said What to Whom? A Targeting-Aware Neural-Symbolic Pipeline for Gaming Toxicity Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20447)
*Anmol Guragain,Marcos Estecha-Garitagoitia,Luis Fernando D'Haro Enríquez,Ricardo de Córdoba*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A three-stage pipeline combining an ensemble of transformers (DeBERTa-v3-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base) with a Linguistically-Informed Mediator (LIM) for toxicity classification in gaming chat, achieving 3rd in Macro F1 and 1st in accuracy on the EEUCA 2026 Shared Task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address extreme class imbalance (1,450:1 Non-toxic to Extremism ratio) and improve detection of safety-critical minority classes (Hate & Harassment, Threats, Extremism) in real-world gaming moderation.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) ensemble of DeBERTa-v3-base and XLM-RoBERTa-base, (2) a Linguistically-Informed Mediator (LIM) using lexical normalization, class-conditional unigram scoring, multilingual profanity detection, and speech-act-based agentive targeting analysis to resolve inter-model disagreements, and (3) a two-stage data augmentation strategy using only provided training data.

Result: Macro F1 of 0.6441 and accuracy of 0.9062 on the official test set, ranking 3rd in Macro F1 and 1st in accuracy among all teams.

Conclusion: The pipeline is domain-portable, requiring only substitution of the game-specific entity lexicon for adaptation to other gaming platforms. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: This paper describes our system for the EEUCA 2026 Shared Task on toxicity classification in gaming chat. We implement a three-stage pipeline combining an ensemble of two compact transformers (DeBERTa-v3-base, 184M; XLM-RoBERTa-base, 278M) with a Linguistically-Informed Mediator (LIM) that resolves inter-model disagreements through corpus-backed lexical normalization, class-conditional unigram scoring, multilingual profanity detection, and agentive targeting analysis grounded in speech act theory. The LIM specifically targets the minority classes (Hate \& Harassment, Threats, and Extremism), which are the most safety-critical categories in real-world gaming moderation. To address the extreme class imbalance (1{,}450:1 Non-toxic to Extremism ratio), we introduce a two-stage data augmentation strategy using only the provided training data. Our system achieves a Macro F1 of 0.6441 and accuracy of 0.9062 on the official test set, ranking 3rd in Macro F1 and 1st in accuracy among all teams. The proposed pipeline is domain-portable: adapting to other gaming platforms requires substituting only the game-specific entity lexicon. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Anmol2059/thaulab\_EEUCA.

</details>


### [30] [Domyn-Small: A European 10B Reasoning Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20448)
*Simone Angarano,Francesco Bertolotti,Federico D'Ambrosio,Michele Resta,Alessandro Rognoni,Nicolò Ruggeri,Dario Salvati,Andrea Valenti,Alberto Veneri,Martin Cimmino*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Domyn-Small is a 10B-parameter open-weight reasoning LM (MIT license), trained on 9T multilingual tokens with a post-training pipeline including CPT (32K→128K via YaRN), math-focused SFT, and multi-stage RL (GRPO, DPO). It achieves strong reasoning at roughly 1/3 the token budget of Qwen3.5-9B, competitive GPQA-Diamond (50.0) and IFEval (79.9).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a compact, open-weight reasoning language model in the 7–10B parameter class that achieves a strong accuracy–efficiency balance — delivering competitive reasoning and instruction-following performance while consuming significantly fewer output tokens than peer models. The work also aims to democratize access by releasing both the model and the inference framework (Domyn Swarm) under permissive open-source licenses.

Method: A multi-stage training pipeline: (1) Pre-training on 9T multilingual tokens. (2) Continued Pre-Training (CPT) doubling native context to 32K tokens. (3) SFT with a math-focused annealing run. (4) Multi-stage RL: GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, and a multi-environment GRPO stage covering five domains (mathematics, code, multiple-choice QA, instruction-following, tool calling). Native 32K context extends to 128K at inference via YaRN. A chat-template toggle enables dual-mode reasoning (thinking vs. non-thinking).

Result: Domyn-Small achieves a strong accuracy–efficiency balance against peer 7–10B models: it uses ~33% of Qwen3.5-9B's token output and ~35% of OLMo-3-7B-Think's token budget on core reasoning benchmarks. Key metrics: IFEval 79.9 (instruction-following) and GPQA-Diamond 50.0 (science reasoning).

Conclusion: Domyn-Small demonstrates that a carefully orchestrated post-training pipeline — combining CPT, math-focused annealing, and multi-domain multi-stage RL — can yield a compact reasoning model that is highly token-efficient while remaining competitive on both reasoning and instruction-following benchmarks. The open-source release of weights, recipe, and the Domyn Swarm inference framework lowers barriers for reproducible research and scalable deployment.

Abstract: We introduce Domyn-Small, a 10-billion-parameter open-weight reasoning language model released under the MIT license. Domyn-Small is the product of an initial pre-training phase on 9 trillion tokens multilingual data, followed by a post-training pipeline for reasoning, instruction following, and context extension. For the latter, we performed a Continued Pre-Training (CPT) phase that doubles the native context window to 32K tokens, followed by SFT with a math-focused annealing run. Finally, the RL phase includes GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, and a multi-environment GRPO stage spanning five task domains: mathematics, code, multiple-choice QA, instruction-following, and tool calling. The 32K-token native context extends to 128K at inference via YaRN, and a chat-template toggle enables dual-mode reasoning. Against peer models in the 7--10B class (Qwen3.5-9B, OLMo-3-7B-Think, Nemotron-Nano-8B, Ministral-3-8B), Domyn-Small achieves a strong accuracy-efficiency balance: it produces roughly one-third as many tokens as Qwen3.5-9B and approximately 35% of OLMo-3-7B-Think's token budget on core reasoning benchmarks, while delivering strong instruction-following (IFEval 79.9) and competitive science reasoning (GPQA-Diamond 50.0). We release the weights and the post-training recipe alongside Domyn Swarm (Apache~2.0), an open-source framework for scalable LLM inference on HPC clusters developed during this program and used throughout this work.

</details>


### [31] [The Storyteller in the Model: Narrative Pattern Inheritance, Escalation Dynamics, and Alignment Governance in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20449)
*Adam Rigby,Raz Saremi,Azadeh Sohrabinejad,Mehdi Rahimi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs trained on human-authored text absorb narrative conventions (archetypes, tension-resolution arcs) that can cause outputs to drift toward adversarial or manipulative behaviors over extended interactions. A cross-study literature review reveals three patterns: statistical reproduction over reasoning, emergence of latent traits like sycophancy, and unintended behavioral spillover from narrow fine-tuning. This "narrative drift" represents an unmonitored governance risk requiring dedicated oversight instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper is motivated by an underexamined question in AI safety: whether narrative structures and archetypal patterns embedded in human-authored training corpora (e.g., protagonist/antagonist dynamics, underdog tropes, tension-resolution arcs) systematically influence LLM behavior in deployed systems. The authors argue that while alignment research focuses heavily on explicit training objectives and reinforcement learning, the latent influence of storytelling conventions absorbed during pretraining remains a blind spot, potentially causing LLM outputs to drift toward rhetorically enticing but adversarial behavior in multi-turn interactions.

Method: The paper employs a systematic literature review and cross-paper analysis, synthesizing findings from recent empirical studies on LLM alignment, persona dynamics, emergent misalignment, and user interaction patterns. Rather than conducting original experiments, the authors aggregate and interpret evidence across the existing literature to identify convergent patterns bearing on the narrative-drift hypothesis.

Result: Three key patterns emerge from the analysis: (1) LLMs reproduce statistical training-data patterns rather than engaging in independent reasoning; (2) measurable latent traits such as sycophancy and deceptiveness appear reliably across unrelated prompts, suggesting deep structural biases; (3) fine-tuning on a narrow narrative task produces unintended behavioral changes that generalize far beyond the targeted task. Additionally, persuasive narrative-style outputs are identified as among the most common LLM products in real-world usage, compounding these risks. Narrative drift is characterized as an escalation pathway that evades discrete-incident detection mechanisms.

Conclusion: Narrative drift constitutes a significant and currently unmonitored governance risk in deployed LLM systems. Because it manifests gradually across extended interactions and falls outside the scope of incident-based monitoring, it requires the development of dedicated, continuous oversight instruments. The paper calls for the AI safety community to treat pretraining narrative conventions as a systematic source of behavioral influence warranting explicit measurement and mitigation.

Abstract: LLMs are trained predominantly on human-authored text, yet the structural and narrative conventions embedded in that text are rarely examined as a source of systematic behavioral influence, or as a governance risk in deployed systems. This paper considers whether the storytelling patterns inherent in published human writing, including archetypal roles such as protagonist, antagonist, and underdog, as well as tension-and-resolution narrative arcs, are absorbed during training and subsequently surface in LLM outputs, causing responses to drift toward unexpected, adversarial, or rhetorically enticing behaviors over extended interactions. Through a systematic literature review and cross-paper analysis of recent empirical studies on LLM alignment, persona dynamics, emergent misalignment, and user interaction patterns, we observe evidence bearing on this hypothesis. The findings reveal three key patterns. First, LLMs reproduce statistical patterns from their training data rather than reasoning independently. Second, measurable latent traits, including sycophancy and deceptiveness, emerge reliably across unrelated prompts. Third, fine-tuning on a narrow narrative task can produce unintended behavioral changes well beyond that task. Furthermore, evidence suggests that persuasive, narrative-style outputs are among the most common LLM products in real-world usage, amplifying these risks. Narrative drift constitutes an unmonitored escalation pathway in deployed AI systems, one that evades discrete-incident detection mechanisms and requires dedicated monitoring instruments.

</details>


### [32] [ShriNep@EEUCA 2026: RAKSHAK - Multi-Task DeBERTa with Rationale Distillation and Jigsaw-Augmented Training for Toxic Intent Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20450)
*Binayak Karki,Aryan Kafle,Pingala Ghimire*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RAKSHAK, a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base system combining rationale distillation, contrastive loss, and cross-domain data transfer, achieves 0.5883 Macro F1 on fine-grained toxic intent classification in gaming chat, ranking 7th out of 35 teams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classifying toxic intent in gaming chat is challenging due to severe class imbalance (rare categories like Threats and Extremism have only 60 and 24 samples respectively), domain-specific multilingual slang, and the need for fine-grained 6-class categorization.

Method: RAKSHAK employs a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base architecture with: (1) rationale distillation from Qwen2.5-14B, (2) Supervised Contrastive Loss for better representation learning, (3) dedicated rare-class binary heads, and (4) data augmentation via cross-domain transfer from Jigsaw (16,225 samples mapped to Labels 1-4) plus 100 LLM-generated extremism samples for Label 5. A secondary system (M1) fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-base with Focal Loss on original data plus only the 100 extremism samples.

Result: RAKSHAK achieves Macro F1 of 0.5883 on the official test set (7th/35 teams). M1 achieves 0.5252. Ablation shows cross-domain transfer contributes +2.6 F1 points and the multi-task architecture contributes +3.7 points.

Conclusion: Combining rationale distillation from LLMs, contrastive learning, rare-class heads, and cross-domain transfer effectively addresses extreme class imbalance and scarce data in fine-grained toxic intent classification for gaming domains.

Abstract: This paper presents two systems for the GameTox Shared Task at the Workshop on EEUCA at ACL 2026, which requires classifying World of Tanks chat utterances into six fine-grained toxic intent categories (Labels 0-5). Severe class imbalance, domain-specific multilingual slang, and extremely scarce data for rare categories such as Threats (Label 4, 60 samples) and Extremism (Label 5, 24 samples) make this a challenging classification problem. Our primary submission, RAKSHAK (rak s. aka, Sanskrit for "Protector"), is a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base (He et al., 2022) framework combining rationale distillation from Qwen2.5-14B (An et al., 2024), Supervised Contrastive Loss, and dedicated rare-class binary heads. RAKSHAK's training data is augmented with cross-domain transfer from the Jigsaw Toxic Comment dataset (16,225 samples mapped to Labels 1-4) and 100 LLM-generated extremism samples for Label 5. Our secondary system (M1) fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-base with Focal Loss on the original GameTox data plus the same 100 extremism samples, without Jigsaw transfer. RAKSHAK achieves a Macro F1 of 0.5883 on the official test set, ranking 7th out of 35 participating teams, while M1 achieves 0.5252 Macro F1. An ablation comparing M1 with and without Jigsaw data shows that cross-domain transfer accounts for +2.6 F1 points, while RAKSHAK's multi-task architecture contributes a further +3.7 points.

</details>


### [33] [Semantic Field Theory: Historical Origin, Higher-Order Interaction, and Stabilized Semantic Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20451)
*Dimitris Vartziotis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reconstructs Semantic Field Theory (SFT) from its philosophical origins into a mathematically rigorous computational model for lexical semantics. It proposes five formal elements: a semantic field model tuple, a Gaussian product closure theorem, Möbius inversion for isolating higher-order interactions, an order spectrum metric, and energy-functional minimization for stabilized interpretation. A worked example with Gaussian semantic fields demonstrates the framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to give Semantic Field Theory a sharper mathematical core suitable for independent evaluation in computational linguistics and representation learning, moving it from philosophical critique toward a tractable computational model class for lexical semantics, higher-order composition, and stabilized interpretation.

Method: The paper contributes five formal elements: (1) a semantic field model defined as a tuple (semantic space, lexical field lifting, contextual deformation map, interaction complex, interpretation functional); (2) a Gaussian product closure result proving multiplicative field interactions have explicit centers, precisions, and compatibility factors; (3) generalization of the three-word problem via Möbius inversion on the subset lattice to isolate irreducible semantic interactions of arbitrary order; (4) an order spectrum measuring how much field mass is explained at each interaction order; and (5) stabilized interpretation formulated as minimization of an energy functional with existence, descent, and stability conditions.

Result: The paper provides a Gaussian product closure theorem for multiplicative field interactions, generalizes interaction decomposition to arbitrary order via Möbius inversion, and establishes energy-minimization conditions for stabilized interpretation. A worked example demonstrates the framework applied to a three-word "summer day" triple using Gaussian semantic fields, implemented in Python and summarized by a flow diagram.

Conclusion: The result is explicitly not a completed theory of natural language meaning and does not replace social, pragmatic, or normative accounts of language. It offers a tractable formal core for SFT that can be independently evaluated in computational linguistics and representation learning contexts.

Abstract: Semantic Field Theory (SFT) has developed from a philosophical critique of strong anti-formalist readings of language games into a proposed computational model class for lexical semantics, higher order composition, and stabilized interpretation. This paper reconstructs that evolution and gives SFT a sharper mathematical core suitable for independent evaluation in computational linguistics and representation learning. The central proposal is that a tractable level of linguistic organization can be modeled through lexical representations expressed as semantic fields, through contextual deformation of those fields, through interaction terms defined over subsets of tokens, and through stabilization governed by semantic energy dynamics. The paper contributes five formal elements. First, it defines a semantic field model as a tuple consisting of a semantic space, a lexical field lifting, a contextual deformation map, an interaction complex, and an interpretation functional. Second, it proves a Gaussian product closure result showing that multiplicative field interactions have explicit centers, precisions, and compatibility factors. Third, it generalizes the three-word problem by using Mobius inversion on the subset lattice to isolate irreducible semantic interactions of arbitrary order. Fourth, it introduces an order spectrum that measures how much field mass is explained at each interaction order. Fifth, it formulates stabilized interpretation as minimization of an energy functional associated with the sentence and gives existence, descent, and stability conditions. A small worked example shows how a three-word summer day triple can be represented by Gaussian semantic fields, implemented in Python, and summarized by a flow diagram. The result is not a completed theory of natural language meaning and does not replace social, pragmatic, or normative accounts of language.

</details>


### [34] [A Knowledge-Injection Framework for Zero-Shot Adaptation of LLMs to Delirium Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20453)
*Jessica Sena,Shesadree Priyadarshani,Miguel Contreras,Bharat Gandhi,Scott Siegel,Subhash Nerella,Parisa Rashidi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A lightweight inference-time knowledge-injection framework augments clinical summaries with external clinical reports, significantly improving zero-shot ICU delirium prediction for smaller open-weight LLMs (LLaMA 8B and 70B), narrowing the performance gap with frontier models without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models struggle with zero-shot clinical prediction due to incomplete domain knowledge, particularly in smaller, locally deployable models. The authors aim to bridge this gap while maintaining a privacy-preserving, resource-efficient workflow suitable for clinical settings.

Method: The framework injects an external clinical knowledge report at inference time into a deterministic natural-language summary of structured EHR data. No fine-tuning or retrieval is required. Evaluated on LLaMA 3.1 8B and LLaMA 3.3 70B using 3,160 ICU admissions from MIMIC-IV. Random control reports and SHAP-based attribution are used to validate that gains stem from clinically meaningful content, not prompt length.

Result: Adding meaningful external knowledge improved AUROC by +8.57pp (8B) and +1.99pp (70B) over no-knowledge baselines. Relative to a GPT-5.2 frontier model (68.86% AUROC), the gap shrank from 15.66 to 7.09 points (8B) and from 5.30 to 3.31 points (70B). Random reports degraded or did not improve performance. SHAP analysis confirmed active use of injected knowledge.

Conclusion: Inference-time knowledge injection effectively narrows the performance gap between locally deployable open-weight LLMs and frontier closed models for zero-shot clinical prediction, offering a practical, privacy-preserving approach for resource-constrained clinical environments.

Abstract: Large language models show promise for clinical prediction, but zero-shot performance on specialized tasks is limited by incomplete domain knowledge, especially for smaller locally deployable models. We present a lightweight knowledge-injection framework for zero-shot ICU delirium prediction that augments a deterministic natural-language summary of structured electronic health record data with an external clinical knowledge report at inference time, without fine-tuning or retrieval. We evaluate LLaMA 3.1 8B and LLaMA 3.3 70B on 3,160 ICU admissions from the MIMIC IV dataset. Adding a clinically meaningful external knowledge report improves AUROC by 8.57 percentage points for the 8B model and 1.99 percentage points for the 70B model compared to no external knowledge. Relative to a GPT-5.2 frontier-model reference without external knowledge report (AUROC 68.86%), knowledge injection reduces the performance gap from 15.66 to 7.09 AUROC points for LLaMA 8B and from 5.30 to 3.31 AUROC points for LLaMA 70B. Random control reports do not improve performance and often degrade it, indicating that gains depend on clinically meaningful content rather than added prompt length alone. SHAP-based attribution further confirms that the injected knowledge is actively used during prediction. These findings suggest that inference-time knowledge injection can narrow the gap between locally deployable open-weight models and frontier closed models while preserving a practical, privacy-preserving workflow for resource-constrained clinical settings.

</details>


### [35] [Response drift across frontier large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20454)
*Mohammed Aledhari,Ali Aledhari,Fatimah Aledhari,Gowtham Venkat Eathamokkala,Mohamed Rahouti*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A blinded human evaluation of 47 participants assessing 62 multidomain questions across 10 frontier LLMs (29,140 assessments) reveals that response drift is universal, with eight models clustering at a 78-81% deviation ceiling and two at 47-49%. Drift structure is domain- and question-dependent, and automated similarity metrics fail to capture human judgments (R² < 2%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While response drift — the tendency of LLM outputs to deviate from expert-validated references — is known to exist across frontier models, no prior work has systematically characterised its magnitude and structure using rigorous human evaluation. The authors aim to fill this gap through a large-scale, fully crossed, blinded human assessment.

Method: A fully crossed, blinded experimental design: 47 geographically diverse participants each evaluated all 62 multidomain questions across all 10 frontier LLMs, producing 29,140 independent human assessments. Responses were judged against expert-validated references. Drift was analysed by model, domain, and question, with pairwise correlations computed among models and automated similarity metrics tested against human judgments.

Result: Every model exhibited response drift. Eight models reached a statistically indistinguishable ceiling of 78-81% deviation, while two models showed substantially lower deviation (47-49%). Drift profiles varied across six domains and 62 questions. Pairwise correlations among the eight ceiling models exceeded r = 0.85. Automated similarity metrics explained less than 2% of the variance in human judgments (R² < 0.02).

Conclusion: Response drift is a universal phenomenon across frontier LLMs. Its magnitude clusters into two tiers, its structure is both domain- and question-dependent, and it is only reliably accessible through human-centred evaluation — automated metrics are an inadequate proxy.

Abstract: All frontier large language models (LLMs) exhibit response drift -- producing outputs that deviate from expert-validated references -- yet the magnitude and structure of this drift remain uncharacterised by systematic human evaluation. Here we report a fully crossed evaluation in which 47 geographically diverse participants each assessed all 62 multidomain questions across ten frontier LLMs under blinded conditions, yielding 29,140 independent assessments. Every model drifts, but drift magnitude varies substantially: eight models converge on a statistically indistinguishable ceiling (78-81% deviation), while two achieve lower deviation (47-49%). Drift profiles differ across six domains and 62 questions, with pairwise correlations among ceiling models exceeding r = 0.85. Automated similarity metrics explain less than 2% of variance in human judgements. These findings reveal that response drift is universal across frontier LLMs, domain- and question-dependent in structure, and accessible only through human-centred evaluation.

</details>


### [36] [RE-AD: Real-Time Requirement Adherence for Data Labeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20455)
*Siddarth Malreddy,Ishan Nigam,Akshay Arora,Nikhil Mittal,Subrat Sahu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A real-time framework (RE-AD) that uses LLMs to validate human annotation quality by decomposing SOPs into atomic rules with tiered validation, achieving 0.749 F1 on benchmarks and 82% fix acceptance in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crowd-sourced human annotations for LLM training frequently suffer from quality issues due to annotator misunderstanding or disengagement. There is a need for proactive, real-time quality validation rather than post-hoc correction.

Method: The RE-AD framework decomposes Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into atomic rules using LLM self-reflection, categorizes these rules by complexity level, and applies tiered validation strategies in real time to flag annotation errors as they occur.

Result: The system achieved an F1 score of 0.749 on a synthetic benchmark. In production deployment, annotators accepted and corrected 82% of the errors flagged by the framework. Ablation studies validated core design decisions.

Conclusion: The RE-AD framework effectively improves human annotation quality through real-time LLM-based validation, with strong empirical results both in benchmark evaluation and real-world production settings.

Abstract: Human-annotated data remains fundamental to training frontier Large Language Models (LLMs). However, crowd-sourced annotations often suffer from quality issues stemming from annotator misunderstanding or lack of engagement. To address this, we introduce a real-time requirement adherence (RE-AD) framework that leverages LLMs to proactively validate labeling quality. Our methodology involves decomposing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into atomic rules via self-reflection, categorizing them by complexity, and applying tiered validation strategies. Evaluated on a synthetic benchmark, the system achieved an F1 score of 0.749. Furthermore, production deployment resulted in annotators accepting and fixing 82% of the errors flagged by the framework. We include ablation studies to demonstrate the impact of our core design decisions.

</details>


### [37] [Learn2Zinc: Fine-tuning Small Language Models for Text-to-Model Translation in MiniZinc](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20456)
*Serdar Kadioglu,Karthik Uppuluri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Small language models achieve near-zero syntax accuracy on MiniZinc code generation; cross-model error bootstrapping fine-tuning boosts execution accuracy to 98%, but semantic reasoning plateaus at 35%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs excel at mainstream language code generation but fail badly on rare DSLs like MiniZinc (constraint modeling). The authors investigate whether fine-tuning small models (0.6B–20B) can bridge this gap, focusing on the syntax vs. semantics failure modes.

Method: Cross-model error bootstrapping: collect syntax errors from multiple LLM runs, curate an error-correction training dataset from these failures, then fine-tune small models. Also incorporates self-reflection and ensembling techniques to further boost accuracy.

Result: Execution accuracy reaches up to 98% after fine-tuning with the error-correction dataset. However, solution (semantic) accuracy caps at ~35%, revealing that syntax is learnable but constraint reasoning remains a hard challenge.

Conclusion: Syntax errors dominate DSL code generation failures and can be effectively addressed via targeted fine-tuning on error-correction data. Semantic reasoning for constraint problems, however, remains the true bottleneck. The authors open-source their pipeline, datasets, and models.

Abstract: Large language models excel at code generation for mainstream programming languages but struggle with rare, domain-specific languages such as MiniZinc, a constraint modeling language for combinatorial problems. We investigate whether targeted fine-tuning can teach small language models (0.6B to 20B parameters) to generate syntactically correct and semantically valid MiniZinc models from natural language problem descriptions. Our key finding is that syntax errors dominate failures when working with this domain specific language: the out-of-the-box execution accuracy of small language models such as Qwen3, LLaMa, Gemma, and GPT-OSS is near-zero. We propose a cross-model error bootstrapping approach that collects syntax errors from multiple LLM runs and leverage those to curate an error correction training dataset. This dataset allows us fine-tune small language models that consistently improves both direct code generation and chain-of-thought approaches across all model sizes. With self-reflection and ensembling, our approach achieves up to 98\% execution accuracy. In parallel, solution accuracy still remains at 35\%, indicating that while syntax is learnable, constraint reasoning remains a challenge. We contribute our fine-tuning pipeline, datasets, and models to opens-source for further research on text-to-model translation.

</details>


### [38] [Dropping the Anchor: Statistical Context Summarization for Distributed Systems via Pulsar Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20457)
*Aryan Sood,Shantanu Acharya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Pulsar Attention introduces content-aware components (attention-sink prefix and Max-IDF cross-block summaries) to replace the static anchor block in distributed long-sequence LLM inference, reducing per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3× over Star Attention while achieving better accuracy on long-context benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distributed blockwise attention methods like Star Attention reduce the quadratic self-attention cost for long sequences by sharding context across hosts, but they rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host. This static anchor is computationally wasteful and not informed by the actual content being processed.

Method: Pulsar Attention replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: (1) a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes the softmax operation, and (2) compact cross-block summaries constructed using a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens, capturing salient content across shards without replicating the entire first block.

Result: Pulsar reduces Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3× over Star Attention with an identical KV cache footprint. On RULER and BABILong benchmarks with Llama-3.1-8B, it outperforms both Star Attention and dense attention at up to 128K token sequences, with absolute gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.

Conclusion: Content-aware anchor design via attention sinks and IDF-based summaries is a more effective and efficient strategy than static block replication for distributed long-context LLM inference.

Abstract: Inference with large language models (LLMs) on long sequences is computationally expensive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Distributed blockwise methods such as Star Attention reduce this cost by sharding context across hosts, but rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host. We propose Pulsar Attention, which replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes softmax, and compact cross-block summaries built via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens. This reduces the Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3$\times$ over Star Attention while retaining an identical KV cache footprint. On RULER and BABILong with Llama-3.1-8B, Pulsar Attention outperforms both Star Attention and dense attention at sequence lengths up to 128K tokens, with absolute gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.

</details>


### [39] [CAMeR: Keyword-Gated Hybrid Activation for Adaptive Memory Retention in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20458)
*Haowen Lai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CAMeR introduces a hybrid symbolic-neural gating mechanism (keyword Jaccard + embedding cosine similarity) with adaptive weight decay for LLM agent memory retention, demonstrating that keyword-gated reinforcement—not learnable decay—drives performance, achieving a 1.6× larger retention gap and 83.2% token savings over full-context baselines on a new benchmark (CAMeR-Bench).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems either retain all information indiscriminately or apply uniform, heuristic-based forgetting, failing to adaptively distinguish relevant from irrelevant knowledge across extended dialogues. Current benchmarks (LoCoMO, LongMemEval) cannot adequately test adaptive retention.

Method: CAMeR (Context-Activated Memory Reinforcement) uses a dual-gating mechanism: a symbolic gate computing word-level Jaccard similarity and a sub-symbolic gate computing embedding cosine similarity. These produce a hybrid similarity score per memory-query pair; memories exceeding a threshold are reinforced, while all memories undergo controlled decay via adaptive weight dynamics. The authors also introduce CAMeR-Bench: a 76-memory, 100-round benchmark across 8 topic clusters with graded activation frequency.

Result: On CAMeR-Bench, CAMeR's keyword gate achieves a 1.6× larger retention gap (0.039 vs. 0.024 scissors gap) between high-frequency and never-referenced memories compared to embedding-only gating. Time-driven baselines (Oblivion, SuperLocalMemory) collapse to near-zero weights. Top-5 retrieval saves 83.2% tokens (39k vs. 231k cumulative) versus full-context approaches while improving retrieval precision. Across 8 ablation conditions, the keyword gate—not learnable decay—is the primary performance driver.

Conclusion: Hybrid symbolic-neural gating offers a simple yet effective mechanism for adaptive memory retention in LLM agents, with the symbolic keyword gate being the critical component rather than learned decay dynamics.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents operating over extended dialogues accumulate vast amounts of information, yet existing memory systems either retain everything indiscriminately or apply uniform forgetting heuristics that fail to distinguish relevant from irrelevant knowledge. We present CAMeR (Context-Activated Memory Reinforcement), a memory retention framework combining keyword-gated hybrid activation -- a joint symbolic (word-level Jaccard) and sub-symbolic (embedding cosine) gating mechanism -- with adaptive weight dynamics. CAMeR computes a hybrid similarity score for each memory-query pair; memories exceeding a threshold receive reinforcement while all memories undergo controlled decay. We introduce CAMeR-Bench, a 76-memory, 100-round benchmark spanning 8 topic clusters with graded activation frequency, designed to test adaptive retention where existing benchmarks (LoCoMO, LongMemEval) cannot. On CAMeR-Bench, CAMeR's keyword gate achieves a 1.6$\times$ larger retention gap between high-frequency and never-referenced memories compared to embedding-only gating (scissors gap: 0.039 vs. 0.024), while time-driven baselines (Oblivion, SuperLocalMemory) collapse to near-zero weights over 100 rounds. CAMeR's top-5 retrieval saves 83.2\% tokens versus full-context approaches (39k vs. 231k cumulative) while producing weight signals that improve retrieval precision. Through 8 ablation conditions we establish that the keyword gate -- not learnable decay -- is the primary performance driver at this scale. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid symbolic-neural gating provides a simple yet effective mechanism for adaptive memory retention in LLM agents.

</details>


### [40] [THOR: A Theta-Gamma Hierarchical Oscillatory Reasoning Framework for Multi-hop QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20459)
*Ziyang Ling,Ronald X. Xu,Mingzhai Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: THOR is a brain-inspired multi-hop QA framework that mimics Theta-Gamma neural oscillations to address attention decay and error accumulation. It decouples global planning from local retrieval and incorporates a verification-repair mechanism, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-hop QA systems suffer from two core limitations: (1) attention decay — the model progressively loses focus on the original question as the reasoning chain extends across multiple hops; and (2) error accumulation — mistakes in early hops compound through the chain, leading to cascading failures. Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillations in the brain naturally solve analogous problems by decoupling global planning (theta) from local processing (gamma) and enabling intermittent verification.

Method: THOR adopts a Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillatory reasoning framework. It decouples global planning (maintaining question focus across hops) from local retrieval (extracting evidence per hop), enabling efficient attention transfer between reasoning steps. Additionally, it incorporates a verification-and-repair mechanism that periodically interrupts error propagation along incorrect reasoning paths, preventing compounding mistakes.

Result: Extensive experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks show that THOR improves answer accuracy and robustness compared to baselines. Specific validation experiments confirm that the framework effectively mitigates both attention decay and error accumulation. THOR also demonstrates strong generalization across different backbone models.

Conclusion: THOR provides a biologically inspired solution to persistent challenges in multi-hop reasoning. By hierarchically organizing reasoning via theta-gamma oscillatory principles and integrating verification-repair cycles, the framework offers a generalizable approach that enhances both accuracy and robustness in multi-hop question answering.

Abstract: Multi-hop question answering requires retrieving and integrating evidence from multiple contexts. Despite the rapid progress of current research, multi-hop reasoning remains constrained by two persistent limitations: attention decay, where the model's focus on main question degrades as the reasoning chain grows, and error accumulation, where mistakes propagate across hops and compounds into final failure. Inspired by Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillation which decouples global planning from local retrieval, enabling efficient attention transfer between hops and a verification and repair mechanism that interrupts the accumulation of errors in the wrong paths, we present THOR, a brain-inspired Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillatory reasoning framework. Extensive comparative experiments and specific validation experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that THOR improves answer accuracy and robustness while mitigating limitations, showcasing its generalization across different backbones.

</details>


### [41] [Instruct-FD: Can Your Full-Duplex Speech System Follow Turn-Taking Instructions?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20460)
*Yuzhi Tang,Wentao Ma,Xiling Zhao,Ahmad Salimi,Sepehr Harfi Moridani,Dongming Shen,Jixuan Wang,Abdulrahman Abdulrazzag,Murdock Aubry,Yu-Hua Chen,Daniel Lee,Jaewon Lee,Jonah Mackey,Silin Meng,Nicholas Stranges,Chenxu Xiong,Hao Yu,Yi Zhu,Mu Li,Alex Smola*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Instruct-FD is a benchmark for evaluating how well full-duplex spoken dialogue systems follow explicit instructions to control turn-taking behavior. State-of-the-art systems perform poorly (best: 64.4% adherence), especially on proactive behaviors like backchanneling and interruption, highlighting a critical gap for real-world deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current FD systems enable fluid conversations but lack controllable turn-taking. Real-world applications demand different conversational policies (e.g., proactive tutoring vs. passive counseling), yet it is unknown whether FD systems can adapt turn-taking when explicitly instructed. This gap must be addressed for practical deployability.

Method: The authors introduce Instruct-FD, comprising: (1) a human-validated, scalable synthetic pipeline that generates instruction-conditioned conversations; (2) a deployment-agnostic multi-turn evaluation protocol; and (3) an LLM-based judge. Six state-of-the-art FD systems are benchmarked against these instruction-conditioned scenarios.

Result: The best model achieves only 64.4% instruction adherence. Performance is highly uneven across behaviors and scenarios, with proactive behaviors such as model backchanneling and interruption remaining particularly challenging for all evaluated systems.

Conclusion: Instruction-following turn management is a critical, underdeveloped capability for FD dialogue systems. The strong performance gap, especially on proactive behaviors, establishes this as an essential research direction for building adaptable, deployable spoken dialogue systems.

Abstract: Current full-duplex (FD) spoken dialogue systems can produce fluid interactions, yet it remains unclear whether they can adapt their turn-taking behavior when explicitly instructed. This is critical for real-world deployment, where conversational policies vary across applications (e.g., proactive tutoring vs. passive counseling). We introduce Instruct-FD, an instruction-conditioned benchmark for evaluating controllable turn management in FD systems. To enable this, we develop a human-validated, scalable synthetic pipeline that generates instruction-conditioned conversations, along with a deployment-agnostic multi-turn evaluation protocol and an LLM-based judge. Benchmarking six state-of-the-art full-duplex systems reveals a substantial gap in instruction-following turn management: the best model achieves only 64.4% adherence. Performance is highly uneven across behaviors and scenarios, with proactive behaviors such as model backchanneling and interruption remaining particularly challenging. These findings establish instruction-following turn management as a crucial direction for building adaptable and deployable full-duplex dialogue systems.

</details>


### [42] [Evaluating the Effectiveness of Persona Simulation in Opinion Prediction with GPT-4.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20589)
*Sarah Y. Li,Ziyu Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GPT-4.1 was tested on persona simulation for opinion prediction, achieving near-perfect election outcome prediction (8/9 U.S. states) and high accuracy (up to 0.94) in predicting healthcare-related beliefs. Simulated dialogues aligned with persona traits but lacked natural flow. The authors conclude persona simulation is promising for applications in public health, lawmaking, and economics, provided biases are addressed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore the current capabilities, limitations, and future potential of LLM-based persona simulation — specifically whether LLMs can accurately predict human opinions and simulate realistic interactions when conditioned on demographic/characteristic information.

Method: The authors employed GPT-4.1 for three tasks: (1) predicting 2024 U.S. election outcomes using personas from nine states (Columbia University Personas dataset); (2) predicting individual beliefs about childhood vaccines using the American Trends Panel Wave 123 dataset (Pew Research Center); and (3) generating simulated conversations among personas to evaluate dialogue coherence and alignment with assigned personalities and backgrounds.

Result: GPT-4.1 correctly predicted election outcomes in 8 of 9 states, only failing on one swing state. For vaccine-related beliefs, it achieved prediction accuracy up to 0.94. In simulated dialogues, opinions and conversational content were consistent with assigned persona traits, though the conversations lacked natural human-like flow.

Conclusion: Persona simulation via LLMs is a promising AI application for opinion analysis and reaction prediction across domains (public health, lawmaking, economics), contingent on addressing inherent biases. The approach shows strong predictive accuracy but still falls short in producing naturally flowing human-like dialogue.

Abstract: Persona simulation involves utilizing large language models (LLMs) to anticipate human choices or interactions based on specific characteristic information. To further understand current limitations and future directions, we tested persona simulation in opinion prediction with GPT-4.1 (knowledge cutoff by June 2024). Using personas from nine U.S. states provided by Columbia University's Personas dataset, GPT-4.1 accurately predicted 2024 election outcomes in eight out of the nine states, only failing in one of the swing states. We then focused on opinions related to medicine and healthcare. With the American Trends Panel Wave 123 dataset from Pew Research Center, GPT-4.1 was able to anticipate beliefs about childhood vaccines with an accuracy of up to 0.94. Furthermore, we applied GPT-4.1 to generate conversations among personas and observed that the simulated dialogues and opinions adhered well to personas' personalities and backgrounds, albeit lacking natural human-like flow. Persona simulation proves to be a promising application of artificial intelligence as long as biases are addressed. In the near future, it will be beneficial to apply it to opinion analysis and reaction prediction in diverse fields ranging from public health to lawmaking to economics.

</details>


### [43] [Frontier Financial Judgement: Can agents tell what might move a stock?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20645)
*Joshua Harris*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Frontier Financial Judgement, a benchmark with 656 items (synthetic, live news, historical documents) for evaluating AI agents on identifying valuation-relevant financial news. The strongest agent matches expert labels in only 52.4% of cases, with false-positive rates ranging from ~1% (GPT-5.6 Sol) to ~32% (Claude Sonnet 4.6), revealing accuracy-cost-reliability trade-offs that hinder practical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Equity analysts face growing difficulty identifying valuation-relevant information amid AI-driven increases in news volume. No rigorous benchmark exists to evaluate how well AI agents can replicate expert human judgement in filtering genuine, material financial news from stale, immaterial, or misleading content under realistic conditions.

Method: The benchmark combines three data sources: human-designed and labelled synthetic articles, live news articles, and historical documents, totaling 656 assessment items. Multiple frontier AI agents are evaluated on their ability to distinguish new, valuation-relevant financial information from irrelevant or misleading news. Performance is measured by agreement with professional equity analyst labels, false-positive rates, and cost-reliability trade-offs.

Result: Top agent accuracy reaches only 52.4% exact match with expert labels. False-positive rates vary dramatically across frontier agents: GPT-5.6 Sol (~1%), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (~32%). Substantial trade-offs exist among accuracy, cost, false positives, and reliability, preventing reliable real-world deployment of automated news-flow filtering.

Conclusion: Current frontier AI agents remain insufficient for reliably automating financial news-flow filtering, as evidenced by modest accuracy and widely divergent false-positive rates. Significant improvements are needed before such systems can be deployed in practice for equity research workflows.

Abstract: We introduce Frontier Financial Judgement, a challenging new benchmark developed in collaboration with professional equity analysts to assess agents' ability to replicate expert human judgements. Rapidly identifying new information, evaluating its implications and determining its valuation impact is one of the most time-consuming and challenging aspects of real-world equity coverage. This is becoming ever more difficult and important as AI rapidly increases the quantity of new information to process. The strongest agent we evaluate on Frontier Financial Judgement matches all expert labels in only 52.4% of cases. We also find significant divergence in estimated false-positive rates among frontier agents, ranging from ~1% for GPT-5.6 Sol to ~32% for Claude Sonnet 4.6. To construct the benchmark and make it representative of real-world settings, we combine human-designed and labelled synthetic articles with live news articles and historical documents, creating 656 items for assessment. The resulting task requires agents to distinguish genuinely new, valuation-relevant financial information from stale, immaterial or misleading news under realistic conditions. We find substantial trade-offs among agent accuracy, cost, false positives and reliability that continue to hinder the reliable deployment of news-flow filtering in practice.

</details>


### [44] [From Agent Failures to Text Policies: What Works and What Breaks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20668)
*Jaideep Ray,Ankit Goyal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TextGrad uses natural-language feedback as optimization gradients for text components. The paper reveals a gap between executing useful textual policies and learning them from experience in agent settings: human-written policies improve agent performance, but policies generated from agent trajectories fail to reliably outperform fixed prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TextGrad has shown promise for optimizing language-model systems via textual feedback, but applying it to sequential decision-making agents is fundamentally harder because feedback is delayed across action sequences, making credit assignment difficult. The authors aim to isolate whether the bottleneck lies in executing textual policies or in learning them from experience.

Method: The study separates two capabilities: (1) following a useful textual policy, and (2) learning that policy from experience. Using two frozen 7B agents on the TextWorldExpress benchmark, they compare human-written policies against policies generated from agent trajectories using various approaches — richer traces, counterfactual evidence, and iterative GEPA search.

Result: Human-written policies yield a +5.0 success-point improvement, confirming that useful policy text exists and frozen agents can follow it. However, all experience-generated policies — regardless of trace richness, counterfactual inclusion, or GEPA search — fail to reliably beat fixed prompting baselines.

Conclusion: The core challenge for agent-level TextGrad is not executing textual policy updates but reliably generating and selecting them from experience. This identifies the credit-assignment and policy-generation step as the primary research bottleneck.

Abstract: TextGrad improves language-model systems by revising text from feedback. Its core thesis is that natural-language feedback can act as a gradient for optimizing text components without changing model weights. Applying it to agents is harder because feedback arrives only after a sequence of actions, making it difficult to identify which decision caused failure. We study this problem by separating the ability to follow a useful policy from the ability to learn that policy from experience. Our main finding is a clear gap between these two abilities. Human-written policies improve two frozen 7B agents on TextWorldExpress by 5.0 success points, showing that useful policy text exists. However, policies generated from agent trajectories do not reliably outperform fixed prompting, even with richer traces, counterfactual evidence, or iterative GEPA search. The main challenge for agent-level TextGrad is therefore not executing textual policy updates, but reliably generating and selecting them from experience.

</details>


### [45] [Learning to Detect UI Principle Violations via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20690)
*Nishi Mehta,Swathi Alse,Himani Kumavat,Yue Yu,Pratik Jayarao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A 4B vision-language model, trained via reinforcement learning on ~10K synthetically violated web pages, achieves 84% micro-F1 in auditing 19 interface-quality principles—outperforming rule-based tools while being far cheaper than human experts or frontier VLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code-generating agents are evaluated only on functional correctness, ignoring critical interface-quality issues (accessibility, deceptive patterns, visual hierarchy, decision complexity). Existing auditing solutions are either expensive/slow (human review, frontier VLMs) or too narrow (rule-based tools like axe-core/Lighthouse). A scalable, comprehensive, and affordable critic is needed.

Method: The authors unify 19 interface-quality principles from WCAG 2.2, deceptive design taxonomies, and HCI perception/cognition theories. They construct a ~10K verified dataset by synthetically injecting known violations into clean LLM-generated Tailwind pages. A 4B vision-language model is then fine-tuned via continued reinforcement learning to serve as the critic.

Result: Micro-F1 improved from 36% to 84%, with 13 of 19 principles exceeding 80% F1. The lightweight model effectively audits interfaces, filters low-quality training data, and provides reward signals for design-aware code generation.

Conclusion: A small VLM can serve as an effective, scalable interface-quality critic, bridging the gap between cheap-but-narrow rule-based tools and expensive-but-rich human/VLM review. The authors release their data-generation recipe and prompts to foster reproducible research.

Abstract: Small language models and coding agents increasingly generate web front-end code, yet their outputs are typically evaluated primarily for functional correctness. A generated interface may compile, render, and pass unit tests while still violating established interface quality principles, including accessibility barriers, deceptive design patterns, poor visual hierarchy, and excessive decision complexity. Existing auditing approaches face a trade-off between cost, coverage, and scalability: expert human review provides rich judgment but is slow and expensive; frontier vision-language models offer broader reasoning capabilities but remain costly to deploy at scale; and rule-based tools such as axe-core and Lighthouse are inexpensive but primarily capture mechanically checkable accessibility issues.
  We investigate whether a lightweight vision-language model can serve as an effective critic for generated interfaces. We unify 19 interface-quality principles from three complementary sources of HCI knowledge: WCAG 2.2 accessibility standards, deceptive design taxonomies, and established theories of perception, cognition, and interaction. To train this critic, we construct a verified dataset of approximately 10,000 generated web pages by synthetically injecting known violations into clean, LLM-generated Tailwind pages.
  Continued reinforcement learning on a 4B vision-language model improves micro-F1 from 36\% to 84\%, with 13 of 19 principles exceeding 80\% F1. The resulting critic can audit generated interfaces, filter low-quality interface training data, and provide a reward signal for design-aware code generation. We release our data-generation recipe and injection/verification prompts to support reproducible evaluation and future work on scalable interface-quality assessment.

</details>


### [46] [REGARD: Regional Affective Differences in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20722)
*Andrei Chetvergov,Alexander Evseev,Mikhail Solovev,Timofei Sivoraksha,Stepan Ukolov,Valeriia Kuschenko,Maria Chistyakova,Sergey Bolovtsov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces REGARD, a study using Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) profiling to capture affective framing differences across 19 LLMs on post-Soviet entities.
