Hybrid models (25% Möbius heads) match baseline perplexity while dramatically improving needle-in-a-haystack retrieval reliability, eliminating the seed lottery (90.3% vs 63.3% at context 512). The effect is specific to the anti-periodic geometry and provides zero-cost retrieval insurance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RoPE suffers from a "retrieval seed lottery" — needle-in-a-haystack accuracy varies wildly across random seeds (e.g., 14% to high values), making long-context retrieval unreliable. The authors seek a positional encoding that maintains perplexity parity while providing consistent, reliable long-range retrieval, fundamentally by changing the boundary condition geometry of the position encoding.

Method: The authors propose Möbius RoPE, which uses an anti-periodic frequency ladder θ_i = π(2i+1)/N. Each rotation plane completes an odd number of half-turns across the context length, yielding holonomy −1 (a Möbius strip topology). This produces a closed-form Dirichlet "dipole" kernel that deterministically couples both ends of the sequence. They pretrain 48 models (160M and 410M parameters, 2B tokens each) comparing: standard RoPE, Möbius RoPE (full and hybrid with 25% of heads), aperiodic controls in the same frequency band, periodic (holonomy +1) controls, and NoPE. Evaluation uses needle-in-a-haystack retrieval with variance testing.

Result: Hybrid Möbius RoPE matches baseline perplexity (29.66 vs 29.72) while dramatically improving retrieval: 90.3±5.7% vs 63.3±31.4% at context 512 (n=6 seeds), worst seed 86% vs 14%. Variance reduction is statistically significant (p=0.013-0.029 unadjusted, Levene p=0.040 at 410M). Aperiodic controls show no effect; periodic controls show only partial effect. Swapping trained models back to standard RoPE frequencies collapses retrieval, confirming dependence on anti-periodic geometry. NoPE achieves better short-context retrieval but incurs a 13% perplexity penalty and poor extrapolation. The effect is scoped to single-needle retrieval within the training window.

Conclusion: An anti-periodic boundary condition in positional encoding (holonomy −1) provides a zero-cost mechanism to eliminate retrieval unreliability in RoPE-based models. A simple one-line frequency swap on 25% of attention heads delivers baseline perplexity with a high reliability floor for needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, effectively insuring against the seed lottery without any architectural changes or training overhead.

Abstract: Möbius RoPE is a rotary positional encoding built on the anti-periodic frequency ladder $θ_i=π(2i+1)/N$: every rotation plane advances by an odd multiple of $π$ across the training context, so the positional holonomy is $-1$ and the two ends of the sequence are deterministically coupled through a closed-form Dirichlet "dipole"; to our knowledge this is the first anti-periodic boundary condition in positional encoding. We verify the theory numerically to $\sim 10^{-6}$ and pretrain 48 models spanning six 160M-class and three 410M-class arms (2B FineWeb-Edu tokens each; the hybrid arm puts Möbius frequencies on 25% of heads). Hybrid perplexity is unchanged (29.66 vs. 29.72), but needle-in-a-haystack retrieval becomes reliable: $90.3\pm5.7\%$ versus $63.3\pm31.4\%$ at context 512 ($n=6$ seeds), observed worst seed 86% versus 14%, robust variance tests $p=0.013$-$0.029$ (unadjusted), recurring at 410M (Levene $p=0.040$). Matched controls isolate the mechanism: an aperiodic ladder in the same frequency band reproduces none of the effect, and a periodic (holonomy $+1$) ladder only a fraction. Swapping trained models' frequency table back to standard RoPE (weights frozen) collapses retrieval, with damage concentrated on far needles: trained models depend on this long-range geometry. A NoPE arm is even more reliable at short context but pays a 13% perplexity tax and extrapolates worst; only the anti-periodic hybrid pairs baseline perplexity with a high reliability floor. The effect is scoped to single-needle retrieval within the training window; a one-line frequency swap thus provides zero-cost insurance against the retrieval seed lottery.

</details>


### [71] [An Evaluation Framework for Structured Audio Captions Validated by Controlled Perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21424)
*Liang-Yuan Wu,Sripathi Sridhar,Mark Cartwright,Magdalena Fuentes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multi-axis evaluation framework for structured audio captioning that combines LLM judges with deterministic metrics across five orthogonal axes, validated via a controlled perturbation testing protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing caption evaluation metrics are designed for flat textual outputs and cannot reliably assess the heterogeneous, multimodal attributes in structured audio descriptions that disentangle acoustic and semantic properties.

Method: A multi-axis evaluation framework built on the AudioCards dataset, assessing outputs across five orthogonal axes (tag-sets, descriptions, logical reasoning, numeric measurements, spectral profiles). It combines LLM-based judges for semantic nuance with deterministic computational metrics for acoustic deviation measurement. A controlled perturbation testing protocol injects typed, graded errors into groundtruth annotations for validation.

Result: The framework successfully distinguishes meaning-preserving paraphrases from genuine semantic and acoustic corruptions under the perturbation testing protocol.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-axis framework provides a reliable evaluation methodology for structured audio captioning, addressing the gap left by traditional flat-text metrics and validated through rigorous perturbation testing.

Abstract: Recent advancements in automated audio captioning (AAC) have shifted from monolithic sentence generation toward structured formats that explicitly disentangle distinct acoustic and semantic properties. However, evaluating this heterogeneous data remains a significant challenge. Existing caption metrics focus on flat textual outputs and fail to reliably assess multimodal attributes. To bridge this gap, we propose a multi-axis evaluation framework tailored for structured audio descriptions. Building on the AudioCards dataset, we evaluate outputs across five orthogonal axes: tag-sets, descriptions, logical reasoning, numeric measurements, and spectral profiles. Our approach combines Large Language Model (LLM) judges to capture semantic nuance with deterministic computational metrics to precisely measure acoustic deviations. To rigorously validate the reliability of this framework, we introduce a controlled perturbation testing protocol that injects typed, graded errors into groundtruth annotations. Our results demonstrate that this framework successfully distinguishes meaning-preserving paraphrases from genuine semantic and acoustic corruptions.

</details>


### [72] [Token Budget Saturation and Mechanistic Early Detection of Reasoning Non-Convergence in Chain-of-Thought Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21433)
*Renuka Oladri,Niveda Jawahar,Abdirisak Mohamed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Chain-of-thought reasoning models show a bimodal convergence pattern where 62% of generations converge with 90.3% accuracy. Linear probes on intermediate hidden states can partially predict convergence fate early (token 150, AUC 0.608), outperforming behavioral baselines, suggesting potential for early-exit inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B exhibit unreliable convergence behavior: some generations terminate successfully while others exhaust the token budget without reaching a conclusion. The authors aim to determine whether this convergence outcome is detectable early in the generation process using internal model representations, enabling potential computational savings.

Method: The authors empirically characterize the bimodal convergence phenomenon on AIME 1983-2024, measuring accuracy by convergence status. They then train linear probes on hidden-state activations from token positions 50–300 across model layers to predict convergence fate. These activation probes are compared against behavioral baselines (token entropy and repetition statistics). Statistical significance is assessed via sweep-level permutation testing with 100,000 permutations.

Result: Converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy vs. 6.6% for non-converged, with a 62.0% overall convergence rate. Layer-20 activations at token 150 yield AUC 0.608 (±0.080, 5-fold CV), above chance as early as token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines. The permutation test yields p=0.063, indicating a modest signal not confirmed at conventional significance thresholds.

Conclusion: Convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate model representations well before generation ends. This opens the path toward early-exit inference strategies and adaptive compute allocation, though the signal strength warrants further investigation with larger sample sizes.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B exhibit a bimodal convergence pattern: generations either terminate within a token budget (converged) or exhaust it without reaching a conclusion (non-converged). We characterize this phenomenon empirically, showing that converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy on AIME 1983-2024 while non-converged ones achieve only 6.6%, with an overall convergence rate of 62.0%. We then ask whether this outcome is detectable early in the thinking chain using internal model representations. Training linear probes on hidden-state activations at token positions 50-300, we find that layer-20 activations at token 150 achieve AUC 0.608 (+-0.080, 5-fold CV), reliably above chance even at token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines derived from token entropy and repetition statistics. A sweep-level permutation test yields p=0.063 (100,000 permutations), consistent with a modest signal that our sample size cannot confirm at conventional thresholds. These findings suggest that convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate representations well before the generation ends, opening a path toward early-exit inference and adaptive compute allocation.

</details>


### [73] [When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21445)
*Anna Mosolova,Djamé Seddah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TriviaRoomQA is a multilingual quiz benchmark spanning 288 topics, used to evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs (7–70B). Models excel on academic topics (history, geography, math) but struggle with everyday popular culture (celebrities, music, movies, news). Performance also varies by language even for identical questions, revealing a knowledge gap not captured by saturated academic benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks are academically focused and saturated, failing to measure LLMs' knowledge of everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail topics. The authors aim to test whether LLMs can compete in real-world quiz settings that span both canonical facts and popular culture, across multiple languages.

Method: The authors introduce TriviaRoomQA, a benchmark with 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages plus 5,340 French-only questions, covering 288 topics. They evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs (7–70B parameters) from European, Asian, and North American providers, analyzing performance across topics, knowledge types, and languages.

Result: LLMs perform well on knowledge-intensive topics (history, geography, mathematics) but significantly underperform on popular-culture topics (celebrities, music, movies, news). Performance is language-dependent: the same question yields different accuracy across languages, indicating factual access is not language-independent.

Conclusion: TriviaRoomQA exposes a critical knowledge gap in LLMs regarding everyday and culturally grounded knowledge, which current academic benchmarks miss. The benchmark provides a more ecologically valid assessment of real-world quiz competence across languages.

Abstract: Quiz rooms, trivia nights, and quiz shows challenge human knowledge across a wide range of topics, from canonical facts to everyday culture. In this paper, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can perform competitively in such settings, using quiz-style questions to test them on both common and niche topics. We introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark designed to evaluate everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge across 288 topics. The benchmark contains 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages and additional 5,340 French-only questions for a more fine-grained case study. We evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs from European, Asian, and North American providers, covering models from 7 to 70B parameters. We find that models are strong on knowledge-intensive topics such as history, geography, and mathematics, but substantially weaker on everyday popular-culture topics such as celebrities, music, movies, and news. Moreover, model performance varies across languages even for the same underlying questions, suggesting that access to factual knowledge is not always language-independent. In sum, our dataset and experiments demonstrate an important knowledge gap which is not captured by existing academic-based saturated benchmarks.

</details>


### [74] [RUMBA: Russian User Memory Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21447)
*Elizaveta Shevtsova,Inna Glebkina,Mark Baushenko,Pavel Gulyaev,Alena Fenogenova*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RUMBA is a Russian-language benchmark for evaluating long-term conversational memory in LLMs, featuring a fine-grained taxonomy of memory-centric question types across session-scoped dialogues. It enables diagnostic analysis of retrieval, temporal reasoning, and cross-session reasoning, with an aligned English subset for comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for long-term memory in LLMs are English-centric and rely on coarse aggregate retrieval metrics, neglecting the interplay between long-range context, temporal information, and reasoning. There is no fine-grained diagnostic tool for analyzing memory mechanisms across diverse question types and temporal scenarios.

Method: The authors construct RUMBA using timestamped, multi-session user-assistant dialogues paired with QA pairs. They introduce a unified taxonomy that categorizes questions by semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning requirements, and explicitness of temporal expressions. An aligned English subset is also produced under the same methodology. Contemporary memory systems and long-context models are evaluated diagnostically across benchmark slices.

Result: RUMBA reveals distinct strengths and failure modes across different memory mechanisms. The fine-grained slicing enables targeted analysis of how models handle retrieval across sessions, temporal reasoning, and the combination of information from disparate dialogue contexts.

Conclusion: RUMBA provides a much-needed diagnostic framework for long-term conversational memory evaluation, extending beyond English and beyond simple retrieval metrics. It highlights that different memory architectures exhibit characteristic failure patterns, underscoring the value of fine-grained, taxonomy-driven benchmarks for advancing memory capabilities in LLMs.

Abstract: The ability to handle long-term memory in LLMs is becoming increasingly critical, yet existing benchmarks remain English-centric and rely on aggregate retrieval metrics, failing to capture interactions between long-range context, temporal information, and reasoning. To address this, we introduce RUMBA (Russian User Memory BenchmArk) - a new benchmark for long-term conversational memory that provides a fine-grained taxonomy of memory-centric question types and a unified methodology accounting for semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning, and the explicitness of temporal expressions. RUMBA consists of timestamped user-assistant dialogues with QA pairs requiring retrieval, combination, and reasoning across sessions. While designed for Russian, we also provide an aligned English subset under the same methodology. We evaluate contemporary memory systems and long-context models, and show how RUMBA serves as a diagnostic tool to analyze model behavior across benchmark slices and identify strengths and failure modes of different memory mechanisms.

</details>


### [75] [What, Where, and How: Disentangling the Roles of Task, Language, and Model in Code Model Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21491)
*Piotr Wilam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A systematic 2×2 study (Python/Rust × Qwen2.5-Coder/DeepSeek-Coder) shows that language models agree on *what* grammatical concepts get dedicated circuits (ρ ≈ 0.65), but disagree on *where* and *how* those circuits are organized — revealing that universality is a property of representational content, not computational organization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether independently trained language models converge on the same internal representations for the same concepts, extending circuit extraction methodology to a cross-model, cross-language design that can disentangle task-driven, language-driven, and model-driven effects.

Method: A 2×2 factorial design: two programming languages (Python, Rust) × two models (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B). The authors extract concept circuits for a complete inventory of grammatical concepts (58 Python, 57 Rust) identically across all four cells using a recently introduced concept-circuit extraction method. They measure agreement via Spearman rank correlation, neuron sharing ratios, Jaccard similarity for neuron clusters, and validate functionality through ablation and linear probes.

Result: Three-part answer: (1) What concepts get circuits is task-driven — models agree strongly (Python ρ=0.638, Rust ρ=0.673, both p<10⁻⁷). (2) Where circuits sit is model-driven — Qwen processes concepts in late layers (~L17-19), DeepSeek at L6-7, regardless of language. (3) How circuits grow across layers is also model-driven — Qwen shows an early spike for atomic concepts absent in DeepSeek. Additional findings: Rust concepts receive 2-3× more circuitry than Python; DeepSeek shares 1.94× more neurons across languages than Qwen; Qwen binds Rust's type-and-trait keywords into a tight semantic cluster (Jaccard 0.535 vs null 0.112, p<0.001). Ablation and probes confirm circuits are functional.

Conclusion: Universality is not all-or-nothing: representational content (What) is largely shared across models, but computational organization (Where and How) is model-specific. Results are scoped to the 2×2 design; testing whether per-model profiles predict a third model is the next step.

Abstract: Do independently trained language models come to represent the same thing in the same way? We answer for code, extending a recently introduced concept-circuit extraction method to a 2x2 design -- Python and Rust crossed with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B -- and measuring a complete inventory of grammatical concepts (58 Python, 57 Rust) identically in all four cells: the smallest design that separates what depends on the task, the language, and the model.
  The answer splits into three parts. What earns dedicated circuitry is set by the task: the models agree on which concepts receive circuits (Spearman $ρ$ = 0.638 for Python, 0.673 for Rust, both p < $10^{-7}$). Where those circuits sit is set by the model: Qwen processes concepts in a late band (~L17-19), DeepSeek at L6-7, for both languages. How circuits grow across layers is also set by the model: Qwen gives its atomic concepts an early spike that DeepSeek does not. "Are circuits universal?" thus has no single answer: yes for What, no for Where and How -- universality is a property of representational content, not of computational organisation.
  None of this structure was fixed in advance. The agreement could have landed anywhere between independence and identity; it lands at $ρ\approx 0.65$. Rust constructs receive 2-3x more concept-specific circuitry than their Python equivalents, in both models. Both models share neurons between the languages (6/7 and 7/7 paired constructs), DeepSeek 1.94x more than Qwen -- a direction no prior result predicts. And Qwen binds nine keywords of Rust's type-and-trait machinery into one tight neuron cluster (Jaccard 0.535 vs null 0.112, p < 0.001), a semantic dimension invisible in surface syntax. Ablation and linear probes confirm the circuits are functional.
  All claims are scoped to this 2x2; whether the per-model profile predicts a third model is the designed next test.

</details>


### [76] [Artificial Epanorthosis: Why large language models overuse a classical rhetorical figure, and how to mitigate it](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21498)
*Federico Boggia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs systematically overuse epanorthosis (rhetorical self-correction, e.g., "This is not X. It is Y.") due to training data rich in promotional prose and RLHF rewarding emphatic phrasing. The paper proposes an Epanorthosis Index to measure genre-specific calibration, finds mis-calibration (overshoot in oratory, undershoot in informal QA), and demonstrates mitigation via prompting and LoRA-based SFT, arguing the goal is calibration to human rates per genre — not elimination — warning that the real risk is humans adopting machine-like writing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit a distinctive rhetorical tic — epanorthosis — that was catalogued by Cicero and Quintilian. The paper seeks to diagnose why this figure appears systematically, measure the extent of deviation from human baselines across genres and model sizes, and provide practical mitigation strategies, while framing the deeper concern that machine rhetoric may reshape human writing.

Method: The paper (1) traces the root cause to training data (promotional prose prevalence) and RLHF rather than left-to-right generation; (2) builds on Fontanier's classification of epanorthosis as a figure of thought; (3) introduces an Epanorthosis Index measuring density relative to human baselines; (4) measures three model sizes of one instruction-tuned family across genres (oratory, argument, journalism, encyclopedic prose, informal QA); (5) surveys and demonstrates mitigation — a one-line instruction prompt and a supervised fine-tuning LoRA adapter — with scaling coefficients to dial back to human rates.

Result: Mis-calibration is bidirectional: models overshoot humans ~2-fold in oratory (~3-fold in Italian, concentrated in larger models) and undershoot in informal QA, while matching humans in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. A one-line instruction reduces the figure by 50–75%; an SFT LoRA adapter removes it almost entirely. A scaling coefficient can tune reduction precisely to the human rate per genre.

Conclusion: The overuse of epanorthosis is a trained disposition, not an architectural inevitability. The proper target is genre-specific calibration to human rates, not elimination. The ultimate stake is that unchecked, machine rhetorical patterns may influence and degrade human writing style.

Abstract: A rhetorical figure that Cicero and Quintilian catalogued two thousand years ago reappears, systematically, in the text of large language models: epanorthosis, the self-correction of the specimen «This is not a course. It is a journey of transformation». This essay argues that the overuse is a trained disposition, driven mainly by a training distribution rich in promotional prose and by preference tuning (RLHF) that rewards confident, emphatic phrasing; the left-to-right nature of generation is an amplifier rather than the root cause. Building on evidence that models diverge from human rhetorical style, and on Fontanier's classification of epanorthosis as a figure of thought, it sets out a programme that scores the figure against genre-specific human baselines through an Epanorthosis Index (density relative to the human rate). A first measurement, on three sizes of one instruction-tuned model family, finds mis-calibration by register in both directions: the models overshoot in oratory (about twofold, near threefold in Italian, concentrated in the larger tiers) and undershoot in informal question-and-answer writing, while matching humans in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. Three constructive contributions follow: a survey of mitigation techniques centred on lightweight LoRA adapters; a demonstration, in Italian, that a one-line instruction cuts the figure by half to nearly three-quarters and that a supervised-fine-tuning adapter removes it almost entirely, with a scaling coefficient that dials the reduction back onto the human rate; and the argument that the target is calibration to the human rate for each genre, not elimination. It closes on the stakes: the real risk is that we begin to write like the machines.

</details>


### [77] [DONDO: Open w2v-BERT Speech-Recognition Base Models for African Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21540)
*Paul Azunre*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DONDO is a family of open-source ASR base models for 27 African language varieties, built on w2v-BERT 2.0, using religious texts for fine-tuning data, achieving 10–13% WER with multilingual models via learning-rate annealing and lightweight language-conditioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many African languages lack transcribed audio resources for ASR development. The authors leverage religious texts (e.g., the Bible) as a broad, license-clear, orthographically consistent source of read speech to build ASR models for under-resourced languages across six African countries.

Method: Uses the w2v-BERT 2.0 self-supervised speech encoder as the foundation. Employs a two-step (and in one family, three-step) learning-rate-annealed fine-tuning procedure: first adapting a shared multilingual model at a high learning rate, then annealing to recover or surpass monolingual baselines. Introduces a lightweight language-conditioning mechanism that prepends a one-hot language ID as prefix frames to acoustic features, enabling a single multilingual checkpoint to be steered to a target language at inference.

Result: Twenty-one monolingual and five multilingual models covering 27 language varieties. Annealed multilingual models achieve average WER of 10–13%, closing most of the performance gap to monolingual models while consolidating many languages into a single checkpoint. All released under Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face.

Conclusion: Religious text-derived read speech combined with careful fine-tuning strategies (annealing, language-conditioning) enables strong, openly licensed ASR for massively under-resourced African languages. The models serve an estimated 100M+ L1 speakers, with broader reach including L2 speakers, and are freely available for both research and commercial use.

Abstract: We present DONDO, a family of open, permissively licensed automatic speech recognition (ASR) base models for African languages, built on the w2v-BERT 2.0 self-supervised speech encoder. DONDO comprises twenty-one monolingual models and five multilingual models spanning twenty-seven language varieties across Ghana, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, Senegal, Kenya and Zimbabwe. Models are fine-tuned primarily on read speech drawn from religious texts, which offer broad, license-clear and orthographically consistent coverage for languages that otherwise lack transcribed audio. We describe a two-step (and, for one family, three-step) learning-rate-annealed fine-tuning procedure that first adapts a shared multilingual model at a high learning rate and then anneals it to recover, and in several cases surpass, strong monolingual baselines. We further describe a lightweight language-conditioning mechanism that injects a one-hot language identity as a sequence of prefix frames prepended to the acoustic features, allowing a single multilingual checkpoint to be steered to a target language at inference. Across the five multilingual families the annealed models reach average word error rates (WER) of 10-13%, closing most of the gap to monolingual models while covering many languages in a single checkpoint. All models are released on the Hugging Face KhayaAI organisation under the Apache-2.0 license (attribution only) so that others may fine-tune them freely, including for commercial use. We provide a conservative estimate that the languages covered are spoken by on the order of one hundred million first-language speakers, and by substantially more when second-language use is included.

</details>


### [78] [Surprisal Theory is Tautological (without Rational Grounding)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21574)
*Ryan Cotterell*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Surprisal theory is a tautology without constraints on the language model: any difficulty pattern can be fit by some model's surprisal. The implicit assumption that the "true" corpus-generating model matters has been empirically undermined. The author argues a rationalist approach—deriving the model from cognitive principles like memory constraints—is needed to make falsifiable predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To expose a fundamental logical flaw in surprisal theory: that without constraining the language model, the theory is unfalsifiable—any pattern of processing difficulty can be perfectly fit by some language model's surprisal. This tautology has been hidden by an implicit assumption that the relevant model is the one that best fits the training corpus, an assumption recent empirical work has contradicted.

Method: Conceptual/mathematical proof: the author demonstrates that for any non-negative difficulty measure over linguistic units in context, there exists a language model (under mild technical conditions) whose surprisal is an affine function of that measure. This is supplemented by a review of recent empirical findings showing that better corpus-fitting models can predict human difficulty worse, undermining the implicit constraint that obscured the tautology.

Result: Surprisal theory, as commonly formulated, is logically a tautology and makes no falsifiable predictions. The implicit assumption equating the "true" language model with the corpus-generating distribution is empirically unsupported. Breaking the tautology requires a rationalist intervention: the language model must be derived from independently motivated cognitive principles (e.g., memory constraints, processing goals) rather than purely from corpus statistics or the behavioral data the theory aims to explain.

Conclusion: Surprisal theory must be rescued by grounding the language model in a rational (cognitive) model of the comprehender, one derived from processing architecture rather than empirical fit to corpora or behavioral data. Only then can the theory produce falsifiable, explanatory predictions about human language processing difficulty.

Abstract: Surprisal theory holds that the human processing difficulty of a linguistic unit in context is an affine function of its surprisal under some language model. I argue this claim is a tautology without further constraint: for any non-negative difficulty measure over units in context, there exists a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it under mild technical conditions. Therefore, because any pattern of difficulty is consistent with some language model, without an additional constraint on the language model, surprisal theory makes no falsifiable predictions. The tautology was long obscured by an assumption implicit in two decades of psycholinguistic work---that the relevant language model is the distribution that generated the training corpus, so that improving corpus fit improves predictions of human behavior. Recent empirical work has undermined this assumption, demonstrating that better corpus models can be worse predictors of processing difficulty. I conclude that breaking the tautology requires a rationalist intervention, i.e., the relevant language model must be derived from a non-empirically motivated model of the comprehender, which could be based on, for instance, memory constraints or processing goals, and that, thus, does not depend on the behavioral data surprisal theory is meant to explain.

</details>

### [79] [AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20452)
*Vinil Pasupuleti,Shyalendar Reddy Allala,Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu,Shrey Tyagi,Srinivasateja Songa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AINTMA is a six-agent AI system for autonomous test management that achieves 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD), 43% cycle time reduction, and 2.1% defect escape rate across 18 months of evaluation on 12 projects. It combines multi-agent coordination, LLM-based quality narratives, and RL-driven test prioritization with zero-trust cloud security, demonstrating 340% ROI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern software quality assurance requires intelligent, autonomous systems for adaptive decision-making in distributed cloud environments. Traditional test management lacks the autonomy and intelligence to scale effectively, motivating an agentic AI approach that transforms test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem.

Method: AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents — Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor — coordinated through a secure multi-agent framework on cloud-native microservices. The RL agent formulates test selection as a Markov Decision Process using 47 features over a rolling 36-month window. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent uses LLMs for quality narratives and defect summaries. Security is enforced via zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation.

Result: Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous projects over 18 months: 88.4% APFD vs. 51.2% random and 82.1% best commercial baseline; 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback; scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time; generative module rated 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness.

Conclusion: Agentic AI combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence, and secure cloud connectivity can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments, as demonstrated by AINTMA's significant improvements across accuracy, efficiency, and defect reduction metrics.

Abstract: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

</details>


### [80] [Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20462)
*Melanie Rieff,Robin Staab,Thibaud Gloaguen,Stefan Hegselmann,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: First rigorous study evaluating how LLM watermarking schemes affect medical performance across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs, introducing a human-expert-validated auditing pipeline. Results show watermarking induces substantial degradation in medical reasoning, lexical precision, and hallucination rates, which aggregate metrics systematically obscure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in clinical workflows, necessitating traceability via watermarking. However, existing watermark evaluations focus solely on general-purpose benchmarks, neglecting high-stakes domains like medicine where small token-level perturbations can cause clinically significant semantic changes. There is a critical gap in understanding whether watermarks degrade medical reasoning quality.

Method: Benchmarked 5 watermarking schemes (KGW, Aaronson, Christ, Unigram, and their variants) across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning tasks. Introduced a human-expert-validated auditing pipeline that systematically evaluates medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and watermark-induced hallucinations — complementing standard aggregate metrics that can mask domain-specific failures.

Result: Watermarking induces substantial degradation across multiple failure modes: lexical corruption, hallucinated medical terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings in multimodal settings. Aggregate metrics systematically obscure these clinically consequential failures, and the absence of domain-specific analyses causes watermark-induced degradations to go undetected by standard evaluation protocols.

Conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a prerequisite for safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine. Current general-purpose benchmarks mask clinically consequential failures, and rigorous medical-domain auditing must accompany any watermarking scheme before clinical integration.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

</details>


### [81] [ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20463)
*Wojciech Michaluk,Tymoteusz Urban,Mateusz Kubita,Soveatin Kuntur,Anna Wróblewska*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A browser extension using a hybrid XGBoost model (combining transformer embeddings with linguistic features and a custom "baitness" score) detects clickbait with 91% F1-score, warns users pre/post-click, explains predictions, and provides a short article spoiler.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional clickbait detection methods are insufficient; users need proactive, explainable tools that warn them before and after accessing misleading articles, not just classify content in isolation.

Method: A hybrid machine learning pipeline: XGBoost classifier trained on features combining transformer-based (LLM) embeddings, linguistically motivated handcrafted features, and a novel "baitness" score. The model is deployed as a browser extension that triggers warnings pre- and post-click, displays a clickbait likelihood percentage, provides interpretable explanations via analyzed metrics, and generates a one-to-two-sentence article spoiler summary.

Result: The XGBoost model achieved an F1-score of 91% on an open combined dataset, outperforming baselines including classic vectorizers and raw LLM embeddings alone.

Conclusion: The hybrid approach effectively balances detection accuracy with user-facing explainability. Integrating the model into a browser extension with pre/post warnings, percentage scores, metric-based explanations, and spoiler summaries provides a practical, transparent tool for combating clickbait in real-time browsing.

Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

</details>


### [82] [Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20464)
*Izhar Ali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-consistency (repeated sampling from one model) provides good per-question uncertainty estimates but reveals no cross-question structure, whereas a diverse ensemble of LLMs surfaces systematic correlations across questions, exposing what the model doesn't know.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether the variation observed when a single LLM is run repeatedly at high temperature carries the same cross-question correlational structure as the variation across a diverse ensemble of different LLMs, and thus whether self-consistency can reveal what a model systematically does not know beyond per-question uncertainty.

Method: The authors compare two regimes on identical question sets: (1) one model run 100 times at τ=1, and (2) an ensemble of 24 LLMs run once each at τ=0. They apply a Marchenko-Pastur random-matrix test to separate signal eigenvalues from sampling noise in the covariance structure of correctness across questions. A matched-difficulty Bernoulli null model is used to assess statistical significance via Monte Carlo draws.

Result: Within any single model, at most one eigenvalue rises above the noise threshold across five model families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while the Bernoulli null produces at most one in 500 Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency yields accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure.

Conclusion: Self-consistency captures per-question aleatoric uncertainty but fails to reveal shared failure modes across related questions. Only a truly diverse ensemble of models can surface the latent structure of what a model does not know, suggesting that single-model repeated sampling is insufficient for understanding systematic knowledge gaps.

Abstract: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

</details>


### [83] [Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20495)
*Anas Mohamed,Kaizan Haque,Azal Ahmad Khan,Chetan Sharma,Shuwen Ge,Ali Anwar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a workload-aware cache eviction policy for multi-agent systems that uses recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency to prioritize cached intermediate results, achieving up to 64.7% latency reduction over uncached baselines and 31.1% improvement over the next-best finite-capacity cache.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cache eviction policies (e.g., LRU, LFU) treat all cached entries uniformly based solely on access history. In multi-agent systems, executions are structured as DAGs of specialized agent calls, creating unique structural and workload signals — such as how expensive an agent is to re-execute, how many downstream agents depend on a cached result, and how frequently an agent type is invoked — that traditional policies ignore. A caching strategy that exploits these domain-specific signals can significantly improve latency without requiring unbounded cache capacity.

Method: The authors design a unified scoring function for cache eviction that integrates three signals: (1) recomputation cost — the computational expense of re-executing an agent; (2) DAG dependency count — the number of downstream agents that rely on a cached intermediate result; and (3) agent invocation frequency — how often a particular agent type is called across queries. When the cache reaches capacity, entries with the lowest combined score are evicted. The method is evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks with varying reuse patterns.

Result: The workload-aware policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% compared to an uncached baseline. On average, it achieves a 31.1% latency reduction over the next-best finite-capacity baseline. It also approaches the performance of an unbounded cache while maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. Additionally, workload-aware caching is shown to be complementary to other optimizations such as plan-level caching and parallel agent execution.

Conclusion: Workload-aware content caching that leverages multi-agent–specific structural and workload signals significantly outperforms generic eviction policies. It is an effective, complementary optimization that targets a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines, working synergistically with plan-level caching and parallel execution.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

</details>


### [84] [JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20466)
*Arya Tschand,Charles Hong,Julian Walker,Nina Cai,Shangkun Wang,Suvinay Subramanian,Sundar Dev,Vijay Janapa Reddi,Amir Yazdanbakhsh,Sethu Sankaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JAXBench is a benchmark suite of 50 JAX workloads for evaluating AI-driven TPU kernel optimization. It includes 17 production ML operators (from Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, etc.) and 33 translated KernelBench operators. Experiments show that curated TPU documentation dramatically improves LLM-generated kernel correctness (5.8%→37.3%), and beam-search pipelines achieve up to 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA, with 1.60x on hand-tuned kernels against a 2.08x expert upper bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While GPU kernel optimization has benefited from rigorous benchmarks (e.g., KernelBench), no equivalent benchmark suite exists for TPUs. This gap hinders systematic progress in AI-generated TPU kernel optimization, particularly as TPU usage grows for large-scale ML workloads.

Method: The authors construct JAXBench with 50 JAX workloads: 17 extracted from production MaxText architectures (Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, AlphaFold2) and 33 adapted from KernelBench, validated for correctness and resized for high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight production operators include hand-optimized Pallas kernels from Tokamax as expert baselines. Four feedback-driven code generation methods are evaluated (including Gemini 3 Flash with documentation conditioning and Autocomp's beam-search), measuring correctness and speedup over XLA.

Result: On Gemini 3 Flash: TPU-specific documentation conditioning raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3%, solving 48/50 benchmarks at 1.28x geomean speedup. Autocomp's beam-search achieves 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA overall. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamak upper bound but trailing on specialized paged and ragged attention operators.

Conclusion: Target-specific context (curated TPU docs) matters more than model scale for sparse-domain DSLs like Pallas. Search structure (beam-search) yields significant gains once baseline correctness is achieved. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging, especially on specialized attention operators. JAXBench is released publicly to spur open-source contributions.

Abstract: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

</details>


### [85] [MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20501)
*Jason Yoo,Rajarshi Saha,Shaowei Zhu,Tao Yu,Wei Tang,Youngsuk Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MKEvolve is a framework that iteratively co-evolves modular decompositions of PyTorch modules alongside LLM-generated kernels, splitting and fusing submodules while refining each subkernel via beam search. It produces configurable, interpretable, and adaptable kernel compositions that outperform end-to-end synthesis baselines on KernelBench L2/L3 in both correctness and speedup, with 35% lower LLM token usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Writing correct, high-performance kernels for hardware accelerators remains a critical bottleneck in scaling ML workloads. End-to-end LLM-based kernel generation struggles with complex multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, motivating a modular, iterative approach that decomposes the problem and independently optimizes subcomponents.

Method: MKEvolve iteratively co-evolves two things: (1) a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules (via splitting and fusing across iterations) and (2) LLM-generated Triton kernels for each submodule. Each subkernel is independently refined using LLM-driven beam search. The final kernel is a programmatic composition of independently verified, swappable subkernels, conferring configurability and interpretability.

Result: On KernelBench L2 (multi-operator sequences) and L3 (full model architectures), MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

Conclusion: Modular, iterative co-evolution of module decomposition and kernel generation is an effective strategy for producing high-quality accelerator kernels, outperforming monolithic generation approaches in correctness, performance, and efficiency.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

</details>


### [86] [DC-Leap: Training-Free Acceleration of dLLMs via Draft-Guided Contiguous Leaping Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20467)
*Yanhua Jiao,Tianyi Wu,Xiaoxi Sun,Yulin Li,HuiLing Zhen,Libo Qin,Baotian Hu,Zhuotao Tian,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DC-Leap is a training-free framework that accelerates Diffusion LLMs by introducing Dynamic Contiguous Verification to overcome the Joint Probability Dependence Error, enabling reliable parallel decoding in moderate-confidence regimes with speedups up to 105x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current parallel decoding in dLLMs relies on conservative confidence thresholds due to the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), causing redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. There is a need for reliable acceleration without sacrificing generation quality.

Method: DC-Leap proposes two key components: (1) Dynamic Contiguous Verification — integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into parallel decoding to progressively validate token dependencies, neutralizing the JPDE; (2) Draft-guided decoding — uses a draft to leap forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context while retaining bidirectional attention benefits during inference.

Result: DC-Leap achieves up to 53.19x speedup on MBPP for long-sequence generation and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache, while maintaining comparable generation quality on standard benchmarks.

Conclusion: DC-Leap demonstrates that training-free, verification-based strategies can unlock substantial inference speedups for dLLMs in moderate-confidence regimes, effectively addressing the JPDE bottleneck without compromising output quality.

Abstract: While parallel decoding is central to the efficiency of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs), current strategies are often hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds. These thresholds, necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), result in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. To overcome this, we propose DC-Leap, a training-free framework that enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in the moderate-confidence regime. DC-Leap introduces a Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process. By progressively validating token dependencies, this mechanism effectively neutralizes the JPDE, enabling reliable acceleration with comparable performance. Furthermore, DC-Leap incorporates the draft-guided decoding mechanism, where the draft helps extend the context by leaping forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context and retaining the structural benefits of bidirectional attention during inference. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DC-Leap achieves substantial speedups, up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache with comparable generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/ffh-wyls/DC-Leap .

</details>


### [87] [ExecuGraph: A Multi-Agent, Execution-Grounded Framework for Reliable Backend Code Synthesis with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20499)
*Sai Deekshith Lekkala,Jothi Prabha Appadurai,Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu,Manpreet Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ExecuGraph is a multi-agent framework for backend code synthesis that centers execution-based validation, using six specialized agents coordinated via a typed directed workflow. Evaluated on DSA, HumanEval, and APPS benchmarks, the framework enables controlled ablation to measure each component's contribution, with multi-agent decomposition showing the strongest gains (+22.5 pp) when paired with a more capable base model (DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-pass LLM code generation lacks correctness and runtime reliability guarantees. The authors aim to replace the single-pass paradigm with an execution-validated, multi-agent workflow and to provide a rigorous, ablation-controlled methodology for measuring each architectural component's marginal contribution.

Method: Six specialized agents — Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer — are orchestrated via a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, built on LangGraph with locally hosted Ollama models and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. The single codebase collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry (Reflexion-style ablation), and full multi-agent conditions, plus per-agent ablations.

Result: On internal-30 (n=30), all three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO; p=0.08 SR vs. SO; 95% bootstrap CIs for pairwise mean differences include zero). On HumanEval (n=64), multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite graph-category accuracy jumps from 57.5% (one-shot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp gain, supporting the hypothesis that multi-agent value scales with base-model capability.

Conclusion: The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a configurable single codebase enabling controlled measurement of each lever. The cross-model scaling result suggests multi-agent decomposition's benefits are contingent on underlying model strength. Statistical insignificance on smaller samples (internal-30) warrants caution and larger-scale replication.

Abstract: Large Language Models generate plausible backend code, but a single-pass paradigm provides no guarantee of correctness or runtime reliability. We present ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework that places execution-based validation at the center of backend code synthesis. Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer) are coordinated by a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. We evaluate on a curated 30-problem DSA suite (internal-30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, contrasting ExecuGraph against a single-agent one-shot baseline and a single-agent execution-retry baseline (a Reflexion-style ablation that isolates the contribution of multi-agent decomposition). On internal-30, the three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (n=30; paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO, p=0.08 SR vs. SO); 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all pairwise mean differences include zero. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy improves from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump that supports a scaling hypothesis: the value of multi-agent decomposition grows with base-model capability. The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation conditions, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. A per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

</details>


### [88] [AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20536)
*Junzhi Chen,Harsh Trivedi,Jane Pan,Michael JQ Zhang,Tejas Srinivasan,Niranjan Balasubramanian,Ashish Sabharwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AppWorld-UL introduces a benchmark of 516 tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions across 9 simulated apps. By systematically introducing ambiguities and constraints into original AppWorld tasks, it tests agents' ability to ask clarifications, seek confirmations, and report infeasibility. Claude Opus 4.7 achieves only 48.6% overall success, dropping to 21.3% on compositional scenario-level tasks, highlighting the challenge of user-in-the-loop interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks for agent-user interaction lack diversity in interaction types and operate in limited environments with few, non-state-changing APIs. They fail to capture the full range of real-world interactions needed for day-to-day digital tasks, such as asking clarification questions, prompting for confirmation, or informing users of infeasible instructions.

Method: The authors build AppWorld-UL on the AppWorld framework with 9 simulated apps (Amazon, Spotify, etc.). They systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints requiring various agent-user interactions. User behavior is simulated by an LLM with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, providing more reliable simulation than unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives from prior work. The benchmark includes 516 tasks with a harder compositional subset and stricter scenario-level metrics.

Result: Claude Opus 4.7 achieves 48.6% success on the full AppWorld-UL benchmark and only 35.7% on the compositional subset. Under stricter scenario-level evaluation, compositional task performance drops to 21.3%. Analysis confirms that correct user interaction is a critical determinant of task success.

Conclusion: AppWorld-UL demonstrates significant difficulty for state-of-the-art agents and exposes user interaction as a key bottleneck. The benchmark offers a robust platform for advancing research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

Abstract: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a ``user-in-the-loop'' benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

</details>


### [89] [InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468)
*Jehyeok Yeon,Ben Rank,Maksym Andriushchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InferenceBench evaluates AI agents on optimizing LLM inference speed under a 2-hour time budget with one GPU. Agents improve over naive baselines but underperform simple hyperparameter search, largely due to insufficient exploration of diverse configurations rather than lack of domain knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks constrain agents to narrow action spaces or prescribed workflows, and even open-ended tasks can be solved via recipe retrieval and hyperparameter tuning. It is unclear whether strong performance reflects genuine optimization ability or memorization. InferenceBench aims to test agents in a truly open-ended AI engineering setting where memorized solutions yield limited gains.

Method: InferenceBench provides each agent with a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a 2-hour wall-clock budget. Agents must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and maximize inference speed. Four scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks: prefill latency, decode latency, concurrent request throughput, and a balanced scenario combining all three. 15 frontier agent configurations are evaluated, with qualitative trajectory analysis performed.

Result: Agents reliably outperform a naive PyTorch baseline (up to 8.08×) and often match or exceed default serving engines like vLLM (4.05×), but fall short of a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to 11.53×). Agents enumerate many relevant techniques but converge on a single inference framework, test few distinct configurations, and spend remaining time on re-measuring, repairing, or fine-tuning hyperparameters rather than exploring diverse strategies.

Conclusion: The primary bottleneck in open-ended AI engineering tasks is not domain knowledge but the ability to propose, systematically evaluate, and select among diverse configurations. InferenceBench provides a benchmark that exposes this limitation and encourages development of agents with better exploration and evaluation strategies.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

</details>


### [90] [StrideDiffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Time-series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20545)
*Du Yin,Estrid He,Julián Jerónimo Bañuelos,Yang Yang,Feng Hu,Yuchen Luo,Hao Xue,Stephan Sigg,Flora Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StrideDiffusion is a training-free, spectral-aware sampler that accelerates diffusion models for time series by adaptively adjusting denoising stride based on per-band spectral activity, achieving up to 18.9× speedup while maintaining or improving generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models for time series suffer from slow inference due to many sequential denoising steps. Existing fast samplers use fixed/generic timestep schedules and ignore a key property: different frequency bands evolve at different rates during the reverse diffusion process.

Method: StrideDiffusion monitors three spectral indicators at each denoising step — relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity — to classify bands as active (high-frequency dynamics present) or inactive (dominated by stable low-frequency structure). It takes fine-grained steps when active bands remain and larger jumps once only coarse components persist. A bandwise stability analysis justifies this, showing inactive bands change only linearly with jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates.

Result: Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses 14–66 function evaluations (vs. 500/1000 baseline), yielding up to 18.9× wall-clock speedup while matching or improving generation quality. For conditional imputation and forecasting, it delivers 5–14× average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy.

Conclusion: Spectral evolution provides a principled, practical signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling, enabling significant acceleration without retraining or quality degradation.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become competitive generators for time series, but their practical use is limited by the large number of sequential denoising steps required at inference time. Existing fast samplers typically use fixed or generic timestep schedules, overlooking a distinctive property of time-series diffusion: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. We introduce StrideDiffusion, a training-free spectral-aware sampler that adaptively selects the denoising stride from band-level activity. At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to identify whether high- frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. It then takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps once only coarse components remain. A bandwise stability analysis shows that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing a local justification for spectral activity as a step-size indicator. Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 denoising steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it further delivers 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy. These results show that spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stridediff-ts.

</details>


### [91] [DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20469)
*Zishan Shao,Lixun Zhang,Kangning Cui,Yixiao Wang,Ting Jiang,Hancheng Ye,Qinsi Wang,Zhixu Du,Yuzhe Fu,Fan Yang,Danyang Zhuo,Yiran Chen,Hai Helen Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DecodeShare identifies a low-dimensional, task-general subspace in LLM hidden states during KV-cached decoding and demonstrates its causal importance: perturbing this subspace severely degrades performance, and steering vectors that overlap with it have distinct functional roles separable via projection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs handle many tasks with a single parameter set, it is unclear whether any task-general structure exists specifically during the decode phase (as opposed to prefill) under KV-cached inference. Understanding this could improve activation steering and mechanistic interpretability.

Method: The authors propose DecodeShare, a protocol that first identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states. They then causally test its role by ablating only that subspace during decoding, comparing the degradation against prefill-derived and random subspaces under the same intervention budget. They further apply this to activation steering by projecting out the shared subspace from steering directions and evaluating decode-time vs. prefill-based steering vectors.

Result: Disturbing the decode-shared subspace degrades decision performance significantly more than disturbing prefill-derived or random subspaces. Projecting out the shared subspace cleanly separates functional roles of steering components. Decode-time steering vectors yield more reliable downstream signals than prefill-based proxies.

Conclusion: A compact, task-general causal channel exists at decode time in LLMs. This shared subspace serves as a high-leverage target for both interpretability and practical activation steering, with decode-time evaluation being more reliable than prefill-based alternatives.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel.
