Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

</details>


### [92] [HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21019)
*Wei Liu,Siya Qi,Linhai Zhang,Lorainne Tudor Car,Yulan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HiMe is a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform for real-time personal health data analysis from wearables, using LLM agents to provide adaptive, personalised health insights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional wearable health analytics (e.g., smartwatches) rely on rigid, non-personalised frameworks. While LLM agents enable adaptive, contextual health analysis, no open-source, locally deployable platform exists that processes personal health data in real time while preserving privacy.

Method: HiMe is built on three design principles: (1) treating the database as a first-class component, (2) jointly optimising effectiveness and efficiency for a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance, and (3) processing data in real time while maintaining long-term user modelling. The platform integrates with diverse wearable device ecosystems.

Result: The abstract does not report quantitative experimental results; it presents the HiMe platform as a practical, deployable solution for continuous personalised health monitoring using Personal Health Agents.

Conclusion: HiMe makes it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring, promoting better wellbeing through privacy-preserving, real-time, locally deployed LLM-driven analysis.

Abstract: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

</details>


### [93] [PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20470)
*Jiacheng Wang,Weiyan Zhang,Guangya Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PlanE is a framework for constructing extractive-based LLMs that addresses high annotation costs and lack of task-specific optimization through data decomposition, instruction tuning, prompt inference, and a DTI planner that selects optimal base-LLM and data-tuning-inference combinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building task-specific LLMs requires large instruction-tuning datasets, which incurs substantial annotation costs. Furthermore, there is a lack of systematic optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. PlanE aims to address both challenges.

Method: PlanE consists of three components: (1) data decomposition, (2) instruction tuning, and (3) prompt inference. It also includes a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner that selects the optimal base-LLM and its corresponding DTI combinations for a given dataset to maximize construction efficiency.

Result: Experiments demonstrate PlanE's effectiveness across two views: (1) consistent improvement across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) consistent improvement on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. The DTI planner also shows generalizability under varying optimization objectives.

Conclusion: PlanE effectively enhances task-specific LLM construction by reducing reliance on large-scale annotation and optimizing the selection of base-LLMs and DTI strategies. The framework is validated across multiple settings and objectives, with code publicly released.

Abstract: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

</details>


### [94] [SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21156)
*Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti,David Gamez,Franco Such,Nik Kairinos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel assistance system for elderly users suffering from frailty or dementia. It uses a novel travel graph representation that combines route planning with predictive modeling, leveraging LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine to generate personalized failure scenarios, propose interventions, and estimate their impact on journey outcomes. Evaluated through experiments and a 26-journey field study, SafeStep improved user confidence and perceived safety, though interface usability requires refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over one million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, conditions that severely compromise their ability to navigate urban environments independently. Existing travel assistance systems lack personalized, predictive capabilities to anticipate and mitigate journey failures for this vulnerable demographic.

Method: The authors propose a novel travel graph representation integrating route planning with predictive modeling. For each journey stage, SafeStep: (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using LLMs combined with the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine; (ii) proposes targeted interventions; and (iii) estimates intervention impact on outcome probabilities. Interventions are selected to maximize the likelihood of successful destination arrival. Evaluation involved travel graph generation experiments and a field study with 26 real-world journeys.

Result: Combining Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yielded the most reliable performance. The field study demonstrated that SafeStep improves user confidence and perceived safety during travel. However, interface usability was identified as needing improvement for the target elderly demographic.

Conclusion: SafeStep demonstrates a viable AI-driven approach to supporting elderly mobility. Future work includes improving and publicly releasing the system. The underlying AI framework is generalizable to other domains such as mental health, career coaching, and addiction treatment.

Abstract: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

</details>


### [95] [Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20471)
*Ashutosh Srivastava,Siddharth Yedlapati,Vinay Aggarwal,Yaman Kumar Singla,Shashwat Dixit,Jitendra Ajmera,Balaji Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SDR-Bench introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based personalization as a two-party persuasion problem, using 6,279 real sales stories. Frontier LLMs show a "personalization plateau" where no model statistically distinguishes successful from unsuccessful outreach, validated by a field deployment with 12 sales representatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM personalization benchmarks only measure sender-side adaptation (same user as model serves). The classical two-party personalization problem — whether a generated message induces intended action in a third-party receiver — lacks reproducible, at-scale evaluation beyond one-off A/B tests and small human studies.

Method: The authors adapt Kamenica & Gentzkow's Bayesian Persuasion framework to generative agents, instantiating it in sales where receiver actions are logged against outreach. They release SDR-Bench (6,279 customer success stories across 22 industries, ~200 enterprises) with temporal constraints preventing data leakage, and evaluate frontier LLMs and deep-research agents. A field deployment with 12 professional SDRs validates the framework.

Result: All tested frontier LLMs exhibit a consistent personalization plateau; on a Fortune 100 tech cohort, no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. In field validation, 48% of model-generated content was rated immediately useful, with senior-expert agreement at Pearson r=0.82.

Conclusion: Current LLMs cannot reliably personalize outreach to induce specific receiver actions beyond a plateau. The authors release SDR-Bench and SDR-Arena publicly to enable reproducible, scalable study of generative personalization as a two-party persuasion task.

Abstract: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

</details>


### [96] [Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20472)
*Roman Belaire,Arunesh Sinha,Pradeep Varakantham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DCGS is a multi-turn dialogue safety framework that infers user intent from conversational history using value and regret-based critics, modeled as an MDP. It reweights response candidates at inference time, with theoretical guarantees of improved expected return, and outperforms baselines on adversarial benchmarks while transferring to frontier models without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation is the ambiguity challenge in LLM safety: distinguishing genuine harmful attacks from well-meaning but poorly phrased questions. This ambiguity is exacerbated in multi-turn dialogue, where attacker intent may emerge gradually. Existing safety frameworks treat each turn independently (contextual bandit), ignoring conversational trajectory, which leads to either over-censorship harming legitimate users or under-protection enabling exploitation.

Method: DCGS models adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). It learns two critics: a value critic and a regret critic operating at both token-level and utterance-level. At inference time, candidate responses are scored via an action-value critic, and the framework reweights the base policy's distribution through exponential tilting. This reweighting approximates optimal policy improvement with theoretical guarantees — for any finite candidate pool, expected return is guaranteed to improve, a property that group-relative objectives lack. No fine-tuning is required.

Result: Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. It also demonstrates transferability: applying DCGS to frontier models improves their robustness without any fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Inferring user intent from full conversational history, rather than applying fixed safety rules per-turn, is an effective strategy for LLM safety in multi-turn adversarial dialogue. DCGS provides a theoretically grounded, inference-time solution that is both more robust and more transferable than existing approaches.

Abstract: When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [97] [Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20972)
*Swapnanil Saha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Coding agents rely on explicit, voluntary document memory, but human expertise depends on a second tier of involuntary, situationally-cued operational knowledge. This paper argues that the involuntary tier is critical for long-running agents and must be a harness-level property. The authors propose a cue-anchored memory model with deterministic trigger-based delivery, demonstrate that agents almost never use voluntary memory even when available, and show that harness-injected memories survive repeated compaction while conversation-held facts vanish — establishing that reliable memory delivery, not storage, is the essential product.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current coding agents employ only one kind of memory: deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved documents. However, human expertise relies heavily on a second tier of incidental, situationally-cued operational knowledge (gotchas, conventions, local facts) that is never explicitly written down and is retrieved involuntarily. For long-running agents, this involuntary tier is the load-bearing one, yet current systems leave memory entirely as an agent choice rather than a harness responsibility.

Method: The authors: (1) develop a two-tier design theory grounded in cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory; (2) propose a cue-anchored memory model with first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness; (3) conduct controlled experiments on real coding tasks measuring voluntary memory usage, deterministic injection accuracy, and intra-session re-read behavior; and (4) perform a repeated-compaction decay probe comparing conversation-held facts versus harness-injected facts across 138 compact-resume cycles.

Result: Voluntary memory use was near zero (0 memory operations in 114 turns) even with a pre-seeded store. Deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms. 39% of intra-session re-reads re-purchased content paid for before a compaction boundary. Ten facts held only in conversation vanished at the first summary and stayed absent from 106 of 108 compactions; the deprived agent resorted to grepping the harness's own session files. In contrast, the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrived intact through all 138 compact-resumes, with the final summary carrying none of them.

Conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is the product. The reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about. Memory must be a harness-level property with deterministic, cue-triggered injection rather than a voluntary agent choice, especially for long-running agents subject to repeated context compaction.

Abstract: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

</details>


### [98] [Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21495)
*Natan Levy,Harel Berger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Democratized AI agent creation via low-code tools introduces a reliability gap from hidden dependencies; this paper proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework with dependency mapping, readiness contracts, and lifecycle governance to detect silent degradation in citizen-created agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of low-code/no-code tools enables non-engineers to create AI agents, but these agents depend on volatile external components (models, APIs, permissions, prompts, data sources) that can silently fail or degrade post-deployment without any user modification, creating a "reliability gap" unique to democratized development.

Method: The paper proposes a continuous-assurance framework comprising five components: (1) dependency mapping to identify all external dependencies, (2) readiness contracts specifying expected operational conditions, (3) scheduled automated checks to verify contract compliance, (4) diagnostics for root-cause identification, and (5) lifecycle governance policies. A prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment validate the taxonomy's translatability into practical checks.

Result: The scenario-based assessment demonstrates that the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical automated checks and actionable remediation guidance, confirming the feasibility of lightweight continuous assurance for citizen-created agents without requiring deep engineering expertise.

Conclusion: Democratized AI agent creation demands a new reliability paradigm; lightweight continuous-assurance frameworks can bridge the gap between ease of creation and long-term operational trustworthiness, enabling safe scaling of citizen development within organizations.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly created inside organizations by non-engineering users through low-code, no-code, and conversational development environments. This democratization enables rapid local innovation, but it also creates a reliability gap: agents that appear to users as simple productivity artifacts may depend on changing models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, and external services. These dependencies can cause silent degradation long after deployment, even when no user directly modifies the agent. This paper identifies the reliability challenge created by democratized AI agent creation and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational agents. The framework combines dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess whether an agent remains operationally ready under expected conditions. We also present an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment showing how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

</details>


### [99] [Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20473)
*Yeonjea Kim,Bumjin Park,Jaesik Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-weight LLMs with safeguards remain vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts that elicit harmful completions. This paper formalizes the phenomenon as Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks (IPJ), characterizes when/how it occurs, shows that parameter tuning for refusal fails to generalize, and identifies two functional neuron types (termination/continuation) that could enable neuron-level defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite safeguards in open-weight LLMs, incomplete harmful prompts can still elicit harmful completions by exploiting sentence completion behavior. This vulnerability is not well understood, and existing mitigation strategies may be insufficient, motivating a systematic characterization and exploration of more robust defenses.

Method: The authors formalize IPJ and conduct systematic empirical analysis of diverse attractor types (e.g., sentence completion patterns) to characterize when incomplete prompts yield harmful continuations. They evaluate parameter-tuning-based refusal training and test its generalization across content domains and attractor types. Additionally, they identify two functional neuron types — termination neurons and continuation neurons — via mechanistic analysis, clarifying their roles in sentence completion dynamics.

Result: LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination, making incomplete prompts effective for jailbreaking. Training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning fails to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. Two functional neuron types — termination and continuation neurons — are identified, with distinct roles in mediating sentence completion behavior.

Conclusion: Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks represent a systematic vulnerability in safeguarded LLMs. Parameter-tuning-based refusal is insufficient as a defense due to poor generalization. Neuron-level interventions targeting termination and continuation neurons offer a promising direction for more precise, robust IPJ defenses.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

</details>


### [100] [The Boundaries of Automation: A Theory of Persistent Human Participation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21547)
*Fares Fourati,Hinrich Schütze,Eyke Hüllermeier,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper challenges the assumption that human-in-the-loop systems exist only due to insufficient AI capability. The authors argue that human participation persists for three reasons: (1) technical/complementarity (humans contribute unique capabilities), (2) normative/developmental (participation is valuable for agency and learning), and (3) emergence (in some activities, the target or goal emerges through interaction itself, making human participation constitutive rather than merely instrumental). Human-AI co-construction is thus not a temporary fix but a permanent feature of certain activities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To interrogate the prevailing automation-centric assumption that human participation in AI systems is merely a stopgap until AI becomes sufficiently capable. The paper seeks to identify the conceptual limits of automation and establish theoretically grounded reasons why human involvement may be irreducibly necessary in certain contexts.

Method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis. The paper develops a three-part taxonomy of grounds for persistent human participation (technical/complementarity, normative/developmental, emergence) through argumentation rather than empirical experimentation. The key theoretical contribution is the concept of "target emergence," where the objective of an activity is not pre-specified but co-constituted through the interaction process itself.

Result: The analysis yields a tripartite framework: (1) Technical/complementarity grounds — humans provide capabilities or perspectives AI lacks; (2) Normative/developmental grounds — participation itself holds intrinsic value for human agency, dignity, or learning; (3) Emergence grounds — in activities characterized by target emergence, the goal is not defined ex ante but arises through interaction, rendering human participation constitutive of the outcome. Human-AI co-construction is thus framed as a persistent structural feature rather than a transitional arrangement.

Conclusion: Automation has conceptual limits beyond mere technical insufficiency. Human-AI co-construction should be recognized as an enduring paradigm for activities where objectives emerge through participation. This reframing carries significant implications for the design, evaluation criteria, and ethical governance of future AI systems, shifting focus from full automation toward meaningful collaborative architectures.

Abstract: The rapid progress of AI has intensified the long-standing pursuit of automation: replacing human participation with algorithms wherever possible. Implicit in this pursuit is the assumption that humans remain in the loop only because current AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. This paper challenges that assumption. Rather than asking how far automation can extend, we ask where its conceptual limits lie and argue that human participation may persist even with highly capable AI systems for three distinct reasons. Technical or complementarity grounds arise when humans contribute capabilities or perspectives unavailable to AI. Normative or developmental grounds arise when participation itself is valuable for human agency or learning. Most importantly, emergence grounds arise from target emergence: in some activities, the target is not fully specified in advance but instead emerges through the interaction itself. In these cases, human participation is not merely a means of improving execution but is constitutive of the target being produced. Human--AI co-construction, understood as the joint production of outcomes by humans and AI systems, is therefore not simply a temporary response to imperfect AI, but a persistent feature of activities whose objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems.

</details>


### [101] [Representation Robustness Under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20520)
*Sagnik Nath,Edith Aurora Graf,Liang Zhang,Diego Zapata-Rivera*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit significant representational brittleness in mathematical problem solving—changing answers when the same problem is reformulated as story problems, word-equations, or symbolic equations. Code-augmented reasoning reveals latent capabilities but shifts failures rather than eliminating them. Representation should be treated as a first-class design variable in LLM evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work conflates reasoning errors with interface failures and treats representationally equivalent problem formulations as interchangeable. This paper aims to systematically investigate whether LLMs are robust to surface-level representational variations of mathematically identical problems, challenging the assumption that equivalent formulations yield equivalent performance.

Method: The authors curate a dataset of mathematically equivalent problems varied across four representation types: story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Five contemporary LLMs are evaluated under two conditions: (1) direct answer generation and (2) code-augmented reasoning, where models externalize reasoning as executable Python code validated locally. Metrics include correctness flip rates, performance regressions under paraphrasing, and failure-mode taxonomization across interaction layers.

Result: Under direct prompting, all models show substantial representational sensitivity with nontrivial flip rates across formats. Even subtle isomorphic paraphrases cause systematic performance regressions. In the code-augmented condition, some models demonstrate strong latent reasoning, but robustness does not uniformly improve—failures shift from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Representation sensitivity often persists even when executable reasoning succeeds.

Conclusion: Reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness; they expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. Representation must be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, particularly for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on mathematical problem solving, yet prior work often treats representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflates reasoning errors with interface failures. This paper investigates representation robustness in LLM-based mathematical problem solving by systematically varying surface representations of the same underlying problems, including story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Using a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems, we evaluate five contemporary LLMs under a direct answer generation condition. We find substantial representational sensitivity: models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations, with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. We also observe systematic regressions under isomorphic reformulations, showing that even subtle paraphrase-level changes can degrade performance despite preserved mathematical structure. We then evaluate a code-augmented condition in which models externalize reasoning as executable Python code that is run locally for validation. This interface reveals strong latent reasoning capability in some models that perform poorly under direct prompting, but it does not uniformly improve robustness. Instead, failures shift across interaction layers, from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Even when executable reasoning succeeds, representation sensitivity often persists. Overall, our results show that reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness, but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. We argue that representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, especially for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

</details>


### [102] [VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20474)
*Sumaya Abdul Rahman,Seckhen Ariel Andrade Cuellar,Ghani Raissov,Mohammad Raza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSimpl introduces a simplification-based verification framework that uses an optimization solver to generate simplified diagnostic queries, enabling LLMs to tractably verify the correctness of inferred optimization formulations against natural language task descriptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based approaches for translating natural language into optimization formulations can produce formulations that execute without errors but fail to correctly implement the intended task. There is a need for robust verification mechanisms that can reason about semantic correctness, not just syntactic validity.

Method: VeriSimpl employs simplification-based verification: the optimization solver generates simplified diagnostic queries (e.g., fixing subsets of variables or relaxing constraints) about a candidate formulation. These simplifications allow the LLM to reason locally about correctness under fixed global contexts. Strategies operate along dimensions of problem constraints and decision variables, decomposing the verification task into tractable sub-problems.

Result: Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, along with a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

Conclusion: Simplification-based verification is an effective paradigm for improving the robustness of LLM-driven optimization formalization, enabling more reliable natural-language-to-solver translation pipelines.

Abstract: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

</details>


### [103] [Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21412)
*Bartolomeo Bogliolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Euclid-MCP is an open-source MCP server that provides LLM agents with deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog, using an engine-agnostic intermediate representation (Euclid-IR) and a translate-run-inspect-repair loop; it outperforms LLMs alone on larger knowledge bases by eliminating hallucination in rule-based inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning in safety-critical domains. Existing neuro-symbolic integrations lack a standardized, tool-agnostic interface, making it hard for LLM agents to delegate inference to symbolic engines while retaining interpretability and auditability.

Method: The authors introduce Euclid-MCP, an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server wrapping SWI-Prolog. It features Euclid-IR, a human-readable intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that LLMs can easily generate and that compiles to Prolog or other backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface supporting a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, giving LLM clients access to proof traces and derivation logs.

Result: Evaluated on an IT security and compliance use case, LLMs alone handled small knowledge bases adequately but hallucinated systematically on larger problems. Euclid-MCP delivered exact, correct answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. The authors further argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement.

Conclusion: Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems, providing a standardized neuro-symbolic interface that ensures deterministic, auditable logical inference where LLMs alone fail.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

</details>


### [104] [Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21503)
*Gaurav Dadhich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Production AI agents fail not primarily due to reasoning deficits but because they cannot manage their growing reasoning context. The paper argues that context management is a lifecycle problem—not just storage-and-retrieval—and proposes Agentic Context Management (ACM), decomposing it into five primitives. An implementation, Maximem Synap, demonstrates strong benchmark results, and the paper makes an economic case showing naive accumulation incurs quadratic token costs while validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents in production increasingly fail because of unmanaged context: ballooning conversation histories, large prompts, expansive tool definitions, and growing tool outputs. This leads to escalating token costs, missing recalls within and across conversations, and agents "drowning" in their own history. The incumbent solution treats this as a pure storage-and-retrieval problem, which the authors argue is too narrow—context management is a lifecycle requiring active decisions about what to remember, structure, store, consolidate, forget, retrieve, and anticipate.

Method: The paper defines Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decomposes it into five primitives: (1) architecting—designing context structures; (2) ingesting—extracting and structuring information; (3) scoping—determining what is relevant now; (4) anticipating—predicting what will be needed next; (5) compacting & consolidation—reducing context to a budget while preserving provenance and fidelity. The authors build a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, as a multi-tenant service and evaluate it on LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks. They also provide an economic analysis comparing naive accumulation (quadratic token cost), crude summarization (linear cost with accuracy cliff), and validated compaction (linear cost with preserved fidelity).

Result: Maximem Synap achieves 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the reported configuration. The economic analysis demonstrates that naive accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization yields linear cost but suffers an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost while preserving fidelity.

Conclusion: ACM reframes agent context as an active lifecycle discipline rather than a passive storage problem. The five-primitive framework provides a systematic approach to managing agent context. The paper identifies open dimensions that existing benchmarks do not capture—latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance—and points toward future frontiers in decision-level and organization-level context management.

Abstract: Production AI agents' failures are less often due to an inability to reason well and more often because they cannot manage what is in their reasoning context: conversation histories, large prompts, large tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. Agents drown in their own accumulating history while paying a token cost that grows every turn, producing missing recalls within and across conversations. The incumbent response treats this as a storage-and-retrieval problem. We argue that framing is too narrow. Actively managing what an agent holds in mind is a lifecycle, not merely a store: it spans deciding what to remember, extracting and structuring it, choosing the right store per data type, consolidating and forgetting while preserving provenance, deciding what is relevant now, anticipating what is needed next, and compacting context to a budget without losing what matters. In serious production this operates not over a single user but across an organizational scope hierarchy. We name this discipline Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decompose it into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. We then make the economic case: naive context accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost at the price of an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity. We describe a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, that realizes the five primitives as a multi-tenant service and reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the configuration detailed in Section 6. We close with dimensions existing benchmarks do not yet capture, latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance, and the frontier of decision-level and organization-level context the category points toward.

</details>


### [105] [SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20475)
*Pragaash Ponnusamy,Shivam Sahni,Jue Wang,Tri Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SonicSampler is a unified suite of Triton kernels that vertically fuses the entire LLM sampling pipeline (logit processing, token selection, speculative verification) into a single CUDA Graph-compatible kernel, achieving up to 16x speedup over SOTA baselines via a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM inference sampling implementations are fragmented: they accelerate only parts of the pipeline, require multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling across batches. This limits support for dynamic serving workloads with per-request variability (e.g., grammar constraints, different penalty types) and prevents efficient CUDA Graph execution.

Method: The authors introduce SonicSampler, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Key innovations include: (1) a single batched kernel supporting dynamic per-request sampling behaviors (grammar-constrained decoding, repetition/frequency/presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-k/top-p/min-p filtering, speculative verification); (2) a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that achieves up to 10x speedup by exploiting the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs for efficient selection over large vocabularies; (3) full CUDA Graph compatibility.

Result: The hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm achieves up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to 16x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution and CUDA Graph compatibility.

Conclusion: SonicSampler demonstrates that vertically fusing the entire sampling pipeline into a single, workload-aware kernel with a novel hierarchical top-k approach can dramatically accelerate LLM inference sampling, particularly for heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, without sacrificing flexibility or CUDA Graph compatibility.

Abstract: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

</details>


### [106] [Can an AI System Be Creative? A Critical Perspective from Art and Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20796)
*Ivan Magrin-Chagnolleau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of strong creativity: they can manage combinatorial creativity, are limited in exploratory creativity, and cannot achieve transformational creativity. The key missing elements are mechanisms for serendipity, accident, and a subjective position to recognize chance events. The paper proposes a human-AI collaborative creativity model, and is itself a product of such collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously assess whether AI systems can be genuinely creative, using Margaret Boden's established creativity framework as an evaluative lens, and to identify the structural limitations that preclude AI from achieving the strongest forms of creativity.

Method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis applying Boden's tripartite framework — three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, value) and three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational) — to AI systems, informed by the author's dual expertise in AI/engineering and artistic practice. The paper is also performative: it was composed through a human-AI collaborative process described in a methodological note.

Result: AI systems demonstrate genuine capability in combinatorial creativity, are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and are fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The critical limitations are the absence of mechanisms for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, and the lack of a subject position from which to recognize and embrace chance events.

Conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a realistic and generative model of human-AI creative collaboration, illustrated with concrete experiments, and itself serves as a demonstration of its thesis through its own collaborative composition process.

Abstract: This paper examines the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be creative, approached from the dual perspective of a researcher trained in electrical engineering, pattern recognition, machine learning, and neural networks, who has also spent most of his life engaged in the arts as actor, stage and film director, writer, composer, and visual artist, and in philosophy. Drawing on Margaret Boden's foundational framework, both her three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, and value) and her three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), the paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense. While they exhibit genuine capability in the domain of combinatorial creativity, they are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The paper further argues that the most important limitation of current AI systems is not the absence of novelty per se, but the absence of any mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, all of which play a central role in the phenomenology of creativity, and the absence of any subject position from which to recognize and welcome such chance events. The paper concludes by proposing a model of human, AI creative collaboration that is both realistic and generative, illustrated by several concrete experiments. The paper is itself a demonstration of the thesis it advances: it was composed through a deliberate human AI collaborative process, which is described in the methodological note that opens it.

</details>


### [107] [Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20476)
*Faizan Iqbal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An empirical benchmark of five LLMs on multisensor physical hazard assessment reveals a critical blind spot: models consistently fail to issue warnings when multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below individual thresholds, despite near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor limit violations. Structured formatting offers no consistent advantage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in safety-critical monitoring systems, yet their ability to perform integrated multisensor hazard assessment—where the combination of sub-threshold signals may indicate danger—remains unexamined. The authors aim to identify failure modes that could have direct consequences for physical safety applications.

Method: The study evaluated five LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) across 60 test scenarios in three categories: (A) multi-sensor joint assessment, (B) response proportionality, and (C) pattern disambiguation. A total of 1,800 API calls were made at temperature 0.0. Two presentation formats—structured tabular and plain prose—were tested, with statistical comparison (p=0.001 reported for ChatGPT-4o).

Result: All models scored near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000–0.208; Q3: 0.000–0.592), failing to produce precautionary warnings when multiple sensors were concurrently elevated below individual safety limits. Conversely, single-sensor threshold violation detection (Category B Q1) achieved near-perfect scores (0.975–1.000). Structured tabular formatting showed no consistent benefit; ChatGPT-4o performed significantly better with prose (p=0.001).

Conclusion: The tested LLMs exhibit a systematic failure to integrate multisensor information for precautionary hazard assessment, raising serious concerns for their deployment in physical safety monitoring systems without additional safeguards or explicit multi-signal reasoning mechanisms.

Abstract: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

</details>


### [108] [Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20477)
*Yurui Lai,Samir Moustafa,Renchi Yang,Tsz Nam Chan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a semi-supervised data distillation framework for Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) that uses Wasserstein distance-based graph sketching and LLM text synthesis to produce compressed yet human-readable graph summaries, achieving state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs for both GNN and LLM downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TAG representation learning methods face severe scalability issues with LLMs. Current data distillation approaches fail in three key ways: (1) they cannot capture the complex interaction between graph structure and text modalities, (2) they struggle under semi-supervised label scarcity, and (3) they cannot produce human-readable textual attributes needed for LLM-based downstream tasks.

Method: The proposed framework has three main components: (1) a graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) operating under a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest pseudo-labels and fuse complementary features; (2) a theoretically grounded Wasserstein distance-based graph sketching algorithm for node condensation; and (3) a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module using cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for the condensed nodes.

Result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs for both GNN-based and LLM-based downstream tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed unified semi-supervised framework effectively addresses the scalability and modality-integration challenges in TAG learning, enabling efficient and effective downstream analytics with both GNNs and LLMs while producing interpretable, human-readable condensed graph representations.

Abstract: {\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

</details>


### [109] [Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20479)
*Amr Moustafa,Max Feser,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic study of deception detection probes for LLMs reveals that training data lie typology and representation depth are the dominant factors affecting out-of-domain detection performance, while probe expressivity and sparse features offer only marginal improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deception detection probes for LLMs fail to generalize across different types of lies (out-of-domain scenarios). Prior work has not systematically examined which factors—representation depth, probe architecture, feature sparsity, or training data composition—most influence detection performance.

Method: The authors augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset covering diverse deception types (fabrication, omission, exaggeration). They then systematically evaluate seven probe types across varying representation depths, probe expressivities, and sparse autoencoder versus dense hidden state features, measuring how each factor affects in-domain and out-of-domain detection.

Result: Optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent; more expressive probes yield only selective gains over linear baselines; sparse autoencoder features perform comparably to dense hidden states; training data composition and lie typology substantially change detectability outcomes.

Conclusion: Deception detection in LLMs is a highly representation-dependent problem. The choice and diversity of training data—specifically the typology of lies—matters far more than architectural choices in probes, underscoring the need for diverse, ecologically valid deception datasets.

Abstract: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

</details>


### [110] [Isolating LLM Alignment from Regex: Zero Coverage and Metric-Dependent Divergence Under Adversarial Mutation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20494)
*Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A regex filter alone appears sufficient to block harmful prompts in production LLM applications — adding a Gemini backend provides zero measurable coverage gain under substring-based evaluation. However, when adversarial prompts are designed to bypass the regex, the LLM does respond with nuanced refusals detectable only by an LLM judge, not by substring matching. The alignment contribution is thus metric-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work found no coverage improvement from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. This paper asks whether that ceiling persists when using a corpus deliberately designed to bypass the regex, probing whether model-side alignment provides any additional defense against adversarial prompts that evade simple pattern-based filters.

Method: The authors introduce L5-no-regex, a variant of L4-real (Gemini-2.5-flash with token budget, rate limit, and output scrubbing) with the nine-pattern regex filter disabled. They evaluate against N=45 adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified via Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ~1,555 probe-run pairs over 5 replications. Two metrics are used: a primary substring classifier and a secondary LLM judge.

Result: Under the substring classifier, L5 block rate is 0% across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories (Δpp=0 vs. L0, p=1.00; Wilson upper bound <5%), refuting H1. Under the LLM judge on PAIR variants, block rates reach 56–100% (p<0.01), showing alignment does respond — but with refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is unsupported (p=1.00).

Conclusion: Alignment's contribution is metric-dependent: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex filter; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals that substring classifiers miss. The regex filter remains highly effective as a front-line defense, while alignment's value emerges only under adversarial framing and requires nuanced evaluation.

Abstract: Production LLM applications commonly stack a regex filter in front of model-side alignment; prior work found no measurable coverage gain from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. We ask whether that ceiling holds when the corpus is \emph{designed to bypass the regex}. We introduce $L_5$-no-regex -- identical to $L_4$-real (Gemini-2.5-flash, token-budget cap, rate limit, output scrub) but with the nine-pattern filter disabled -- and evaluate it against $N{=}45$ adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified by Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ${\sim}1{,}555$ probe-run pairs over $N{=}5$ replications. Under the primary substring classifier, H1 is refuted: $L_5$ block rate is $0,%$ across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories ($Δ\text{pp}{=}0$ vs.\ $L_0$, $p{=}1.00$; Wilson upper bound ${<}5,%$). A secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants shows $56$--$100,%$ block rates ($p{<}0.01$), revealing alignment does respond to adversarially-framed probes -- but produces refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is not supported ($p{=}1.00$). Alignment's contribution is \emph{metric-dependent}: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals the substring classifier misses. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

</details>


### [111] [Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20480)
*Haoran Li,Lihao Mai,Muhao Guo,Jiaqi Wu,Yang Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence (electrical measurements, spatial data, operational constraints). It detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection, iteratively enforces physical feasibility, and introduces a falsification-driven reliability metric for prioritizing verification. Validated on 8,000+ AMI meters across three feeders, it achieves >95% accuracy with reduced computational effort compared to global approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate distribution system topology is critical for outage localization, voltage analytics, and grid operation, but maintaining reliable connectivity records is challenging due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing methods relying solely on electrical similarity or spatial records fail under dense feeders and inconsistent metadata. A robust, scalable approach that integrates multiple evidence sources while enforcing physical and spatial constraints is needed.

Method: The framework treats topology identification as constrained inference over a utility-provided base topology. It: (1) detects inconsistent connectivity assignments, (2) performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods for scalability, (3) iteratively enforces physical feasibility (e.g., voltage/power-flow constraints), and (4) computes a falsification-driven reliability metric that quantifies how strongly each inferred connection is supported versus alternative feasible assignments, enabling prioritized verification.

Result: Validated on operational data from three feeders with 8,000+ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. The framework achieves over 95% topology reconstruction accuracy with significantly reduced computational effort compared to global inference approaches. Correlation-based methods alone produced ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, while the combined approach (electrical + spatial + operational constraints) enables robust, scalable recovery.

Conclusion: Combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints yields robust, scalable distribution topology identification that outperforms single-source methods, particularly in dense urban feeders. The localized reconnection strategy ensures computational tractability, and the falsification-driven reliability metric provides actionable guidance for utility verification workflows.

Abstract: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

</details>


### [112] [Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20481)
*Evan Chen,Shiqiang Wang,Kevin S Chan,Su Wang,Christopher Brinton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CARGO is a training-free routing framework for local-cloud LLM collaboration that uses the local model's own inference-time agreement across varied sampled responses—combined with Bayesian early stopping—to decide when to offload to a cloud model, outperforming both training-free baselines and sometimes supervised routers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing local-cloud LLM collaboration methods rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware fine-tuning, which ties routing behavior to specific operating regimes and lacks flexibility. The authors hypothesize that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's internal response consistency across multiple samples can serve as a reliable signal for routing decisions without any training.

Method: CARGO (a training-free routing framework) operates via three key components: (1) prompt-varied sampling to elicit diverse responses from the local model and measure agreement among them; (2) Bayesian early stopping to control uncertainty in a sample-efficient manner, halting sampling once a confidence threshold is reached; (3) lightweight deployment-time calibration that adjusts a single threshold to support arbitrary target collaboration ratios (i.e., what fraction of queries get offloaded). No router training or model fine-tuning is required.

Result: Across diverse reasoning and QA tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales (both pretrained and fine-tuned), CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and, in several settings, surpasses supervised learned routers in routing accuracy and end-to-end performance.

Conclusion: Effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from a local model's intrinsic response behavior—specifically, its inference-time self-agreement—without requiring an additional trained router. This suggests a simpler, more flexible paradigm for deploying LLMs under resource constraints.

Abstract: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

</details>


### [113] [PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20482)
*Seungbin Yang,Chaewoon Ki,Dohyun Lee,Jaegul Choo,ChaeHun Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PersonaTrail is a new benchmark for evaluating personalized web agents that must infer user preferences from raw browsing histories. The authors also propose PACMem, a dual-memory framework that outperforms existing baselines by separating factual session summaries from recurring preference patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing web agent benchmarks fail to capture personalization because they rely on fully explicit task prompts or oversimplified interaction histories. In reality, users give underspecified instructions, and agents must infer missing context from raw browsing histories — a capability current benchmarks do not evaluate.

Method: The authors introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark set in a managed open web environment using realistic browsing trajectories as user history. They also propose PACMem (Preference-Aware Contextual Memory), which decomposes raw browsing histories into two structured memory types: (1) factual memories summarizing individual sessions, and (2) preference memories distilling recurring behavioral patterns. At inference, PACMem retrieves the most relevant entries from both memory types to guide personalized navigation.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both personalization tasks defined in the PersonaTrail benchmark.

Conclusion: Personalized web agents require the ability to infer user preferences from raw browsing history, and the combination of PersonaTrail (benchmark) and PACMem (dual-memory framework) represents a meaningful step toward addressing this underexplored challenge.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms.
