To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

</details>


### [114] [Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20483)
*Max Scribner,Antonio Vergari,Vaishak Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a polynomial-time method for constraining LLM autoregressive generation to satisfy any LR(k) context-free grammar, improving upon previous exponential-time approaches for such grammars.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Integrating LLMs into formal systems requires syntactically valid output. For languages like SQL and JSON (often LR(k) grammars), ensuring validity is a prerequisite for downstream processing. Existing methods for constrained generation are exponential-time for LR(k) grammars.

Method: The authors distill the LLM into a tractable probabilistic model, then steer and mask autoregressive generation by incorporating the probability of satisfying logical constraints. They prove that satisfaction of any finite-duration LR(k) grammar can be computed in polynomial time.

Result: Satisfaction of LR(k) grammars of finite duration is shown to be computable in polynomial time, a significant improvement over the exponential time required by previous methods.

Conclusion: The polynomial-time result enables efficient constrained generation, steering LLMs toward outputs that satisfy formal syntactic constraints, facilitating integration into formal systems like program synthesis.

Abstract: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

</details>


### [115] [The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20484)
*Yiheng Tao,Kaiwen Cheng,Yao Lu,Chang Liu,Jie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs suffer from representation collapse in long-context scenarios, manifesting as either homogenization collapse or isolation collapse. The authors derive a fundamental spectral trade-off between mixing efficiency and information capacity, and propose TRSP — a non-invasive, topologically regularized side-path with a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism — to achieve spectral balance, yielding substantial gains on long-context benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard attention mechanisms face an intrinsic dilemma: they risk either homogenization collapse (rank deficiency from attention sinks, degrading expressivity) or isolation collapse (context disconnection from local attention, impairing long-range mixing). Existing solutions cannot balance mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) simultaneously, creating a bottleneck for long-context LLM performance.

Method: The authors propose TRSP (Topologically Regularized Side-Path), a non-invasive architectural intervention that operates alongside core attention. It uses a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight length-aware gate, to regularize token interaction topology. Proximal coupling preserves effective rank, while distal propagation ensures non-degenerate mixing, together promoting a geometrically healthier transition operator.

Result: TRSP yields significant improvements on general capability and long-context benchmarks. On NoLiMa at 8× training length, TRSP retains 83% accuracy, outperforming Differential Transformer by ~30 percentage points and Gated Attention by ~50 percentage points.

Conclusion: The spectral trade-off between mixing efficiency and information capacity is a fundamental limitation in LLMs. TRSP resolves this by topologically regularizing attention dynamics without altering the core mechanism, offering a practical and effective solution for long-context modeling.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83\%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

</details>


### [116] [Expectation Alignment of Language Models for Real-World User Expectations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20485)
*Miaomiao Li,Yang Wang,Bin Liang,Shudong Liu,Zhiwei Zhang,Kam-Fai Wong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies a misalignment between LLM performance on standard benchmarks and actual user expectations, introduces ExpectBench (a benchmark grounded in real user expectations), and proposes LENS, a lightweight framework for expectation-aware response generation that improves user satisfaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation relies on model-based heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, all of which fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations. This leads to models appearing competent on benchmarks while being misaligned with what users actually want, motivating the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions.

Method: The authors (1) conduct a systematic study to extract semantically rich user expectations from real-world LLM interactions using a principled procedure; (2) construct ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in these real expectations; (3) propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework that enables models to internalize and respond according to user expectations.

Result: Analysis reveals that current LLMs struggle to both satisfy and anticipate user expectations, exposing a fundamental source of human-AI misalignment. LENS consistently improves expectation satisfaction, demonstrating the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling user expectations is crucial for realistic human-AI alignment. The LENS framework shows that expectation-aware generation can bridge the gap between benchmark competence and real user satisfaction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, yet it remains largely unexplored whether they truly meet user expectations. Existing evaluation approaches, relying on model heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing models to appear competent while misaligning with what users actually seek. We present the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, proposing a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and introducing ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations. Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

</details>


### [117] [OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20486)
*Zhongzheng Li,Tiancan Feng,Wenhao Li,Qingsong Ran,Shikun Feng,Xiaoyuan Zhang,Yue Wang,Xiaoguang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPTScientist is a multi-agent framework that discovers neural network optimizers through a typed DSL, combining evolutionary search with automatic DSL extension. It produced RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated optimizer discovery methods face a fundamental trade-off: unconstrained code search is flexible but yields invalid or uninterpretable programs, while parameterized-family search is stable but stifles novelty. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a structured, theory-guided discovery process that balances expressiveness with correctness.

Method: OPTScientist uses a typed domain-specific language (DSL) that decomposes optimizer updates into six modular components: direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping. Four role-specialized agents (Theorist, Designer, Engineer, Reviewer) collaborate in a loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile/evaluate optimizers, and critique results. Evolutionary search operates over DSL programs, and a second-stage mechanism proposes DSL extensions when repeated failures indicate representational bottlenecks.

Result: The framework discovered RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining performance over strong baselines under the authors' native evaluation protocol.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates a viable path toward automated optimizer science that is grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation, suggesting that structured DSLs with agentic search can yield both novel and practically useful optimizer designs.

Abstract: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

</details>


### [118] [Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20487)
*Chendi Wang,Liam Cunningham,Tom Yishay,Jieying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a framework for auditing ideological bias in LLMs by treating hallucinations in document-grounded QA as diagnostic signals. Analyzing 21,727 political articles across left, center, and right sources with four LLMs, the authors find that while hallucination rates show modest source-ideology differences, hallucinated content exhibits a consistent leftward drift. This drift is linked to high-entropy generation contexts, suggesting an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism with implications for election-adjacent AI deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed for answering political information queries, including in high-stakes election settings where factual errors and ideological distortions carry significant consequences. Existing bias audits focus primarily on overt outputs, but subtle ideological drift occurring specifically during hallucination events remains underexplored. The authors aim to quantify whether hallucinations systematically slant in particular ideological directions and to understand the token-level mechanisms driving such drift.

Method: A five-step reproducible measurement pipeline: (1) Generate article-specific questions from 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from the QBias dataset (covering left, center, and right sources). (2) Elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model. (3) Detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison against the source articles. (4) Classify ideological valence of hallucinated sentences using a fine-tuned stance classifier. (5) Probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty (entropy) to both hallucination occurrence and ideological drift direction.

Result: Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious political topics. Source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. However, hallucination content shows robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, even when generated from right-leaning source articles. Logit-level analysis reveals that hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models, higher uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, supporting an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism.

Conclusion: Hallucinations in LLM-based political QA are not ideologically neutral; they exhibit systematic leftward drift, particularly under high-uncertainty generation conditions. This suggests that model uncertainty triggers a defaulting behavior toward left-leaning content. The findings carry significant implications for auditing AI-mediated political information systems and designing safeguards for election-relevant LLM deployments, emphasizing the need to monitor not just whether models hallucinate, but what ideological content those hallucinations convey.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

</details>


### [119] [Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20488)
*Bronislav Sidik,Chaya Levi,Nizzan Kimhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATM introduces runtime topology mutation for multi-agent LLM frameworks, using telemetry-driven overload detection and safety invariants to dynamically factorize overloaded agents into specialized sub-agents, improving code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7% while eliminating high-privacy memory exposure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM frameworks suffer from rigid topologies fixed at boot time. When agents become overloaded at runtime (e.g., mixing too many action categories, tool errors, queue buildup), no mechanism exists to restructure the system dynamically. This rigidity limits robustness and scalability under shifting workloads.

Method: ATM combines: (1) a six-signal Bottleneck Index (queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, cross-agent wait time) with warmup-calibrated thresholds; (2) three safety invariants — capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation; (3) privacy-level-aware memory routing; and (4) factorization of overloaded agents into specialized sub-agents with the parent hot-swapped into a coordinator. Shadow validation gates all live traffic. Evaluated on 720 DeepSeek-V3 runs across four ablation conditions and three workloads.

Result: Code-task success rose from 3.3% (baseline) to 61.7% with factorization. Full rail-and-distillation system reduced high-privacy memory exposure from 2.0 to 0.0 events/task under regex classification while preserving task quality. Invariant-checking latency adds <500 μs p99 on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution confirmed external validity.

Conclusion: Runtime topology mutation is feasible and beneficial for multi-agent LLM systems. ATM's guarded factorization mechanism substantially improves task success rates and eliminates privacy leaks with negligible latency overhead, demonstrating that dynamic structural adaptation can be both safe and effective.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality. The runtime rails carrying ATM's invariants add less than 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution is included as an external-validity check. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

</details>


### [120] [EvoSQL: Memory-Augmented Critic-Generator Co-Evolution for Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20489)
*Jiawei Zhou,Jianwei Wang,Chenyu Zhou,Chaojian Shi,Ming Dong,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoSQL is a co-evolution framework for Text-to-SQL that iteratively refines SQL queries through generator-critic interaction, using candidate memory, execution signals, and LLM critique, with a SDPO fine-tuning stage; it achieves consistent gains over Maj@16 baselines on Spider and BIRD datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex database queries require reasoning beyond one-shot generation — including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction — which existing Text-to-SQL approaches fail to adequately support.

Method: EvoSQL employs a co-evolution framework where a generator and critic iterate on SQL synthesis. It maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates via execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates memory through utility-guided aggregation. Additionally, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning injects execution-aware supervision into coding LLM backbones.

Result: EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines on Spider and BIRD, with BIRD-Dev gains ranging from +1.37% (Qwen3-4B) to +9.19% (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B). SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev.

Conclusion: Memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective approach for building more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems.

Abstract: Text-to-SQL has advanced rapidly with large language models, but complex database queries still require reasoning beyond one-shot generation, including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. We present EvoSQL, a co-evolution framework that formulates SQL synthesis as an iterative interaction between a generator and a critic. EvoSQL maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates with both execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates its memory through utility-guided aggregation. To strengthen the underlying generator-critic pair, we further introduce a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones. Experiments on Spider and BIRD show that EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with particularly large gains on BIRD-Dev, ranging from +1.37% for Qwen3-4B to +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev. These results suggest that memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/EvoSQL.

</details>


### [121] [CRAWO: Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20490)
*Eugênio Santos,Daniel Maia,Stefano Loss,José Manoel Silva,Aluizio Rocha Neto,Thais Batista,Everton Cavalcante,Nélio Cacho,Eduardo Nogueira,Daniel Araújo,Frederico Lopes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRAWO is a Kubernetes-based orchestration framework for edge AI that uses a control-loop model with a pluggable hardware-aware allocator to dynamically place AI pipeline workloads across heterogeneous edge devices, demonstrated via license plate recognition in smart city surveillance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing edge orchestration platforms focus narrowly on deployment automation and infrastructure management, lacking the intelligence to adaptively allocate AI workloads across devices with vastly different capabilities (microcontrollers to accelerators) under dynamic conditions. This inefficiency limits real-time application performance in smart cities.

Method: CRAWO employs a control-loop architecture decoupling allocation intelligence from execution. It uses Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) on K3s (lightweight Kubernetes) for domain modeling, a dedicated operator for state reconciliation, and a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that consumes real-time infrastructure metrics for adaptive workload placement across distributed edge nodes.

Result: Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrated improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing for latency-sensitive tasks.

Conclusion: CRAWO provides an effective architectural framework for adaptive AI workload orchestration at the edge, bridging the gap between heterogeneous hardware capabilities and dynamic placement requirements through a decoupled, metrics-driven control-loop approach.

Abstract: Edge Intelligence has emerged as a key paradigm for enabling real-time applications in smart cities by shifting computation from centralized cloud data centers to the network edge, thereby reducing latency and bandwidth consumption. However, deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures remains challenging due to the wide range of device capabilities, from low-power microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems. Existing edge orchestration platforms primarily focus on deployment automation and infrastructure management, but these approaches are often inefficient and limit the ability to adaptively allocate resources under dynamic conditions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces CRAWO (Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration), an architectural framework for coordinating AI pipelines across distributed edge environments. CRAWO follows a control-loop-based model that separates allocation intelligence from execution by managing placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows while instantiating services on edge nodes. The framework incorporates a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that leverages real-time infrastructure metrics to enable adaptive workload placement. The reference implementation adopts a microservices architecture deployed on a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation. Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.

</details>


### [122] [DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20491)
*Raffi Khatchadourian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DFAH-Bench measures behavioral instability in financial AI agents through replay testing, assessing not just decision outcomes but also tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration. Testing 10 models across 8,127 episodes reveals an 18-percentage-point gap between outcome agreement (95%) and trajectory consistency (77%), identifying three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers, stable executors, and trajectory divergers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard evaluation benchmarks for tool-using agents only assess final decisions, ignoring whether agents arrive at those decisions through consistent, reproducible processes. This creates a blind spot: agents may appear reliable based on outcome agreement while exhibiting significant behavioral instability in their underlying decision-making pathways, which is particularly concerning in high-stakes domains like finance.

Method: The authors introduce a replay-based benchmarking framework with three observable stability channels: (1) tool-call trajectory divergence — whether the agent follows the same sequence of tool invocations; (2) evidence contacts — consistency in which information sources are accessed; and (3) decision concentration — whether the agent's decisions cluster similarly across runs. None of these channels require access to hidden reasoning text, making the approach model-agnostic. The benchmark comprises 8,127 replay episodes across 10 models and 3 financial tasks.

Result: Outcome agreement alone proves insufficient: frontier models achieve 95% decision agreement but only 77% trajectory consistency, yielding an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]). Among case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. Three behavioral profiles emerge: pattern matchers that collapse to a single output irrespective of input variation; stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes; and trajectory divergers that reach identical conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts.

Conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation is an incomplete stability signal for tool-using agents. DFAH-Bench demonstrates that measuring process-level consistency — through tool trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration — reveals substantial behavioral instability that conventional benchmarks miss, with implications for reliability and auditability in financial AI deployments.

Abstract: Standard evaluation benchmarks measure what a tool-using agent decides, not whether it arrives at that decision through the same process each time. We introduce DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark that measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across three channels -- tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration -- none of which require access to hidden reasoning text. Across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks, we find that outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal: frontier models can agree on decisions 95% of the time while following the same tool path only 77% of the time -- an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) that outcome-only evaluation misses entirely. Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. We identify three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers that achieve near-perfect agreement by collapsing to a single output regardless of input, stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and trajectory divergers that reach the same conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts. The benchmark code, metric scripts, replay logs, benchmark card, dataset README, and release manifest are released in the accompanying repository.

</details>


### [123] [Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20493)
*Quentin Besnard,Nicolas Ragot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a continual learning framework for time series forecasting that uses Attention-guided Experience Replay to enable dynamic model adaptation while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, demonstrated on standard benchmarks and a piezometric dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional neural networks rely on large, stationary datasets, but real-world applications involve dynamic, evolving environments where data distributions shift over time. There is a need for forecasting models that can adapt incrementally without forgetting prior knowledge, under computational constraints.

Method: The authors propose a continual learning framework that extends static time series forecasting models by integrating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This enables the model to revisit and retain important past experiences while adapting to new temporal contexts, balancing stability and plasticity.

Result: The framework was evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks and a piezometric dataset with diverse temporal behaviors. Results demonstrate increased or maintained predictive performance over time, alongside reduced retraining costs and lower data requirements.

Conclusion: The proposed Attention-guided Experience Replay framework effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting in continual time series forecasting, making it suitable for deployment in dynamic, real-world settings where data is non-stationary and computational resources are limited.

Abstract: Deep learning has led to remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, particularly in robotics, imaging and sound processing. However, a major limitation of neural networks remains their strong dependence on large and stationary datasets. In many real-world applications, these conditions are rarely met due to evolving and dynamic environments where data distributions change over time. Continual learning aims to address this challenge by developing models capable of adapting incrementally while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under computational constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for continual time series forecasting, designed to extend existing static forecasting models commonly used in the literature by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This approach allows the model to adapt dynamically to new contexts while preserving prior knowledge, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks as well as on a piezometric dataset exhibiting diverse temporal behaviors. Results show that our approach effectively increases or maintains predictive performance over time while reducing retraining costs and data requirements, thus facilitating the deployment of forecasting models in dynamic and real-world settings.

</details>


### [124] [From Errors to Rules: Iterative Prompt Optimization for Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20497)
*Yueying Cui,Renhao Xue,Yi Zhang,Mukul Prasad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic comparison of prompt optimization paradigms (demonstration selection, exploration-based search, error-driven diagnosis) reveals task-type complementarity. The authors propose ERGO, an error-guided method that excels on "boundary-learnable" tasks by diagnosing confused label pairs and generating decision rules, while showing no single paradigm dominates across all task types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt optimization paradigms for text classification have incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. There is no systematic understanding of which method works best under which task conditions, nor a principled framework to guide practitioners in paradigm selection.

Method: First, a comprehensive empirical study comparing demonstration-based ICL, exploration-based search, and error-driven diagnosis across classification benchmarks (2–150 classes) with quantitative and qualitative analysis. Second, ERGO (Error-Guided Optimization): an iterative method processing the full training set in non-overlapping batches, using a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop that identifies classification failures and generates targeted decision rules for confused label pairs.

Result: ERGO achieves top accuracy on boundary-learnable tasks (TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%) and converges in 3–5 iterations with interpretable rules. Broader findings: demonstration-based ICL excels on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search on many-class intent tasks, and ERGO on boundary-learnable tasks. No single method dominates across all benchmarks.

Conclusion: The three paradigms are complementary rather than competitive. The paper provides a complementarity framework linking task characteristics (coverage-dependence, many-class intent, boundary-learnability) to optimal paradigm selection, offering actionable guidance for practitioners deploying prompt optimization in text classification.

Abstract: Prompt optimization for text classification spans diverse approaches, from demonstration selection to exploration-based search to error-driven diagnosis, each with known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (2 to 150 classes) comparing these paradigms through both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces, revealing that each paradigm excels on structurally different task types and that no single method dominates. Guided by these insights, we propose Error-Guided Optimization (ERGO), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules through a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop. ERGO achieves the best accuracy on tasks where errors concentrate in specific confused label pairs (which we term boundary-learnable tasks): TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%, converges in 3-5 iterations, and produces interpretable decision rules. While ERGO does not achieve the highest overall average, it fills a complementary role: demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent, and ERGO wins where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns. We provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical guidance for practitioners.

</details>


### [125] [AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20498)
*Fanjin Zhang,Zhengyang Wang,Ruixuan Huang,Kefan Zhang,Amy Xin,Yuanchun Wang,Shu Zhao,Evgeny Kharlamov,Jie Tang,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AISE-Bench is a real-world benchmark with 1,133 QA pairs for evaluating LLM agents on complex, multi-step API-based information seeking over academic knowledge graphs, featuring full execution trajectories, validated parameters, and grounded answers. Even the strongest model achieves only moderate performance, highlighting significant challenges in API planning and execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-using benchmarks for academic graph information seeking rely on synthetic templates, simplified solutions, or narrow paper-centric tasks, leaving underexplored challenges such as realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive process-outcome evaluation.

Method: The authors construct AISE-Bench with 1,133 QA pairs featuring query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. They design a customized agent workflow enabling annotators to efficiently plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows. A comprehensive evaluation protocol assesses answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success across 14 methods.

Result: Among 14 evaluated methods, the strongest (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and frequently struggles with API planning and execution, indicating that multi-step API-using LLM agents remain far from reliable autonomous operation on realistic information-seeking tasks.

Conclusion: AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents on academic knowledge graphs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with tools are emerging as autonomous agents capable of using Web engine, APIs, and code to solve complex, long-horizon tasks. Current tool-using benchmarks for information seeking on academic graphs rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow tasks such as paper-centric tasks, leaving key challenges underexplored - realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling for APIs, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive evaluation of both the process and the outcome. We introduce AISE-Bench, a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs. AISE-Bench release contains 1,133 QA pairs, including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. To support high-quality annotation, we design a customized agent workflow to enable annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows efficiently. We develop a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Among the 14 evaluated methods, even the strongest model (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution. AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving the stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents. Our code and data are available at https://aise-bench.github.io/.

</details>


### [126] [FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20500)
*Sizhe Tang,Guangyu Jiang,Yu Li,Rongqian Chen,Ioannis G. Kevrekidis,Tian Lan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlowEdit is a framework that enables LLMs to handle ill-posed problems with conflicting constraints by regulating internal reasoning flows via information-theoretic objectives, generating multiple diverse and valid alternative responses in a single pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world problems are often ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements. Current LLMs, constrained by next-token prediction, struggle to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses across reasoning branches, and produce multiple alternative responses simultaneously.

Method: FlowEdit uses two dual information-theoretic objectives on internal reasoning representations: (1) maximizing information flow from each selected hypothesis to its branch outcome, and (2) minimizing overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches. This is operationalized via tractable variational bounds under ε-sufficient boundary embeddings, optimizing conditional mutual information during the LLM reasoning process.

Result: FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68% and overall response informativeness by 24%. Token-level analysis reveals that flow regulation manifests as a redistribution of next-token entropy concentrated within branches, amplified at flow boundaries, and scaling with the number of flows required.

Conclusion: Regulating internal reasoning flows via information-theoretic principles is a viable and effective approach for enabling LLMs to handle ill-posed, conflict-laden problems, producing diverse and informative alternative responses beyond the capabilities of standard next-token prediction.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

</details>


### [127] [Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20502)
*Jan Speller,Malte Luttermann,Marcel Gehrke,Tanya Braun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a formal extension scheme for comparing probabilistic graphical models defined over different variable sets by completing unmatched components with conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions, lifting both models to a minimal common measurable space while preserving probabilistic semantics under projection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets cannot be directly compared using standard distributional discrepancy measures. A principled method is needed to lift two such models to a common measurable space without distorting their original probabilistic semantics, enabling well-defined quantitative comparison.

Method: The authors introduce conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions to complete unmatched components between two models. This ensures the extended joint distributions differ from the originals only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. A deterministic algorithm minimially extends the factor graphs to the smallest common measurable space and a shared graphical structure. Structural and measure-theoretic properties are formally analyzed.

Result: The proposed extension scheme is invariant under projection and produces joint distributions that preserve the original models' semantics up to multiplicative constants. The method yields a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smallest common measurable space, enabling principled comparison via established discrepancy measures.

Conclusion: The Laplace extension framework provides a sound measure-theoretic foundation for comparing probabilistic graphical models with mismatched variable sets, opening the door to rigorous model comparison methodologies grounded in distributional discrepancy measures.

Abstract: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

</details>


### [128] [LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20503)
*Lazar Milikic,Simon Guilloud,Khanh Nguyen,Viktor Kuncak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LeanFlow is an LLM agent system that translates mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Through case studies in number theory and measure theory, the authors evaluate runtime mechanisms (queuing, proof workflows, toolsets) using Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5, finding the full workflow completes projects within budget and minimizes token costs. LeanFlow also achieves 75.7% on a benchmark slice and solves all five challenge projects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing verifier-in-the-loop systems can produce large formal artifacts, but it is unclear which runtime mechanisms — such as queuing strategies, proof workflows, and tool configurations — most affect completion, auditability, and efficiency in the end-to-end document-to-project formalization pipeline. This paper aims to systematically study these factors.

Method: The authors build LeanFlow, an LLM agent system for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. They conduct ablation studies on two previously unformalized papers (one in number theory, one in measure theory) using two models (Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5). Ablations span proof-workflow design, queuing mechanisms, and toolset variations. Metrics include task outcome, API call count, input tokens, and output tokens, with a 2000-call budget. Complementary evaluation uses the PFR slice of RLM25 (reporting BEq+) and five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects.

Result: With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants exhaust the budget. With GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow achieves the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in GPT5.5 runs.

Conclusion: Runtime design choices — particularly queuing mechanisms — significantly impact formalization efficiency and completion. The full LeanFlow workflow with queuing enables budget-constrained completion and token-cost minimization, demonstrating that careful system engineering is critical for scaling document-to-project formalization.

Abstract: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

</details>


### [129] [Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20506)
*Houda Khrouf,Pedro Fillastre,Sebastiao Correia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperGraphRAG improves knowledge retrieval by representing n-ary facts with hypergraphs, but suffers from LLM extraction errors and poor chunk retrieval. This paper proposes self-consistency prompting for extraction and Personalized PageRank over hypergraphs for retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard GraphRAG structures knowledge as pairwise graphs, which cannot adequately capture n-ary (multi-entity) facts. HyperGraphRAG addresses this via hypergraphs but introduces two key weaknesses: error-prone LLM-based fact extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. The authors aim to mitigate both issues.

Method: Two improvements are proposed: (1) Self-consistency prompting for fact extraction, where multiple LLM generations are sampled and aggregated to reduce extraction errors; (2) Personalized PageRank algorithm applied over the hypergraph structure to enhance relevance-based chunk retrieval, leveraging hypergraph topology for better ranking.

Result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper claims the proposed method addresses the identified weaknesses of HyperGraphRAG.

Conclusion: The combination of self-consistency prompting and Personalized PageRank over hypergraphs offers a more robust HyperGraphRAG pipeline, improving both extraction fidelity and retrieval quality for n-ary fact reasoning.

Abstract: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

</details>


### [130] [MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20507)
*Jingquan Chen,Jinghua Piao,Jie Feng,Shaogang Hu,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MiniCache is a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought outputs into parameterized cache objects, using a small model to handle semantic variable extraction and speculative drafting, thereby reducing expensive LLM invocations while achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput in structured task execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision-making, and structured task execution, but these applications incur high inference costs. Prior caching approaches fail to address the challenge of structurally similar but semantically distinct requests, where naive exact-match caching yields low hit rates and cannot exploit partial computational overlap across related queries.

Method: MiniCache introduces a parameterized caching framework for Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs. It extracts semantic variables from incoming requests using a small model, matches them against cached program templates, and on cache hits reuses the parameterized program structure. The same small model also performs speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing the number of expensive calls to the large target model while preserving output quality.

Result: Experiments on WebShop, Formula, CodeTAT-QA, and shopping-style request datasets demonstrate up to 3.1x lower inference latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving, while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full target-LLM inference.

Conclusion: Small models are most effective not as direct replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching, significantly improving cost-latency-accuracy trade-offs in LLM-powered structured task execution.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

</details>


### [131] [Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20510)
*Dmitrii Khizbullin,Zaid Alyafeai,Abdelrahman Eldesokey,Nourah AlSultan,Raghad Alshalan,David R. Pugh,Bernard Ghanem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual (English/Arabic) benchmark with 100 human-verified QA tasks for evaluating tool-using agents on real telecom data, requiring multi-hop reasoning over HTML, SQL databases, and web archives. Even the strongest LLM solves only 71% of tasks, with visually grounded categories scoring below 30%, highlighting significant room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of rigorous, reproducible, closed-domain benchmarks for evaluating tool-using AI agents in real-world enterprise settings, particularly one that spans multiple modalities, languages, and heterogeneous data sources without relying on LLM-as-a-Judge for scoring.

Method: The authors construct Telco-GAIA, a sandboxed Docker environment containing 100 QA tasks (English/Arabic) over three heterogeneous sources: a static telecom website snapshot (HTML, images, PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives. Tasks require multi-hop reasoning (avg 4.2 hops) across text, image, and tabular modalities. Evaluation uses deterministic normalized exact string matching. A reference agent was tested across 12 commercial and open LLMs under both unlimited and moderate cost budgets.

Result: The strongest model achieves only 71% task success; under a moderate cost budget, performance drops to ~40%. Visually grounded categories are the weakest, with average backend scores below 30%. The benchmark proves challenging across all evaluated LLMs, with substantial headroom remaining in document and image understanding.

Conclusion: Telco-GAIA provides a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise tool-using agents and serves as a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks. Current LLMs still struggle significantly with multi-modal, multi-hop reasoning in realistic enterprise contexts, especially on visually grounded tasks.

Abstract: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

</details>


### [132] [SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20511)
*Keonhee Park,Gunhee Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SiGMA proposes sign-guided adaptive tuning and merging to reduce negative interference in Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning, outperforming prior Mixture-of-Experts and expansion-merge methods on UCIT and DCL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MCIT methods (MoE, expansion-merge) address catastrophic forgetting but still suffer from negative interference at inference, where new updates overwrite useful prior knowledge, degrading overall performance.

Method: SiGMA consists of two components: (1) Sign Guided Adaptive Tuning during training, which reduces collisions with past knowledge and minimizes drift while learning new tasks; (2) Sign Guided Merging at inference, which selectively scales salient parameters to preserve and amplify task-specific knowledge.

Result: Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks demonstrate that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing MCIT methods.

Conclusion: SiGMA effectively mitigates negative interference in MCIT through sign-guided training and merging, advancing the continual adaptation of MLLMs to sequential downstream tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

</details>


### [133] [Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20515)
*Jingyi Huang,Ruohan Zong,Yujun Feng,Liran Ma,Lanyu Shang,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RGPO addresses inconsistent human annotations in RLHF by estimating annotator reliability, inferring latent ground truth, and dynamically weighting training based on annotation consensus, outperforming standard RLHF baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human feedback used in RLHF is inherently noisy, inconsistent, and subjective. Existing methods like DPO treat all preference pairs equally regardless of annotator disagreement, forcing models to overfit ambiguous or contradictory supervision signals, which leads to suboptimal alignment with human preferences.

Method: RGPO consists of two key components: (1) estimation of annotator reliability and inference of latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences; (2) reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on annotation consensus level, prioritizing high-consensus signals over low-consensus ones.

Result: Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks show that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines.

Conclusion: RGPO provides a robust alternative to standard preference optimization by explicitly modeling and mitigating annotation noise, leading to more reliable alignment of LLMs with human preferences.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

</details>


### [134] [CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20518)
*Xue-Jian Gao,Deng Pan,Yueming Su,Jiasheng Li,Bin Du,Fengming Zhu,Chengdi Ma,Junyi Fan,Qichen Liao,Chengqiu Hu,Xinxian Chen,Lingchao Zheng,Jun Li,Jiwei Yang,Yuwei Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANN Bench is an open benchmark for AI-generated operator kernels on Huawei's Ascend NPU, covering 53 operators and 1060 test cases across four difficulty tiers and multiple precision formats. It introduces a three-dimensional composite score (compilation, correctness, performance) with hardware-anchored performance limits to resist reward hacking, providing a reproducible evaluation standard for the Ascend ecosystem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI kernel-generation benchmarks (e.g., for CUDA, Triton) leave hardware platforms with less-exposed programming models — notably Huawei's Ascend NPU — without a common evaluation baseline. A dedicated benchmark is needed to quantitatively assess and drive AI operator-authoring capability on Ascend hardware.

Method: CANN Bench provides 53 operators and 1060 test cases across four difficulty tiers (elementwise primitives → MoE dispatch → FlashAttention), spanning FP16/BF16/FP32/INT8. Evaluation uses a three-dimensional weighted composite score on compilation success, functional correctness, and performance. Performance is graded against a PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit computed per case on real NPU hardware. The harness is designed from the ground up to resist reward hacking.

Result: The benchmark is versioned within the official CANN repository, supporting long-term community co-construction. The three-dimensional scoring framework provides a principled reward signal that reflects genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts.

Conclusion: CANN Bench provides the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability, filling a critical gap left by CUDA/Triton-centric benchmarks.

Abstract: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

</details>


### [135] [Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20524)
*Sagar Dangal,Manoj Shakya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mean cross-positional attention degradation over distance is widely observed but causally untested. Through six experiments across multiple transformer architectures, the authors find that attention degradation follows a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern, but causally manipulating attention toward function tokens (Relay-Aware Attention) produces null or harmful effects on prediction. Function tokens contribute via hidden-state computation, not attention mass received — challenging interpretability methods and KV-cache eviction strategies that rely on attention scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability literature, but whether this degradation causally limits contextual retrieval has never been empirically tested. The paper aims to move from descriptive characterization to causal intervention, questioning whether attention-score-based analyses are prescriptively meaningful.

Method: Six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2: (1) characterization of short-term (5–100 token) attention degradation patterns with exponential-then-plateau fitting; (2) function token anchoring analysis across absolute positional encoding, RoPE, and other schemes; (3) causal intervention via strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries; (4) Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), a causal mechanism that biases attention logits toward function token positions; (5) multi-fact retrieval probes to test whether degradation rate predicts retrieval accuracy.

Result: Attention degradation follows a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern inversely correlated with depth. Function token anchoring is architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion causally reduces degradation in the 40–80 token range via syntactic boundary alignment. Critically, RAA increases attention mass by 16–24% but yields null effects on GPT-2/LLaMA-1B, harm on LLaMA-3B, and net-zero mixed effects on OPT-1.3B. Multi-fact retrieval probes show degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy.

Conclusion: Mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive. Function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive. This has significant implications for interpretability methodology and for attention-score-based inference optimizations such as KV-cache eviction, which may be targeting the wrong signal.

Abstract: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

</details>


### [136] [Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20525)
*Yichen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an autonomous AI agent (GPT-5.5 Pro) using a three-stage prompting pipeline that successfully generated correct disproofs of the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over ℝ in 7/8 trials, producing diverse proofs including both unit-based and novel algebraic-integer approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Following OpenAI's disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture, the authors aim to demonstrate autonomous proof generation capabilities by targeting another major open problem — the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over ℝ — as a benchmark for AI-driven mathematical reasoning.

Method: A simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro employs a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline: (1) proof-plan proposal, (2) proof construction, and (3) review. No problem-specific tuning was used. The system averaged 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial across 8 independent runs.

Result: In 7 out of 8 independent trials, the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over ℝ. In the remaining trial, it correctly identified an unresolved gap. The proofs exhibited diversity: some resembled known unit-based constructions, while others used novel L^p-type regions of algebraic integers avoiding units entirely.

Conclusion: The work provides a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation. Code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs are released, establishing a benchmark for AI mathematical reasoning and demonstrating that general-purpose prompting pipelines can yield novel, diverse proofs for major conjectures.

Abstract: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

</details>


### [137] [ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20526)
*Matthew ffrench-Constant,Daniel Yang,Xinmeng Huang,Sanyam Kapoor*

Main category: cs.AI
