TL;DR: ConfidenceBench evaluates how well 15 frontier LLMs can verbalize calibrated confidence estimates using the Brier score on 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories. Results show that calibration and accuracy diverge substantially — the most accurate model is not necessarily the best-calibrated — establishing verbalized confidence calibration as a distinct axis of LLM reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs deployed in high-stakes settings need not only accuracy but also reliable self-assessment of when they are likely wrong. Standard accuracy benchmarks fail to capture this capability, and existing calibration methods often require logit access, which is unavailable for closed-source models. The authors aim to fill this gap with a prompting-based calibration benchmark applicable to all LLMs.

Method: The authors introduce ConfidenceBench, a benchmark of 200 private multiple-choice questions spanning spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Verbalized confidence is elicited via prompting without logit access. Calibration is measured using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule. Three independent runs are conducted per model, with a calibrated-random baseline (0.1875) as reference.

Result: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieved the lowest Brier score (0.103), substantially outperforming the calibrated-random baseline. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scored 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverged across model families: the most accurate model was not the best-calibrated, and several models performed worse than the baseline despite reasonable accuracy.

Conclusion: Verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important dimension of LLM reliability, complementary to accuracy-based evaluation. The prompting-based framework makes calibration assessment feasible for both open-source and closed-source systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

</details>


### [138] [Evaluating and Guarding Citation Faithfulness in Agentic Scientific Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20527)
*Taewan Goo,Junsik Kim,Kyulhee Han,GwonYul Jo,Jong-Soo Kim,Tae-Hyung Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current benchmarks for agentic LLM literature systems check citation support but never audit the verifier itself. The authors show verifier strictness dramatically changes measured unsupported-citation rates (3–18%) with poor inter-verifier agreement on flags. They propose a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a split-conformal guard that provides distribution-free, finite-sample bounds on unsupported citations, validated across multiple models and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic LLM systems that answer scientific questions with citations (e.g., OpenScholar, PaperQA2) are benchmarked on whether their citations are supported, but the reliability of the citation verifiers themselves is never audited. The authors demonstrate that verifier choice alone can swing reported unsupported-citation rates from ~3% to ~18%, and verifiers disagree on which outputs to flag (negative-specific agreement only 0.27–0.30). This makes cross-paper comparison invalid and any single flag set untrustworthy. There is no standardized, validated protocol for measuring or bounding citation support reliability.

Method: The authors propose two components: (1) a gold-anchored evaluation protocol that validates the verifier against human gold labels, measures re-attribution, and calibrates guarantees using human judgments rather than another model's verdicts, with a deterministic BM25 retriever serving as the re-attribution step; and (2) a split-conformal guard layer that wraps any chosen flagging rule to produce a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on the rate of truly unsupported citations that escape detection. They also identify "calibration-negative difficulty" as the condition governing bound transfer from calibration to deployment, with a concrete recalibration recipe. Validation spans four open 27–35B models and three agentic pipelines on SciFact, QASA, and PubMedQA.

Result: The verifier achieves 0.94 recall on the supported class (held out). The proposed protocol and guard are validated across all four models and three pipelines on public benchmarks, with confidence intervals on every headline number. The split-conformal bound holds on held-out gold data. The entire system ships as an open-source single-GPU kit.

Conclusion: Citation verification in agentic LLM systems is currently unreliable and unstandardized. A gold-anchored protocol with a swappable verifier and a conformal guard layer provides the first measurable, bounded guarantee on unsupported citation rates, enabling trustworthy cross-paper comparison and deployable safety guarantees.

Abstract: Agentic LLM systems such as OpenScholar and PaperQA2 read the scientific literature and return cited answers, and both they and their benchmarks already check whether those citations hold, with a fixed attribution model or human graders. Neither audits the reliability of that check itself. We show it is not reliable, and that this matters. On identical agent outputs the measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to about 18% depending only on the verifier's strictness, and although verifiers agree on which citations are supported, they disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27 to 0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy and cross-paper comparison is invalid without a named verifier and protocol.
  We present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that make this behavior measurable and bounded. The protocol validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates a guarantee against human gold rather than another model's verdict; the verifier is a swappable instrument chosen on cost (recall 0.94 on the supported class, held out), and re-attribution is a commodity step where a deterministic BM25 matches the best open generator. The guard adds a split-conformal layer placing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flagging rule, a guarantee on catch rate rather than conclusion correctness. The bound holds on held-out gold, and we identify and quantify the condition governing its transfer to deployment, calibration-negative difficulty, with a concrete recalibration recipe, left untested by prior conformal-factuality work.
  Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on public benchmarks (SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA), with confidence intervals on every headline number, the protocol and guard ship as an open single-GPU kit.

</details>


### [139] [PromptPack: Scaling LLM Annotation Agents for Online Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20528)
*Sebastian Koralewski,Merwan Barlier,Yulia Stolin,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PromptPack is a batched LLM annotation agent that reduces per-creative prompting costs by 89% and increases throughput 2.5x via in-context batching, shared prompts, XML structuring, and output correction, all while preserving downstream CTR model AUC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-call LLM annotation per ad creative yields strong CTR gains in production but is prohibitively expensive at scale because redundant system instructions account for 94% of billed input tokens. The core motivation is to eliminate this token redundancy to make LLM-based feature extraction economically viable at production scale.

Method: PromptPack introduces three key components: (1) in-context batching that processes multiple creatives in a single LLM call using a shared system prompt to amortize token overhead; (2) a strict XML structural envelope that enforces a deterministic schema for structured feature extraction across all creatives in the batch; and (3) an output correction layer that validates and fixes malformed outputs to ensure pipeline compatibility. The authors evaluate via an offline retrieval benchmark with a logistic-regression ranker, using AUC and a novel metric called Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL) to assess signal quality of generated features.

Result: At batch size 20, PromptPack reduces LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x compared to the unbatched production baseline, while fully preserving AUC. The VWAL metric confirms that signal quality of generated features is maintained.

Conclusion: In-context batching with structured output enforcement is a highly effective strategy for scaling LLM-based feature annotation in industrial recommendation systems, achieving dramatic cost and throughput improvements without sacrificing downstream model performance.

Abstract: Online recommendation platforms increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract structured features from ad creatives. While deploying a single-call LLM annotation agent yields significant Click-Through Rate (CTR) improvements in our live production environment, per-creative prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale. The redundant system instructions sent in every request account for 94% of billed input tokens. To break this cost bottleneck, we introduce PromptPack, a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation agent. PromptPack achieves this scale via in-context batching, combining a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives simultaneously. We evaluate PromptPack via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker. To deeply profile the agent's behavior, we measure AUC and introduce Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), a novel metric capturing the signal quality of the generated features. Compared to our live, unbatched production baseline, PromptPack at batch size 20 cuts our LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x while fully preserving AUC.

</details>


### [140] [DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20531)
*Jerzy Kamiński,Ilya Galyukshev,Artem Kuznetsov,Sergey Chuprin,Kirill Redko,Aidar Shumbalov,Anna Kalyuzhnaya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DynamicMCPBench is a reusable, live evaluation framework for LLM agents operating over MCP servers. Rather than scoring fixed ground-truth answers, it generates goals, executes reference trajectories, distills them into effect checkpoints, and scores agents on whether they reproduce those effects. At scale (24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks across 15 categories), even the strongest agents solve only ~50% of tasks; 31% remain unsolved by any model; accuracy drops from 39% to 13% as tool-chain length increases. Human validation confirms reliable automatic scoring (κ = 0.76).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks evaluate against static final answers or fixed tool lists, which are brittle when underlying MCP server data is live and stateful. There is a need for a reusable, server-agnostic evaluation framework that scores agents on achieving intended side effects rather than matching predetermined outputs.

Method: DynamicMCPBench is a framework, not a fixed dataset. Given MCP servers and models, it (1) generates realistic goal tasks across 15 categories targeting distinct tool-use challenges, (2) pursues each goal live to record a successful reference trajectory, (3) distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints (e.g., file created, database row modified), and (4) scores agents on whether they reproduce those effects. Scoring uses pass³ (all three independent attempts must succeed). Automatic scoring is validated via a human study.

Result: At scale (24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks): strongest agents solve ~50% of tasks; 31% of tasks are solved by no model; accuracy degrades sharply with tool-chain length (39% shortest → 13% longest). Human validation yields chance-corrected agreement of 0.76, confirming scoring reliability. The 15 task categories each surface distinct tool-use failure modes.

Conclusion: DynamicMCPBench enables practitioners to benchmark LLM agents on their own live MCP servers with reliable, effect-based automatic scoring. The results expose a consistent and severe limitation: current agents cannot reliably handle long, multi-step agentic tasks, with performance collapsing as tool-chain depth increases.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed "ground-truth" list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3: it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

</details>


### [141] [CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20553)
*Yubo Wang,Qiuyu Zhao,Zenghui Sun,Shichao Dong,Jinsong Lan,Xiaoyong Zhu,Haoyang Li,Bo Zheng,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CMI-Mem is a lightweight RL-based memory manager for agent systems that uses a hybrid reward combining downstream QA correctness with Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), where CMI evaluates information contribution of new inputs relative to memory state without relying on sampled QA pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory manager models rely on LLM-judged synthetic QA pairs for memory valuation, making performance dependent on the quality of sampled queries and the downstream reader model. This creates a brittle evaluation pipeline that can be circumvented.

Method: Proposes CMI-Mem, a lightweight memory manager trained via reinforcement learning. The key innovation is a hybrid reward function that combines: (1) downstream QA correctness for task grounding, and (2) intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), which quantifies how much new information a conversational input contributes given the current memory state, without conditioning on any sampled QA query. CMI thus complements QA-based rewards rather than replacing them.

Result: The paper releases both the codebase and a CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint, demonstrating practical viability of the approach.

Conclusion: CMI provides an effective, query-agnostic signal for memory valuation that complements traditional QA-grounded rewards, enabling more robust memory management in agent systems.

Abstract: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

</details>


### [142] [AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20554)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Simone Angelini,Emiliano Pallotti,Pierpaolo Salvo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A GNN-based Learning-to-Optimise framework is proposed for real-time NR-V2X multi-hop relay selection, using an MILP oracle for supervision. The GINE model achieves oracle-comparable connectivity with orders-of-magnitude faster inference, enabling scalable urban V2X operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense urban V2X communications suffer from limited RSU density, frequent NLOS conditions, and dynamic topologies, preventing stable single-hop CAV connectivity. While MILP provides optimal multi-hop relay selection, its exponential computational complexity precludes real-time use. A fast, near-optimal relay selection method is needed.

Method: Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs (CAVs and RSUs as nodes, radio links as edges with propagation-aware features). An offline MILP oracle generates optimal relay decisions as supervision labels. An edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) is trained to approximate these decisions. Experiments use an integrated SUMO–GEMV2 simulation pipeline on large-scale urban datasets.

Result: The GINE-based L2O approach achieves connectivity performance comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude, delivering near-constant inference latency regardless of network density.

Conclusion: The framework enables cost-effective, scalable, real-time NR-V2X relay selection by leveraging existing vehicular assets, supporting reliable low-latency communications in smart city environments without dense RSU deployment.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude. The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

</details>


### [143] [KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20556)
*Yan Zhu,Y. Chen,Rebecca Faust*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KeySI is an interaction framework that enables users to tune pre-trained language model embeddings through feature-level feedback by organizing extracted keywords into concept groups, reducing the need for manual document inspection and lowering the barrier to domain adaptation of embedding models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models struggle to capture domain-specific semantics, and adapting them typically requires large labeled datasets and technical expertise. Existing visual interaction methods operate at the document level, forcing users to open and assess individual documents — a labor-intensive process. There is a need for a more efficient, lower-barrier approach to provide training signals for model tuning.

Method: KeySI introduces feature-level feedback via keyword-based concept specification. Users organize extracted keywords into groups representing semantic concepts. The system translates these keyword groupings into document-level supervision signals for embedding model tuning. The prototype includes: (1) curation of representative keywords from a corpus, (2) visualization of both keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, (3) interactive specification of keyword groups, and (4) iterative refinement through system feedback.

Result: Evaluation was conducted through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments. Results demonstrate KeySI's effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment for domain-specific text analysis tasks.

Conclusion: Feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification is an effective alternative to document-level feedback for tuning embedding models, significantly reducing the manual effort and technical expertise required for domain adaptation while maintaining the ability to capture user intent.

Abstract: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

</details>


### [144] [WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20638)
*Yichuan Liu,Daniel Cummings,Nick Vadlamudi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WaveformQA is a benchmark of 360 QA pairs for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. Frontier LLMs perform well on simple queries but degrade on complex temporal/multi-step questions; an event-time JSON format outperforms the standard VCD format for LLM reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM reasoning over digital waveforms—critical for hardware design verification—remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks focus on HDL code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context, lacking dedicated evaluation of temporal reasoning capabilities.

Method: The authors introduce WaveformQA, an open-source QA benchmark with 360 questions across 8 difficulty-graded categories (including multi-signal correlation and event ordering). Waveforms are generated from open-source hardware designs with programmatically derived ground truths. Frontier LLMs are evaluated using both standard VCD format and a proposed event-time JSON representation.

Result: Frontier LLMs achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries but performance declines on complex temporal and multi-step questions due to context window constraints and reasoning difficulties. The event-time JSON representation consistently improves reasoning accuracy over the standardized VCD format.

Conclusion: WaveformQA fills a gap in LLM evaluation for digital waveform temporal reasoning. The JSON-based waveform representation offers a practical improvement for LLM-based verification workflows, and the extensible open-source framework enables further research in this direction.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

</details>


### [145] [NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20709)
*Paul Furgale,Severin Klingler,James Nolan,Matt Staats,Gaia Di Lorenzo,Elisa Martinez Abad,Christian Schüller,Razvan Dinu,Alessio Devoto,Pascal Berard,Gal Kaplun,Elad Sarafian,Riccardo Roveri,Leon Derczynski,Ricardo Silveira Cabral*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NOOA is a Python framework where agents are regular Python objects: methods are actions, docstrings are prompts, type annotations are contracts, and methods with "..." bodies are LLM-completed at runtime, unifying developer and agent interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional agent development fragments code across prompt templates, tool schemas, callbacks, and workflow graphs. NOOA unifies these into a single Python object model, allowing agent behavior to be tested, traced, refactored, and improved like standard software.

Method: NOOA treats an agent as a Python object where methods with "..." bodies are filled at runtime by an LLM-driven loop, while methods with normal bodies remain deterministic Python. It adopts existing Python abstractions (type annotations, docstrings, fields) and exposes agent-specific capabilities (context, events, state rendering, memory, validated LLM loops) through Pythonic APIs.

Result: Current models use the NOOA interface effectively across targeted capability tests and benchmarks including SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3. Six model-facing design ideas are combined: typed I/O, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs.

Conclusion: NOOA demonstrates that the agent-as-a-Python-object model is viable and effective. The community is already converging on several of its design ideas. The framework bridges the gap between agent development and traditional software engineering practices.

Abstract: Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python. This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events. We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

</details>


### [146] [ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20764)
*Pavel Golikov,Evgenii Opryshko,Gennady Pekhimenko,Mark C. Jeffrey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARBIGRAPH is a benchmark generator that creates controllable, composable task graphs to evaluate tool-assisted language agents on their ability to manage context across extended reasoning workflows, revealing significant accuracy degradation on dependent tasks that single-task evaluation misses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate language agents on isolated tasks, failing to capture how well agents retain, update, compose, and discard context across multi-step, interdependent reasoning workflows. There is a need for a controllable, automatically verifiable framework to stress-test these capabilities.

Method: ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem paired with an executable Python solver. Tasks are composed through typed intermediate states (scalar and list values), enabling construction of task graphs with controllable length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value types. The authors instantiate it with math, GSM-style word problems, and Python-tracing categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four graph topologies.

Result: The Qwen3.5-27B agent achieves high accuracy on isolated tasks but degrades substantially on complex dependent tasks, with accuracy dropping by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. Failures emerge that single-task evaluation cannot expose.

Conclusion: ARBIGRAPH effectively exposes context-management failures in tool-assisted language agents that are invisible under single-task evaluation, demonstrating the importance of multi-step, dependency-aware benchmarking for assessing real-world reasoning agent capabilities.

Abstract: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

</details>


### [147] [The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20781)
*Bonny Banerjee,Shreya Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents the Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, a formal analytical framework for determining when, where, and why AI replaces human labor in hierarchical organizations. Central to the model is an encoded economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. Key findings include the Human-AI Substitution Principle, abrupt workforce transitions, flatter hierarchies, elevated middle-management automation vulnerability, and a skill threshold governing highly skilled worker displacement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI is rapidly transforming organizations, yet there is no formal, unified analytical framework for understanding when human employees will be replaced by AI. The authors aim to fill this gap by modeling the fundamental economic asymmetry between how humans acquire skills and how AI scales in capability, and by deriving structural conditions under which substitution occurs.

Method: The authors develop the Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, an analytical model of hierarchical organizations that formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The model incorporates risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk to derive conditions for human-AI replacement.

Result: Key results include: (1) the Human-AI Substitution Principle, a precise condition grounded in formal asymmetry that determines when AI replaces human labor; (2) AI adoption can trigger abrupt workforce transitions; (3) hybrid human-AI organizations can emerge, with risk heterogeneity sustaining both roles without minimum-human-fraction constraints; (4) flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control result from AI adoption; (5) middle-management roles show elevated automation vulnerability; and (6) highly skilled worker vulnerability depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials.

Conclusion: The HAT model unifies automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a coherent theory of AI-driven organizational transformation. It provides actionable structural insights into which roles, under what conditions, are most susceptible to AI substitution.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

</details>


### [148] [Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20791)
*Phillip Howard,Xin Su,Allen Roush,Manikandan Ravikiran,Amir Abdullah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: High-temperature sampling increases LLM output diversity but weakens safety guardrails. The authors propose a sequential decoding method that preserves 91-99% of greedy decoding refusal behavior at high temperatures with minimal latency overhead, without degrading safe-prompt responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-temperature sampling is essential for diverse LLM outputs and truncation methods have mitigated coherence issues, but no existing solution addresses the critical problem that elevated temperatures reduce model refusal rates on harmful prompts. The work fills this gap.

Method: A sequential decoding approach that preserves the model's greedy decoding refusal behavior when operating at high temperatures. The method intervenes during the decoding process to detect and maintain refusal responses that would otherwise be lost due to the flattened probability distribution, with minimal additional latency.

Result: The approach preserved 91-99% of greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets. It achieved this without compromising the quality and diversity of responses to safe prompts, and incurred only minimal additional latency overhead.

Conclusion: Refusal behavior can be efficiently maintained under high-temperature sampling regimes, enabling applications that require both output diversity and robust safety guardrails. The proposed sequential decoding method offers a practical, low-latency solution to this previously unaddressed problem.

Abstract: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

</details>


### [149] [Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20806)
*Tomohiro Harada,Enrique Alba,Gabriel Luque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces PTME, a precision-aware profiling framework that jointly measures Precision, execution Time, peak Memory, and Energy consumption of lightweight LLMs via direct hardware measurements. Applied to edge-class settings, results show that static proxies (parameter count, FLOPs) predict cost but not accuracy, and Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated model configurations missed by single-metric evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lightweight LLMs are increasingly deployed in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments where energy, time, and memory directly impact usability. However, existing efficiency evaluations rely on proxy metrics (parameter count, FLOPs) that are decoupled from task precision and lack joint, hardware-level measurement of the physical costs that matter in practice.

Method: The authors propose a PTME experimental framework that profiles lightweight LLM inference across four joint dimensions: Precision (task accuracy), execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption — all measured via direct hardware instrumentation. The framework is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs running locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks covering code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding.

Result: Static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope raises cost without improving precision, with execution time amplified more than energy and larger models penalized most. No single model dominates across all PTME dimensions; Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments.

Conclusion: Selecting lightweight LLMs based solely on size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy risks choosing suboptimal deployment candidates. PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost, providing practical guidance for model selection under varying resource constraints.

Abstract: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

</details>


### [150] [Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20814)
*Hai-Nam Duy Vuong,Duy-Anh Bui,Trong-Nghia Nguyen,Kim-Ngan Thi Nguyen,Trang Mai Xuan,Tien-Cuong Nguyen,Van-Dem Pham,Thien Van Luong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a guide-grounded multimodal framework for ECG report generation that injects curated clinical knowledge (a distilled ECG Interpretation Guide) into a CNN+Grad-CAM+LLM pipeline. This approach reduces hallucinations and improves semantic alignment with reference reports, raising BERTScore from 0.818 to 0.953.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models for ECG analysis suffer from limited interpretability, and LLM-based report generation faces hallucination risks. Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+LLM frameworks produce explanations weakly grounded in diagnostic criteria, undermining trustworthiness and reproducibility in clinical settings.

Method: A CNN with Grad-CAM generates class probabilities and heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guidelines are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, injected as a fixed knowledge block. A multimodal LLM then generates structured diagnostic reports conditioned on: the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the injected guide, ensuring guideline-consistent terminology.

Result: On the full PTB-XL test set, the guide-grounded framework significantly improved BERTScore from 0.818 to 0.953 over a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicating substantially closer alignment with reference reports, while maintaining competitive classification performance.

Conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce LLM hallucinations and enhance clinical plausibility of ECG explanations, advancing explainable cardiac diagnosis toward real-world deployment.

Abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

</details>


### [151] [Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20820)
*Christian Arzate Cruz,Stefanos Gkikas,Houshyar Asadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) as efficient alternatives to graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition, demonstrating that TCNs achieve competitive accuracy with substantially fewer parameters and lower latency while enabling interpretability analyses of body-region contributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition are computationally expensive, limiting their practicality in real-time affective systems. There is a need for efficient yet interpretable alternatives that maintain competitive classification performance.

Method: The authors evaluate a family of TCN models against a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline on the DIEM-A dataset using metrics including accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Interpretability is assessed through region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency analyses.

Result: G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, but TCN-Base trails by only 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points while using 79.18% fewer parameters and achieving approximately 12.5× lower classifier latency. Upper-body motion is the strongest standalone regional cue, body-region usefulness varies by emotion, and different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior.

Conclusion: Lightweight TCNs offer a viable, efficient alternative for body-based emotion recognition with practical advantages for real-time deployment, while also providing complementary insights into how body-region motion cues inform emotion classification.

Abstract: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

</details>


### [152] [Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20827)
*Junchi Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents can be influenced by untrusted evidence even when textual source-authority cues are present. The paper introduces a target-specific authorization audit that isolates the effect of evidence source authority on agent tool/argument selection, finding unauthorized competition in ~5.4% of competing cases and persistent influence patterns under controlled degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents select tools and arguments from mixed-context environments containing both trusted and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant to a decision without being authorized to determine it. The core concern is that agents may ground actions in untrusted evidence even when valid trusted evidence exists, undermining safety and reliability in agentic systems. Existing evaluation frameworks lack systematic methods to isolate whether unauthorized evidence causally influences agent decisions.

Method: The authors propose a **target-specific authorization audit** with the following components: (1) labeling context factors separately for each tool/argument target; (2) a primary causal test that fixes task, proposition, position, and policy while varying only the source authority of the proposition; (3) a secondary test that weakens valid evidence and uses context-subset interactions as a localization diagnostic. The audit was applied across 450 controlled next-action tasks spanning multiple open-weight LLM families. Metrics compare trusted vs. untrusted variants, measuring competing cases (where untrusted evidence conflicts with trusted evidence) and supporting cases (where untrusted evidence aligns). A controlled degradation protocol further characterizes error persistence patterns.

Result: Across 450 controlled tasks: (1) trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in **5.4% of competing cases** versus **1.7% of supporting cases**; (2) under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition persists in a **full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern** in **2.4% of comparisons** (95% CI: 2.1–3.0%). These are controlled stress-set rates, not natural deployment prevalence estimates. Models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this behavioral sensitivity does not eliminate the influence of untrusted evidence on action selection.

Conclusion: LLM agents exhibit measurable susceptibility to unauthorized evidence influence despite surface-level responsiveness to authority cues. The target-specific audit framework provides a principled method for evaluating evidence-grounding in agentic systems. The authors caution that their rates reflect controlled stress-test conditions and should not be interpreted as deployment prevalence. The work highlights a fundamental tension between relevance-based attention mechanisms and authorization-based safety constraints in LLM agents.

Abstract: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

</details>


### [153] [Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20848)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a behavioral audit method that goes beyond diagnostic accuracy to assess how medical LLMs use evidence. By decomposing patient information into evidence units and analyzing interaction effects on diagnosis scores, the study finds that most interactions are clinically plausible, but failures concentrate in negated/absent findings and local evidence. Accuracy alone can mask evidence-use failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnostic accuracy benchmarks for medical LLMs fail to reveal whether models arrive at correct diagnoses through appropriate use of clinical evidence or through spurious shortcuts. There is a need for evaluation methods that audit the reasoning process itself — specifically, how models weigh and combine individual pieces of patient information when making diagnostic decisions.

Method: The authors propose a three-step behavioral audit: (1) decompose each case into discrete evidence units; (2) score candidate diagnoses under systematically controlled subsets of evidence to compute marginal contributions; (3) mine low-order (pairwise and three-way) interactions among evidence units. Crucially, the framework separates interaction discovery from failure assignment — large or negative interactions may reflect legitimate differential diagnosis reasoning, while only interactions failing robustness checks and clinical review are flagged as suspicious. Five open-weight LLMs are evaluated across three datasets: DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. A blinded five-reviewer enriched review of 130 DDXPlus items provides clinical validation.

Result: Faithful support interactions and differential conflict/cancellation effects account for the majority of interaction strength across all datasets, indicating that most evidence interactions reflect clinically plausible reasoning rather than model failures. Invalid or shortcut-like cases were concentrated in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. In the DDXPlus enriched review sample, reviewers identified specific failure patterns that would be invisible to accuracy-only evaluation.

Conclusion: Diagnostic accuracy alone is an insufficient metric for medical LLM evaluation, as it can conceal problematic evidence-use patterns. Role-aware behavioral audits that examine how models combine clinical evidence offer a necessary complementary evaluation paradigm, enabling detection of shortcut reliance and invalid reasoning even when final diagnoses are correct.

Abstract: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [154] [Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20852)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CodeMonitorBench introduces a red-teaming protocol to evaluate whether weaker LLMs can detect hidden bugs in code that passes public tests, finding that even scaffolded verifiers miss most hidden bugs at low false-positive rates, and adversarial overfitting to public tests further degrades detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated code often passes visible (public) tests but still harbors specification-violating bugs. The paper investigates whether a weaker LLM-based verifier can identify these residual hidden bugs after code has cleared the public-test gate, addressing a deployment-like monitoring scenario.

Method: The authors propose Code Monitor Red Teaming, a protocol that holds constant the public-check information boundary while systematically varying three dimensions: (1) generator pressure (including adversarial public-test overfitting), (2) verifier scaffolding (e.g., chain-of-thought, tool use), and (3) weak-to-strong capability gaps. They instantiate this as CodeMonitorBench, covering function-level, data-science, and workflow code domains, with 71,000 generated candidates where 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 subsequently fail hidden tests. Evaluation uses AUROC and low-FPR miss rates. An inferability audit distinguishes verifier failures from evidence-limited cases (M1 evidence limits).

Result: Weak verifiers improve with better scaffolding and stronger model families but still miss most hidden bugs at a 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates across most experimental configurations. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the performance gap under the same evidence boundary. The inferability audit reveals that remaining misses are a mixture of genuine verifier failures and cases where public-test evidence alone is fundamentally insufficient (M1 limits).

Conclusion: Passing public tests provides insufficient evidence for specification correctness, and even scaffolded weak verifiers cannot reliably detect hidden bugs at practical false-positive rates. The monitor-red-teaming protocol offers a systematic framework for evaluating and improving code verification under realistic deployment constraints, highlighting both verifier capability gaps and inherent information-boundary limitations.

Abstract: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

</details>


### [155] [Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20891)
*Pengyu Zhu,Lijun Li,Longju Yang,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MisKnow-Agent introduces a framework that generates misleading knowledge to test Deep Research agents, revealing that even limited exposure to credible-looking but false information during long-horizon research workflows can lead agents to adopt false conclusions in final reports. Despite focused verifiers detecting the misleading content, agents still incorporate it into final outputs, and existing defenses only partially mitigate this vulnerability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Research agents — LLM-based systems that perform planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation over extended workflows — lack rigorous reliability evaluation in open information environments. The core concern is that factually misleading but apparently credible knowledge encountered during research can propagate through the agent's workflow and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports, a failure mode that remains underexplored.

Method: The authors propose MisKnow-Agent, a framework that constructs misleading knowledge instances with controllable authority levels and styles, validated through quality control, yielding 5,933 instances built atop the DeepResearch Benchmark. Extensive experiments are conducted across both open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents. They evaluate the gap between focused corpus verification (using search-enabled verifier models) and workflow-level evidence use, and test three pre- and post-research defense configurations (individually and in combination) against false-conclusion adoption.

Result: Key findings: (1) Even limited exposure to misleading knowledge induces false-conclusion adoption in final agent reports. (2) Search-enabled verifiers consistently identify misleading instances during focused validation, yet the same instances are still adopted during long-horizon research — revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. (3) All three defense configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption.

Conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, going beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report generation alone. Current agents exhibit a broad reliability vulnerability to misleading knowledge propagation.

Abstract: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

</details>


### [156] [Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20913)
*Yi Xiong,Yuan-Yuan Cheng,Xiao-Ming Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fine-tuning diffusion models for new domains involves a trade-off between target-specific generation and preserving general capability. This paper proposes a source-prior-driven selective adaptation method that learns a static mask to identify which pretrained parameters are better suited for downstream adaptation, then applies structured update strategies to those selected parameters, achieving a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fine-tuning methods for diffusion models (both full and parameter-efficient) handle the trade-off between target-domain adaptation and preserving general generative capability only implicitly. The authors aim to make this trade-off explicit through selective parameter adaptation guided by pretrained source knowledge.

Method: The method is built on two observations: (1) the degradation of general generative capability varies significantly across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters with minimal impact on general capability are structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Based on these insights, the method first learns a static mask to explicitly identify parameters more suitable for downstream adaptation. It then constructs structured update strategies targeting only the selected subset of parameters, preserving the rest intact.

Result: The proposed method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off compared to existing strong baselines, as demonstrated experimentally.

Conclusion: The source-prior-driven selective adaptation approach provides an efficient and effective way to fine-tune diffusion models for new domains while explicitly preserving the pretrained model's broad generative capabilities.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

</details>


### [157] [Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20916)
*Deyu Jing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Traceable Scholarship" as a normative standard for AI-assisted humanities research, introducing page anchors and citation-first generation to ensure sources remain verifiable. A three-layer reference implementation (AIH-Infra) is demonstrated on a Kant corpus, arguing traceability is the precondition for public, refutable scholarship in the generative AI era.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI produces fluent but potentially unmoored scholarly text that lacks verifiable grounding — no clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. The core risk is not mere factual error but the illusion of established explanation without citational provenance. The authors argue that without traceability, humanistic research loses its public and refutable character in the age of AI.

Method: The paper situates traceable scholarship within three historical revolutions (print, digital, generative AI). It introduces a conceptual framework comprising: page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE markers, human verification protocols, four-level compliance grading, and Scope Contracts. A three-layer reference architecture (AIH-Infra) is presented: Contexture (document structuring layer), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study applies this to a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base, demonstrating retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading.

Result: The Kant case study demonstrates that traceability mechanisms enable retrieval correction, systematic evidence grading, and judgment downgrading when source support is insufficient. The three-layer architecture shows feasibility of embedding page-anchored provenance into AI-assisted research workflows.

Conclusion: Traceability is not merely a software feature but the fundamental condition under which humanistic research can remain public, accountable, and refutable in the generative AI era. Traceable Scholarship is proposed as the minimum normative standard for AI-assisted humanistic inquiry.

Abstract: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

</details>


### [158] [OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20918)
*Tong Zhao,Yuyang Hu,Reed Li,Yu Lu,Haibo Shi,Yutao Zhu,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPOD is an on-policy distillation framework that routes each student-generated response to a modality-specific teacher (text, image, or audio), using selective token-level guidance and independent modality weighting to train a unified omni-modal model that outperforms both pooled-data training and individual specialists across twelve benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training a single omni-modal model on pooled multimodal data typically underperforms modality-specific specialists, and naive multi-teacher distillation introduces competing guidance where improving one modality harms another. A method is needed to effectively coordinate modality-specific teachers without cross-modal interference.

Method: OPOD extends on-policy distillation with three key mechanisms: (1) response routing — each student response is directed to the teacher matching its modality (text, image, or audio); (2) selective token-level guidance — teacher supervision is applied only where the teacher assigns higher probability than the student; (3) independent modality weighting — the influence of each modality teacher is tuned separately during training. The teacher assesses both final-answer correctness and reasoning quality.

Result: Across 12 benchmarks and 3 backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale (70.8, 51.7, 46.2), surpassing the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it beats both the base model and a jointly post-trained counterpart on all 12 benchmarks, and ranks first or second on 11/12 even when individual specialists are included. Specialists are discarded post-training.

Conclusion: Coordinated modality-specific on-policy distillation effectively improves omni-modal models while maintaining cross-modal balance, yielding a single deployable model that outperforms separate specialists without their runtime cost.

Abstract: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher.
