OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

</details>


### [159] [Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20925)
*Shen Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues that entity importance in AI knowledge systems should not be collapsed into a single scalar score. It proposes a dual-signal representation distinguishing audience evaluation from structural authority, and empirically demonstrates—using IMDb ratings, Wikipedia PageRank, and Wikidata—that these two dimensions are statistically distinct, weakly correlated, and non-redundant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI knowledge systems typically reduce entity importance to a single score (from human judgments or graph topology), discarding meaningful distinctions between how audiences evaluate an entity and how the knowledge graph structurally positions it. This compression may harm performance in downstream tasks like retrieval, recommendation, or evidence selection where different importance signals matter.

Method: The authors propose a minimal dual-signal framework: (1) an audience-evaluation dimension operationalized via IMDb user ratings, and (2) a structural-authority dimension operationalized via PageRank on Wikipedia hyperlink graphs. They align 482 movie entities across IMDb, Wikidata, and Wikipedia, constructing 13,690 directed relationships, then compare the two rankings using Spearman correlation and top-k overlap analysis.

Result: The two dimensions show a statistically significant but weak correlation (Spearman ρ = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Overlap is only 10% in the top 10 entities and 34% in the top 100. Entity-level divergence occurs in both directions, confirming that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals.

Conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority should not be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is a minimal knowledge-representation framework and empirical evidence supporting its dimensional necessity. The authors advocate for task-aware AI systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

Abstract: AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

</details>


### [160] [SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20926)
*Yinhao Tang,Youqing Fang,Yanan Sun,Wenran Liu,Weiming Zhang,Bin Liu,Kuikun Liu,Wenwei Zhang,Kai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciExplore is a benchmark with 103 expert-curated tasks across 10+ scientific disciplines, evaluating LLMs and agents on four progressively harder task types: database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source knowledge synthesis. Current models show sharp performance degradation as complexity increases, with very low accuracy on the hardest synthesis tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on general-domain retrieval or static QA, failing to capture the complex, multi-step information-seeking and reasoning workflows that characterize real scientific research. There is a need for a benchmark that probes higher-level capabilities like evidence grounding and cross-source synthesis.

Method: The authors constructed SciExplore with four task types of increasing difficulty: (1) scientific database navigation (entity-level reasoning), (2) ambiguous literature retrieval (document-level identification), (3) missing reference completion (evidence-level grounding), and (4) cross-source structured knowledge synthesis (domain-level synthesis). Over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents were evaluated across 103 tasks spanning 10+ disciplines.

Result: Performance degrades sharply as task complexity increases across all evaluated models and agents. The most challenging structured synthesis tasks yield extremely low accuracy, exposing significant limitations in current systems' ability to handle realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

Conclusion: Current LLMs and autonomous agents exhibit substantial performance gaps in realistic scientific research workflows, particularly in tasks requiring cross-source synthesis and evidence grounding. SciExplore provides a rigorous testbed for advancing scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

</details>


### [161] [Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20937)
*Chinmaya Kumar Dehury,Boris Sedlak,Alaa Saleh,Ilir Murturi,Lauri Loven,Satish Narayana Srirama,Praveen Kumar Donta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), a paradigm shift where derived intelligence becomes a first-class, independently manageable and shareable entity across the edge-cloud continuum, supported by a three-layer architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Edge Intelligence research is limited to AI-for-resource-management and lightweight on-device AI deployment. There is no framework that treats intelligence itself as a first-class entity that can be described, discovered, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge environments — a gap as society moves from the information age to the intelligence age.

Method: The authors introduce the Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI) conceptual framework with a three-layer architecture. They identify and examine key enabling technologies and research dimensions including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication protocols, discoverability mechanisms, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

Result: The paper is visionary/conceptual in nature, so it presents a novel architecture and research roadmap rather than empirical results. Key outcomes include the CEI architectural blueprint and a structured research agenda spanning ten enabling dimensions.

Conclusion: CEI represents a necessary evolution toward intelligence-centric edge computing, where intelligence is treated as an independently manageable, shareable, and reusable asset. Realizing this vision requires advances across multiple research dimensions, from semantic representation to marketplace mechanisms and standardization.

Abstract: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

</details>


### [162] [From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20970)
*Weihan Zhang,Xuan Zhao,Yenwen Peng,Yuqi Chen,Jun Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes reformulating implicit neural representations for time-varying volumetric data by replacing dense spatiotemporal point-wise sampling with spatially indexed time series trained via sequence-level supervision. This reduces training cost, improves reconstruction quality, and synergizes with mixture-of-experts architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard INRs for time-varying volumetric data rely on dense coordinate-wise sampling over space and time, which is computationally expensive and inefficiently leverages temporal structure. The authors argue this design choice is suboptimal and that full spatiotemporal sampling density is unnecessary.

Method: Instead of sampling individual (x,y,z,t) coordinates, the data is represented as a collection of spatially indexed time series. INRs are trained with sequence-level supervision over each spatial location's full temporal evolution, using structured losses over entire sequences rather than scalar point-wise predictions. This reformulation is architecture-agnostic and is further extended with a mixture-of-experts (MoE) instantiation that allocates capacity based on heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

Result: The sequence-level reformulation consistently improves reconstruction quality across various existing INR architectures while significantly reducing training cost. The proposed MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality over both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods.

Conclusion: Dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Structured, sequence-level training over spatially indexed time series is a more efficient and effective paradigm that can be combined with MoE architectures for stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

</details>


### [163] [Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20981)
*Jay Gor,Karm Dave,Akshita Abrol,Rajesh Gupta,Sudeep Tanwar,Zhengkui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey examines the interdependent design challenges in efficient multimodal inference, arguing that techniques like visual token compression, MoE routing, KV-cache optimization, quantization, and edge deployment cannot be treated in isolation due to their complex cross-interactions. It organizes the literature around these couplings, identifies key accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models, and outlines open problems in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, and hardware-aware co-design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient multimodal inference faces constraints beyond model quality and FLOP count—namely the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy budgets. Current approaches treat optimization techniques as independent, but in practice they interact in ways that can undermine expected gains (e.g., token compression affecting routing, quantization altering router logits, hardware constraints turning compute savings into memory bottlenecks). The field lacks a unified perspective on these couplings.

Method: This is a survey/review paper that synthesizes recent advances across multiple sub-areas: visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. The authors organize the literature around the interaction effects among these techniques, identifying design trade-offs (accuracy vs. token budget, static vs. adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency vs. expert collapse, low-bit inference vs. modality-specific degradation). They also propose a new diagnostic metric, Temporal Routing Consistency, for evaluating video MoE models.

Result: The survey reveals that multimodal efficiency techniques exhibit strong interdependence: visual token compression shifts downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions; routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity; quantized router logits influence expert assignment; KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence; and hardware constraints often convert computational savings into memory/communication bottlenecks. The paper maps these interactions systematically and identifies Temporal Routing Consistency as a meaningful diagnostic for temporal coherence in video MoE routing.

Conclusion: Efficient multimodal inference requires holistic co-design rather than isolated optimization of individual components. The paper calls for research in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence. It positions these interaction-aware approaches as necessary for practical deployment under real-world latency, memory, and energy constraints.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

</details>


### [164] [GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20982)
*Vishal Ishwar Naik,Chenyu Xu,Donna Dong,Hussein Hassan,Abhishek Pradhan,Ofer Mendelevitch,Tallat Shafat,Humayun Irshad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GABench is a benchmark of 580 scenarios across 6 domains for evaluating LLM agent safety. Even the best model achieves only 74.8% accuracy. Stronger models under-call required tools, weaker models over-call and mis-select tools. A guardrail implementation recovers 19.9% of failures at 0.5% FPR, outperforming system-prompt defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents gain autonomy with tool access and external environment interaction, ensuring safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. No comprehensive benchmark existed for evaluating agent safety across multiple frameworks and adversarial conditions.

Method: The authors introduce GuardianAgentBench (GABench), comprising 580 scenarios spanning six domains, evaluated across three production-ready frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vectara). The benchmark uses rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Six SOTA models are tested. A structural guardrail intervention is compared against system-prompt-based defenses, measuring failure recovery and false positive rates.

Result: The best configuration achieved only 74.8% overall accuracy. Two distinct failure regimes emerged: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with increased tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning as the steeper bottleneck. The guardrail implementation consistently outperformed system-prompt defenses, recovering 19.9% of failures at a 0.5% false positive rate.

Conclusion: Execution-time structural intervention (guardrails) improves LLM agent safety without disrupting correct behavior, and proves more effective than prompt-based defenses. The benchmark reveals significant safety gaps in current agentic systems, particularly in long-horizon planning and tool selection.

Abstract: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

</details>


### [165] [Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20999)
*Zibin Lin,Shengli Zhang,Taotao Wang,Yihan Xia,Deen Ma,Guofu Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WML introduces a workflow-localized mechanism learning framework that pinpoints failures in agent workflows to specific nodes and mechanisms, then applies targeted fixes by reusing third-party Skill knowledge. It achieves strong results on SpreadsheetBench, WikiTableQuestions, and Compiler-Supported50, with significant cost and token savings via compiled execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Skill optimizers for frozen LLM agents fail to jointly localize workflow failures, identify their causal mechanisms, and reuse relevant third-party Skill knowledge for local repair. There is no unified approach that connects failure attribution to mechanism-level debugging and provenance-aware knowledge reuse.

Method: WML uses Node–Mechanism Attribution to identify the failed workflow node, the implicated mechanisms, and the minimal valid edit target. Single-mechanism defects are routed to L3 (execution-level) resources, while cross-mechanism relational defects go to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified results in optimizer-side memory.

Result: On SpreadsheetBench, WML achieves 90.33±1.53 (DeepSeek) and 74.67±3.51 (Qwen3.6-Flash) Hard Accuracy. Skills transfer zero-shot to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00±2.00 and 83.00±2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML achieves the highest hard-PASS rate and lowest cost per successful task, with compiled execution sharply reducing tokens and API calls versus direct SkillAgent while preserving most successful tasks.

Conclusion: WML demonstrates that precise, mechanism-level attribution of workflow failures combined with provenance-aware third-party knowledge reuse enables effective and efficient Skill optimization for frozen LLM agents, yielding both state-of-the-art accuracy and substantially lower inference costs.

Abstract: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

</details>


### [166] [Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000)
*Hyuk Lim,Seunghyun Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Naju introduces a factorized recurrent update for sequence modeling that decouples the forget gate from the write gate, removing the inherent trade-off between memory retention and overwriting that constrains coupled single-gate designs (like SSMs). By parameterizing discrete transitions directly, Naju achieves strong performance on both long-range retention and active overwriting tasks, outperforming Mamba baselines while maintaining linear complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-sequence memory tracking requires simultaneously (1) near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons and (2) active overwriting of stale information. Existing efficient models, including continuous-time SSMs like Mamba, tend to solve only one side of this dilemma. The authors identify a fundamental structural limitation: coupled single-gate recurrences tie effective retention and write gain through the inequality |r|+w≤1, meaning near-complete retention forces weak writing. This motivates a decoupled design.

Method: Naju factorizes the recurrent update as x_n = f_n ⊙ x_{n-1} + i_n ⊙ (B_n u_n), where f_n is an explicit discrete forget gate (sigmoid, satisfying 0<f_n<1), i_n is an independent write gain, and B_n u_n provides input-dependent write/read maps. Unlike SSMs that derive discrete recurrences from continuous-time systems via zero-order-hold discretization, Naju parameterizes the discrete transition directly. The sigmoid pole ensures each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound without needing stability regularizers.

Result: In diagnostic evaluations, Naju is the only model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4× the training length. On WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming Mamba baselines in principal comparisons while matching Transformer competitiveness and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

Conclusion: Decoupling the forget and write gates eliminates the retention-overwriting trade-off inherent in coupled designs. Naju demonstrates that direct discrete parameterization is not only viable but preferable for memory tracking, achieving the best of both worlds: strong long-range retention and effective overwriting, all with linear complexity and without stability regularizers.

Abstract: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

</details>


### [167] [Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21010)
*Vasudha Bhatnagar,Purnima Bindal,Vikas Kumar,Raj Kumari Bahl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM-based summarizers by measuring summary stability across multiple dimensions (semantic and factual alignment). Empirical testing across three LLMs and three document genres reveals statistically significant differences in generation-level variability, highlighting a trustworthiness problem in zero-shot LLM summarization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot LLM summarization produces coherent summaries, but the inherent stochasticity of LLMs raises concerns about stability and trustworthiness. This is especially critical in educational settings where students and researchers rely on LLM-generated summaries of complex academic materials. The authors aim to formally diagnose and quantify this stability problem.

Method: A two-level diagnostic protocol: (1) Lower level — document-level stability analysis where multiple summaries are generated under controlled conditions, a stability coefficient is computed, and each summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the source document across multiple dimensions. (2) Upper level — observations from a stratified sample of documents are consolidated to estimate a stability index for the LLM-summarizer, serving as a proxy for trustworthiness.

Result: Empirical investigation across three LLM-summarizers and three document genres reveals statistically significant differences in generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics, confirming that stability varies meaningfully by model and context.

Conclusion: The study provides evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-generated summaries and calls for further research toward developing robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

Abstract: Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

</details>


### [168] [EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21013)
*Lihuang Fang,Yuchen Zou,kebin Jin,Jinghui Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EmoAgent-R1 proposes a reinforcement learning framework with dynamic agent specialization for multimodal emotion recognition. It uses a cold-start strategy for preliminary abilities, then applies a two-step agentic workflow (agent selection and specialization) optimized via a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) algorithm. P-GRPO combines group-based relative advantages with progressive token-level modulation to address sparse reward issues in GRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based emotion recognition methods rely on fixed prompts, which fail to capture the dynamic and complex nature of emotion sources in multimodal inputs. This rigidity limits the model's ability to reason about emotions adaptively.

Method: The framework, EmoAgent-R1, proceeds in stages: (1) Cold-start training using synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought and agent routing data to instill preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and routing abilities. (2) Reinforcement learning with a two-step agentic workflow — agent selection followed by agent specialization. (3) A novel P-GRPO algorithm that combines group-based relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to convert sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, overcoming the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment problem in standard GRPO.

Result: Extensive experiments on multimodal emotion recognition benchmarks show that EmoAgent-R1 achieves stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: Dynamic agent specialization via reinforcement learning, enabled by the P-GRPO algorithm, effectively enhances MLLMs' emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization capabilities by adaptively handling the complexity of multimodal emotional inputs.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

</details>


### [169] [Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21042)
*Muyang Du,Shuang Yu,Junjie Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates the IndexTTS-2 autoregressive TTS model using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM, achieving up to 5.0× speedup on the GPT component and 3.6× end-to-end, with minimal quality degradation, while also enabling streaming and batched inference for production deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive TTS models like IndexTTS-2 produce high-quality speech but suffer from slow, sequential token generation that barely reaches real-time, hindering deployment in low-latency production applications. The goal is to significantly accelerate inference while preserving synthesis quality.

Method: The authors optimize all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 (GPT backbone, flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and vocoder) using NVIDIA TensorRT for non-autoregressive components and TensorRT-LLM for the autoregressive GPT. They further introduce streaming synthesis for interactive use cases and batched inference across all components to improve GPU utilization and throughput.

Result: On the Seed-TTS benchmark (English and Chinese), Faster IndexTTS-2 achieves up to 5.0× speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6× end-to-end speedup, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness.

Conclusion: The proposed optimization methodology effectively accelerates autoregressive TTS models for GPU-based production deployment, providing a practical reference for accelerating similar autoregressive speech models with TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM.

Abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

</details>


### [170] [Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21101)
*Jie Peng,Yanping Zheng,Zhewei Zhe,Bin Tong,Guan Wang,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper diagnoses the cold-start limitations of Semantic ID (SID)-based generative recommenders under a temporal split protocol. It finds that while SID models can reach future items sharing observed tokens/prefixes, they fail on unseen atomic tokens and unsupported paths, interpreting this boundary through a hierarchical semantic bucketing lens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SID-based generative recommendation assumes closed-world recombination of shared semantic tokens, but real-world item catalogs evolve temporally — new items may introduce unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. The paper aims to systematically diagnose whether SID generation can truly perform open-ended cold-start induction under temporal dynamics, or whether it remains bounded by the compositional constraints of its token vocabulary.

Method: The authors adopt an absolute-time temporal protocol that strictly separates seen (training) and unseen (future) targets. They conduct three diagnostic analyses: (1) seen/unseen-hit analysis measuring token- and path-level reachability of cold items, (2) a coldness taxonomy categorizing failure modes (unseen atomic tokens vs. unsupported SID paths), and (3) oracle-prefix probing that feeds ground-truth prefixes to isolate where generation breaks down. They frame SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing — early tokens coarsely select semantic regions, later tokens refine item-specific paths — to explain the observed boundary.

Result: SID-based models can occasionally reach future items whose SIDs are fully composed of observed tokens and supported prefixes. However, they consistently fail on items containing unseen atomic tokens or requiring unsupported SID path compositions. The hierarchical bucketing interpretation reveals that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended: the coarse-to-fine token structure constrains the generation space to combinations that were implicitly covered during training.

Conclusion: SID generation is compositional but bounded by its learned token co-occurrence structure. True open-ended cold-start induction remains unsolved. The authors suggest future work on more independent SID token spaces, scoring-based interfaces (rather than autoregressive generation), and dynamic integration of textual side-information to expand cold-item reachability.

Abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

</details>


### [171] [AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21106)
*Qinfeng Li,Yuntai Bao,Xinyan Yu,Hongze Chen,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AttriMem proposes an attribution-guided RL framework for learning memory-construction policies in LLM agents, using token-level contribution signals to address the fine-grained credit-assignment problem that plagues outcome-reward-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-construction policies for LLM agents either rely on heuristic rules (subjective, task-specific, poor cross-task generalization) or RL with coarse outcome/module-level rewards. The latter creates a credit-assignment bottleneck: outcome rewards cannot identify which intermediate memory operations actually contributed to the final answer. While process-level feedback would be ideal, it is hard to construct because memory decisions lack ground-truth targets and appropriate credit depends on the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory.

Method: AttriMem augments global outcome rewards with local rewards derived from token-level attribution of the final answer. These attribution signals measure each token's contribution to the final output, providing fine-grained process feedback for RL-based memory policy learning without requiring pre-specified ground-truth for intermediate memory decisions.

Result: On long-horizon dialogue question answering tasks, AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines. It demonstrates generalization across benchmarks and answer models, and stabilizes RL optimization.

Conclusion: AttriMem effectively addresses the credit-assignment bottleneck in RL-based memory policy learning by leveraging token-level attribution as process rewards, yielding superior and more stable performance in long-horizon agent tasks.

Abstract: Effective memory is crucial for LLM agents, yet constructing it effectively remains challenging. A memory-construction policy decides what information to extract, store, update, compress, or discard as interactions accumulate. Heuristic memory methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules, which can misalign with downstream objectives and limit cross-task adaptability. RL-based methods, by contrast, learn from task feedback but mainly use outcome- or module-level rewards. These coarse signals indicate task success but cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck. However, constructing such process feedback is prohibitively difficult because intermediate memory decisions lack unique ground-truth targets, while the appropriate credit varies with the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory and therefore cannot be specified in advance. We propose AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer. Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, stabilizes RL optimization.

</details>


### [172] [V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21151)
*Zhetong Zhang,Honghao Fu,Miao Xu,Yiwei Wang,Yujun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Video LLMs exhibit a counterintuitive safety vulnerability where harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than with explicitly harmful queries. The authors propose V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework analyzing model behavior, understanding, and internal representations, revealing that visual understanding activates weaker refusal tendencies than textual understanding. A prompt injection intervention reduces attack success rates by ~48 percentage points, matching fine-tuning-based defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, making safety alignment critical. The authors observed a counterintuitive phenomenon: harmful video content paired with benign natural-language queries yields higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with overtly harmful queries. Understanding the mechanism behind this vulnerability—and developing an effective mitigation—motivates this work.

Method: The authors propose V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that analyzes: (1) model behavior (attack success rates under different query-video pairings), (2) model understanding (whether perception failures explain the vulnerability, tested via recognition accuracy), and (3) internal representations (hidden-state analysis comparing refusal tendencies triggered by visual vs. textual understanding). They further introduce a prompt injection intervention method that injects safety-oriented prompts to counteract the weak refusal signal from visual processing.

Result: Across six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks, models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate under harmful-video/benign-query pairings reaches 48.33%. Hidden-state analysis reveals that visual understanding activates a significantly weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. The prompt injection intervention reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points, achieving performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods.

Conclusion: The safety vulnerability in Video LLMs stems not from perception failure but from a modality gap in refusal tendencies—visual inputs trigger weaker safety refusals than textual inputs. The proposed prompt injection method offers a practical, effective, and lightweight defense, matching fine-tuning approaches without requiring model retraining.

Abstract: As Video Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. Counterintuitively, we find that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with explicitly harmful queries. To understand the underlying mechanism of this vulnerability, we present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. By progressively ruling out perception failure and quantifying the model's internal refusal tendency, V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing the underlying mechanism of the observed vulnerability. We tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks and observed that models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81\% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33\% under the condition pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis further shows that visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a prompt injection intervention method that reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods, providing an effective and practical means to address such safety risks in Video LLMs.

</details>


### [173] [Safeguards for Speech2Speech LLM-Assistants: A Case Study in Automotive Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21180)
*Gregor Endler,Sebastian Kraus,Lukas Stappen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: End-to-end speech-to-speech assistants enable natural in-car dialogue but resist domain-specific guardrails. The authors evaluate transcript-based and tool-based safeguarding approaches, finding both suffer from prohibitive latency (0–1.4s per answer) and technical issues like non-deterministic tool calls, making them unsuitable for industrial automotive deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Integrating end-to-end speech-to-speech conversational assistants in vehicles enables humanlike interaction (including non-verbal cues), but the end-to-end architecture severely constrains the ability to insert programmable, domain-specific safeguards — a critical requirement for industrial automotive applications where safety and compliance are paramount.

Method: The paper presents two implementation strategies for S2S guardrails: (1) transcript-based, where the spoken output is transcribed and checked post-hoc; and (2) tool-based, where guardrails are embedded as callable tools within the model's reasoning loop. These are evaluated empirically, focusing on latency overhead and technical reliability.

Result: Both strategies prove inadequate for industrial deployment. Latency penalties range from 0 to 1.4 seconds per response, even for computationally inexpensive checks. Tool-based approaches additionally suffer from non-deterministic tool call behavior, undermining reliability.

Conclusion: Neither transcript-based nor tool-based guardrails currently meet the requirements for automotive-grade S2S systems. The authors outline open challenges that the research community must address to enable safe, compliant deployment of end-to-end speech-to-speech assistants in vehicles.

Abstract: Recent advances have introduced speech-to-speech (S2S) conversational assistants capable of producing natural-sounding interactions, including non-verbal cues like tonality and mood. In the automotive domain, this enables intuitive and humanlike in-car dialogue experiences. However, integrating these end-to-end assistants limits architectural options for programmable domain-specific safeguards. This paper discusses two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails: transcript-based and tool-based. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that both strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment in most cases due to prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks) and technical impediments (like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior). Finally, we outline open challenges for S2S guardrails in the automotive context.

</details>


### [174] [Explaining Weather Bulletins via ILP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21184)
*Enrico Santi,Alessandro Dal Palù,Agostino Dovier,Talissa Dreossi,Andrea Formisano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a pipeline that uses Inductive Logic Programming (specifically FastLAS2) to learn interpretable, explanatory hypotheses from meteorological data and human-issued weather bulletins. The learned hypotheses clarify the rationale behind experts' choices of pictogram symbols in forecast maps, and the approach is designed to be generalizable across regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge the gap between complex meteorological raw data and the human-expert reasoning embedded in weather bulletins, providing transparent, interpretable explanations for the symbol choices in forecast pictograms. This addresses the need for explainability in domain-specific, declarative knowledge-driven forecasting.

Method: A pipeline that: (1) extracts simulated meteorological raw data and OSMER FVG bulletins (ground truth) into ASP (Answer Set Programming) facts; (2) generates ILP examples from these facts; (3) uses FastLAS2 — a mature, non-monotonic ILP framework — to infer an explanatory hypothesis; and (4) translates the learned hypothesis into natural language to explain the experts' pictogram symbol selections.

Result: The pipeline successfully learns a hypothesis that explains the rationale behind human experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram. The approach is demonstrated on data from OSMER FVG (Friuli Venezia-Giulia) but is designed to be region-agnostic.

Conclusion: FastLAS2 and the proposed ILP-based pipeline can effectively generate simple, interpretable hypotheses that explain expert meteorological forecasting decisions. The generality of the method supports its application to different regions and bulletin sources beyond the Italian case study.

Abstract: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) originated within the Logic Programming community in the Nineties as a framework for combining symbolic learning with declarative knowledge representation. Nowadays, mature ILP frameworks exist and they are capable of learning complex, non-monotonic hypotheses, thus broadening both the modeling capabilities and the scope of real-world applications of ILP. This work is primarily based on the FastLAS2 framework and aims to generate simple, interpretable hypotheses to help clarify the weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG, the Regional Meteorological Observatory of the Italian region of Friuli Venezia-Giulia. In this paper we present a pipeline that, starting from simulated meteorological raw data and from OSMERs' bulletins (used as ground truth), extracts data as ASP facts and generates ILP examples. From such examples an explanatory hypothesis is then inferred via FastLAS2. Such a hypothesis (translated into natural language) explains the weather forecast issued by human experts, and in particular the rationale behind experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram (the symbol-annotated meteorological map of the forecast). The proposed approach is general, not specific to any particular region and it can equally be applied to bulletins from other sources and to different regions.

</details>


### [175] [Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21185)
*Akihiro Takemura,Katsumi Inoue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A matrix-based differentiable logic programming approach is proposed to mitigate two types of reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems: constraint satisfaction shortcuts and cognition shortcuts. One-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to soft probability distribution methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic systems, despite their promise for generalization and interpretability, are vulnerable to shortcut reasoning behaviors where constraints are satisfied superficially (constraint satisfaction shortcuts) or biased data yields semantically incorrect concept mappings despite valid logic (cognition shortcuts). Prior work lacks effective mitigation strategies for both phenomena simultaneously.

Method: The authors propose a matrix-based differentiable logic programming framework that encodes rules and constraints in a unified single matrix. They introduce one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms (instead of soft probability distributions), analyze connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and their gradient flow properties, and conduct experiments on MNIST variants to evaluate shortcut mitigation under different architectural choices for coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning.

Result: One-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both constraint satisfaction shortcuts and cognition shortcuts compared to prior approaches using soft probability distributions. Architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation effectiveness.

Conclusion: Matrix-based differentiable logic programming with one-to-one grounding offers a principled way to reduce reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems, and careful architectural design of the neural-symbolic interface is essential for robust shortcut mitigation.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems integrate neural networks with logical reasoning to achieve both generalization and interpretability, but recent work has shown they are susceptible to shortcut reasoning behaviors.  We propose a novel method using matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in two phenomena: constraint satisfaction shortcuts, where constraints are satisfied without achieving the intended task, and cognition shortcuts, where biased data leads to semantically incorrect concept mappings despite logically sound inference. Building on recent matrix-based logic programming semantics, we introduce design elements to mitigate shortcuts, including a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix.  We also identify connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and empirically compare their gradient flow properties. Through carefully designed experiments on MNIST variants, we show that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to previous methods that rely on soft probability distributions.  We then confirm that architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

</details>


### [176] [Identifying Good Rules for Efficient SAT Encodings of Single-Constant Multiplication Using Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21188)
*Chufeng Jiang,Neng-Fa Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic framework that uses a graph neural network to accelerate SAT encoding for the Single Constant Multiplication (SCM) problem. By predicting promising operator types to prune poor choices during decomposition, the method achieves 1–2 orders of magnitude faster encoding, >97% memory reduction, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching on 17–32 bit constants, while maintaining near-optimal encoding quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional dynamic programming methods for SCM produce near-optimal SAT encodings but incur prohibitive encoding costs for large constants. The authors aim to reduce this cost by intelligently guiding the symbolic search, thereby improving scalability without sacrificing solution quality.

Method: A neuro-symbolic framework combining a Graph Neural Network (GNN) with symbolic search. The GNN is trained to predict promising operator types (add, subtract, shift) from constant decompositions. The resulting confidence scores are used to prune unpromising (no-good) operator choices during the symbolic decomposition search, reducing the search space dramatically.

Result: On unseen 17–32 bit constants, the method achieves 1–2 orders of magnitude reduction in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality measured by number of additions.

Conclusion: Learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM SAT encoding. The approach demonstrates that neuro-symbolic methods are a promising direction for tackling hard combinatorial optimization problems in hardware design.

Abstract: The Single Constant Multiplication problem is a fundamental NP-hard optimization task in hardware design, which seeks to decompose a fixed constant using only additions, subtractions, and bit-shifts. Although dynamic programming methods can produce near-optimal SAT encodings for SCM, their encoding cost remains high for large constants. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that accelerates SCM SAT encoding by identifying good rules for guiding operator selection during decomposition. Our approach employs a graph neural network model to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, and exploits the resulting confidence scores to prune no-good choices in the symbolic search. Experimental results on unseen 17-32 bit constants demonstrate one to two orders of magnitude reductions in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions. These results show that learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Chufeng-Jiang/SCM_MLDP

</details>


### [177] [Bound-Founded Semantics for Answer Set Programming with Difference Constraints: Preliminary Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21201)
*Pedro Cabalar,Jorge Fandinno,Nicolas Rühling,Torsten Schaub,Sebastian Schellhorn,Philipp Wanko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb) to unify the semantic foundations of hybrid ASP systems with linear constraints, applies it to difference constraints to characterize clingo[DL], formalizes foundedness for numeric variables, and reveals the semantic roots of behavioral differences among clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid Answer Set Programming solvers that integrate linear constraints (e.g., clingcon, clingo[DL], flingo) rely on disparate, ad-hoc semantic formalisms without a unified logical foundation. This fragmentation hinders rigorous comparison, formal analysis of program simplifications, and principled integration of diverse semantic principles across systems.

Method: The authors develop a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), a non-monotonic logic extending HT with bound-foundedness. This framework uses sorts to distinguish Boolean and numeric domains, defines equilibrium models parameterized by alternative semantic choices, and is instantiated for difference constraints to formally characterize clingo[DL]'s semantics. The notion of foundedness for numeric variables is formalized and used to analyze how different hybrid systems justify constraint atoms.

Result: The many-sorted HTb framework successfully captures equilibrium models across a spectrum of alternative semantics for ASP extensions with linear constraints. Applied to difference constraints, it provides a precise semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. The analysis reveals that the varying behaviors of clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo stem from fundamentally different notions of foundedness for numeric variables, now made explicit and comparable within a single unified framework.

Conclusion: The proposed many-sorted HTb provides the first unified logical foundation for hybrid ASP systems with linear constraints, enabling rigorous comparison of disparate semantics, formal study of program simplifications, and principled future integration of diverse semantic principles in ASP constraint solving.

Abstract: While the integration of linear constraints has significantly expanded the reach of Answer Set Programming (ASP), existing hybrid solvers often rely on disparate semantic underpinnings that lack a unified logical foundation. We address this gap by introducing a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), providing a versatile framework capable of characterizing equilibrium models across a wide spectrum of alternative semantics for extensions of ASP with linear constraints. We apply this framework to the setting of difference constraints, focusing on the semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. Central to our approach is the formalization of foundedness for numeric variables. By investigating how different hybrid systems - such as clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo - justify constraint atoms, we uncover the semantic roots of their varying behaviors. This investigation results in a single, consistent framework that not only formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates the rigorous study of program simplifications and the future integration of diverse semantic principles.

</details>


### [178] [A New Well-Supported Semantics for Description Logic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21203)
*Spencer Killen,Jia-Huai You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a new stricter well-supported semantics for description logic programs that maintains NP-completeness (instead of rising to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy), provides a reduct-based characterization, and preserves well-supportedness while aligning more closely with traditional logic programming semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The current well-supported semantics for DL programs has two key limitations: (1) the consistency problem jumps in computational complexity to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, and (2) it lacks a reduct transformation characterization, which is a fundamental property in logic programming semantics (e.g., answer set semantics). The authors aim to address both issues simultaneously.

Method: The authors introduce a new semantics that evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the existing well-supported semantics. They characterize this semantics via a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. They also identify a syntactic subclass of DL programs for which the new and old semantics coincide, establishing that the new semantics is a strict subset of the current one.

Result: The new semantics keeps the consistency problem NP-complete, avoiding the complexity increase. It yields a stricter notion of well-supportedness that the authors argue is preferable due to its closer analogy with standard logic programming. The reduct transformation characterization bridges a gap left by the prior semantics.

Conclusion: The proposed semantics successfully addresses both limitations of the prior well-supported semantics for DL programs: it restores NP-completeness and provides a reduct-based characterization, all while maintaining the core principle that answer sets should not rely on cyclic dependencies.

Abstract: Description logic programs are a powerful formalism for combining rules with ontologies. The well-supported semantics for description logic programs ensures that no answer sets rely on cyclic dependencies. Most popular semantics for logic programming have this property of well-supportedness. We recognize two limitations of the current well-supported semantics for DL programs: its increased computational complexity for the consistency problem and its lack of a reduct transformation characterization.  In this work, we present a new semantics which evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the current semantics. This keeps the complexity of its consistency problem NP-complete, rather than increasing it to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Additionally, we identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which our new semantics is equivalent to the current semantics. We characterize our semantics using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. Our new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, so it maintains the prior notion  of well-supportedness while inducing its own stricter notion. We prefer our new notion of well-supportedness due to its similarities with logic programming.

</details>


### [179] [How Rules Represent Causal Knowledge: Causal Modeling with Probabilistic Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21208)
*Kilian Rueckschloss,Felix Weitkaemper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper extends Pearl's causal theory from Bayesian networks to probabilistic logic programming (PLP), proposing a formal causal semantics, an intervention notion, and an implementation for PLP, while showing alignment with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pearl's theory of causality is confined to Bayesian networks and acyclic causal relationships, limiting its applicability. Transferring these ideas to other formalisms like PLP risks misinterpretation. The paper aims to bridge this gap by bringing causal reasoning into the PLP paradigm without relying on temporal notions.

Method: The authors develop a formal causal semantics for probabilistic logic programs grounded in atemporal philosophical foundations (all events assumed simultaneous). They define a notion of intervention tailored to PLP and provide an implementation. The semantics is compared against P-log semantics, particularly for stratified and non-stratified ProbLog programs and other PLP formalisms.

Result: The proposed causal semantics coincides with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs but may diverge in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms, highlighting boundaries of semantic alignment.

Conclusion: Pearl's causal framework can be coherently transferred to probabilistic logic programming under an atemporal interpretation. The resulting semantics is sound for stratified cases but reveals important divergences in non-stratified settings, underscoring the need for careful adaptation when extending causality beyond Bayesian networks.

Abstract: Pearl famously argues that causal knowledge enables the prediction of intervention effects. By contrast, purely descriptive knowledge supports only conclusions drawn from observations. His theory of causality, however, is developed exclusively within Bayesian networks and causal models. Consequently, it is largely restricted to acyclic causal relationships, and transferring its ideas to other formalisms risks misinterpretation or inconsistency.
  This paper brings Pearl's approach to causality into probabilistic logic programming (PLP). To this end, such programs are aligned with philosophical foundations established in prior work that do not rely on temporal notions; that is, all relevant events are assumed to occur simultaneously. A formal causal semantics for these programs, together with a notion of intervention and an implementation, is proposed. It is shown that this semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while the two may differ in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms.

</details>


### [180] [ICAE-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Interactive Project Builders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21217)
*Zhongyuan Peng,Dan Huang,Chuyu Zhang,Caijun Xu,Changyi Xiao,Shibo Hong,David Lo,Lin Qiu,Xuezhi Cao,Jiyuan He,Yixin Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICAE-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents in interactive, project-building scenarios where agents must transform vague product requirements into working software, using an automated User Agent to simulate realistic interaction and multi-dimensional diagnostics for fair evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from "vibe-coding" — where agents merely complete code under fully specified instructions — to interactive project-building workflows demands benchmarking that reflects this new paradigm. Existing benchmarks evaluate only static, fully specified tasks, failing to capture agents' abilities in planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction under ambiguous requirements.

Method: ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs: (1) deriving ambiguity from precise real open-source repositories with executable behavior to avoid unconstrained fuzzy requirements; (2) grounding interaction through User Agent Data, enabling automated User Agents to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts; (3) evaluating via standardized black-box tests and multi-dimensional diagnostics covering functional correctness, semantic/API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

Result: The benchmark introduces ICAE-Bench as a reproducible, realistic framework for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings, moving beyond static task completion to dynamic, requirement-clarifying workflows.

Conclusion: ICAE-Bench fills a critical gap in coding agent evaluation by aligning benchmarks with the emerging vibe-coding paradigm, enabling robust assessment of agents' holistic project-building capabilities through ambiguous yet grounded requirements and comprehensive diagnostic metrics.

Abstract: The recent emergence of vibe-coding workflows is changing what coding agents are expected to do. Instead of merely completing code under fully specified instructions, agents are increasingly expected to transform incomplete product intent into working software by combining various abilities including planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction. Yet existing benchmarks have not fully caught up with this shift, evaluating agents on static, fully specified tasks.
  In this paper, we introduce ICAE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings. The basic idea is to start from a fuzzy product requirement, simulating the dynamic paradigm with an automated User Agent. To make this setting both realistic and evaluable, ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs. First, to avoid the ambiguity of unconstrained fuzzy requirements, each task derives ambiguity from a precise real open-source repository with executable behavior. Second, to ensure high-quality and reproducible user simulation, ICAE-Bench grounds interaction through User Agent Data, allowing the User Agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts. Third, to evaluate open-ended repositories fairly, ICAE-Bench uses standardized black-box tests together with multi-dimensional diagnostics, including functional correctness, semantic and API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

</details>


### [181] [Logic Programming Semantics for Causal Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21233)
*Felix Weitkämper*

Main category: cs.AI
