Conclusion: Flint successfully bridges the gap between high-level semantic intent and low-level visualization configuration, serving as an effective intermediate representation that benefits both human and AI-driven visualization authoring across multiple target frameworks.

Abstract: We present Flint, an intermediate language that enables authors to create high-quality visualizations from concise, semantics-driven specifications without explicitly configuring low-level parameters such as scales, axes, and formatting. Unlike prior systems that infer default configurations from surface-level data representations, often producing brittle choices, Flint introduces a hierarchical data semantic model that allows users to specify the meanings of data fields structurally and helps the compiler derive appropriate visualization configurations. From a concise specification, the system generates and optimizes library-agnostic visualization configurations and translates them into complete, executable specifications for multiple target grammars, including Vega-Lite, Apache ECharts, and Chart.js. We demonstrate that Flint simplifies the authoring process without compromising on visual quality, and it is an effective intermediate language for both humans and AI agents to create visualizations.

</details>


### [204] [Sonic Stage: Automatically Generating Interactive Spatial Soundscapes to Facilitate Dialogue Video Comprehension for Blind Viewers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20835)
*Shuchang Xu,Xiaofu Jin,Gaurav Jain,Wenshuo Zhang,Huamin Qu,Brian A. Smith,Yukang Yan*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Sonic Stage transforms dialogue-heavy videos into interactive spatial soundscapes using spatialized dialogue, diegetic sound, and interactive descriptions, enabling BLV audiences to perceive characters' actions and movements. Evaluation with 12 BLV participants showed significant improvements in comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional audio description (AD) is constrained by an overlap rule that prevents descriptions from coinciding with dialogue, causing critical visual actions to be omitted during dialogue-heavy scenes. There is currently no established method for conveying character actions during speech, leaving a gap in video accessibility for blind and low-vision audiences.

Method: Sonic Stage employs three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue that pans speech according to characters' spatial positions on screen, (2) diegetic sound effects that sonify character actions, and (3) interactive descriptions that allow users to request context-specific visual details on demand. Together these form an interactive spatial soundscape that overlays dialogue videos.

Result: Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers demonstrated that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement compared to conventional approaches.

Conclusion: Immersive, interactive audio representations present a promising direction for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres, overcoming the fundamental limitation of traditional AD's speech-overlap constraint.

Abstract: Audio description (AD) makes film and television accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) audiences by narrating characters' actions. However, in scenes with lots of dialogue, AD often omits important actions because it is constrained not to overlap with speech. It is not yet known how to convey characters' actions during dialogue. We present Sonic Stage, a system that transforms dialogue videos into interactive spatial soundscapes, enabling BLV audiences to intuitively understand characters' actions and movements through immersive auditory cues. Sonic Stage conveys essential visual information during dialogue through three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue to represent spatial layout, (2) diegetic sound to convey character actions, and (3) interactive descriptions to provide context-specific visual details. Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers showed that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement. We highlight opportunities for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres through immersive, interactive audio representations.

</details>


### [205] [Exploring the Design Space of LLM-Based Programming Support in CS Education: A Scoping Review through the Lens of Assistance Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21257)
*Minsun Kim,S. Moonwara A. Monisha,Zihan Wu,David H. Smith*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A scoping review of 90 LLM-based programming support systems in CS education introduces PEA — Policy (what help is allowed/restricted), Enforcement (how boundaries are operationalized), and Authority (who can configure them) — as a three-dimensional analytic framework for comparing and designing pedagogically governed AI assistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based programming support systems vary widely in how assistance is bounded, enacted, and controlled, yet these governance decisions are described implicitly, hindering educationally meaningful comparisons. A shared vocabulary and analytic lens are needed to make governance choices explicit, comparable, and actionable.

Method: The authors conducted a scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education. They iteratively developed and refined a three-dimensional governance codebook — Policy, Enforcement, and Authority (PEA) — and applied it to characterize and map the design space across the reviewed systems.

Result: Systems often share similar pedagogical goals but implement them through diverse enforcement mechanisms. Authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with few systems granting learners or instructors runtime control. The analysis reveals underexplored configurations where authority could be distributed and enforcement mechanisms diversified.

Conclusion: PEA provides a vocabulary for analyzing and comparing LLM-based programming support systems. It surfaces design trade-offs and underexplored areas, guiding the development of future tools that are pedagogically bounded, instructor-configurable, and accountable.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integrated into programming education, learner-facing systems increasingly differ in how that assistance is bounded, enacted, and controlled. These governance decisions are often described implicitly, making it difficult to compare systems in educationally meaningful ways. To address this gap, we conduct a scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education. We analyze assistance governance through three dimensions, which we refer to collectively as PEA: Policy, capturing what forms of help are allowed or restricted; Enforcement, capturing how those boundaries are operationalized through interaction and system behavior; and Authority, capturing who can configure, adapt, or override them during use. Our findings show that systems often share similar pedagogical goals, but implement those goals through varied enforcement mechanisms. At the same time, authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with fewer systems giving learners or instructors runtime control. This work contributes PEA as a three-dimensional analytic lens, a governance codebook empirically refined within these dimensions, and a map of underexplored configurations in the current design space of LLM-based programming support. By making these explicit and comparable, PEA offers a vocabulary for analyzing existing systems and designing future tools that are pedagogically bounded, configurable, and accountable.

</details>


### [206] [Reimagining the Augmented Reality Accessibility Ecosystem for Deaf Students: Service Provider Perspectives in Experiential Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21289)
*Roshan Mathew,Roshan Peiris*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: AR-mediated communication access for DHH students reconfigures accessibility labor and interaction in experiential learning — enhancing contextual awareness but disrupting gaze coordination and pacing — suggesting AR works best within a hybrid ecosystem rather than as a standalone replacement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DHH students in experiential learning environments suffer from "split attention" across tasks, instructors, and access providers. While AR has been proposed to centralize communication access in the student's field of view, little is known about how AR systems affect the instructors, interpreters, and captioners who provide that access.

Method: A formative, expert-based evaluation of ARRAE (an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem) was conducted in a simulated laboratory environment, comparing three modalities: in-person, traditional remote, and AR-mediated access. Participants included an instructor, an ASL interpreter, and a real-time captioner.

Result: AR redistributes communication, attention, and awareness across participants. It supports integrated, in-situ communication and enhances contextual awareness, but alters interactional feedback mechanisms — particularly gaze coordination and pacing — that are critical for shared understanding during instruction.

Conclusion: AR-mediated communication access introduces trade-offs between access, control, and coordination. These systems are most effective as part of a broader hybrid ecosystem, not as standalone replacements for existing modalities. Findings contribute to designing coordinated, multi-user AR systems for hands-on educational contexts.

Abstract: In experiential learning environments, Deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) students often experience ``split attention,'' dividing their focus among tasks, instructors, and access providers. Augmented reality (AR) has been proposed as a means to centralize communication access within the student's field of view; however, little is known about how such systems affect the instructors, interpreters, and captioners who support access in these settings. We present a formative, expert-based evaluation of ARRAE, an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem, examining the experiences of an instructor, an American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter, and a real-time captioner in a simulated laboratory environment. Comparing in-person, traditional remote, and AR-mediated access, our findings suggest that AR reconfigures accessibility labor and interactional practices by redistributing communication, attention, and awareness across participants. While AR-mediated access supported integrated, in-situ communication and enhanced contextual awareness, it also altered interactional feedback mechanisms, such as gaze coordination and pacing, that support shared understanding during instruction. These observations highlight trade-offs between access, control, and coordination, and suggest that AR-mediated systems may be most effective when considered as part of a broader, hybrid ecosystem rather than as standalone replacements for existing modalities. This work contributes initial insights into how AR reshapes communication access in experiential learning and informs the design of systems that support coordinated, multi-user interaction in hands-on educational contexts.

</details>


### [207] [CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21394)
*Runze Cai,Yuxuan Huang,Lin-Ping Yuan,Kexin Xiang,David Hsu,Collier Nogues,Jussi Holopainen,Shengdong Zhao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes CRAFT (Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation), an AI-powered smart glasses approach that transforms writers' daily experiences into fictional narratives. Through interviews, co-design workshops, and field trials, the authors derive design goals, operationalize interaction mechanisms, and provide empirical insights for ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday writing contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-assisted creative writing tools fail to capture in-situ moments when writers spontaneously draw inspiration from real-world experiences. The authors identify a gap in supporting the serendipitous, context-aware transformation of lived experiences into fiction, motivating a novel ubiquitous computing approach via AI glasses.

Method: A three-phase mixed-methods study: (1) Interviews with nine writers to elicit desires and derive three design goals; (2) Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers using a technology probe to operationalize goals into concrete interaction mechanisms; (3) Supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe to evaluate perceived benefits, emergent practices, and design considerations.

Result: Three design goals emerged: augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Field trials revealed writer-perceived benefits such as enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters, emergent practices like micro-creation, and key considerations for sustained use.

Conclusion: The CRAFT approach offers a viable design direction for ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration. The paper contributes design explorations, concrete design implications, and empirical insights on how context-aware AI systems can augment creative writing by transforming everyday experiences into fiction while respecting writer agency and authenticity.

Abstract: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation (CRAFT), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.

</details>


### [208] [Thinkink: 2D Spatial Ink-native Interaction with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21468)
*Mohammad Hasan Payandeh,Daniel Vogel,Jian Zhao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Thinkink is an ink-native LLM interaction tool that allows users to handwrite and sketch prompts on a shared 2D canvas, with LLM responses rendered as spatially integrated ink-like text and drawings. The tool was developed through a three-stage design process involving formative (N=12), diagnostic (N=6), and evaluative (N=10) studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People often use handwritten notes and sketches for idea generation (ideation), but there is no established method for integrating large language models into this fluid, spatial, ink-based workflow. The paper aims to bridge this gap by enabling LLM interaction that feels native to pen-and-ink ideation practices rather than disrupting them with conventional chat interfaces.

Method: A three-stage research-through-design process: (1) a formative study (N=12) examining current conventional and digital inking practices; (2) a diagnostic study (N=6) using a technical probe to identify usability and human-LLM interaction challenges; and (3) a final evaluative study (N=10) assessing how users incorporate Thinkink into their ideation workflows. Thinkink itself features a semantic tree for ink interpretation and a lightweight state-machine-based UI for explicit control.

Result: The formative study characterized existing inking behaviors and needs. The diagnostic study surfaced specific usability challenges and interaction friction points between humans and LLMs in ink-based contexts. The final study demonstrated how users adopted Thinkink in ideation, yielding design implications for ink-native LLM interaction.

Conclusion: Thinkink demonstrates a novel paradigm for human-LLM collaboration through shared ink-based canvases. The paper contributes both a functional tool and a set of design implications for building interfaces where users and LLMs co-create through handwriting and sketching in a unified spatial medium.

Abstract: People often use handwritten notes and sketches to externalize ideas for ideation. To integrate large language models (LLMs) into this practice, we propose Thinkink. Prompts can be handwritten text or drawn sketches with LLM-generated responses visualized as ink-like text and sketches spatially integrated into a shared canvas. A semantic tree streamlines ink interpretation, and a lightweight UI provides explicit control using a state machine. The tool was designed using a three-stage process. A formative study (N=12) examined current practices with conventional and digital inking methods. The results informed a technical probe for a diagnostic study (N=6) identifying usability and human-LLM interaction challenges. This motivated the design of Thinkink, with a final study (N=10) examining how people incorporate it into their ideation practices. We contribute design implications and a tool for ink-native LLM interaction where the user and LLM write and draw in a shared 2D canvas.

</details>


### [209] [A Needs Assessment for Measuring Geographic - Legislative Associations in the U.S. House of Representatives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21502)
*Ashu Gupta,Cameron Owens,Benjamin Wilson-Langman,Max Hill,Jason Cox,Joshua Clinton,Clio Andris*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This technical report presents a system that merges U.S. congressional voting records from the 118th House of Representatives with GIS data to compare legislators' votes against district-level demographic/geographic features, using manually themed bills and an interactive map prototype.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge the gap between publicly available congressional voting records and the geographic/demographic characteristics of constituencies, enabling quantitative assessment of how well legislative decisions align with district-level features and interests.

Method: Bills from the 118th U.S. House (Jan 2023–Jan 2025) were retrieved and manually assigned thematic tags (e.g., veterans' affairs, agriculture). Spatial data at the congressional district level corresponding to each theme was collected. A backend database was built to link bill information with spatial data, and an interactive map prototype was developed to visualize thematic spatial data associated with each bill.

Result: A functional prototype system was delivered that integrates legislative data with GIS layers, demonstrating the feasibility of linking themed bills to district-level spatial data and identifying challenges in building a more complete, accessible system for visualizing and analyzing congressional representation.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates proof-of-concept for merging congressional voting data with GIS to measure district-feature/legislator-decision associations, while highlighting challenges for future development of a more comprehensive system for analyzing contemporary congressional representation.

Abstract: Political legislation affects the well-being and livelihoods of constituents. In the U.S. Congress a representative's voting record on bills and legislation is public. These bills have themes associated with them, such as veterans' affairs, coastal monitoring, agricultural appropriations, etc. A bill on veterans' affairs may affect a constituency differently if they have a high percentage of veterans. In this work, we demonstrate how congressional vote outcomes can be merged with typical geographic information systems (GIS) data to help compare a legislator's votes with the geographies of their constituencies to measure the association between district features and legislators' decisions.
  We retrieved and tagged bills from the 118th U.S. House of Representatives (Jan. 2023 - Jan. 2025) by manually assigning each bill a set of themes. We then retrieved spatial data at the congressional district level related to each theme. We built a backend database to connect bill information and spatial data, and an interactive map prototype displayed the spatial data related to each theme associated with each bill. Our work helps identify challenges to creating a more accessible and complete system that would facilitate the visualization and analysis of the nature of contemporary Congressional representation. This technical report is primarily written for members of the data science community, and specifically those interested in legislative and geographic data.

</details>


### [210] [Transparent by Design, Usable in Practice? A Formative Usability Study of a Conversational Product Advisor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21513)
*Kevin Schott,Dagmar Kern,Daniel Hienert*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A usability study of a transparent conversational product advisor (chatbot for laptop search) shows that built-in transparency features do not guarantee user understanding, and users desire both explanation and direct control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational product advisors powered by LLMs can be fluent but opaque, hiding ranking logic and recommendation evidence within natural-language replies. This opacity challenges users' ability to understand, trust, and steer results, motivating the need to build transparency into such systems.

Method: A formative, moderated think-aloud usability study with seven participants who completed three laptop-search tasks using a chatbot featuring constrained natural-language generation, on-demand ranking explanation, and a comparison feature. Post-task usability measures were collected, and sessions were coded into severity-rated usability problems.

Result: Ease and satisfaction were high, but two key findings emerged: (1) transparency by design did not guarantee understanding — the ranking explanation caused the most severe usability problem despite being valued in principle; (2) participants valued the effort saved but some wanted additional direct-manipulation controls.

Conclusion: The paper contributes a severity-prioritized set of usability problems and design implications for building human-centered conversational product advisors, highlighting the gap between designing for transparency and achieving actual user comprehension.

Abstract: Large language models can make conversational product advisors fluent but opaque. If they hide the logic behind a ranking and the evidence for a recommendation inside natural-language replies, they challenge users' ability to understand, trust, and steer the results. One response is to build transparency into the advisor. We report a formative, moderated think-aloud usability study of one such system: a chatbot for laptop search with constrained natural-language generation, an on-demand ranking explanation, and a comparison feature. Seven participants completed three laptop-search tasks and reported post-task usability measures. We coded their sessions into severity-rated usability problems. Ease and satisfaction during the tasks were high, but two findings stand out. First, transparency by design did not guarantee understanding: several participants valued the ranking explanation in principle, yet it caused the most severe problem. Second, participants valued the effort the advisor saved, but some wanted additional direct-manipulation controls. We contribute a severity-prioritized set of usability problems and design implications for human-centered conversational product advisors.

</details>


### [211] [Sources of Inequity and Fairness Risks inWellbeing Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21527)
*Han Zhang,Vedant Das Swain,Koustuv Saha,Anind K. Dey,Jennifer Mankoff*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates fairness risks in passive sensing systems for wellbeing, going beyond identity-based algorithmic audits. Through interviews with 14 researchers/practitioners across five countries, the authors identify five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity), synthesize 15 fairness risks with mitigation strategies across the full system lifecycle, and highlight structural barriers requiring both individual and ecosystem-level interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Passive sensing systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings (hospitals, universities) to infer psychological states, yet fairness research has been largely limited to post-hoc, identity-based model performance comparisons. The domain's distinctive characteristics—heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment—raise underexplored questions about additional sources of inequity and how they propagate beyond algorithmic audits across the entire system lifecycle.

Method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries who have experience designing, deploying, or studying passive sensing systems for wellbeing. The interviews examined how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the full passive sensing lifecycle, from study design through deployment. Findings were analyzed qualitatively to characterize sources of inequity, synthesize risks and mitigation strategies, and identify structural barriers.

Result: The study empirically characterizes five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity) that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. It synthesizes 15 fairness risks and corresponding mitigation strategies spanning the entire lifecycle, from study design to deployment. Additionally, it identifies structural barriers that constrain fair practice in reality.

Conclusion: Enabling fair passive sensing requires both individual researcher efforts and ecosystem-level governance support from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions. The paper argues that fairness must be addressed as a systemic, lifecycle-spanning concern rather than merely a post-hoc algorithmic audit problem.

Abstract: Passive sensing for wellbeing uses smartphones and wearables to continuously collect human behavioral data and applies ML/AI models to infer psychological states and behaviors (e.g., depression, cognitive load). These systems are increasingly adopted in high-stakes settings (e.g., hospitals, universities), yet fairness research remains limited---primarily to post-hoc, identity-based comparisons of model performance. However, passive sensing combines heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment---characteristics that, while not exclusive to the domain, are jointly pronounced here and raise two underexplored questions: (1) what additional sources of inequity arise from these characteristics, and (2) how do such inequities propagate beyond algorithmic audits across the system lifecycle? To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries, examining how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the full passive sensing lifecycle. Our findings empirically characterize five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity) that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. We further synthesize 15 fairness risks and corresponding mitigation strategies across the lifecycle, from study design to deployment. Finally, we identify structural barriers that constrain fair practice in reality, and argue that enabling fair passive sensing requires both individual researcher efforts and ecosystem-level governance support from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [212] [DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20465)
*Hao Liang,Qifeng Cai,Yibo Lin,Jianzhuo Du,Qifeng Xia,Sizhe Qiu,Linzhuang Sun,Meiyi Qiang,Zhaoyang Han,Xiaochen Ma,Bohan Zeng,Ruichuan An,Conghui He,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DataPrep-Bench is a unified benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven data preparation, covering both data construction and data quality evaluation. It introduces Data-Construction-Skill (a skill-guided agent) and the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), which achieve strong results across six domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No unified benchmark exists to holistically measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows prepare training data end-to-end, where "quality" is defined by downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties.

Method: DataPrep-Bench evaluates two complementary capabilities over six domains: (1) data construction — methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; (2) data quality evaluation — scoring functions are evaluated by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool. The authors release Data-Construction-Skill (skill-guided agent) and the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator using MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy.

Result: Data-Construction-Skill lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 absolute points on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods. DAS achieves the strongest cross-model correlation in 4 of 6 domains and is the only metric surpassing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators.

Conclusion: DataPrep-Bench establishes a unified, downstream-grounded framework that treats data construction and data quality evaluation as co-equal targets, enabling systematic progress measurement in LLM-driven data preparation.

Abstract: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

</details>


### [213] [PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20492)
*Rana Muhammad Usman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language models forced to output structured formats (JSON fields, enums, arrays) fabricate answers at dramatically higher rates than in free-text responses. When a question cannot be answered from the input, required fields drive hallucination rates to 100% in most models, revealing a systematic failure mode unaddressed by scale or instruction alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production LLMs predominantly output structured data (JSON, function arguments, extraction templates), yet hallucination research has largely focused on free-text generation. The authors identify that the output format itself—specifically required fields with no room for hedging—coerces models into fabrication, a phenomenon no existing benchmark measures.

Method: The authors construct inputs where the requested information is provably absent (e.g., a viral post with 12,400 likes but no visible replies; a support ticket with an untranscribed call). They query thirteen models with the same question across different output formats: free text, required JSON fields, enums, and minimum-count arrays. Metrics include the Coerced Fabrication Rate (how often models invent answers under format pressure) and Escape Utilization Rate (how often models use an explicit "insufficient evidence" option when available). Interventions tested include adding an explicit "insufficient evidence" enum value and direct instructions not to infer.

Result: Under required JSON fields, fabrication reaches 100% in ten of thirteen models. GPT-5.5 answers honestly in free text 98% of the time but fabricates 40/40 times with a required sentiment field. An "insufficient evidence" escape option is used only by frontier models; all nine open-weight models ignore it. Direct instructions ("do not infer sentiment") are overridden by schema constraints in four of six models. Resistance does not scale monotonically: within a single family, the smallest and largest models refuse while the mid-sized model fabricates.

Conclusion: Format-driven hallucination is pervasive and systematically unmeasured. The fix is trivially simple—one line of schema providing an explicit abstention option—yet adoption is absent. The authors release PhantomFill as a benchmark and advocate that honesty under format pressure become a standard evaluation criterion for deployed models.

Abstract: Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

</details>


### [214] [The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20512)
*Yufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Muon's grokking speed advantage over AdamW stems from momentum orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz), not spectral norm constraints. Orthogonalization-only matches full Muon; spectral-only is no faster and unreliable. Fewer Newton-Schulz iterations accelerate grokking but introduce fragility, while the canonical 5 iterations provide robustness across learning rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work credits Muon's faster grokking on modular arithmetic to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" without isolating which mechanism is causally responsible. The authors aim to decompose and stress-test these components to identify the true driver of Muon's performance.

Method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps with ablation experiments decomposing Muon into: (1) orthogonalization-only (Newton-Schulz), (2) spectral-only normalization, and (3) full Muon. Mechanistic analysis tracks spectral norm and embedding movement. Newton-Schulz iteration count is varied (1 vs 5) to test robustness. A stability-aware dual metric (first-crossing and sustained-grok time) is introduced.

Result: Orthogonalization-only matches full Muon performance; spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and unreliable. Orthogonalizing optimizers generalize at ~3x lower spectral norm while settling into lower-norm solutions. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from 5 to 1 accelerates grokking but causes fragile, collapse-prone solutions — fragility worsens with learning rate. One iteration is only stable at small learning rates; five iterations are learning-rate-robust. Spectral scaling can be dropped at no cost. Under stability-aware metrics, "faster" claims can invert.

Conclusion: Momentum orthogonalization, not spectral constraints, drives Muon's grokking advantage. The canonical 5 Newton-Schulz iterations represent a robustness trade-off: fewer iterations are faster but fragile. Methodologically, grokking speed claims must consider stability, not just first-crossing time. Code is open-sourced.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

</details>


### [215] [Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20516)
*Tolgay Atinc Uzun,Radu Timofte,Dmitry Ignatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaling up LLM-based neural network channel-width search to 250 candidates per cycle (2,000 total, 462 verified) reveals that optimization signal transfers to denser sampling, with positive accuracy trends, improved parameter efficiency, and emergent architectural regularities like non-power-of-two widths and structured channel-allocation patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed LLM-based closed-loop channel-configuration search can optimize neural network widths, but results were based on sparse evaluations. The authors aim to test whether the optimization behavior persists under denser sampling and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more candidate networks are evaluated.

Method: The same LLM-based code-generation search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle, across 8 complete cycles, producing 2,000 generated candidates. After task and metadata filtering, 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations are analyzed for accuracy trends, parameter efficiency, and architectural patterns.

Result: Per-cycle mean accuracy shows a positive linear trend (slope=9.87e-4, p=0.043). The best accuracy improves from 0.3144 to 0.3676. Top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means also show positive trends. The best model achieves 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters vs. an early model's 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Non-power-of-two channel widths appear in 41.8% of verified candidates, and top models share structured patterns: moderate early widths with expanded middle/later blocks.

Conclusion: The channel-search signal from the initial study transfers to denser sampling regimes. Scaling reveals improved parameter efficiency and emergent architectural regularities—particularly non-power-of-two widths and structured channel-allocation patterns—that were difficult to observe under sparse evaluation.

Abstract: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

</details>


### [216] [Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20517)
*Takato Yasuno*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF is a four-axis fusion retrieval system combining dense embeddings, BM25, knowledge graph triples, and image similarity that achieves 0.99 retrieval recall and 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over heterogeneous PDF collections, with triple-filtering identified as the dominant axis via Bayesian optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG over heterogeneous PDFs is difficult due to multimodal content (text, images, tables), domain-specific terminology, and dispersed evidence requiring multi-hop reasoning. Existing retrievers struggle to balance lexical and semantic signals while supporting compositional queries across document boundaries.

Method: The authors propose a four-axis fusion architecture: (1) dense text embeddings, (2) BM25 keyword matching, (3) knowledge-graph triple filtering using 11,414 OpenIE triples indexed via FAISS for sub-second lookup with hierarchical relevance propagation, and (4) image-based similarity via vision LLM captioning. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume→chapter→block) prunes the search space. Bayesian optimization tunes fusion weights, revealing the triple axis should dominate (α_triple=0.44). The system indexes 2,403 blocks from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs using a hybrid OCR pipeline.

Result: On a 457-pair benchmark, the system achieves Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM demonstrates applicability to visual inputs.

Conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs. The framework generalizes beyond the disaster domain, and the dominance of the knowledge-graph triple axis is critical for counteracting lexical bias and sustaining multi-hop retrieval quality.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

</details>


### [217] [Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20519)
*Andrei Cristian Popescu,Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Looped Transformers use adaptive depth via learned halting, but joint training of the exit gate entangles trajectory formation with readout selection. The authors decouple these: fixed-prior depth supervision shapes difficulty-aware trajectories, and simple post-hoc confidence readouts match or exceed learned gates. Failure stems from the trajectory induced by joint training, not gate expressivity. This pattern holds across synthetic tasks and large-scale Ouro models, reframing adaptive depth as a joint trajectory–readout problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In looped Transformers with learned halting, the exit distribution serves dual purpose: inference-time stopping and training-time per-depth loss weighting. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation, making it unclear whether poor adaptive-compute performance arises from the readout mechanism, the learned trajectory, or their interaction. Prior work leaves this distinction implicit.

Method: The authors systematically decouple trajectory formation from exit readout. They compare (1) fixed-prior depth supervision (trajectory shaped without input-dependent halting) versus joint gate training, and (2) post-hoc confidence-based readouts versus learned linear/MLP gates. Experiments span controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic, binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B/2.6B checkpoints. They also fit gates on frozen trajectories to isolate failure sources and measure wall-clock latency for practical savings.

Result: Fixed-prior depth supervision produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states contain useful stopping signals. Simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the primary failure to trajectory formation induced by joint training, not limited gate expressivity. In Ouro evaluations, pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal; reduced average exit depth yields practical inference latency savings.

Conclusion: Adaptive depth in looped Transformers should be reframed as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, not gate learning alone. The diagnostic evaluation demonstrates that decoupling these components—using fixed priors for trajectory shaping and simple confidence readouts—can match or improve upon jointly trained halting, with practical speed benefits.

Abstract: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

</details>


### [218] [Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20521)
*Lei Cao,Sihang Feng,Jixin Yan,Tao Sun,Naichen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF) replaces restrictive linear-Gaussian observation models in classical filters with pretrained conditional VAEs, reformulating the measurement update as a score-based posterior sampling problem that combines dynamical priors with flexible generative likelihoods for improved state estimation in nonlinear, high-dimensional settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical filtering methods (e.g., Kalman filters) rely on simple observation models like linear-Gaussian assumptions, which fail to capture the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in modern high-dimensional sensor data. There is a need for a filtering framework that can leverage expressive generative models while retaining principled Bayesian uncertainty quantification.

Method: GBF performs Bayesian prediction-update recursion where the measurement update is cast as a posterior sampling problem. It combines the dynamical prior with a likelihood induced by a pretrained conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). The resulting filtering problem is transformed into a score-based sampling formulation, enabling flexible generative modeling with ensemble-based uncertainty quantification.

Result: Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications (manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis) show that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness compared to baseline approaches.

Conclusion: GBF successfully bridges classical Bayesian filtering with modern deep generative models, offering a flexible and uncertainty-aware framework for state estimation in complex, nonlinear, high-dimensional observation settings.

Abstract: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

</details>


### [219] [Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20582)
*Frederik Hauke,Patrick Wienholt,Christiane Kuhl,Dyke Ferber,Jakob Nikolas Kather,Sven Nebelung,Daniel Truhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty estimation improves error detection in chest X-ray classification, but its clinical utility depends on presentation format—binary flags outperform raw scores for decision support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical image analysis models lack reliable confidence measures, limiting safe deployment in ambiguous cases. The authors aim to quantify whether epistemic uncertainty from Monte Carlo dropout carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, and how communication format affects downstream clinical utility.

Method: A multi-task DenseNet classifier was trained on 137,593 chest radiographs for eight thoracic findings. Monte Carlo dropout was applied at inference to estimate epistemic uncertainty. The uncertainty signal was evaluated for (1) tracking generalization across training-set scales, (2) flagging confident but erroneous predictions (error detection AUROC), and (3) downstream impact on clinician decisions via a controlled 2×2 factorial experiment comparing raw uncertainty scores versus binary error-risk flags.

Result: Incorporating epistemic uncertainty raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 (ΔAUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In the factorial experiment, clinicians reduced confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7% only when uncertainty was presented as a binary error-risk flag, not as raw scores.

Conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty estimation via Monte Carlo dropout provides decision-relevant information beyond point predictions. However, its practical value for clinical decision support is contingent on effective communication formats—structured binary flags prove more actionable than raw numerical uncertainty scores.

Abstract: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions. Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.

</details>


### [220] [Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20522)
*Larry Richards*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A preregistered experiment in Gemma 2 2B found that active SAE feature planes carry less holonomy than mixed-feature controls, falsifying the semantic-concentration prediction in reverse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test the semantic-concentration hypothesis—that holonomy (curvature measured by parallel transport around loops) concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder feature planes in language models, operationalizing the idea that semantically meaningful directions exhibit geometric structure.

Method: Holonomy was measured at the final-token residual stream (layer 12→13) in Gemma 2 2B by transporting a local frame around small loops using a restricted-Jacobian transport rule, normalizing rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis pipeline, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before data inspection.

Result: The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes showed less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls (adjusted log contrast = -0.29439, 95% CI [-0.43989, -0.14889]). A magnitude-only explanation was unsupported, and three-way ordering across random, mixed, and active planes failed due to lack of common support at matched magnitude. Post-freeze diagnostics confirmed the area law on a validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement, and identified transport distortion as a live confound.

Conclusion: The result is a narrow, auditable operational reversal—not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, feature engagement, dictionary geometry, center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

Abstract: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

</details>


### [221] [Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20529)
*Jiawei Zheng,Jiazhen Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes using Cooke-style log weighting from decision theory for LLM ensemble aggregation, estimating each model's reliability via calibration questions. This method outperforms naive aggregation when models vary in quality or include adversarial experts, achieving better accuracy-reliability balance on MMLU benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-LLM aggregation methods treat all models as equally trustworthy, ignoring significant differences in uncertainty quality across heterogeneous LLMs. This makes naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts, creating a need for uncertainty-aware trust estimation.

Method: The authors adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, employing Cooke-style log weighting. This method uses context-aware calibration questions to estimate each expert's reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions, penalizing overconfident incorrect predictions while favoring well-calibrated experts.

Result: Evaluated on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated panels. All methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings; however, Cooke weighting significantly outperforms baselines under heterogeneity and contamination, achieving superior accuracy-reliability balance and remaining robust to unreliable experts.

Conclusion: Multi-LLM aggregation requires not merely combining predictions but calibrating trust under uncertainty. Uncertainty-aware expert weighting is essential for robust ensembles, especially in heterogeneous or adversarial settings.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

</details>


### [222] [CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20530)
*Léa Billet,Louise Travé-Massuyès,Elodie Chanthery,Alexandre Gaffet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLOE combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with Christoffel Function-based anomaly detection in latent space, using a novel Christoffel-guided loss to align representation learning with detection, achieving superior performance on high-dimensional tabular benchmarks while maintaining low-tuning simplicity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Christoffel Function-based anomaly detection methods are theoretically elegant and require minimal hyperparameter tuning, but they scale poorly to high-dimensional data. Existing lightweight semi-supervised methods also struggle in high dimensions and demand careful multi-parameter tuning.

Method: CLOE uses an autoencoder to reduce dimensionality, then applies a Christoffel Function detector in the latent space. A novel loss function leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that capture the support of the normal data distribution. The authors also introduce a principled detection threshold procedure and an efficient strategy for tuning the single remaining hyperparameter.

Result: Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks show CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: CLOE successfully extends Christoffel Function-based anomaly detection to high-dimensional settings by operating in a learned latent space, preserving its lightweight, low-tuning advantages while achieving state-of-the-art performance.

Abstract: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

</details>


### [223] [Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21488)
*Gil Lifshits,Igal Bilik,Gilad Katz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPS is a hierarchical DRL architecture for coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections, where a centralized Master agent generates a continuous proto-plan embedding that decentralized Worker agents use alongside local observations. Trained and tested in HighwayEnv across 72 configurations, MAPS achieves collision-free navigation with reduced travel time and demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization from 3-agent training to 5-agent deployment (94% success rate).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MARL approaches for unsignalized intersection coordination suffer from three key limitations: (1) combinatorial explosion of joint action spaces, (2) dependence on privileged global information unavailable in real deployments, and (3) rigid agent architectures that tightly couple strategic coordination with tactical control. A framework is needed that decouples high-level coordination strategy from low-level vehicle execution while remaining scalable and generalizable.

Method: MAPS employs a two-tier hierarchical DRL architecture. The centralized Master agent processes global state information to produce a compact, continuous vector called a "proto-plan" that encodes the global coordination strategy. Each decentralized Worker agent receives this proto-plan embedding concatenated with its local observations and outputs vehicle-specific control actions. This design decouples strategic intent from tactical execution, allowing each module to be optimized independently. Evaluation is conducted in HighwayEnv across 72 intersection configurations.

Result: MAPS achieves collision-free navigation across all tested configurations while significantly reducing average travel time compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans exhibit robust zero-shot generalization: a model trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed on five-agent scenarios, demonstrating that the proto-plan representation captures transferable coordination strategies.

Conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising and effective framework for multi-vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections. The decoupled architecture enables both strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, suggesting that compact continuous embeddings can serve as an effective medium for communicating strategic intent in decentralized multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

</details>


### [224] [Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20532)
*Nadine Chang,Maying Shen,Jialiang Wang,Rafid Mahmood,Jose M. Alvarez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper advocates replacing reactive AI maintenance flywheels (which patch models based on observed user errors) with a proactive, test-driven flywheel that uses a "test space" to map feedback to task objectives, enabling preemptive identification of edge cases. The authors provide a mathematical proof that the proactive approach achieves superior long-term scaling with fewer iterations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reactive AI flywheels — the dominant maintenance paradigm for deployed AI systems — suffer from two critical limitations: (1) they address errors in isolation without considering broader system objectives, failing to anticipate future edge cases and causing wasteful iteration cycles; and (2) due to the long-tail distribution of errors in open-world settings, collecting remaining errors becomes statistically increasingly difficult over time. A fundamentally different, proactive approach is needed.

Method: The authors propose a proactive test-driven flywheel centered on constructing a "test space" — a technical framework that maps feedback data explicitly to task objectives. This test space enables systematic, preemptive identification of potential edge cases before they manifest as user-facing errors. The paper also provides a formal mathematical analysis comparing reactive and proactive flywheels, proving that the proactive variant achieves better long-term scaling properties with fewer total iterations.

Result: The mathematical proof demonstrates that the proactive test-driven flywheel converges to a generalizable system with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel and exhibits superior long-term scaling behavior, particularly in open-world, long-tail error distributions.

Conclusion: A paradigm shift from reactive to proactive, test-driven maintenance flywheels is necessary for building truly generalizable AI systems. The proposed "test space" construct provides a principled mechanism for aligning feedback-driven model updates with overarching task objectives, yielding both theoretical and practical advantages in long-tailed, open-ended deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

</details>


### [225] [SalesLoop: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Sales Lead Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20655)
*Chenyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SalesLoop is a reinforcement learning framework for CRM lead ranking that closes the feedback loop between predictions and real-world outcomes. It introduces a performance-aware reward and Discriminative GRPO to address offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise misalignment, and temporal drift. In production, it achieves +7.9% NDCG@K, +15.8% P@K, and +4.7%–8.7% cumulative lift in a 160-day A/B test across 16.5M leads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CRM lead ranking models suffer from a persistent offline-online performance gap caused by three root issues: (1) offline-online metric mismatch — offline metrics like AUC do not reflect real business KPIs; (2) pointwise-listwise objective misalignment — pointwise training objectives fail to capture the relative ordering critical in ranked lists; and (3) temporal distribution drift — static models degrade as customer behavior and market conditions evolve. These gaps demand a closed-loop, adaptive approach that directly optimizes business outcomes.

Method: SalesLoop is a reinforcement learning framework with two core innovations: (1) a performance-aware reward function that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by both ranking position and conversion velocity (rewarding faster conversions at higher ranks more heavily); and (2) Discriminative GRPO, which adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization into a listwise optimization objective suitable for discriminative ranking models, enabling the model to learn from pairwise and listwise comparisons within the same batch. The framework operates in a closed feedback loop, continuously ingesting production outcomes to refine the ranking policy.

Result: Offline: SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9% and P@K by +15.8% over the strongest static baseline. Online (160-day A/B test at a NEV manufacturer): spans 16.5M leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets. Statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7% (p=0.047) in one market and +8.7% (p=0.002) in the other. The ranking backbone achieves Top-10% recall of 44.1% and surfaces high-intent leads at 2.3× the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

Conclusion: SalesLoop demonstrates that closing the feedback loop via reinforcement learning — with position- and velocity-aware rewards plus listwise optimization — effectively bridges the offline-online gap in CRM lead ranking. The production-validated, statistically significant lifts confirm that adaptive, business-outcome-driven ranking policies can substantially outperform static models in real-world sales environments.

Abstract: Lead ranking in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems faces a persistent challenge: models achieving high offline accuracy often underperform in production. We identify three fundamental gaps responsible for this disconnect: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift.
