To address these gaps, we propose SalesLoop, a reinforcement learning framework that establishes a closed feedback loop between model predictions and real-world business outcomes. Our approach introduces (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.
  SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9\% and P@K by +15.8\% over the strongest static baseline. A 160-day production A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer, spanning 16.5M leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets, validates statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7\% ($p=0.047$) and +8.7\% ($p=0.002$). In production, the ranking backbone achieves Top-10\% recall of 44.1\% and surfaces high-intent leads at $2.3\times$ the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

</details>


### [226] [Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20533)
*Marcos Florencio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a method that uses neural predicates—compositional, probabilistic structures operating on financial analysis data—to automatically generate the view inputs (pick matrix, return vector, and uncertainty matrix) required by the Black-Litterman portfolio model, replacing subjective human specification with a data-driven, interpretable, and fully differentiable pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specifying views and their associated uncertainty in the Black-Litterman model remains a highly subjective, manual process that does not scale well. The authors aim to automate and ground this process in data through a structured, probabilistic mechanism, removing the reliance on investor intuition for uncertainty elicitation.

Method: The authors propose a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates that consume structured financial analysis data. Each neural predicate outputs a probability distribution over market stances. These distributions are then algorithmically mapped to the three key Black-Litterman inputs: the pick matrix P, the view return vector q, and the view uncertainty matrix Ω. View confidence is directly derived from the predicate's output distribution entropy or spread, and the entire architecture is designed to be end-to-end differentiable.

Result: The resulting framework yields a fully differentiable pipeline that can be trained end-to-end. It provides interpretable portfolio weights, as any weight can be traced back through the neural predicate logic chain to the original data sources. View uncertainty is generated in a data-driven manner rather than subjectively.

Conclusion: Neural predicates offer a viable, scalable, and principled alternative to subjective view specification in Black-Litterman portfolio construction, enabling interpretable and learnable portfolio optimization grounded in structured financial data.

Abstract: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

</details>


### [227] [Cardinality-Decomposed Loss: Matching Training Objectives to Relation Structure in Heterogeneous Recommendation Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20737)
*Parul Maheshwari,Amulya Paruchuri,Yiqing Zou,Alireza Sahami Shirazi,Farhad Farahani,Prakhar Mehrotra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard BPR loss in heterogeneous bipartite graph recommendation systems causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry, silently degrading user representations. The authors propose Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL), combining Cross Entropy and BPR, to jointly optimize across one-to-one and one-to-many relations. CDL improves attribute embedding quality, and a trade-off parameter governed by semantic alignment and topology leakage determines when ranking metrics also benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In recommendation systems using heterogeneous bipartite graphs, a single loss function (typically BPR) is applied uniformly to all edge types. The authors discover that while BPR excels at the one-to-many recommendation task, it causes one-to-one attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry — a silent failure invisible to standard ranking metrics. This collapse pollutes user node embeddings (which aggregate signals from both edge types), degrading downstream tasks like personalization and segmentation.

Method: The authors propose Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL), which applies Cross Entropy loss to one-to-one attribute edges and BPR loss to one-to-many preference edges, jointly optimizing both in a shared encoder. They demonstrate a "CE-BPR conflict" by showing the two losses compete in the shared parameter space. A lambda parameter balances the trade-off between attribute discriminability and ranking performance. Two graph properties are introduced to explain dataset behavior: semantic alignment (whether attributes predict preferences) and topology leakage (whether graph connectivity already encodes that predictive signal).

Result: CDL consistently improves attribute embedding discriminability across five datasets (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing, Yelp) spanning two structural configurations (attributes on user nodes vs. item nodes). NDCG ranking improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal (high semantic alignment), but conflicts with attribute optimization when correlation is weak. A lambda-sweep confirms that semantic alignment and topology leakage govern this trade-off.

Conclusion: The CE-BPR conflict in heterogeneous graph learning is a previously unidentified failure mode. CDL resolves this by decomposing the loss along cardinality boundaries. Practitioners should assess semantic alignment and topology leakage to determine whether attribute-aware training will benefit ranking, rather than blindly applying a uniform loss.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks trained on heterogenous bipartite graphs form a common basis in recommendation systems. These graphs often express relations that vary in cardinality, for example, user-item preferences are one-to-many and user-attribute features are one-to-one. Traditionally, a unique loss function is applied for all of the network components which is often Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR). While BPR works well for the recommendation task, we find that it causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry -- a silent failure that leaves standard ranking metrics largely unaffected and therefore invisible to conventional evaluation. This in turn pollutes user node embeddings, which are shaped by both edge types simultaneously, hurting downstream tasks like personalization, segmentation, etc. Here we propose a Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) that combines both Cross Entropy (CE) and BPR to enable the model to collectively optimize for relations across cardinalities. We confirm this CE-BPR conflict by showing the two losses compete in the shared encoder's parameter space. We evaluate CDL on five datasets spanning two structural configurations -- one-to-one attributes on user nodes (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing) and on item nodes (Yelp) -- and find that CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings. We also show that ranking (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal, but conflicts with it when the correlation is weak. We use a lambda parameter to navigate this trade-off, and a lambda-sweep reveals that dataset behavior is governed by two graph properties -- semantic alignment and topology leakage. Semantic alignment measures whether the attribute predicts preferences, while topology leakage measures whether the graph's connectivity already encodes it.

</details>


### [228] [A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20535)
*Alicia Tierz,Icíar Alfaro,David González,Elías Cueto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A zero-shot digital twin framework that combines real-time visual perception with a Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (TIGN) to simulate diverse physical systems on unseen geometries without retraining, achieving ~25ms per frame with augmented reality visualization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional digital twins are geometrically rigid and require extensive retraining or fine-tuning when physical domains or boundary conditions change. The authors aim to create a system that generalizes zero-shot to novel, unseen geometries while maintaining physical consistency and real-time performance.

Method: The framework consists of three main components: (1) A Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (TIGN) solver based on metriplectic thermodynamics formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production via local graph message passing; (2) An auxiliary GNN that infers unobservable fields (stress tensors, velocity/energy distributions) from sparse visual boundaries to mitigate start-up transients; (3) A closed-loop data assimilation mechanism using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow to track macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time, dynamically correcting autoregressive rollouts to eliminate numerical drift.

Result: The unified framework successfully demonstrated extreme generalization across two disparate physical regimes: large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both cases, physically accurate simulations were instantiated on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating at approximately 25ms per frame with direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

Conclusion: The proposed Zero-Shot Digital Twin framework successfully bridges the sim-to-real gap by coupling geometry-agnostic physics-informed learning with real-time visual perception and closed-loop data assimilation, enabling instant, physically accurate simulation on arbitrary geometries without retraining.

Abstract: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

</details>


### [229] [ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20537)
*Huei-Chung Hu,Hsin-Tai Wu,Koyo Kobayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReliableTableQA is a framework for training LLMs to annotate whether tabular QA results are statistically meaningful (not merely answerable). Using a ten-category reliability taxonomy and a program-generated dataset of 50K examples, the authors show that a small, schema-stratified SFT set (~200 examples) is remarkably sufficient, driving reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and eliminating unreliable confident answers. GRPO fine-tuning provides benefit only when SFT is under-trained and yields no gains once SFT is adequate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In enterprise analytics, syntactically correct SQL queries can return statistically unreliable answers — e.g., based on small samples, wide confidence intervals, or confounded data — yet existing QA systems answer confidently in all cases. The authors quantify this failure as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR) and argue that LLMs must be trained to flag statistical reliability, not just answerability.

Method: The authors propose: (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1–R10) covering hazards like small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline generating 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study measuring how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation requires, comparing SFT and GRPO across varying training sizes, in-distribution and out-of-distribution (H&M) settings, and using multiple metrics including exact-flag-set match and a hard compound-flag slice.

Result: A schema-stratified SFT set of just 200 examples raises reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98, improves parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drives UCAR to zero, and generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). GRPO helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06–0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate — a null result confirmed across a hard compound-flag slice, strict exact-match, and OOD evaluation.

Conclusion: Reliability annotation is fundamentally a data-efficiency problem. A small, well-stratified SFT dataset can achieve near-perfect reliability annotation, and reinforcement fine-tuning (GRPO) adds value only under data-scarce, under-trained conditions — delineating precisely when and when not to invest in RL-based post-training for this task.

Abstract: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

</details>


### [230] [Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20538)
*Yitao Jiang,Yaoqing Yang,Luyang Zhao,Muhao Chen,Devin Balkcom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Codec-Gauge introduces a post-training, lightweight orthogonal channel transformation layer that learns optimal coordinate representations for KV-cache compression/quantization. By concentrating energy into low-frequency components via a DCT spectral-centroid loss and a rate proxy, it significantly reduces compression distortion (e.g., 44% KL divergence reduction with zfp) across multiple models and bit-widths, without modifying model weights, attention, or backend codecs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV-cache compression and quantization are critical for efficient long-context Transformer inference, but the fidelity of compressed caches depends heavily on the channel basis in which key/value vectors are represented. Existing backends operate on raw coordinates, which may not be optimal for energy compaction under a given codec. The authors aim to learn a favorable coordinate geometry post-training to maximize compression fidelity without altering model weights or backend rules.

Method: Codec-Gauge inserts a small, learnable orthogonal transformation matrix per layer before an existing compression/quantization backend. Training uses a frequency-distribution objective combining: (1) a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss that concentrates KV energy into low-frequency bins, and (2) a smooth rate proxy to encourage compact codec-facing layouts. The transforms are learned post-training on calibration data. Evaluation uses measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring to assess actual compression-decompression fidelity.

Result: Across six models at 3, 4, and 6 bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average versus raw coordinates, outperforming random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT baselines. Improvements also hold for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. On a 27B model with long-context prompts, the quality trend is reproduced, and serial storage/timing measurements validate the practical compressed-cache implementation.

Conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry is a practical and effective post-training axis for improving KV-cache compression fidelity. Learning small orthogonal transforms tailored to specific codec backends yields significant distortion reductions without touching model weights or attention semantics, establishing a new lightweight optimization dimension for efficient long-context inference.

Abstract: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

</details>


### [231] [Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20539)
*Kyunghoon Hur,Eunjung Jeon,Hyun Woo Kim,Gyubok Lee,Seongjun Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A systematic study comparing two strategies for injecting biokinetic ODE prior knowledge into neural networks to address data scarcity in biomanufacturing: simulation-based decoder pre-training (data-level prior) versus architecturally embedding ODEs (architecture-level prior). Both outperform baselines and are found to be substitutable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning has had limited impact on biomanufacturing due to severe data scarcity — bioreactor experiments are expensive, slow (days to weeks), and rarely shared publicly, leaving researchers with only a handful of experiments per study. However, the domain possesses rich prior knowledge in the form of biokinetic ODE models that have described microbial growth for decades. The gap is that no systematic study has investigated how to inject this ODE knowledge into neural networks.

Method: The authors conduct the first systematic study comparing two approaches for incorporating biokinetic ODE priors into neural networks: (1) a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves, and (2) an architecture-level prior that directly embeds the ODE structure within the decoder network itself. Both are benchmarked against no-prior baselines across 11 datasets spanning 7 microbial species.

Result: Both prior-injection strategies consistently outperform no-prior baselines across all 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. The key finding is that the two approaches are substitutable — a generic decoder pre-trained on simulation data matches the performance of a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data.

Conclusion: Simulation pre-training provides a simple, data-efficient recipe for applying deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity, eliminating the need for complex, bespoke bio-structured architectures while achieving equivalent performance.

Abstract: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

</details>


### [232] [From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20540)
*Luca Ambrogioni,Giulio Franzese,Alberto Foresti,Gabriel Raya,Bac Nguyen,Georgios Batzolis,Yuhta Takida,Naoki Murata,Chieh-Hsin Lai,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a statistical framework for optimizing noise-level allocation in diffusion model training, proving that optimal schedules concentrate on finitely many noise levels under standard assumptions. The authors derive an information-theoretic proxy—square root of generative entropy rate—that approximates the optimal schedule and demonstrate its practical effectiveness across controlled experiments and larger-scale settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current noise schedules in diffusion model training are largely heuristic or empirically tuned, despite the critical importance of which noise levels to train on and how much computational budget to allocate to each. There is no principled statistical framework for understanding or optimizing this allocation.

Method: The authors develop a general statistical framework analyzing two regimes: (1) a fully coupled regime where information flows across time points, for which they prove atomic (finite-support) minimizers under convexity or Polyak-Łojasiewicz conditions; (2) an idealized independent-learner regime modeling neural network temporal specialization, where a random-matrix analysis under a feature-noise decoupling condition yields the entropic proxy. They validate predictions in controlled settings (Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, MNIST) and test the entropic schedule at scale.

Result: In controlled settings, directly optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, and the entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural networks while breaking down in fully coupled parametric cases (as predicted). In larger-scale experiments where full optimization is intractable, square-root entropy scheduling substantially improves training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM heuristics on continuous images.

Conclusion: The work establishes that optimal noise schedules for diffusion training are fundamentally atomic (finite-support) and can be well-approximated by a square-root entropy rate proxy in neural network settings, offering a principled alternative to heuristic noise scheduling that improves training efficiency.

Abstract: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

</details>


### [233] [AI Assistants Overassist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21306)
*Verona Teo,Raghav Jain,Tobias Gerstenberg,Max Kleiman-Weiner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Int-Bench is a simulation-based benchmark that evaluates how LLMs decide when and how to intervene during problem-solving. LLM "teachers" are tested on their intervention strategies with simulated "students" across code debugging, math, and brain teasers. Results show LLMs intervene more frequently, earlier, and with complete solutions rather than targeted hints compared to humans, optimizing for short-term success over deeper learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as AI tutors, but their intervention strategies—when, how often, and in what manner they assist—are poorly understood. Poorly timed or overly frequent interventions, such as giving away full solutions, may undermine genuine learning and cognitive engagement. There is a need to systematically benchmark how LLMs navigate these pedagogical decisions.

Method: The authors introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark featuring a "student" agent solving problems while an LLM "teacher" monitors reasoning and decides on interventions (whether, when, and how to intervene). The benchmark spans three domains: code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers. LLM teachers are evaluated on intervention frequency, timing, and impact on both immediate task success and generalization to unseen problems. LLM behavior is also directly compared against human teacher baselines.

Result: LLM teachers intervene significantly more frequently and earlier than human teachers. Unlike humans, LLMs tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints or scaffolded guidance. These intervention patterns improve short-term task success but fail to support generalization, suggesting a trade-off where LLMs optimize for immediate performance at the expense of deeper learning and reasoning development.

Conclusion: Current LLM assistants are calibrated for short-term success rather than fostering the reasoning processes essential for deeper learning and long-term retention. The findings highlight a critical gap in AI tutoring: the need for intervention strategies that scaffold thinking through hints and partial guidance rather than premature, complete solutions.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

</details>


### [234] [HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20541)
*Dimitrije Ždrale,Cassie An Jeng,Katie Wang,Sonia Vanier,Alexandre Bayen,Hossein Nick Zinat Matin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HypNO is a graph neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws that uses physics-informed message passing on space-time graphs to accurately capture shocks and discontinuities, demonstrated on traffic-flow models (LWR and ARZ).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing operator-learning methods struggle with hyperbolic conservation laws because these systems exhibit simultaneous global transport and shock formation. Standard neural operators often fail to respect the underlying physics — specifically upwinding and entropy conditions — leading to poor shock resolution. There is a need for a data-driven surrogate that is both accurate across varying initial conditions and faithful to the mathematical structure of hyperbolic PDEs.

Method: The authors propose HypNO, a graph-based neural operator that operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells. The key architectural innovation is adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing, which explicitly encodes upwinding (information propagates along characteristic directions) and entropy admissibility (ensuring physically correct shock selection). The model learns a mapping from initial conditions to solution snapshots without requiring a traditional numerical solver at inference time.

Result: HypNO accurately predicts solution snapshots across a range of initial conditions on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models — both prototypical stress tests featuring global transport and shock formation. The architecture successfully captures shocks and discontinuities that conventional neural operators typically smooth over or misplace.

Conclusion: HypNO demonstrates that embedding physics-informed inductive biases — specifically upwinding and entropy conditions — directly into the message-passing mechanism of a graph neural operator yields a surrogate model capable of faithfully approximating hyperbolic conservation laws, even in the presence of shocks.

Abstract: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

</details>


### [235] [Beyond Heavy Log Curation: Perplexity-Based APT Detection via Unsupervised, Context-Augmented Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20832)
*Shoya Otsu,Kei Suzuki,Toshiaki Koike-Akino,Jing Liu,Ye Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAPTAIN is a perplexity-based APT detector that uses pre-trained language models with minimal preprocessing, encoding recent history via a Q-Former-style bridge to inject temporal context into perplexity scoring, achieving competitive detection performance while drastically reducing the cost of log curation and pipeline engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: APT detection is hindered by the rarity of attack events in large-scale logs and the high cost of investigation. Existing ML-based methods require heavily curated training data and complex preprocessing pipelines that demand substantial domain expertise and engineering effort. The authors aim to reduce this development and operational burden while maintaining robust detection performance.

Method: CAPTAIN uses a perplexity-based detection approach with three key components: (1) domain-agnostic, minimal preprocessing of log entries; (2) a context-augmented architecture where an encoder model captures recent history and a Q-Former-style bridge compresses it into compact context tokens fed into the decoder input, so that perplexity reflects temporal context; and (3) smoothing filters applied to the perplexity time series to improve stability.

Result: CAPTAIN achieves competitive performance against strong existing baselines on APT-oriented benchmarks while maintaining robustness under substantially less curated input conditions.

Conclusion: By leveraging general pre-trained language models and avoiding complex domain-specific preprocessing, CAPTAIN lowers the cost of building and maintaining APT detection systems, making scalable log-based threat detection more accessible without sacrificing detection quality.

Abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) remain difficult to detect because only a small fraction of events in large-scale logs are attack-related, and investigation is expensive and hard to scale. Prior machine-learning approaches can reduce analyst workload, but they often rely on heavily curated training data and sophisticated preprocessing pipelines. Building and maintaining such pipelines require substantial domain expertise and engineering cost. Motivated by insights from a study of a strong APT detection baseline, we propose CAPTAIN (Context-Augmented Perplexity-based Threat Activity log detectIoN), a perplexity-based detector that leverages general, pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing, enabling robust scoring of long, minimally processed log entries. CAPTAIN encodes recent history with an encoder model and a Q-Former-style bridge, then injects the compact context tokens into the decoder input so that perplexity reflects temporal context. To improve stability, CAPTAIN additionally applies smoothing filters to the perplexity time series. Across APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs, that reduces the development and operational cost of advanced log preprocessing.

</details>


### [236] [Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20542)
*Angel Tsai-Hsuan Chung,Jatu Abdulai,Patrick Bayoh,Lawrence Sandi,Francis Smart,Hamsa Bastani,Osbert Bastani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A decision-aware machine learning framework using multi-task learning and catalytic priors was developed for essential medicines allocation in Sierra Leone. Nationwide deployment led to a 19% increase in medicine consumption, ultimately scaling to cover 2 million women and children.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient and equitable allocation of scarce essential medicines in LMICs is hindered by limited high-quality data, making traditional data-driven methods impractical. There is a pressing need for allocation frameworks that work under severe data constraints while ensuring equitable distribution.

Method: The authors propose a decision-aware machine learning framework that integrates multi-task learning for sample efficiency and catalytic priors to promote equitable allocation. The system was deployed as a decision support tool through a staggered, nationwide rollout in collaboration with the Sierra Leone government, followed by econometric evaluation.

Result: The econometric evaluation estimated a 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts. The tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering approximately 2 million women and children under five.

Conclusion: Machine learning methods can significantly improve resource allocation efficiency and access to essential medicines at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings, offering a scalable solution for LMICs.

Abstract: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

</details>


### [237] [Agree on the Model, Verify the Inference: GKR Protocols for HND-Based Transformer Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21162)
*Xiaolong Liang,Juanjuan Li,Rui Qin,Yisheng Lv*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GKR-HND is a verification protocol for transformer inference that uses GKR proofs and registered model weights, delegating expensive public evaluations to a separate computation worker while a lightweight retained verifier checks proofs without replaying dense matrix operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outsourced transformer inference suffers from two attack vectors: model substitution (a malicious server swaps the model) and incomplete execution (the server skips computation). Existing solutions either require full replay (negating outsourcing benefits) or lack efficient verification for real transformer architectures.

Method: The authors propose GKR-HND, which combines: (1) GKR (Goldwasser-Kalai-Rothblum) interactive proofs to verify the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic-Nonhomomorphic Decomposition (HND) transformers, (2) registered-model weights with cryptographic openings for model integrity, and (3) a two-party architecture where a retained verifier checks GKR transcripts and weight openings while delegating costly public evaluations to an untrusted computation worker under a non-collusion assumption. The worker's response must be signed and request-bound.

Result: Experiments on pretrained HND models demonstrate that the proof path is valid and that public computation can be delegated successfully without requiring dense-matrix replay, preserving the computational benefits of outsourcing.

Conclusion: GKR-HND enables verifiable outsourced transformer inference under honest-verifier and prover-worker non-collusion assumptions, achieving practical verification without the overhead of full dense-matrix replay.

Abstract: Outsourced Transformer inference exposes clients to model substitution and incomplete execution, while direct replay removes the computational benefit of delegation. We present GKR-HND, a registered-model protocol for verifying the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic--Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers. The retained verifier checks the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings, but delegates expensive public evaluations to an assigned computation worker. Assuming an honest retained verifier and prover--worker non-collusion, the verifier accepts only when the worker's signed, request-bound response agrees with the proof claims. Experiments with pretrained HND models validate the proof path and the delegated public computation without dense-matrix replay.

</details>


### [238] [When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20543)
*Todd Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLVR training improves one-sample accuracy but often reduces pass@k at large k — solving fewer distinct problems under repeated sampling. The authors diagnose this as an absence-of-evidence failure on "boundary prompts" (where correct trajectories are rare but exist in the base model) and propose Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA), a simple method that preserves base-distribution behavior on risky prompts while sharpening on safe ones. PBA improves both pass@1 and high-budget coverage over GRPO on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR post-training (e.g., GRPO with outcome verifiers) is known to improve pass@1 but can degrade pass@k — i.e., after training, the model solves fewer distinct problems under repeated sampling than the base model. This inversion is poorly understood, and the authors seek to diagnose its mechanism, arguing it is an absence-of-evidence failure where rare correct trajectories are lost because RLVR's finite rollout groups fail to sample and reinforce them often enough.

Method: The paper proposes a diagnostic framework distinguishing "safe" prompts (abundant correct evidence) from "boundary" prompts (rare correct trajectories). The proof-of-concept method, Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA), sharpens safe prompts via RLVR while anchoring boundary prompts to the frozen base model's distribution. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study isolates the effect across three seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary validation benchmark.

Result: PBA improves both pass@1 and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO baselines. The diagnostic study consistently shows that standard GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves these rare verifier-positive trajectories. Results are consistent across three training seeds.

Conclusion: Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize but also which prompts are safe to optimize. The pass@k inversion risk generalizes beyond math to vision-language agents where repeated attempts are checked by external verifiers. PBA demonstrates that simple per-prompt anchoring strategies can mitigate the trade-off between one-sample accuracy and sampling diversity.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

</details>


### [239] [Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20547)
*Esrat Farhana Dulia,Syed Arbab Mohd Shihab,Caleb Adams,Ruben Del Rosario*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A DQN-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework enables decentralized conflict resolution for heterogeneous UAS and eVTOL aircraft in structured 3D corridors under degraded surveillance, with policies evaluated across traffic densities and separation thresholds, revealing safety-capacity trade-offs via Pareto-optimal configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) operations require reliable separation assurance even when surveillance data is degraded — noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. Existing conflict resolution approaches often rely on ideal sensing assumptions, motivating the need for decentralized, learning-based methods robust to realistic sensing imperfections.

Method: A Deep Q-Network (DQN) based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework trains separate decentralized policies for two heterogeneous aircraft types (small UAS and eVTOL) in a structured 3D corridor. Each agent uses local observations and a discrete 14-action space (maintain course, turn, vertical maneuver, land, speed control). Training incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy constraints, corridor boundaries, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. Evaluation spans 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds.

Result: Loss-of-separation frequency and duration increase with traffic density and separation requirements, though most events resolve within 1 second. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of the time. During conflicts, action distribution is: turning 33%, maintain motion 29%, speed control 25%, vertical maneuvers 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity.

Conclusion: The MARL framework effectively supports simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions, demonstrating that learned decentralized policies can handle realistic sensing degradations while balancing safety and operational efficiency.

Abstract: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

</details>


### [240] [SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20548)
*Mikail Khona,Aditya Vavre,Boxiang Wang,Deyu Fu,Hao Wu,Mike Chrzanowski,Bryan Catanzaro,Dheevatsa Mudigere,Jeff Pool,Michael Lightstone,Mohammad Shoeybi,Mostofa Patwary,Nima Tajbakhsh,Tijmen Blankevoort*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper adapts preconditioned gradient methods (SOAP, Muon) for large-scale LLM pretraining, addressing stability issues at large batch sizes, proposing fair optimizer comparisons via update-RMS matching, and introducing a distributed layer-wise implementation compatible with Megatron-LM that preserves convergence benefits while being memory-efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Higher-order optimizers like Muon and SOAP converge faster than AdamW but suffer from high computational cost and numerical instability, limiting their adoption at scale. The work aims to overcome these practical barriers to enable effective large-scale LLM pretraining with these methods.

Method: (1) Algorithmic modifications to SOAP including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning to eliminate loss spikes at large batch sizes. (2) Update-RMS matching for fair learning rate transfer across AdamW, Muon, and SOAP in a unified empirical study. (3) A layer-wise distributed optimizer built for Megatron-LM that balances memory and hides communication without approximating optimizer computations. (4) System-level optimizations to accelerate the distributed implementation.

Result: SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens. At batch sizes up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, SOAP and Muon maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. The layer-wise distributed implementation achieves efficient scaling without sacrificing convergence.

Conclusion: Preconditioned gradient methods can be made practical for large-scale LLM pretraining through targeted algorithmic and systems-level innovations. The released codebase (Emerging-Optimizers) provides the research community with production-ready implementations of these advanced optimizers.

Abstract: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

</details>


### [241] [SevDiff: Severity-Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Tail Conflict Trajectory Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20549)
*Eni Solomon Laughter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SevDiff is a severity-conditioned diffusion model that generates vehicle interaction trajectories with a target Time-to-Collision (TTC), achieving near-perfect hit rates for TTC values ≤2.5s and producing physically plausible kinematic features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ADAS evaluation datasets are dominated by routine driving and lack rare but safety-critical vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events. Existing generative methods condition on scene-level properties (spatial goals, agent structure, adversarial objectives) but none accept a target TTC as a direct conditioning signal with measurable accuracy, leaving a gap for controlled generation of specific conflict severities.

Method: SevDiff is a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that takes a scalar minimum TTC value as conditioning input and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories. Performance is evaluated via a hit-rate metric measuring how often the realized TTC falls within ±0.5s of the target. The model is trained on 468 interaction windows from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations).

Result: SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate (±0.5s) for TTC targets of 0.5–1.5s, 97–99% for 2.0–2.5s, and degrades gracefully to 39% at TTC=5.0s. Generated kinematics are physically plausible: maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features, with no negative speed or gap values in >96.5% of samples.

Conclusion: The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the weakening of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, providing a precision characterization of generator capability rather than a binary pass/fail judgment. SevDiff enables targeted generation of safety-critical scenarios for ADAS evaluation.

Abstract: Trajectory datasets used in ADAS evaluation are heavily biased toward routine driving; genuine vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events are rare, and the rarer the event, the higher the cost when an ADAS system fails to handle it. Existing generative approaches address this imbalance by conditioning on scene-level properties - spatial goals, agent structure, or natural-language adversarial objectives - but none can accept a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value as input and be held to producing it within a measurable error. This paper introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that accepts a requested minimum TTC value as a scalar conditioning signal and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories whose realized conflict severity matches the request, evaluated through a hit-rate metric. Trained on 468 interaction windows extracted from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing), SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s and 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s, with graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematic features are physically plausible, with a maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features and no negative speed or gap values in more than 96.5% of samples. The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the strength of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, making it a precision characterization of the generator rather than a pass/fail result.

</details>


### [242] [Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20550)
*Tianming Han,Zhijie Pan,Wenchi Ge,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as the key computational framework for overcoming the challenges of rational polypharmacological drug design, surveying architectures from invariant GNNs to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that enable shared pocket characterization, multi-target bioactivity prediction, and de novo dual-target ligand generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm fails for multifactorial diseases (cancer, neurodegenerative disorders) due to compensatory signaling and drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a therapeutic solution, the rational design of single ligands that simultaneously satisfy geometric constraints of multiple binding sites remains a major computational bottleneck that current methods cannot adequately address.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic review positioning GDL as an integrative framework, surveying architectures across: (1) invariant graph neural networks for molecular representation, (2) SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models for 3D structure-aware learning, (3) geometric embeddings for shared binding pocket characterization, (4) heterogeneous graph fusion for multi-target bioactivity prediction, and (5) structure-conditioned generative algorithms combining diffusion models with reinforcement learning for de novo dual-target ligand design. They also evaluate multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures.

Result: The review synthesizes methodological advances demonstrating that GDL enables a paradigm shift from serendipitous drug discovery to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, providing a structured guide across three core application dimensions: shared pocket characterization, multi-target prediction, and de novo generation.

Conclusion: Geometric deep learning, particularly SE(3)-equivariant architectures and diffusion-based generative models augmented with reinforcement learning, represents a transformative computational paradigm for rationally designing polypharmacological ligands. The integration of multimodal omics data with specialized geometric benchmarks is critical for model validation and clinical translation of these next-generation therapeutic strategies.

Abstract: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

</details>


### [243] [SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20551)
*Tianming Han,Li Zhang,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SenCos-GEM is a 3D geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that combines physics-guided geometric consistency (law of cosines) with SENet-based dynamic feature modulation to achieve state-of-the-art molecular property prediction, particularly on 3D conformation-sensitive tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D SSL methods for molecular representation learning suffer from two key weaknesses: (1) lack of explicit physical constraints, making them vulnerable to geometric noise from coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training; and (2) neglect of dynamic feature modulation during downstream fine-tuning, leading to catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer.

Method: SenCos-GEM introduces two core components: (1) a physics-guided geometric consistency loss derived from the law of cosines to enforce high-fidelity, mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors; and (2) lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules integrated as task-specific adapters into the backbone, coupled with a dual-modulation prediction head combining Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms for dynamic feature recalibration during downstream adaptation.

Result: SenCos-GEM achieves state-of-the-art results on MoleculeNet benchmarks, with particularly strong performance on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks: 12.9% relative RMSE reduction on FreeSolv, 5.3% relative RMSE reduction on Lipophilicity, and 8.2% relative MAE reduction on QM9. The model also demonstrates superior stereoisomer discrimination and conformational perturbation robustness.

Conclusion: SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in molecular property prediction by explicitly decoupling geometry enhancement (physics-guided priors) from dynamic feature modulation, achieving robust and accurate performance across diverse molecular tasks.

Abstract: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

</details>


### [244] [Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20552)
*Chitraansh Pandey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper frames grokking as a thermodynamic phase transition in attention logits, uses the peak in attention logit variance (specific heat Cv) as a precursor signal, and introduces CvAdamW—an optimizer variant that dynamically scales weight decay at the phase transition to accelerate generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. The authors aim to detect an early, reliable signal of impending generalization and leverage it to trigger intervention, thereby enabling grokking within a fixed compute budget where standard methods fail.

Method: Building on the thermodynamic isomorphism of Transformer attention, the variance of attention logits is treated as a specific heat Cv. CvAdamW monitors Cv online and dynamically scales weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Three failure modes (initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, slingshot blinding) are resolved via a memorization gate and an EMA shock absorber. A scale-invariant z-score reformulation removes task-specific hyperparameters.

Result: On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 within a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. The cold-start z-score variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds. Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds.

Conclusion: Neural networks expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions. A physically motivated, proportional intervention (CvAdamW) can facilitate grokking within a fixed compute budget, suggesting a principled approach to triggering and accelerating delayed generalization.

Abstract: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

</details>


### [245] [Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20555)
*Bryce A. Christopherson,Jack Baretz,Darian Colgrove,Salah Dandan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper revisits the strong lottery ticket hypothesis, identifies layerwise sparsity selection as a key bottleneck in edge-popup methods, and introduces "double-scoring"—an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces per-layer sparsity selection with optimization over enlarged score tensors. This approach substantially improves strong-ticket extraction, reduces sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters, and outperforms existing baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing theory confirms that strong lottery tickets (accurate subnetworks within randomly initialized networks without any weight training) exist, but reliable extraction remains challenging. Edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method, is a leading approach, but its performance is hindered by a layerwise sparsity selection bottleneck that is poorly understood.

Method: The authors propose double-scoring: an augmented parameterization where score tensors are enlarged, allowing fixed-density masking in the augmented space while preserving access to all original-coordinate masks. The method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. The approach replaces the need for careful layerwise sparsity allocation with optimization over the expanded score space, inducing effective original sparsity through score-space competition.

Result: Double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines. It also improves upon rewound sparse-training topologies and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablation studies confirm the gains stem from augmented score-space competition rather than merely additional trainable parameters.

Conclusion: The layerwise sparsity selection is a critical bottleneck in strong lottery ticket extraction. The double-scoring method effectively addresses this bottleneck through score-space augmentation, enabling more reliable extraction of strong tickets and reducing hyperparameter sensitivity.

Abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

</details>


### [246] [Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20557)
*Hesen Chen,Xinyu Su,Xiaomeng Yang,Yuetan Lin,Zixiong Yang,Junyi An,Fenglei Cao,Yifeng Jiao,Yunqi Zhang,Yuan Cheng,Zhiyu Tan,Hao Li,Libo Wu,Yuan Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MKB is a unified scientific multimodal model built on a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored encoders/decoders, covering six scientific domains (DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, medical imaging) and supporting both understanding and generation of native scientific outputs. It uses a two-stage modality-then-language training curriculum and retains strong general capabilities while achieving competitive domain-specific performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific discovery increasingly requires multi-domain reasoning, but existing AI systems are either domain-specialized or unify scientific data superficially through text tokenization, failing to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, or support joint understanding and generation across domains.

Method: MKB employs a shared Transformer backbone with modality-specific encoders, adapters, and decoders. Training uses a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with a frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. The model covers DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, producing native outputs like biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks.

Result: MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding on biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone.

Conclusion: Shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components offer a promising foundation for cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration, demonstrating the feasibility of a unified paradigm for scientific AI.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora.
