Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

</details>


### [247] [StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20558)
*Emma Kondrup,Zachary Yang,Anne Imouza,Reihaneh Rabbany*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StabilityBench transforms static single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn conversational histories with realistic user simulations (demographic proxies, sycophantic baits). Applied across four benchmarks and nine LLMs, it reveals consistent performance instability, motivating more realistic evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation protocols rely on static, single-turn benchmarks that fail to capture real-world conversational variability. AI assistants deployed in high-stakes settings (healthcare, government) exhibit strong context dependence, yet existing evaluation layers—from traditional benchmarks to adversarial testing—do not adequately simulate realistic multi-turn interactions. There is a need for a model-agnostic method to stress-test LLMs under conversational conditions without requiring entirely new benchmarks.

Method: StabilityBench is a benchmark operator that augments existing single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories by injecting realistic user simulations along two axes: (1) demographic proxies—varying user identity attributes such as age, gender, or profession; and (2) sycophantic baits—user utterances designed to probe whether models alter responses to agree with or flatter the user. Crucially, these injections preserve the original task intent of the underlying benchmark. The authors also introduce StabilityBench-Mini, a cost-preserving variant that samples across diversification axes to enable realistic multi-turn evaluation without increased computational expense.

Result: When applied to four benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, health QA, and safety) across nine LLMs, StabilityBench reveals consistent performance instability. Three out of four benchmarks showed considerable performance degradation under the injected conversational conditions, demonstrating that model capabilities measured in static settings do not reliably transfer to multi-turn, socially situated interactions.

Conclusion: Static, single-turn evaluations are insufficient for assessing real-world LLM reliability. StabilityBench provides a principled, model-agnostic framework to stress-test models under realistic conversational dynamics, exposing brittleness that traditional benchmarks miss. The authors advocate for adopting more dynamic evaluation settings, with StabilityBench-Mini offering a practical path forward that balances realism with cost.

Abstract: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent. We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

</details>


### [248] [Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20559)
*Aditya Dutt,Paul Gader,Aditya Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deep learning framework (JuGAAD) integrates Indian census and geospatial data with survey data to predict high-resolution socioeconomic indicators, overcoming scale mismatches between coarse survey data and fine-grained census data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a critical scale mismatch between geographically comprehensive census data and infrequent, coarse-resolution socioeconomic surveys (e.g., NSSO), hindering effective poverty and food security monitoring in developing nations.

Method: A three-step framework: (1) census and geospatial data are aggregated into village-cluster tessellations to reduce noise and handle boundary changes; (2) an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional NSSO survey data into a low-dimensional latent representation; (3) a regression model maps the upscaled census/geospatial data to this latent representation, then applied to fine-grained census data for high-resolution predictions, validated against district-level NSSO ground truth.

Result: The methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine spatial scales with strong accuracy, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators.

Conclusion: The JuGAAD framework effectively bridges the scale gap between census and survey data, enabling reliable high-resolution prediction of poverty and food security indicators.

Abstract: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

</details>


### [249] [Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20560)
*Muntaser Syed,Marius Silaghi,Sheikh Abujar,Sharun Akter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chronofy is a neuro-symbolic framework that embeds temporal validity into RAG systems at three layers—representation, retrieval, and reasoning—to combat temporal hallucination by making fact age structurally encoded, applying learnable exponential decay grounded in Bayesian decision theory, and using Signal Temporal Logic to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RAG systems treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of when they were generated, leading to temporal hallucination where obsolete facts corrupt LLM outputs. The core insight is that recency critically determines relevance—yesterday's clinical lab result is actionable, but a six-month-old reading is noise.

Method: Chronofy implements a three-layer Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA): Layer 1 reserves a temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings so fact age is structurally inseparable from the representation; Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, with decay coefficient β_j derived from Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate; Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate temporal validity of retrieved knowledge and enforces a possibilistic weakest-link principle, bounding output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain.

Result: Evaluated on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, Chronofy demonstrates improved retrieval precision, reduced temporal hallucination, and principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

Conclusion: Explicit temporal decay modeling through a neuro-symbolic architecture significantly improves RAG reliability by structurally preventing obsolete facts from corrupting outputs, and enables automated re-acquisition decisions when temporal context is insufficient.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation. Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

</details>


### [250] [CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20561)
*Keumseo Ryum,Joonhyuk Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CT-Merging is a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that constructs consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales, addressing the coefficient mismatch in SVD-based merging. It achieves superior accuracy on CLIP adapter benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SVD-based LoRA merging methods inherit coefficients directly from original task SVDs, causing a mismatch: while they preserve component order with high rank correlation, their magnitudes differ substantially from those induced by actual task updates. This limits merged model performance.

Method: CT-Merging estimates consensus directions by averaging task subspace projectors (repeated support across task SVD subspaces) to construct a common basis. After direction construction, it assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update, deliberately reducing reliance on rank-wise SVD magnitudes.

Result: On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy over state-of-the-art merging methods, outperforming DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 with KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

Conclusion: Decoupling basis construction from coefficient assignment — using subspace projectors for directions and RMS-based task-level scaling for magnitudes — is a more effective strategy for LoRA adapter merging than directly inheriting SVD coefficients.

Abstract: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

</details>


### [251] [AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20577)
*Mengda Xing,Jean-Marie Lagniez,Alejandro Franco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Swin3D Transformer-based deep learning surrogate with Gaussian Positional Encoding and a Temporal Encoding module is proposed to dramatically accelerate physics-based battery simulations while maintaining high prediction accuracy for spatiotemporal discharge dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-based electrochemical simulations of lithium-ion battery electrode discharge are computationally prohibitive, hindering high-throughput battery design and optimization. A fast yet accurate surrogate model is needed.

Method: The authors propose a deep learning surrogate pipeline built on the Swin3D Transformer architecture. Two key innovations are introduced: (1) Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE) to better represent spatial features in complex electrode microstructures, and (2) a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution of discharge dynamics. The model predicts spatiotemporal discharge behavior directly from volumetric electrode data.

Result: Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset shows the proposed pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy, while reducing computational overhead by orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: The proposed Swin3D-GPE framework provides a scalable and efficient surrogate for electrode-scale discharge simulation, enabling high-throughput LIB design and optimization.

Abstract: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

</details>


### [252] [Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20578)
*Vu Khac Ky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds via two complementary functionals: the primal Fisher width (induced by the Fisher metric) and the inverse-Fisher width (induced by the inverse Fisher metric). The Fisher width governs learning by measuring local parameter fluctuations, while the inverse-Fisher width governs recovery under anisotropic Gaussian measurements. Key results include a scale-attainment theorem for Fisher-regular losses, two-sided estimates for the statistical dimension in sparse recovery with support-sensitive guarantees, and a sharp uncertainty-like inequality: \(w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) \geq w(T)^2\), showing Fisher anisotropy can shift but not eliminate complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical models naturally carry Riemannian geometry via the Fisher information metric, yet classical complexity measures (e.g., Gaussian width) are typically Euclidean. The authors aim to bridge this gap by systematically developing Fisher-geometric analogues of Gaussian width, capturing how the intrinsic geometry of the statistical manifold affects both learning (parameter estimation) and recovery (sparse signal reconstruction).

Method: The paper defines two functionals: the primal Fisher width \(w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)\) and the inverse-Fisher width \(w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)\), where \(G\) is the Fisher information matrix. For learning, it analyzes Fisher-regular losses and proves scale attainment on small Fisher balls. For recovery, it studies anisotropic Gaussian measurements with covariance \(G^{-1}\), deriving two-sided bounds on the statistical dimension and support-sensitive recovery estimates. A product inequality linking the two widths is then proved for any compact coordinate set \(T\).

Result: Three main results: (1) For Fisher-regular losses, the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt{n}\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls. (2) In sparse recovery, the geometry depends on both sparsity and the position of active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum, yielding two-sided statistical dimension estimates, support-sensitive recovery guarantees, and a curvature-based ordering of supports. (3) The inequality \(w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) \geq w(T)^2\) holds on any common compact coordinate set, implying Fisher anisotropy can transfer complexity between geometries but cannot simultaneously reduce both below the Euclidean scale.

Conclusion: Fisher information geometry fundamentally shapes both learning and recovery complexity, but in complementary ways governed by the metric and its inverse. The product inequality acts as a conservation principle: anisotropy may redistribute complexity but never eliminates it. The framework provides a unified geometric lens for understanding statistical trade-offs in high-dimensional inference.

Abstract: We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

</details>


### [253] [Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20586)
*Boldsaikhan Bolorkhuu,Tsogtgerel Gantumur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proves that vector-valued affine refinement operators with compactly supported piecewise linear data admit exact fixed-width ReLU network realizations of depth O(n), using a novel "residual memory controller" that converts noninvertible residual dynamics into an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay for Horner-type evaluation of affine forcing sums.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish that iterated affine refinement operators—common in subdivision schemes, wavelet constructions, and fractal modeling—can be exactly represented by ReLU neural networks with depth scaling linearly in the number of iterations, thereby bridging classical refinement theory with modern deep learning architectures.

Method: The authors build on a homogeneous realization theorem (B≡0 case). The key innovation is a residual memory controller that replaces noninvertible residual dynamics with an injective skew-product dynamical system. This enables exact backward replay of residual states needed for Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align forcing atoms away from residual seams, and complementary loop readouts recover values exactly. Branch-selection ambiguity is shown to occur only where the accumulated affine state vanishes. The construction handles M≥3 for arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing, and M=2 with ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing.

Result: For M≥3, every finite affine iterate admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization of depth O(n) for arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing. For M=2, the same holds under seam-separation conditions. A stage-dependent extension covers forcing terms in fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear spans, yielding linear-depth upgrades for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

Conclusion: Affine refinement operators with piecewise linear data can be exactly embedded into ReLU networks with depth linear in iteration count and fixed width, establishing a tight connection between classical subdivision/refinement schemes and neural network expressivity. The residual memory controller technique provides a general tool for handling noninvertible dynamics in exact network realizations.

Abstract: We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

</details>


### [254] [Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20590)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural network failures exhibit "Spectral Drift" — heightened frequency-domain instability in internal layer activations invisible at the output. The authors propose Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a lightweight monitoring framework (5% overhead) that uses multi-scale spectral features and curriculum learning to detect misclassifications, achieving ~79% AUROC vs. ~52% for confidence-based baselines on CIFAR-10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Confidence-based failure detection methods (e.g., MaxSoftmax, Energy Score) perform poorly because the spectral signatures of misclassifications are masked at the output layer. The authors identify that failures manifest as characteristic spectral instability in internal activations — termed "Spectral Drift" — which remains invisible to output-layer methods, motivating a detection framework that monitors internal spectral dynamics.

Method: SDNN monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features from internal activations. A lightweight detector network (5% additional parameters) is trained via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations. The detector learns to identify failure-indicative spectral patterns.

Result: On CIFAR-10, SDNN achieves 79.0 ± 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, outperforming MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by 25–30 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm wavelet decomposition and statistical features contribute consistently, while STFT's contribution remains unclear. The 1.9% increase in Spectral Drift for failures is statistically significant (p < 0.001).

Conclusion: Spectral analysis of internal activations reveals diagnostic failure information inaccessible to output-based approaches, establishing a promising direction for neural network reliability. SDNN demonstrates that lightweight spectral monitoring can substantially improve failure detection over traditional confidence-based methods.

Abstract: Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

</details>


### [255] [STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20592)
*Jan Linnenbrink,Jakub Nowosad,Marvin Ludwig,Anna Frederike Jablotschkin,Fabian Schumacher,Teja Kattenborn,Hanna Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) is proposed as a standardized reporting framework for spatio-temporal machine-learning models in environmental research, addressing the current lack of such protocols. It provides both a documentation structure and a guided workflow, accompanied by an R-package with a web application that semi-automates protocol completion and flags common pitfalls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatio-temporal machine-learning models in environmental research are highly sensitive to training data characteristics and methodological choices (e.g., cross-validation strategy), yet standardized reporting protocols for such models are currently absent. This lack of transparency and comparability undermines trust in machine-learning-based environmental maps, especially as they transition from science into practice.

Method: The authors designed STeMP, a protocol structured into three sections: Overview (metadata), Model (predictors, evaluation, software), and Prediction (elements of the modelling workflow). The protocol is hosted on GitHub and implemented via an accompanying R-package featuring a web application for manual or semi-automated completion using provided modelling objects. The tool issues warnings when common pitfalls are detected, serving as guidance for authors and reviewers.

Result: The protocol delivers a dual-purpose framework: standardized reporting for understanding model functioning and actionable guidance during the modelling process by highlighting critical decisions and parameters. The R-package and web application enable practical adoption, while the GitHub-hosted definition encourages community contributions and feedback.

Conclusion: STeMP fills a critical gap by providing the first standardized protocol for spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling in environmental research, promoting trust, transparency, and comparability. Its open-source, community-driven approach via GitHub and the R-package facilitates widespread adoption and iterative improvement.

Abstract: Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

</details>


### [256] [When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20594)
*Tong Zhang,Junhao Hu,Yun Peng,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzes weight-tied looped transformers on group word problems, revealing four findings: a budget law linking training data to computation speed; architecture prior (not expressivity) determining algorithm selection; barriers from group order (not circuit complexity); and portable, transferable mechanisms. Introduces a convergence-time scaling instrument for mechanistic analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when and how weight-tied looped transformers implement actual algorithms, moving beyond expressivity theory to characterize the algorithms SGD actually discovers, their scaling laws, mechanistic properties, and barriers to learning.

Method: Controlled experiments on group word problems (symmetric groups S5, alternating group A5) using weight-tied looped transformers trained with different budget contracts (n_train, T_train). Introduced convergence-time scaling τ(n,i) as a head instrument, validated causally via damage cones. Tested architectural variants (tied vs. untied, with/without positional addressing), curricula, and warm-starting across budget contracts.

Result: (1) Budget law: v ~ n_train/T_train with exponent 0.98, R²=0.99; T* = ceil(n/v̂) as principled halting rule. (2) Weight tying flips algorithm selection from parallel to serial; untied models extrapolate poorly and fail on A5. (3) NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes), but group order blocks learning (S5's 120×120 operator); operator-first curriculum dissolves this wall. (4) Mechanisms transfer via warm-starting across budgets; imposing seriality through input schedule fails. Head instrument τ(n,i) predicts OOD behavior where tail metrics fail.

Conclusion: Weight-tied looped transformers learn serial algorithms governed by a precise budget law, with architecture prior (tying) determining algorithm selection. Barriers are empirical (group order), not complexity-theoretic. Standard tail metrics are inadequate; the convergence-time scaling instrument provides reliable mechanistic insight and predicts out-of-distribution behavior.

Abstract: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

</details>


### [257] [Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20596)
*Seonglae Cho,Zekun Wu,Kleyton Da Costa,Rishi Kalra,Ilham Wicaksono,Adriano Koshiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Single-token SAE features across families show that cross-family causal roles are sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale, with decoder-space clustering and depth-dependent ablation effects revealing systematic differences in feature interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether the causal role of sparse autoencoder (SAE) features is stable across different SAE families, using single-token features (which activate on one vocabulary item) as a diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct, controlled comparison.

Method: Analyzed 3.9 million features across six models and three SAE families (GemmaScope, BatchTopK, LlamaScope) using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Measured decoder-space clustering, per-layer ablation effects on logit outputs, target token rank recovery, and conducted a controlled activation-function comparison within the same base model.

Result: Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers. Ablation yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178/208 full-layer conditions. Depth controls whether damage cascades downstream or shapes output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. Target token rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96–98% of the time post-ablation. A controlled activation-function comparison reversed the sign within the same model.

Conclusion: Cross-family interpretability claims are sensitive to training methodology (the residual explanatory factor), not merely activation function or scale. This challenges the assumption of causal stability across SAE families and has implications for using SAE features in interpretability and steering applications.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

</details>


### [258] [One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20641)
*Afsaneh Mahanipour,Hana Khamfroush*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity, where clients only annotate subsets of disease categories. It replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations—balanced label projection, per-class absolute aggregation, and optional analytic pseudo-label refinement—requiring at most two communication rounds. On ChestXray14, it outperforms FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC and 13.24 AUC points while drastically reducing communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real-world federated medical imaging, institutions annotate only pathologies within their expertise, creating task heterogeneity where each client has labels for a strict subset of disease categories. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail here because they need hundreds of communication rounds and lack mechanisms to correct systematic false-negative bias from missing class labels.

Method: The authors propose an analytic FL framework with three closed-form operations: (1) Balanced label projection — normalizes positive and negative contributions to equal total mass, neutralizing class-imbalance bias; (2) Per-class absolute aggregation law — independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease from sufficient statistics uploaded by annotating clients; (3) Optional analytic pseudo-label refinement — propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure completes in at most two communication rounds.

Result: Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations show the method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points.

Conclusion: The analytic FL framework effectively addresses task heterogeneity in multi-label medical image classification, achieving superior performance with dramatically fewer communication rounds compared to gradient-based alternatives, making it highly practical for real-world cross-institutional collaborative learning.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity. The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients. Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

</details>


### [259] [Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20652)
*Andrew Mack,Kraig Yuheng Tou,Mark Henry,Zhengxun Wu,Lauren Greenspan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The ParityTransformer introduces a hardware-efficient sparse bottleneck (DPB) that makes per-layer interpretability practical at scale, replacing learned over-complete dictionaries with a parameter-free algebraic structure, achieving native interpretability that matches or exceeds post-hoc SAE methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models exhibit superposition (representing more features than dimensions), and while SAEs can recover features post-hoc, training interpretable-by-construction models is impractical due to the prohibitive memory/compute costs of per-layer over-complete bottlenecks.

Method: The Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces learned over-complete bases with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary using hierarchically structured sparse bottlenecks and a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach, providing deterministic incoherence guarantees. This is implemented in a GPT-2-scale ParityTransformer with hardware-aware sparsity to minimize the interpretability tax.

Result: ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, and outperform on feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Features are native to the forward pass, confirming they are actually used during computation.

Conclusion: This work represents progress toward models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post-hoc, with the DPB approach closing the cost gap between sparse and dense training to a manageable level.

Abstract: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

</details>


### [260] [Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20656)
*Manoosh Samiei,Doina Precup,Paul Masset*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multi-horizon RL approach that adaptively selects and combines multiple temporal discount factors, enabling robust adaptation to changing reward structures without manual tuning, and demonstrates its effectiveness on MiniGrid continual learning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL uses a fixed discount factor that imposes a single exponentially discounted horizon, which is inflexible. Biological agents exhibit flexible, multi-timescale temporal discounting, suggesting that adaptive multi-horizon planning could improve adaptability, particularly in non-stationary and continual learning settings.

Method: A multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines multiple temporal horizons (discount factors). The method dynamically adjusts which discount factors are used based on the current reward structure, eliminating the need for manual discount-factor tuning.

Result: The method successfully identifies effective discount factors across various MiniGrid environments and in a continual learning setting with three sequentially changing tasks, demonstrating robust adaptation to task switches.

Conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems, offering a more flexible alternative to fixed discount factors in RL.

Abstract: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

</details>


### [261] [End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20674)
*Xingjian Li,Kelvin Kan,Deepanshu Verma,Krishna Kumar,Stanley Osher,Samy Wu Fung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a scalable method for training neural network controllers with hard safety constraints via control barrier functions (CBFs), combining operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to overcome computational bottlenecks, enabling end-to-end training on systems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior approaches that incorporate CBF-based safety filters into end-to-end policy training rely on embedding a quadratic program (QP) as a differentiable optimization layer. This creates computational and differentiation bottlenecks that restrict applicability to low-dimensional systems (typically ≤16 state dimensions). There is a clear need for a scalable methodology that extends CBF-constrained policy learning to high-dimensional settings.

Method: The authors combine operator splitting techniques with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to bypass the need to differentiate through the QP safety filter. JFB replaces exact Jacobian computation with an identity-like surrogate, while operator splitting efficiently solves the underlying QP. Nonsmooth analysis is used to theoretically justify the training methodology.

Result: The proposed approach is demonstrated on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400, showing effective end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees.

Conclusion: The combination of operator splitting and JFB enables scalable, safe end-to-end policy learning with CBF constraints for high-dimensional systems, significantly expanding the applicability beyond prior low-dimensional limitations.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

</details>


### [262] [Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20675)
*Omran Ayoub,Carlos Natalino,Ali Al Housseini,Felix Foschum,Philipp Morger,Tiziano Leidi,David Hock,Paolo Monti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes explanation-based runtime verification for ML-driven optical network automation, using XAI-derived explanations to assess decision soundness before execution, filtering uncertain predictions while maintaining high automation rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As ML models become integrated into optical network control loops, incorrect predictions can directly degrade service quality and network stability. Existing XAI methods provide post-hoc interpretability but are not leveraged for real-time decision validation at deployment time.

Method: Explanation-based runtime verification framework that evaluates (1) explanation coherence and (2) physics grounding consistency of ML predictions at runtime. Decisions flagged as uncertain based on these criteria are deferred or rejected before control-plane execution. Validated on lightpath QoT classification use case.

Result: The approach intercepts a significant fraction of erroneous ML decisions while preserving a high automation rate, demonstrating effective discrimination between reliable and unreliable predictions.

Conclusion: Explanation-based verification offers a practical mechanism for safe deployment of ML in optical network control loops, bridging the gap between XAI interpretability and operational reliability requirements.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

</details>


### [263] [Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20694)
*Salavat Ishbulatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a quasi-linear Fisher market framework to bridge planned task budgets with logged actions, using fused text/structural/temporal signals. Introduces market instruments yielding conservation and budget guarantees, extends to concave completion utility with satiation-threshold fixed-point analysis, identifies sensitivity to affinity noise via a de-circularized benchmark, and resolves it with an entropy-regularized generalization featuring a noise-adaptive regularization rule.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personal and organizational planning systems suffer from a structural disconnect: planned effort budgets and logged actions drift apart. Existing systems use exclusive, all-or-nothing links that either strand genuinely related effort or falsely report active goals as stalled. A principled, market-based approach is needed to establish soft, partial matching between plans and actions with formal guarantees.

Method: The core formulation casts the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market where planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers and logged actions are divisible goods. Fused text, structural, and temporal signals define buyer valuations. Two market instruments — a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option — provide conservation, hard budget caps, and a provable junk filter. A concave completion utility is introduced to discount progress near plan completion, with a satiation-threshold fixed point proven via Brouwer's theorem and local uniqueness under diagonal dominance. An entropy-regularized generalization unifies the sharp equilibrium with entropy-regularized optimal transport. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark with independently corrupted affinity evaluates noise sensitivity. A noise-adaptive rule tunes regularization strength.

Result: The market instruments yield conservation, hard budget caps, and a provable junk filter as theorems. The satiation-threshold fixed point has guaranteed existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated on random and adversarial instances. The de-circularized benchmark reveals that the market's zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport. The entropy-regularized generalization with noise-adaptive regularization resolves this sensitivity.

Conclusion: The Fisher market formulation provides a theoretically grounded, flexible bridge between planning and logging systems with formal guarantees. The entropy-regularized extension unifies sharp and smoothed matching regimes, and the noise-adaptive rule makes the approach robust. Connections to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms suggest broader applicability.

Abstract: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

</details>


### [264] [CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20696)
*Mohammad Fesanghary*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CEDAR is a constraint-based causal discovery method for sparse autoregressive time series that uses distance correlation screening followed by targeted conditional independence tests to identify lagged causal edges, requiring O(d²) CI tests in sparse regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal discovery methods for time series either rely on rich conditioning sets that become statistically inefficient when data are scarce, or fail to exploit the typical sparsity and lag-1 self-dynamics common in real-world time series. CEDAR is designed to fill the gap for sparse, low-sample settings where variable count may exceed time points.

Method: CEDAR operates in three phases: (1) screening cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation to identify candidate edges; (2) applying two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant candidate, accepting at most one lag per ordered pair; (3) a stable MCI (Momentary Conditional Independence) pruning step to remove indirect edges, with optional deterministic C-nodes to handle trend-like nonstationarity.

Result: CEDAR achieves O(d²) CI tests after screening in sparse regimes. It is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics, outperforming richer conditioning-set methods in these settings, though those methods become preferable as sample size grows or when higher-order autoregressive and simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

Conclusion: CEDAR provides an edge-level interpretable, statistically efficient alternative for lagged causal discovery in sparse, small-sample autoregressive time series, with clear delineation of the regimes where it excels versus where denser conditioning methods should be preferred.

Abstract: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

</details>


### [265] [Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20708)
*Hongju Pae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An active inference agent with separated fast (z) and slow (g) latent variables shows that integrated information (Φ_r) concentrates architecturally in g, decreases with training, and reveals learning effects only at the atom-compositional level — arguing against interpreting scalar Φ_r as a direct measure of learned integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work found that Φ_r from Integrated Information Decomposition grows with training and tracks reward in RL agents. This paper tests whether similar information-theoretic signatures emerge in reward-free active inference, probing how predictive organization relates to Φ_r without reward-driven learning.

Method: An active inference agent with a hierarchical architecture: a fast perception latent z and a slow global latent g, where g is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. The agent operates under a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol. Φ_r is analyzed at both aggregate (scalar) and atom-compositional levels.

Result: Φ_r concentrates in g architecturally, not as a function of learning. Aggregate Φ_r decreases with training. At the atom-compositional level, decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment. Scalar Φ_r fails to capture these dynamics.

Conclusion: g is the architectural locus of Φ_r-relevant temporal organization. Scalar Φ_r should not be read as a direct index of learned integration, since substantive learning effects are only visible through compositional analysis. The work bridges active inference and integrated information decomposition in a reward-free setting.

Abstract: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

</details>


### [266] [LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20734)
*Jihoon Tack,Philippe Laban,Jennifer Neville*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs perform well on static, single-turn tasks but fail significantly when user intent evolves dynamically across multi-turn conversations, revealing a critical gap in their ability to track and act on changing user intent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as collaborative agents in iterative dialogues, but real interactions involve users disclosing, revising, and reshaping intent over time. Current evaluation paradigms remain static and single-turn, leaving unaddressed the question of whether LLMs can faithfully track evolving user intent.

Method: The authors introduce a framework that converts static, single-turn benchmark tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations where user intent incrementally emerges, is revised, and is redirected mid-conversation, while preserving the original evaluation protocol so existing benchmarks can serve as controlled testbeds without new annotation.

Result: Across multiple tasks and model families, strong performance in static settings consistently fails to transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial performance drops observed universally.

Conclusion: There is a fundamental gap between static evaluation and real-world collaborative demands: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on evolving user intent, a capability critical for future collaborative agents but invisible to current static benchmarks.

Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, they are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, taking on user-delegated tasks through iterative interaction. Yet genuine interaction is inherently dynamic: users rarely specify their intent upfront, instead disclosing, revising, and reshaping it as the conversation unfolds. Despite this, LLMs are still predominantly evaluated or trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings, leaving open a fundamental question: how well do LLMs track and act on user intent as it evolves over the course of a conversation? To study this, we introduce a framework that transforms static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations in which the user's intent evolves across turns--incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation--while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol, enabling existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without new annotation. Across multiple tasks, we surface a consistent phenomenon: strong static-setting performance does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial drops across model families. Our findings point to a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on the user's evolving intent, a capability invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

</details>


### [267] [Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion for Trustworthy Multi-Omics Multimodal Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20742)
*Mohammad Raahemi,Ali Sekhavati,Alireza Maleki,Hamid Nasiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ACE introduces a dual-level confidence mechanism for multimodal fusion that generates complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations, then adaptively reweights modalities by reliability before fusion and estimates a global trust score. It outperforms SOTA on four multi-omics datasets in both classification and confidence calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal learning improves medical prognosis but suffers under noisy/uninformative data streams. Existing fusion approaches lack dynamic data quality assessment and trustworthy confidence scores, limiting their deployment in safety-critical clinical settings.

Method: ACE first augments the multimodal space by generating new complementary modalities derived from intra-modality correlations. It then applies a dual-level confidence mechanism: (1) adaptive reweighting of all modalities based on their reliability prior to fusion, and (2) estimation of a global trust score over the fused final decision.

Result: ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms on four multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, ROSMAP) in both classification performance and confidence calibration.

Conclusion: ACE provides a more stable and robust fusion method that enhances trustworthiness, facilitating the use of multimodal learning in high-stakes problems such as clinical prognosis.

Abstract: Multimodal learning is a robust approach to improve predictive performance in applications such as medical prognosis. However, the clinical applicability of models that use multimodal learning is hampered by their poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams. Present fusion approaches often lack robust mechanisms for the dynamic assessment of data quality and for the provision of a trustable confidence score on the final prediction. This dissuades their deployment in safety-critical settings. To address these limitations, we introduce Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE), a novel framework to enhance the trustworthiness of multimodal fusion models. ACE first enhances the multimodal space by generating new, complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweighs all modalities by their reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused, final decision. To evaluate ACE, we used four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, and ROSMAP). ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration. Our framework provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates the use of multimodal learning in addressing high-stakes problems.

</details>


### [268] [GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20757)
*Miguel P. Bento,João Seabra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GaugeQuant introduces a training-time method that breaks internal symmetries in Transformers using a LogSumExp regularization term, selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. This improves quantization performance dramatically — e.g., W4A4 perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73 on LLaMA-2 7B — without requiring calibration data or quantization simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers possess continuous internal symmetries that allow weight matrices to be rotated without changing the model's output, yet different rotations produce different quantization error profiles. Existing quantization methods either rely on post-training calibration data or simulate quantization during training. The authors aim to exploit these symmetries during training to learn a representation inherently robust to quantization, without altering the language modeling objective or requiring calibration data.

Method: GaugeQuant adds a LogSumExp-based regularization term to the training loss that breaks the internal symmetries of Transformer layers. This term penalizes activation outliers, effectively selecting a basis (rotation) that minimizes extreme activation values. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only the rotation matrices (not the core weights) are updated by this auxiliary loss, leaving the language modeling objective entirely unaltered. The method operates during standard training with negligible overhead and without quantization simulation or calibration data.

Result: On LLaMA-2 7B: under W4A4 quantization (group size 128), perplexity improves from 8.22 (baseline) to 6.73; under W4A16, from 11.16 to 5.45. These results compete with post-training quantization methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets.

Conclusion: GaugeQuant demonstrates that exploiting internal Transformer symmetries during training can yield representations inherently more robust to quantization, achieving strong results without calibration data or quantization simulation, at negligible training cost.

Abstract: Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

</details>


### [269] [Memory-Computation Tradeoffs in Semi Amortized Parametric Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20769)
*Shijie Pan,Agustin Castellano,Zeyu Shen,Enrique Mallada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes fundamental memory–computation–accuracy tradeoffs in amortized parametric optimization: it proves tight upper and lower bounds on how much offline memory is required to guarantee ε-accuracy under a fixed online gradient descent budget K, revealing a phase transition for convex (but not strongly convex) objectives beyond which extra memory yields no benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning-enabled decision systems increasingly rely on offline precomputation to reduce online inference cost, yet there is no general theory quantifying how much offline memory is necessary and sufficient to achieve a target accuracy under a fixed online computation budget. The authors aim to fill this gap for parametric optimization problems.

Method: The authors formalize the problem as amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite set of previously solved instances, and an online phase uses a nonparametric predictor (nearest-neighbor retrieval from stored solutions) to warm-start K steps of projected gradient descent.
