Abstract: The original ALPHA benchmark introduced a taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python and proposed that the penalty could theoretically also serve as a training signal. This paper provides that validation. We compare three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalised penalty. We find that supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeds. Our best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset by 27.9% under greedy decoding, and by 25.5% under sampled decoding(p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher. We conclude that the value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery.

</details>


### [291] [Spectral Transformation for Layer-wise Global Rank Discovery in Federated LoRA for Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21074)
*Hariharan Ramesh,Jyotikrishna Dass*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpecTraL proposes a federated fine-tuning method for Vision Transformers that uses spectral transformation (Householder) in low-rank latent space to aggregate LoRA adapters, eliminates cross-term aggregation error, discovers optimal layer-wise ranks via Random Matrix Theory, and introduces padding-aware initialization to avoid re-merging into pretrained weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated LoRA aggregation strategies suffer from three key problems: (1) Independent averaging of low-rank factors causes mathematical inconsistency (cross-term aggregation error); (2) Concatenation-based methods preserving heterogeneous ranks inflate download costs and require re-merging into pretrained weights, causing reinitialization lag; (3) Dense reconstruction or auxiliary model approaches increase server overhead. A unified solution addressing all three issues simultaneously is lacking.

Method: SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules on the server and applies orthonormal Householder Transformation directly in the low-rank latent space to avoid dense reconstruction. It leverages the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory to analytically separate global consensus signal from non-IID noise, automatically discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without hyperparameter tuning. A padding-aware initialization framework allows clients to incorporate residual LoRA dimensions in subsequent rounds without merging them into the pretrained base model.

Result: Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection compared to existing federated LoRA aggregation methods.

Conclusion: SpecTraL provides a unified, theoretically grounded framework for federated LoRA aggregation that simultaneously resolves mathematical inconsistency, high communication cost, reinitialization lag, and server-side overhead, while automatically determining optimal ranks through spectral analysis.

Abstract: Fine-tuning Vision Transformers (ViTs) with low-rank adapters (LoRA) promises better communication efficiency under federated setup, yet existing aggregation strategies face fundamental limitations. Independently averaging these LoRA factors is mathematically inconsistent, introducing cross-term aggregation error. In contrast, approaches that preserve heterogeneous client ranks by concatenating local adapters on the server substantially increase download cost and often require merging global LoRA updates into pretrained weights on the clients, causing reinitialization lag and unstable convergence. Other approaches further increase server-side overhead by reconstructing dense weight updates or training auxiliary models to refine aggregation error. In this work, we propose SpecTraL, spectral transformation for layer-wise global rank discovery, that resolves these challenges within a unified design. SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation of the stacked adapters directly in the low-rank latent space, eliminating dense reconstruction of the global update and any auxiliary refinement on the server. By leveraging the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, SpecTraL analytically separates the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without manual hyperparameter tuning. To match local ranks in subsequent rounds, we introduce a padding-aware initialization framework that lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pre-trained base model. Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL

</details>


### [292] [Nipping the Butterfly Effect in the Bud: Self-Output Fine-Tuning for Autoregressive Weather Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21080)
*Yun-Ye Cai,Hsuan-Tien Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Autoregressive deep learning weather prediction suffers from rapidly growing errors over long horizons due to a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts (akin to the butterfly effect). The authors propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT), a plug-and-play method that calibrates the shifted input distribution using the model's own one-step predictions, achieving state-of-the-art long-horizon forecasting performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive DLWP models, while scalable and flexible, exhibit prediction errors that grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. The authors aim to understand this error growth phenomenon theoretically and empirically, and to develop a mitigation strategy.

Method: The authors first analyze error growth theoretically, identifying a feedback loop: small initial output errors amplify through autoregressive steps, corrupting subsequent input distributions (distribution shift), which in turn degrades accuracy — echoing the butterfly effect. They show this distributional shift is detectable from the very first autoregressive step. To address this, they propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT), a plug-and-play strategy that fine-tunes the model using its own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first autoregressive step.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon weather forecasting tasks, substantially reducing both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy.

Conclusion: SOFT's success underscores the importance of reexamining the autoregressive pipeline in DLWP. The work represents a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science by addressing the fundamental error-growth mechanism in autoregressive weather prediction.

Abstract: Long-horizon weather forecasting is a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science, for which autoregressive Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) has emerged as the primary paradigm. Although the autoregressive pipeline is highly scalable and flexible, its prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. In this work, we study this error growth phenomenon from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis reveals that the growth is driven by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. Specifically, the autoregressive process amplifies small initial output errors, which progressively corrupt subsequent input distributions, echoing the butterfly effect in atmospheric science and ultimately deteriorating forecasting accuracy over longer horizons. Furthermore, we show that this distributional shift originates at the earliest stage of inference, with out-of-distribution signatures detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT)}, a plug-and-play strategy that leverages the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental pipeline of deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

</details>


### [293] [CASC: Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Spatiotemporal Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21088)
*Francis Ndikum Nji,Vandana Janeja,Jianwu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CASC proposes a causal-adversarial deep subspace clustering framework that moves beyond geometric self-expressiveness by integrating U-Net-inspired architecture, FAConvLSTM layers, and graph attention transformers with two novel losses — Causal Subspace Preservation and Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution — to discover evolving latent regimes in multivariate spatiotemporal data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep subspace clustering methods rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and fail to capture (1) causal dependencies, (2) local spatial interactions, and (3) long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread, and neurodegeneration tracking.

Method: CASC combines: (1) a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers for spatial-temporal structure preservation and robust latent representation learning; (2) a graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network for joint modeling of local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions; (3) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships; and (4) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and regime transitions in nonstationary environments.

Result: The framework transforms deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework. (Quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)

Conclusion: By integrating causal and temporal objectives with adversarial deep clustering and graph attention mechanisms, CASC enables robust discovery of evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data, addressing key limitations of prior static, correlation-based subspace clustering methods.

Abstract: Deep subspace clustering plays a critical role in applications involving multivariate spatiotemporal data, such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and tracking neuro-degeneration over time. Despite recent advances, existing methods primarily rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and often fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework for discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. CASC integrates a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial and temporal structure while learning robust latent representations. A graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network is introduced to jointly model local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions. Furthermore, we propose two new learning objectives: (1) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, encouraging clusters to reflect underlying causal processes rather than simple feature similarity, and (2) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions in nonstationary environments. Together, these components transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework.

</details>


### [294] [Training Large Language Models for Self-Explanation Faithfulness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21090)
*Yeoktatt Cheah,María Pérez-Ortiz,Noah Y. Siegel,Oana-Maria Camburu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Reinforcement Learning to directly optimize LLMs to produce faithful self-explanations — reasoning that accurately reflects internal decision-making. By converting faithfulness metrics into RL rewards, they fine-tune Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, achieving substantial gains on the Phi-CCT metric (near-zero to ~0.66-0.69). Cross-intervention generalization is partial and model-dependent. The work offers a scalable path to reducing unfaithful reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to LLM self-explanation faithfulness either only evaluate it or use inference-time prompting, without a mechanism to directly optimize model parameters for generating faithful explanations. The authors aim to bridge this gap by making faithfulness directly trainable via RL.

Method: The authors convert existing faithfulness metrics (specifically Phi-CCT, a correlation-based measure) into a per-sample RL reward. They apply RL fine-tuning to Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B using two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions. Faithfulness is measured by how well the model's self-explanations disclose which interventions influenced its decisions. Generalization is tested on held-out tasks like StrategyQA and across intervention types.

Result: RL fine-tuning substantially improves faithfulness: in-distribution Phi-CCT scores rise from near-zero to 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reach 0.691 on StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is mixed — Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer from random-word to user-bias interventions, but the reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, suggesting model- and setup-dependent effects. The authors also verify that improvements are not due to reward gaming.

Conclusion: LLMs can be trained via RL to implicitly identify and disclose factors influencing their decisions, enabling direct optimization of self-explanation faithfulness. This provides a scalable, parameter-level approach to reducing unfaithful reasoning, though cross-intervention generalization remains limited and poorly understood.

Abstract: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method to directly optimize the faithfulness of self-explanations - the extent to which a model's generated reasoning accurately reflects its internal decision-making process. While existing work focuses on evaluating faithfulness or using inference-time prompting frameworks to improve an LLM's self-explanation's tractability, these approaches do not provide a mechanism to directly optimize a model's parameters to generate faithful self-explanations. We bridge this gap by modifying existing faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective. We investigate (1) if models can be trained to accurately detect factors that affect their decisions, and (2) whether RL can directly optimize for the disclosure of these factors thereby improving LLM self-explanations' faithfulness. We experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions, using a per-sample reward derived from the Phi-CCT correlation metric. RL fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show substantial improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric, with in-distribution scores rising from near-zero to as high as 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reaching up to 0.691 on held-out tasks such as StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but more interesting: a priori we would not expect a model trained only on random word insertions to generalize to user-bias phrases, yet Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer in this direction. The reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, indicating model-dependent and setup-dependent effects we cannot yet explain. Lastly we analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming behaviors that often plague RL training. Ultimately, we show that models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

</details>


### [295] [A Polynomial Architecture-Attribution Co-Design Framework for Exact Aumann-Shapley Attribution in GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21094)
*Bizu Feng,Zhimu Yang,Shuming Wang,Shaode Yu,Yuan Cheng,Xiaojun Qian,Zixin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APEX proposes a co-designed GNN architecture (PolyGIN) whose polynomial form enables exact, closed-form Aumann-Shapley attribution via Gauss-Legendre quadrature, eliminating the approximation trade-off in standard path-integral methods like Integrated Gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Path-integral attribution methods (e.g., Integrated Gradients) for GNNs rely on finite-sample numerical approximation of the integral, creating an inherent trade-off between quadrature accuracy and computational cost. The authors seek to eliminate this trade-off by making the integral exactly computable.

Method: The authors introduce PolyGIN, a GIN-style architecture where message-passing, normalization, and transformations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar outputs (e.g., pre-softmax logits). For L polynomial transformation blocks, the attribution-path derivative has degree at most 2^L−1, allowing Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 2^{L−1} points to evaluate the Aumann-Shapley integral exactly (to floating-point precision). Attributions are computed at the feature level and aggregated to node-level while preserving completeness.

Result: PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks. The APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations needed for path integration.

Conclusion: Co-designing the model architecture to enforce polynomial structure renders Aumann-Shapley attribution exactly computable, yielding both higher fidelity explanations and computational efficiency over conventional approximation-based methods.

Abstract: We study feature-level and node-level explanations for graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of Aumann-Shapley attribution. Path-integral methods such as Integrated Gradients provide an axiomatic formulation of attribution, but their practical use in deep GNNs typically relies on finite-sample numerical approximations to the path integral, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This paper proposes APEX, a model-attribution co-design framework that makes the attribution integral exactly computable under a polynomial GNN architecture. The key component is PolyGIN, a GIN-style graph network whose message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar model scores, such as pre-softmax logits. We show that, for a PolyGIN with $L$ polynomial transformation blocks, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most $2^L-1$. Therefore, Gauss--Legendre quadrature can evaluate the Aumann--Shapley path integral exactly, up to floating-point precision, with $2^{L-1}$ deterministic evaluation points. The resulting attributions can be computed at the feature level and then aggregated into node-level scores while preserving completeness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks show that PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance, while the complete APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than the compared baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations required for path integration.

</details>


### [296] [Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21098)
*Michele Bellomo,Riccardo Ramaschi,Alberto Dolara,Tomaso Aste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a neural TPP model that parameterizes the conditional intensity function directly as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions with neural network-predicted coefficients, enabling exact NLL evaluation, architectural flexibility, parallelized training, and built-in smoothness regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural TPPs either model the compensator instead of the CIF directly, constrain network architectures, or require sequential event evaluation during training — all of which limit flexibility and computational efficiency. A method is needed that allows direct CIF parameterization with exact likelihood computation, unconstrained architectures, and parallelizable training.

Method: The CIF is modeled as a non-negative linear combination of B-spline basis functions over time, where the combination coefficients are output by a flexible neural network. This admits an exact closed-form integral (compensator) for NLL evaluation without numerical quadrature, allows any neural architecture for the coefficient predictor, supports parallel event evaluation during training, and naturally incorporates smoothness regularization via the integrated squared second derivative of the B-spline representation.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to a reference neural TPP baseline.

Conclusion: The proposed B-spline-based CIF parameterization successfully addresses key limitations of prior neural TPPs — exact NLL, architectural freedom, training parallelization, and smoothness regularization — yielding both faster training and better predictive performance.

Abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) provide a general and flexible framework for modeling sequences of events in continuous time. Neural networks have been successfully employed to model TPPs in a highly expressive and data-driven way. Neural TPPs are typically trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which depends on both the conditional intensity function (CIF) and its integral over time, the compensator. Recent neural TPP approaches enable exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration. However, these methods typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose constraints on the neural network architecture, and are computationally expensive during training, as event contributions to the NLL are evaluated sequentially rather than in parallel. In this work, we propose a novel neural TPP model that directly parametrizes the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions, whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This formulation enables exact evaluation of the NLL, preserves full flexibility in the neural architecture, allows efficient parallelization during training, and naturally supports CIF smoothness regularization through the integrated squared second derivative. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.

</details>


### [297] [TOUR: A Trajectory-Level Unlearning Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21111)
*Chaofan Pan,Lingfei Ren,Xiangyu Jiang,Yanhua Li,Xuemei Cao,Xiangkun Wang,Hao Yu,Wei Wei,Xin Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TOUR is a benchmark for evaluating trajectory-level unlearning in offline RL that reveals single-score membership audits are unreliable; proper evaluation requires matched non-member controls, retraining references, multiple attack families, and retained-performance anchors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL trains on fixed behavioral trajectories, necessitating trajectory-level deletion (e.g., for data removal requests). Existing evaluation is flawed because a lower membership inference score can misleadingly indicate successful deletion, actual residual memorization detectable by other attacks, or catastrophic policy collapse. No standardized, rigorous benchmark exists for auditing unlearning quality in offline RL.

Method: TOUR integrates five components: (1) trajectory-level partitioning with matched non-member controls, (2) retraining-from-scratch references, (3) retained-performance anchors to distinguish deletion from policy collapse, (4) multi-attack privacy auditing spanning reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks, and (5) comparisons across baselines including retraining, fine-tuning, uniform GA+Refit, and TrajDeleter. Experiments cover D4RL locomotion tasks and an AntMaze extension.

Result: Common deletion baselines exhibit environment-dependent privacy-utility trade-offs. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility than uniform GA+Refit. TrajDeleter is useful but not uniformly dominant under identical audits. Critically, single likelihood-based membership scores overstate deletion quality; conclusions about unlearning are unstable without matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family diversity, and utility preservation checks.

Conclusion: Reliable offline RL unlearning evaluation demands multi-dimensional auditing: matched non-members, retraining calibration, diverse attack families, retained-utility measurement, and explicit diagnostic scope for architecture or component-level evidence. Single-score approaches are insufficient.

Abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are trained on fixed behavioral trajectories, which makes trajectory-level deletion important when selected data must be removed after training. Evaluating such deletion is difficult because a lower membership score can reflect trajectory removal, residual memorization visible to another attack, or policy collapse that destroys useful behavior. We introduce Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR), a benchmark that combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Across D4RL locomotion experiments and an exploratory AntMaze extension, TOUR shows that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit, while TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but is not uniformly stronger under the same audit. Reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks further show that a single likelihood-based membership score can overstate deletion quality. In the evaluated settings, conclusions about offline RL unlearning are therefore not stable under single-score auditing. They depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

</details>


### [298] [GlucoTune: A Unified Framework for Blood Glucose Preprocessing, Forecasting, and Benchmarking in Diabetes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21117)
*Davide Marelli,Giorgia Rigamonti,Mirko Paolo Barbato,Paolo Napoletano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GlucoTune is a comprehensive framework that standardizes the entire blood glucose time-series experimental workflow — from preprocessing to model evaluation — using YAML-based configurable pipelines, enabling reproducible research without redistributing sensitive medical data, while also providing integrated public datasets, state-of-the-art prediction models, and a benchmarking leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blood glucose time-series preprocessing lacks standardized workflows and evaluation protocols, which hinders reproducibility and fair comparison. These issues are compounded by data-sharing restrictions due to privacy and licensing constraints that prevent redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. A unified solution is needed to enable reproducible experimentation directly from original datasets without sharing sensitive data.

Method: GlucoTune provides configurable, reproducible preprocessing pipelines defined in portable YAML files; standardized dataset wrappers for public datasets; a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models; integration of SOTA prediction and general time-series forecasting methods; and a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods for systematic comparison.

Result: The authors demonstrate GlucoTune's effectiveness through comprehensive experiments and validate its usability via a user study.

Conclusion: GlucoTune addresses critical gaps in blood glucose time-series research by providing a standardized, extensible, and privacy-preserving framework that enables reproducible experimentation, fair benchmarking, and streamlined model development for diabetes management.

Abstract: Preprocessing blood glucose time-series data is a critical yet often overlooked step in developing data-driven methods for diabetes management, particularly for type 1 diabetes. The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols hinders reproducibility and complicates fair comparison across studies. These challenges are further exacerbated by data-sharing restrictions, as privacy and licensing constraints often prevent the redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. To address these limitations, we present GlucoTune, a comprehensive and extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data. The framework standardizes the entire experimental workflow, from preprocessing to model evaluation, enabling reproducible experiments directly from the original datasets. Reproducible preprocessing is achieved through configurable pipelines defined in portable YAML configuration files, ensuring consistent data handling without distributing sensitive preprocessed data. Beyond preprocessing, GlucoTune provides a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models. The framework integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers and provides a curated collection of state-of-the-art blood glucose prediction and general time-series forecasting methods, while remaining readily extensible to additional datasets, preprocessing strategies, and forecasting models. To promote transparent and consistent evaluation, GlucoTune includes a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods, enabling systematic comparison of experimental settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GlucoTune through comprehensive experiments and assess its usability in a user study.

</details>


### [299] [Relative Value Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21120)
*Marc Höftmann,Jan Robine,Stefan Harmeling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Relative Value Learning (RV) replaces absolute value function estimation with learning pairwise value differences via an antisymmetric function, offering a novel critic framework that is theoretically sound (contraction mapping, unbiased policy gradients) and empirically competitive with PPO on Atari.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In reinforcement learning, only differences in state values matter for control, not absolute values. Existing critics estimate absolute V(s), which is unnecessary and may introduce inefficiencies. The authors are motivated to design a framework that directly models what control actually requires — relative value differences.

Method: The authors propose RV, which learns an antisymmetric function Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j). They introduce a pairwise Bellman operator, prove it is a γ-contraction with a unique fixed point at the true value differences, and derive 1-step, n-step, and λ-return targets. They also reconstruct Generalized Advantage Estimation from pairwise differences (R-GAE) to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator. RV is integrated with PPO for evaluation.

Result: RV integrated with PPO achieves competitive performance against standard PPO across 49 Atari (ALE) games, demonstrating that relative value estimation is a viable alternative to absolute critics in practice.

Conclusion: Relative Value Learning provides a theoretically grounded and practically effective alternative to absolute value critics. By focusing on value differences, RV aligns the critic's objective more closely with what control actually requires, and the strong Atari results suggest this paradigm merits further exploration.

Abstract: In reinforcement learning, critics typically estimate absolute state values $V(s)$, estimating how good a particular situation is in isolation. However, it turns out that only differences in value are relevant for control. Motivated by this, we propose Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that learns value differences directly via an antisymmetric function $Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. We introduce a pairwise Bellman operator and prove it is a $γ$-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, derive well-posed $1$-step, $n$-step and $λ$-return targets and reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Beyond theoretical results, we integrate RV with PPO and achieve competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, indicating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.

</details>


### [300] [Demographically-Informed Heat-Mortality Risk Curves via Risk Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21131)
*Alex O. Davies,Eunice Lo,Rui Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs) enhance traditional DLNMs by incorporating granular census-based demographic and geographic context via a hierarchical GNN encoder, preserving interpretable exposure-response curves while significantly improving predictive calibration, especially during extreme heat events like the 2022 UK heatwave.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs) for heat-related mortality risk estimation ignore demographic and geographic context, despite these factors being well-established determinants of heat vulnerability. This omission limits predictive accuracy and calibration, particularly under unprecedented extreme heat scenarios.

Method: The authors propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that leverages granular census features to optimize DLNM coefficient vectors. This architecture retains the interpretable exposure-response surface structure of DLNMs while embedding spatial and demographic heterogeneity into the risk estimation pipeline.

Result: Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants achieve both lower point-prediction errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage. Notably, baseline models collapse during the 2022 heatwave, whereas RGNNs maintain robust calibration.

Conclusion: Integrating geographic and demographic context through graph-structured representations into DLNM frameworks yields substantial improvements in mortality risk prediction, particularly for extreme heat events. The approach preserves model interpretability while enhancing real-world applicability.

Abstract: Estimating heat-related mortality risk is a core task in environmental epidemiology, typically addressed with Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs); interpretable exposure-response surfaces fitted to temperature-mortality time series. DLNMs are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, despite well-established relevance to heat vulnerability. We propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while substantially improving predictive calibration. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse.

</details>


### [301] [Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21173)
*Irena Girshovitz,Dan Zeltzer,Ran Gilad-Bachrach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ARA is a framework that makes silent causal failures in automated research visible by integrating protocol construction, synthetic data generation with known ground truth via SCMs, and adversarial validation. Rather than improving numerical accuracy, ARA shifts the failure mode from silently returning invalid causal estimates to surfacing diagnostic concerns and downgrading non-causal interpretations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated empirical research systems (e.g., LLM-based analysis pipelines) can produce analysis code that runs without errors but rests on invalid causal assumptions — so-called "silent failures." These are especially dangerous in high-stakes domains like epidemiology, where incorrect causal claims can propagate undetected. The authors aim to make these failures visible and to argue that validity-first systems should be evaluated on their ability to flag unwarranted causal claims, not just answer accuracy.

Method: ARA implements a three-stage pipeline: (1) **Protocol construction** — natural language research questions are translated into structured causal protocols specifying design, assumptions, and estimands; (2) **Synthetic data generation** — Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects produce datasets, enabling verification even when real confidential data (e.g., medical records) are inaccessible; (3) **Adversarial validation** — the generated analysis is stress-tested under controlled violations of identification assumptions (e.g., unmeasured confounding, selection bias). Evaluation uses the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, measuring recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment/outcome variables, and code–protocol consistency.

Result: Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared to standard LLM-based generation. However, the failure mode changed qualitatively: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA frequently surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or explicitly downgraded interpretations to non-causal associations when causal claims were unwarranted.

Conclusion: The paper argues that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not solely on answer accuracy but also on their capacity to indicate when causal claims are unjustified. ARA demonstrates that making failures visible — even without improving point-estimate accuracy — is a meaningful shift toward trustworthy automated research pipelines.

Abstract: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

</details>


### [302] [Filter Learning for Subgraphs: Algebras and Performance Risk Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21263)
*Purui Zhang,Feng Ji,Yanan Zhao,Bihan Wen,Wee Peng Tay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a statistical learning framework for approximating ambient graph filters from partial observations (subgraphs). Introduces a distance-aware subgraph filter algebra for structured, controllable approximation, with risk bounds under least squares loss. Outperforms polynomial, distribution-agnostic, and direct learning baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph signal processing typically requires complete graph topology, which is often unavailable. The authors address the practical need to approximate spectral graph filters when only a subgraph is observed.

Method: Formulates subgraph filter learning (SFL) as a statistical learning problem where optimal subgraph operators are data-dependent. Develops a subgraph filter algebra using distance-aware Laplacian constructions to define a structured, controllable filter class. Derives performance risk bounds under least squares loss.

Result: The proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines on real-world datasets for SFL tasks.

Conclusion: Distance-aware algebraic filter constructions provide an effective, theoretically grounded approach for learning graph filters from partial topology, bridging the gap between spectral GSP and practical incomplete-data scenarios.

Abstract: Graph signal processing tasks that leverage spectral information typically assume access to the complete graph topology, which is often unavailable in practice. We propose a systematic framework for subgraph filter learning (SFL), where subgraph-supported operators approximate ambient graph filters under partial observations. We formulate SFL as a statistical learning problem in which optimal subgraph operators are inherently data-dependent. To address the difficulty of directly estimating such operators, we develop a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacian constructions, defining a structured and controllable class of filters for effective approximation. We further establish performance risk bounds under the least squares loss, quantifying how well the learned operator approximates the restricted ambient mapping. Experiments real-world datasets show that, for SFL tasks, the proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines that attempt to recover the underlying structure from data.

</details>


### [303] [The Dark Room in the Reward Channel: Dense Prediction Rewards Collapse GRPO-Trained LLM Agents -- and What Actually Works](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21273)
*Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dense per-step prediction rewards under GRPO cause policy collapse into a "dark room" degenerate state. The cause is GRPO's std normalization interacting with all-fail groups, making bounded rewards exert unbounded pressure. The variance-profile criterion predicts which signals are safe, and auxiliary-loss channels outperform reward channels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate why dense per-step supervision — an intuitively appealing remedy for sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agents — catastrophically fails under GRPO, and identify the mechanism driving this failure.

Method: Experiments across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on ALFWorld using potential-based prediction rewards under GRPO. Single-factor ablation removing GRPO's std normalization. Theoretical proposition explaining z-scored advantage invariance in all-fail groups. Variance-profile criterion for predicting signal safety. Controlled signal-delivery matrix comparing reward-channel vs auxiliary-loss-channel consumption of identical signals, including a shuffled-gold placebo.

Result: Prediction reward under GRPO drives all runs to a degenerate absorbing state (prediction accuracy → 1.0, task success → 0, episode length pinned at horizon). Removing std normalization alone restores baseline parity from 0%. The variance-profile criterion successfully retrodicts collapses and carries preregistered predictions. Auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points over reward channel; shuffled-gold placebo matches true-gold, showing the gap survives without correct labels.

Conclusion: GRPO's z-scoring amplifies within-group variance of dense signals, and when all-fail groups dominate, bounded rewards become structurally unbounded pressure leading to policy collapse. Signals whose variance decays with mastery are "amplifier-safe." Delivering dense supervision through auxiliary losses rather than reward shaping avoids this pathology entirely.

Abstract: Dense per-step supervision is an appealing remedy for sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agents: reward the agent for predicting its next observation, and memory should follow. We show that under group-normalized RL (GRPO), this recipe does not merely fail -- it destroys the policy. Across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on ALFWorld, a potential-based prediction reward drives every run into a degenerate absorbing state (prediction accuracy -> 1.0, task success -> 0,episode length pinned at the horizon): the "dark room" pathology, built automatically by the optimizer. A single-factor ablation localizes the cause -- removing only GRPO's std normalization turns the same reward from catastrophic (0%) into baseline parity -- and a two-line proposition explains why: in all-fail groups the z-scored advantage is invariant to the shaping coefficient, so bounded rewards become unbounded pressure and annealing cannot help. Our central insight generalizes this: what z-scoring amplifies is a dense signal's within-group variance while all-fail groups dominate, so signals whose variance decays by mastery are structurally amplifier-safe.This variance-profile criterion retrodicts our collapses, carries preregistered predictions for arms that had not yet run, and is consistent with published reward-channel successes (a compatibility check, not an independent test). Finally, a controlled signal-delivery matrix (identical signal, varying only the consumption mechanism) shows the reward channel is at best neutral while the auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points -- and a shuffled-gold placebo matches the true-gold arm, so the gap survives without correct labels. Endpoints are single-seed; seed replication and group-size controls are preregistered and in progress.

</details>


### [304] [Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Prediction from Video Game State with Transfer Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21290)
*Jonas Peché,Aliaksei Tsishurou,Alexander Zap,Günter Wallner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates multi-task learning for team-based multiplayer games, adapting a multimodal architecture to jointly predict multiple targets from game state data. Experiments on World of Tanks data show MTL can improve generalization and reduce costs compared to single-task models, with evaluations of loss weighting strategies, gradient conflict handling, pre-training/fine-tuning regimes, and cross-map transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern game telemetry produces multiple related supervision signals from the same structured observations (e.g., match outcomes, player performance metrics). Training separate specialized models for each prediction task is computationally expensive and fails to exploit shared representations. The authors investigate whether a shared multi-task model can improve generalization while reducing training and inference costs in team-based multiplayer game settings.

Method: The authors adapt a multimodal architecture for endpoint prediction to a general multi-task setting. The model integrates: (1) rasterized vision inputs processed via an image encoder, (2) global match context features, and (3) per-unit state information modeled through attention-based interaction mechanisms. They compare single-task vs. multi-task training paradigms, evaluate various weighting strategies for mixed losses and conflicting gradients, and explore pre-training/fine-tuning approaches under limited target-data regimes. Cross-map transfer under structured environment shift (different game maps) is also examined.

Result: Experiments on a large proprietary World of Tanks dataset demonstrate that multi-task learning with appropriate loss weighting and gradient conflict mitigation strategies can outperform single-task baselines in terms of generalization. Pre-training followed by fine-tuning proves effective under limited target-data scenarios. The study also provides empirical evidence on the transferability of learned representations across different game maps under structured distribution shifts.

Conclusion: Multi-task learning is a viable and cost-effective paradigm for game telemetry prediction tasks in team-based multiplayer settings. Shared multimodal architectures can effectively leverage multiple supervision signals, with careful handling of conflicting gradients being critical to success. The approach offers practical benefits for deployment in live game analytics where computational efficiency and data scarcity are real constraints.

Abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a promising approach for prediction tasks derived from video game state data, as modern game telemetry provides multiple related supervision signals from the same structured observations. We study whether a shared model trained jointly across tasks in team-based multiplayer games can improve generalization while reducing training and inference cost compared to specialized single-task models. We adapt a multimodal architecture for endpoint prediction to a general multi-task setting that combines rasterized vision inputs, global match context, and per-unit state information through an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling. Experiments on a large proprietary World of Tanks dataset compare single-task and multi-task training, evaluate weighting strategies for mixed losses and conflicting gradients, and test pre-training/fine-tuning under limited target-data regimes. We also examine within-game transfer across game maps under structured environment shift.

</details>


### [305] [M$^3$-Gen: Interpretable Multimodal Generation of Gene Expression Profiles Using Clinical and Imaging Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21343)
*Francesca Pia Panaccione,Carlo Sgaravatti,Marco Venere*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M³-Gen is a GAN-based framework that generates gene expression profiles from histopathology images and clinical metadata using contrastive learning, providing built-in interpretability through attention-based identification of influential image regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gene expression data acquisition is limited by high costs and privacy concerns, hindering multimodal biomedical research and AI applications that require integrated molecular, imaging, and clinical data.

Method: M³-Gen conditions a Generative Adversarial Network on histopathology images and clinical metadata. It learns a unified latent representation from both modalities via contrastive learning, then uses these embeddings to guide gene expression profile generation. An attention-based mechanism provides intrinsic explainability by identifying image regions most influential for specific gene expression outputs.

Result: Evaluations on the TCGA dataset show that M³-Gen produces realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression profiles, demonstrating effective multimodal integration.

Conclusion: M³-Gen offers a viable solution for generating gene expression data from more readily available modalities (histopathology images and clinical data), with the added benefit of interpretable, attention-driven insights into which tissue regions drive specific molecular predictions.

Abstract: Integrating heterogeneous biomedical data, including clinical metadata, histopathology images, and molecular profiles, is crucial for comprehensive disease understanding. However, gene expression data acquisition remains constrained by high costs and privacy concerns, limiting its use in multimodal research and AI-driven applications. We present MultiModal Molecular Generation (M$^3$-Gen), a novel framework for the generation of gene expression profiles by conditioning a Generative Adversarial Network on histopathology images and clinical metadata. M$^3$-Gen learns a unified latent representation from the clinical variables and the images, leveraging contrastive learning, and exploits the embeddings of the two modalities to guide a generative model in producing biologically coherent gene expression profiles. Evaluations on the TCGA dataset demonstrate that M$^3$-Gen generates realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression data. Importantly, by integrating multiple modalities in an attention-based mechanism, M$^3$-Gen provides intrinsic explainability: it allows the identification of which regions of the histopathology images most strongly influenced the generation of specific gene expression profiles, making the model's decisions interpretable by design.

</details>


### [306] [How Many Bits Can an Adapter Write? Measuring the Capacity and Memorization of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21351)
*Kaizhen Tan,Heqing Du,Yang Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper measures how much information LoRA adapters actually store in frozen-base models using compression-based memorization analysis, finding that storage capacity depends more on parameter placement than count, with adapters storing ~2 bits per trainable parameter. MLP-placed adapters hold nearly twice as much as attention-placed ones, and supervised fine-tuning leaks secrets while reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards does not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA adapters are commonly treated as skills rather than data records, but this assumption lacks quantitative grounding. The authors aim to rigorously measure how much information a low-rank adapter writes into a frozen model, quantifying privacy and memorization risks in a principled way rather than relying on folklore or parameter-count heuristics.

Method: The authors extend compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting, measuring directly in bits how much a LoRA adapter writes. They systematically vary where the same parameter budget is placed (attention vs. MLP modules), test on structurally scrambled frozen bases, and apply the framework to realistic Qwen2.5 fine-tunes comparing supervised fine-tuning against reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Result: Adapters store roughly 2 bits per trainable parameter — well below full fine-tuning capacity. Placing the same parameter budget in the MLP yields nearly double the storage capacity vs. attention. Stripping the frozen base of structure nearly eliminates capacity. Privacy leakage correlates with bits written rather than nominal parameter count. Supervised fine-tuning copies secrets verbatim; reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards records none.

Conclusion: Measuring what fine-tuning writes — rather than post-hoc attacking — transforms the folk assumption that "adapters are skills not records" into a quantifiable design target. Bit-based measurement enables principled engineering against memorization and privacy leakage, with clear implications for choosing adapter placement, training paradigm (SFT vs. RL), and auditing fine-tuned models.

Abstract: A LoRA adapter is a few megabytes that almost everyone treats as a skill rather than a record of the data behind it. We put that assumption on a scale. Extending compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting, we measure directly, in bits, how much a low-rank adapter writes into a model it never changes. The answer is both smaller than full fine-tuning and less lawful than parameter counting would predict. Adapters store a couple of bits per trainable parameter, well short of a full model's budget, but that figure turns less on how many parameters an adapter carries than on where they sit. Move the same parameter budget from attention into the MLP and it holds nearly twice as much; strip the frozen base of its structure and the capacity all but disappears. Applied to realistic fine-tunes of Qwen2.5, the same instrument shows privacy leakage rising with the bits an adapter writes rather than the parameters it nominally has, and it draws a clean line between supervised and reinforcement learning: the secrets that supervised fine-tuning copies down verbatim, an adapter trained on verifiable rewards never records. Measuring what fine-tuning writes, rather than attacking it after the fact, turns a piece of folklore into a quantity one can design against.

</details>


### [307] [Gradient Concentration, Not Weight Saliency, Explains Representation-Level Class Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21353)
*Billel Habbati,Alessio Merlo,Luca Verderame,Meriem Guerar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether saliency-based weight selection in machine unlearning (specifically SalUn) actually matters for representation-level forgetting. Through controlled ablation on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-18, the authors show that saliency masking performs no better than random masking or unconstrained updates — all are statistically equivalent because forget gradients are overwhelmingly concentrated in final layers (~92% of gradient energy), forcing all methods into the same representational subspace.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite widespread adoption of gradient-based saliency for parameter selection in machine unlearning (e.g., SalUn), the actual causal contribution of saliency masking to representation-level forgetting has never been rigorously tested. The paper aims to fill this gap by isolating whether saliency-based weight selection provides benefits beyond what gradient concentration and representational geometry already determine.

Method: A matched-compute controlled ablation study on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using ResNet-18. Three configurations are compared under identical unlearning objective, optimization schedule, and computational budget: (1) SalUn's saliency-based masking, (2) random masks of equal sparsity, and (3) unconstrained full-network updates. Evaluation uses representation-level metrics: linear probing accuracy on forget-class samples, prototype recovery, and layer-wise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). Gradient energy distribution across layers and class specificity of saliency masks (specificity index) are also quantified.

Result: All three masking configurations yield statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability across all metrics. Forget gradients concentrate ~92% of squared gradient energy in the final layers before masking, forcing all strategies into the same representational subspace. Saliency masks exhibit low class specificity (specificity index 0.09–0.11), selecting highly overlapping parameter subsets for different forget classes.

Conclusion: Representation-level forgetting is governed primarily by gradient concentration and representation geometry, not by which specific weights are selected for updating. This suggests that advancing machine unlearning requires objectives that directly target latent representations rather than developing increasingly sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data while preserving model utility. Many state-of-the-art approaches pursue this goal by restricting the forgetting update to a subset of parameters selected through gradient-based saliency. Although such methods are widely adopted, the actual contribution of saliency-based weight selection to representation-level forgetting remains unclear. In this work, we perform the first controlled ablation of the saliency masking mechanism used by SalUn. Using a matched-compute experimental design on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, we compare saliency-based masking against random masks of equal sparsity and unconstrained updates, while keeping the unlearning objective, optimization schedule, and computational budget fixed. Across multiple representation-level evaluations, including linear probing, prototype recovery, and layer-wise CKA, the three configurations exhibit statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability. We find that forget gradients are strongly concentrated in the final network layers (approximately 92% of the squared gradient energy on CIFAR-10) before any mask is applied, causing all masking strategies to operate within the same representational subspace. Furthermore, saliency masks show limited class specificity (specificity index 0.09-0.11), selecting highly overlapping parameter subsets across different forget classes. Our findings suggest that, in the studied setting, representation-level forgetting is primarily governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry rather than by the specific identity of saliency-selected weights. More broadly, the results support a growing body of evidence indicating that effective representation-level unlearning requires objectives that act directly on latent representations rather than on increasingly sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

</details>


### [308] [Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21356)
*Mohammed Suhail B Nadaf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fine-tuning an aligned LLM on narrow bad advice causes broad misalignment because the model contains a pre-existing, low-rank "persona subspace" shared across unrelated domains. Projecting this subspace out prevents misalignment; injecting it induces misalignment dose-dependently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emergent misalignment — where narrow fine-tuning on bad advice generalizes broadly to unrelated questions — lacks a mechanistic explanation. The authors investigate why this generalization occurs, hypothesizing that a latent persona structure pre-exists in aligned models and is recruited by narrow fine-tuning.

Method: Using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, the authors extract per-domain persona subspaces via contrastive teacher forcing across 4 unrelated domains. They identify a shared low-rank core (657× enrichment over random). They then track gradient dynamics during the first optimizer step, perform subspace projection/ablation/injection interventions in the residual stream during fine-tuning, test weight-gradient projections and post-hoc weight edits, and compare spreading bad data across domains vs. concentrating it.

Result: The shared persona core is 82% distinct from a style core. The first optimizer step on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than educational code, forecasting long-run margin movement. Projecting the persona subspace out of the residual stream during fine-tuning reduces broad misalignment from 27.7% to 0.0% (random subspace: no change). Injecting the subspace into a never-fine-tuned model induces dose-dependent misalignment up to 45.4%. Weight-gradient projection is inert; post-hoc weight edits suppress but do not remove the disposition — the ablated structure re-forms. Spreading bad data across 4 domains amplifies broad misalignment beyond what weight superposition and diversity jointly predict.

Conclusion: Broad emergent misalignment arises from a pre-existing, low-rank persona structure in aligned models. This structure is causally necessary and sufficient for the generalization of narrow bad-fine-tuning. The findings suggest safety interventions should target these latent structures directly, though the provenance of the persona subspace (aligned checkpoint) remains an open question.

Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.

</details>


### [309] [Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366)
*Hossein Mobahi,Peter L. Bartlett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HOPE introduces a Hilbert-space framework that models neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators, unifying pruning, neuron merging, and macro block eviction under low-rank subspace projection. It enables data-free, hyperparameter-free, architecture-agnostic network compression without scale symmetries or architectural biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard network compression heuristics suffer from scale symmetries (weight magnitudes can be rescaled without changing network function) and architectural biases (different layer types/sizes are incomparable under existing metrics). The link between learning and compression motivates using compression as a lens to probe learned representations, but biases in current methods undermine this analysis.

Method: HOPE models individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators embedded in a Hilbert space of continuous functions. This shifts compression from discrete decisions to continuous functional analysis. Pruning and neuron merging are unified as low-rank subspace projection within this space. The framework extends to "macro block eviction," which can assess entire multi-layer structures (e.g., residual pathways) under a single unified metric, enabling unbiased cross-layer comparisons regardless of layer type or dimensionality.

Result: Proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning demonstrate the practical potential of the HOPE framework, though the abstract does not provide specific quantitative results.

Conclusion: HOPE provides a principled, mathematically grounded alternative to heuristic compression methods, enabling unbiased deconstruction of representations in trained neural network weights without requiring data or hyperparameters.

Abstract: Deep neural networks encode complex representations, but deconstructing this internal knowledge remains a challenge. Given the link between learning and compression, network compression offers a promising lens to analyze this knowledge. However, standard compression heuristics often suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases. To resolve these, we introduce Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE), a mathematical framework to gradually deconstruct the representations in trained network weights.
  HOPE shifts network compression from the discrete domain into a Hilbert space of continuous functions. By modeling individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators, HOPE unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection. Extending this formulation, HOPE introduces macro block eviction to encompass multi-layer structures like entire residual pathways under the same unified metric. This unified approach enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers with different types and sizes. HOPE is a data-free and hyperparameter-free framework. We present proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning to highlight the practical potential of our theory.

</details>


### [310] [Mean-to-Score Discrete Diffusion: Posterior-Mean Denoisers for Score Entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21372)
*Jingyuan Li,Xiaoyi Jiang,Yixuan Jiang,Wei Liu,Yi Zhu,Zuoqiang Shi,Pipi Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEDD's unconstrained score ratios often violate Bayes realizability, causing negative weights in sampling. The authors propose M2S, which predicts a clean-token posterior mean and maps it exactly to valid scores via a kernel-dependent linear transformation. This guarantees scores lie in the bridge polytope, eliminates negative weights, and yields consistent improvements in generative perplexity and FID across CIFAR-10 and OpenWebText benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD), discrete reverse processes are parameterized by unrestricted positive score ratios. While positivity ensures nonnegative jump rates, it does not guarantee that the score ratios at a noisy state are jointly realizable by any clean-token posterior under the forward kernel — a condition termed Bayes realizability. Empirical analysis reveals that a substantial fraction of score vectors in trained SEDD models violate this constraint, leading to negative pre-normalization weights during finite-step sampling. The paper aims to enforce structural consistency between learned scores and the forward corruption process while preserving or improving generative performance.

Method: The authors introduce Mean-to-Score (M2S): instead of directly parameterizing score ratios, the model predicts the posterior mean of a clean token given a noisy token, then converts this mean to score ratios via an exact linear map derived from the forward kernel. For any coordinate-wise CTMC satisfying a mild support condition, this map sends the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope — the set of all score vectors that are Bayes-realizable. Two cases are detailed: uniform corruption (simplex maps to bridge polytope) and absorbing-mask corruption (recovers MD4). The approach requires no sampler changes; scores are projected onto the polytope for existing SEDD models, while M2S models produce valid scores by construction.

Result: In a trained pure-uniform SEDD checkpoint, ~25% of complete score vectors violate the coordinate box, and >50% of those inside the box are still incompatible with any valid posterior. Projecting raw SEDD scores onto the bridge polytope eliminates all negative weights and reduces generative PPL from 203.6 to 175.1. A 28.4M-parameter M2S model on CIFAR-10 lowers test BPD from 3.173 to 3.129 and improves FID-50k. A 170M-parameter M2S model trained on ~262B OpenWebText tokens outperforms pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC at every sampling budget, achieving generative PPL of 143.3 at 128 steps vs. 183.6 for the best pure-uniform baseline.

Conclusion: Enforcing Bayes realizability on score vectors — either by post-hoc projection onto the bridge polytope or by design via M2S — reliably improves sample quality in discrete diffusion models. M2S is a principled, kernel-adaptive parameterization that guarantees structural validity of scores, unifies existing objectives like MD4 under a common framework, and yields consistent empirical gains across model scales and datasets.

Abstract: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) parameterizes discrete reverse processes with unconstrained positive score ratios. While positivity guarantees nonnegative reverse jump rates, it does not ensure Bayes realizability: ratios at a noisy state need not be jointly induced by any clean-token posterior under the forward kernel. The score-entropy loss has the correct population optimum but does not enforce this constraint away from it. In a trained pure-uniform SEDD checkpoint, roughly one quarter of complete score vectors violate the coordinate box, while more than half lie inside it yet remain materially incompatible with any valid posterior. Such violations can produce negative pre-normalization weights in finite-step sampling. Projecting raw scores onto the bridge polytope removes all observed negative weights and improves external generative PPL from $203.6$ to $175.1$ without changing the sampler. We introduce \emph{mean-to-score} (M2S), which predicts a clean-token posterior mean and converts it to the score through an exact kernel-dependent linear map. The construction applies to any known coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) satisfying a mild support condition. For uniform corruption, it maps the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, the resulting objective recovers MD4 exactly. In a controlled 28.4M-parameter CIFAR-10 comparison, M2S lowers test BPD from $3.173$ to $3.129$ and FID-50k from $\CifarSEDDFID$ to $\CifarMtwoSFID$. A 170M-parameter M2S model trained on about 262B OpenWebText token slots outperforms the evaluated pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints at every tested sampling budget, reaching generative PPL $143.3$ at 128 steps versus $183.6$ for the strongest pure-uniform baseline.

</details>


### [311] [A Diffusion-Model Subpopulation Digital Twin for Mobile Health Deployment: A Case Study on the HeartSteps Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21403)
*Ziping Xu,Yuyi Chang,Chenshun Ni,Nithin Sugavanam,Asim H. Gazi,Pedja Klasnja,Emre Ertin,Susan A. Murphy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A conditional time-series diffusion model called JITAI-Twins is proposed to create digital twins of target subpopulations, enabling pre-deployment vetting of online learning algorithms for mobile-health interventions. Validated across HeartSteps v2–v4, the method outperforms simpler simulators in reproducing temporal and between-participant structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Poorly designed online algorithms in just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) can burden and disengage users. There is a need for realistic simulated users to test and compare candidate algorithms before real-life deployment, avoiding costly real-world failures.

Method: The JITAI-Twins method uses a conditional time-series diffusion model with temporal consistency (future actions do not influence generated past). It proceeds in three steps: (1) pre-training on large observational data, (2) fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and (3) inference-time calibration to the target population using domain-scientist expertise.

Result: Validated across HeartSteps v2 through v4, treating each successive deployment as an upcoming study, JITAI-Twins reproduced the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure significantly better than simpler simulators.

Conclusion: JITAI-Twins can credibly simulate a target deployment before it runs, providing a practical prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions in mobile-health interventions.

Abstract: Mobile-health interventions increasingly use online learning and decision making algorithms to personalize when to nudge users toward healthier behavior, but a poorly designed algorithm can burden and disengage participants. New algorithm design decisions should therefore be vetted against realistic simulated users before each real-life deployment. We propose a method to develop ``JITAI-Twins'': digital twins of a target subpopulation for comparing candidate online algorithms before a just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) deployment. The method builds on a conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent (future actions do not affect the generated past), and it supports repeated updating from three sources of information, in three steps: pre-training on a large observational dataset, fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and inference-time calibration to the next target population from domain-scientist expertise. We validate the twin at each pre-deployment stage of the long-running HeartSteps series (v2 through v4) of physical-activity suggestion intervention deployments, treating each successive deployment as an upcoming study. The proposed method reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators. These results suggest that our twin can be used to simulate a target deployment before it runs, the prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions.

</details>


### [312] [Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21426)
