*Ahmad Halimi Razlighi,Maximilian H. V. Tillmann,Edgar Beck,Bho Matthiesen,Armin Dekorsy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a semantic-aware task clustering method for cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) to prevent destructive cooperation. It uses hierarchical density-based spatial clustering after an initial training phase to group semantically aligned tasks, then conducts joint training within clusters, yielding accuracy gains over unclustered and individual training baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication can be either constructive or destructive depending on semantic relationships among tasks. The authors aim to ensure that only semantically aligned tasks cooperate, thereby avoiding negative transfer and destructive cooperation that degrade task performance.

Method: A sequential multi-stage optimization framework: (1) a short initial training phase to obtain task representations; (2) semantic clustering of tasks using hierarchical density-based spatial clustering (HDBSCAN); (3) end-to-end joint training conducted exclusively within the discovered task clusters (intra-cluster CMT-SemCom learning).

Result: Simulation results show that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy improvements compared to both unclustered multi-tasking and individual task training baselines.

Conclusion: Semantic-aware task clustering is an effective strategy for CMT-SemCom, ensuring that only semantically compatible tasks share representations during joint training. This approach transforms destructive multi-task cooperation into constructive cooperation, leading to measurable performance gains.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

</details>


### [313] [Context-weighted Discrete Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21427)
*Daniil Cherniavskii,Daniel Severo,Karen Ullrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Discrete flow matching suffers from variable token difficulty during training. The authors propose context-weighted sampling and a scaled cross-entropy loss based on local CTMC context density, achieving up to 63% generative perplexity reduction on OpenWebText while matching block diffusion quality with full order flexibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard factorized training in discrete flow matching exposes the model to tokens of widely varying predictability — some are trivially conditioned while others are highly ambiguous. The authors empirically show that token uncertainty correlates strongly with the density of available context in its neighborhood, motivating context-aware modifications to both sampling and training.

Method: Two modifications to the continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) framework: (1) a context-weighted sampler that uses local context density to modulate the noising/sampling process, and (2) a scaled cross-entropy loss that reweights training signals per token based on contextual informativeness, with negligible computational overhead.

Result: The scaled cross-entropy loss reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. The approach matches the generation quality of a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline while preserving arbitrary-order generation capability.

Conclusion: Local context is a critical factor in discrete generative modeling. Simple context-aware modifications to CTMC-based discrete flow matching can substantially improve both sampling quality and training efficiency without sacrificing flexibility.

Abstract: Discrete flow matching provides a flexible framework for generative modeling on discrete structures. However, the standard factorized training objective exposes the model to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned, predictable tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. We empirically demonstrate that the uncertainty over the value of each token is closely related to the density of available context in its neighborhood. Motivated by this observation, we propose a simple modification to the underlying continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) that incorporates local context information. Our context-weighted sampler improves generation quality with negligible computational overhead, while our scaled cross-entropy loss function reweights the training signal from different tokens and reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. Moreover, our approach matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while retaining the ability to perform generation in any order. These results highlight the role of local context as an important factor in discrete generative modeling and show that simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency.

</details>


### [314] [Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21475)
*Peng Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deterministic KV-cache eviction methods are inherently unidentifiable — they cannot estimate their own error — while randomized eviction with Poisson sampling restores identifiability. A survey-sampling variance estimator yields per-step error certificates with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. The certificate excels at attribution (separating cache-induced from inherent failures, AUC 0.73–0.75) but not prediction; randomization buys attribution, not predictive power.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV-cache eviction is critical for efficient LLM inference, but existing deterministic top-k methods lack any principled way to estimate the error they introduce. The authors identify a fundamental identifiability problem: deterministic eviction cannot know what it destroyed, since evicted values can be adversarially perturbed without changing any retained observable, making error estimation impossible. This motivates a randomized framework that enables statistical inference on eviction-induced error.

Method: The paper proposes randomized KV-cache eviction using Poisson sampling with known inclusion probabilities. Key components: (1) a Hájek-corrected logit offset inside the softmax to debias attention computation from the subsample; (2) a survey-sampling variance estimator (Horvitz-Thompson style) over retained tokens that produces per-step error certificates; (3) certificate-gated budget escalation for dynamic allocation. The authors pre-registered seven claims and tested them on real workloads.

Result: Three of seven pre-registered claims were rejected: question-aware eviction at 25–50% budgets is nearly cost-free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survived: the error certificate achieves 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost and separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73–0.75 vs. 0.47–0.54 for output confidence). It also schedules recomputation better than random or confidence-based gating. Randomization enables attribution, not prediction.

Conclusion: Randomized KV-cache eviction is necessary for identifiability and enables principled error attribution through survey-sampling variance estimators. However, the resulting certificates are better at diagnosing failures post-hoc than predicting them in advance. The core insight is that randomization buys attribution, not prediction — a trade-off with significant implications for how LLM serving systems should monitor and respond to cache-induced errors.

Abstract: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the Hájek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

</details>


### [315] [KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21446)
*Yann Bouquet,Alireza Khodamoradi,Kristof Denolf,Mathieu Salzmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KroQuant introduces a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform for W4A4 post-training quantization of diffusion transformers, operating on 32-element blocks with lower parameter cost than per-channel scaling. Combined with LoRaQ weight calibration, it achieves faster inference than SmoothQuant while outperforming SVDQuant and LoRaQ in output fidelity on PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training quantization of DiTs to W4A4 degrades quality due to activation outliers in linear layers. Existing solutions force an online invertible transform at each denoising step, creating a trade-off: SmoothQuant is cheap but harms accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms improve accuracy but incur high online cost; learned full-rank transforms are best but require prohibitive per-layer per-step dense GEMMs. A method is needed that combines high quantization accuracy with low inference overhead.

Method: KroQuant applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of activations, using fewer than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure executes as small tensor-core GEMMs, yielding a quantizer kernel up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant on MI350 GPU. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs residual per-weight quantization error.

Result: On PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI benchmarks, while preserving or improving image quality.

Conclusion: KroQuant resolves the accuracy-cost trade-off in DiT quantization by using Kronecker-structured transforms that are both computationally efficient and highly accurate, making W4A4 inference practical for diffusion transformers without sacrificing output quality.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

</details>


### [316] [Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21453)
*Rajiv Shailesh Chitale,Rahul Madhavan,Taneesh Gupta,Deepanway Ghosal,Aravindan Raghuveer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TTEL is an inference-time scaling algorithm that uses token-level error localization via conditional probability comparison to truncate incorrect reasoning trajectories at the error step and branch new generations from the valid prefix, achieving superior pass@k vs. token-cost Pareto frontiers compared to independent sampling and sequential refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard test-time scaling approaches (independent sampling and multi-turn refinement) lack token-level credit assignment, leading to computational waste because valid reasoning prefixes that precede an error are discarded and recomputed from scratch.

Method: TTEL performs error localization by comparing token-level conditional probabilities under two contexts: (1) a null-context baseline and (2) informed feedback (fixed or environment-based). When a significant divergence in probability is detected at a token, that token is identified as the error location. The trajectory is then truncated at the preceding valid prefix, and a new generation is branched from that point, maximally reusing correct reasoning steps.

Result: On LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-8B, TTEL achieves pass@64 of 71.0% using ~360.4k tokens versus 735.0k tokens for independent sampling (roughly half the cost). TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains. On AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 math benchmarks, TTEL outperforms competing test-time baselines with both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

Conclusion: Token-level error localization enables more efficient test-time compute scaling by preserving and reusing valid reasoning prefixes, yielding strictly better performance-cost trade-offs than prior methods across code and math reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

</details>


### [317] [Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535)
*Alagappan Valliappan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: At million-token context lengths, Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP) draft heads in speculative decoding become prohibitively expensive due to full-attention KV cache reads. The authors propose Windowed-MTP, a training-free, drop-in solution that applies StreamingLLM-style sliding window + attention sink to the draft head only, bounding its KV working set to a constant size. This yields 28-44% per-step cost reduction at 1M context across diverse architectures while preserving the target model's full-attention verification and output distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLMs increasingly ship with built-in MTP draft heads for speculative decoding, assuming the draft is negligibly cheap. This assumption breaks at long contexts (~1M tokens): the MTP draft head runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, causing its read cost to grow linearly with context length. The problem compounds with deep draft lengths (can become net-negative vs. no speculation) and is exacerbated under hybrid/linear-attention targets where cheap verification exposes the draft's full-attention cost. The core insight is that speculation is most valuable precisely where the draft becomes most expensive.

Method: Windowed-MTP applies a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink exclusively to the draft head's attention mechanism, while keeping the target model's full-attention verification completely intact. This is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which tokens are accepted. The draft's KV working set is bounded to a constant size, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M context. Additionally, the unread draft KV entries are reclaimed via a compact ring buffer with no acceptance or quality cost.

Result: Evaluated across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%. This margin is input-invariant and widens with context. End-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount at matched acceptance, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance. The unread draft KV accounts for 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M and is successfully reclaimed.

Conclusion: Windowed-MTP is a simple, training-free, lossless technique that restores the viability of built-in MTP speculative decoding at extreme context lengths by bounding draft attention cost to a constant, with no degradation to the verified output distribution.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

</details>


### [318] [Finite-Sample Coverage Audits for High-Recall Candidate Generation: Certification and Learning-Theoretic Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21480)
*Martin Anthony,Kaveh Salehzadeh Nobari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the label complexity of certifying that a high-recall screening stage misses few relevant items, proving that auditing the excluded pool is minimax rate-optimal and providing exact finite-sample certification tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In empirical pipelines with a high-recall screening stage (e.g., systematic reviews, e-discovery, information retrieval), items filtered out are lost to all downstream stages. The authors aim to provide finite-sample valid guarantees on the number of missed relevant items, addressing the question of how many audit labels are needed to certify that the missed mass is small.

Method: The authors establish theoretical lower bounds on label complexity: first showing that no procedure using only in-candidate labels can certify non-trivial missed-mass bounds, then deriving a finite-corpus lower bound proving excluded-pool auditing requires order N₀/m labels — establishing minimax rate-optimality in the zero-miss regime. They then develop exact finite-sample certification tools using binomial and hypergeometric inversion (avoiding asymptotics), supporting two-pool designs, simultaneous certification of nested candidate generators, and stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms.

Result: Excluded-pool auditing is proved minimax rate-optimal for missed-mass certification. The finite-sample toolkit provides exact binomial/hypergeometric-based certificates for missed mass, recall conversion, simultaneous family certification, and perturbation stress-testing, all under a pre-registration discipline where the candidate generator and audit rule are fixed before label examination.

Conclusion: Auditing the excluded pool is not merely convenient but theoretically necessary and rate-optimal for certifying small missed mass. The proposed finite-sample toolkit enables practitioners to select the least burdensome candidate generator that meets a missed-mass target with rigorous, non-asymptotic guarantees, provided pre-specification is maintained.

Abstract: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

</details>


### [319] [Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21542)
*Yakun Wang,Leyang Wang,Song Liu,Taiji Suzuki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a two-sample test (ZF2ST) based on a zero-flow discrepancy that learns local misalignment patterns between distributions using neural networks, while maintaining valid statistical calibration through separation of witness learning and hypothesis evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing two-sample tests often struggle to balance flexibility (e.g., using deep learning) with rigorous statistical validity. There is a need for tests that can detect structured distributional differences with high power while maintaining calibrated type-I error control.

Method: The authors introduce the zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD), a statistical divergence grounded in the zero-flow criterion. The ZF2ST framework separates the witness function learning phase from hypothesis evaluation. Two witness learning strategies are developed: a regression-based approach and a power-maximized approach. Flexible neural networks can be used for witness learning without compromising the validity of the downstream test.

Result: ZF2ST achieves strong testing power for detecting structured distributional changes on both synthetic and image datasets, while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error, as demonstrated experimentally.

Conclusion: The separation of witness learning from hypothesis testing enables the use of flexible neural networks while preserving statistical guarantees, making ZF2ST a practical and powerful two-sample testing framework.

Abstract: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

</details>


### [320] [X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21550)
*Dongjie Fu,Di Cao,Xize Cheng,Zihan Zhang,Wenxu Jia,Yifu Chen,Shengpeng Ji,Yu Zhang,Tao Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: X³-OPD is a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers logical reasoning capabilities from a text-based teacher LLM to an audio-language student model using a three-tier symmetric corpus, significantly improving audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio-language models lag behind text-based LLMs in deep logical reasoning due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. The key challenge is effectively transferring reasoning capabilities from text models to audio models without requiring large-scale annotated audio reasoning datasets.

Method: The framework uses on-policy distillation where the audio-language student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while a text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. A three-tier symmetric corpus is constructed: (1) textual reasoning rendered into speech, (2) audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and (3) spoken-dialogue reasoning with paralinguistic cues. This enables distillation beyond textually recoverable content to non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context.

Result: Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR benchmark datasets show substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality, while preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

Conclusion: X³-OPD effectively bridges the reasoning gap between text and audio-language models through cross-modal on-policy distillation with a carefully designed multi-tier training corpus, achieving strong performance without sacrificing general capabilities.

Abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

</details>


### [321] [Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21561)
*Aaron Feller,Kris Deibler,Maxim Secor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EnsembleEGNN is a pretrained molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes conformational ensembles via shared EGNN layers and Set Attention pooling, achieving strong cyclic-peptide property prediction when combined with a sequence encoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most molecular property prediction methods rely on a single representative conformation, ignoring the reality that molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. This limits predictive accuracy, particularly for flexible molecules like cyclic peptides.

Method: EnsembleEGNN uses shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers to encode each conformer in an ensemble, then pools representations via a Set Attention Block. The model is pretrained on the CREMP cyclic peptide ensemble dataset with a multi-task self-supervised objective: masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. For downstream prediction, it can operate standalone or be co-trained end-to-end with a BERT sequence encoder.

Result: Training from scratch yields R²=0.005 (complete failure). Pretrained EnsembleEGNN achieves R²=0.477 and Pearson r=0.699, surpassing the sequence-only BERT baseline (R²=0.439, r=0.667). Co-training with BERT further boosts performance to R²=0.538 and Pearson r=0.737 on the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB benchmark.

Conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding significantly improves cyclic-peptide property prediction, and combining ensemble structural information with sequence representations yields the best results.

Abstract: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

</details>


### [322] [Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21573)
*Hongnan Ma,Yiwei Shi,Mengyue Yang,Weiru Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TimePNS is a two-stage framework for time-series explanation that refines sufficiency-based saliency maps by incorporating counterfactual necessity: Stage I learns a causal generative model with an initial explanation mask, and Stage II uses counterfactual interventions to identify necessary temporal factors, suppressing spurious subsequences and improving the sufficiency-necessity trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing explanation methods for time-series classifiers focus on sufficiency—finding subsequences that preserve the prediction—but can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that are sufficient yet not necessary. There is a need for explanations that also capture necessity as defined by Pearl's counterfactual framework.

Method: TimePNS has two stages. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process along with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors, measuring whether prediction is disrupted to derive necessity signals. These signals supervise a temporal gate that refines the mask by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones.

Result: On synthetic and real-world benchmarks, TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

Conclusion: Incorporating counterfactual necessity into time-series explanation yields more faithful and precise identification of decision-critical subsequences, overcoming the limitations of purely sufficiency-oriented approaches.

Abstract: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

</details>


### [323] [Expanding Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21585)
*Sophia Tang,Pranam Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EFlows introduces generative flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality, and EFMs distill these into efficient few-step generative models using expand and transport operators, enabling variable-size generation across continuous and discrete domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-based generative models are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths, limiting their applicability to tasks where output size is itself a variable degree of freedom, such as variable-size graphs or variable-length sequences.

Method: The authors propose Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows) that define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality via an expanding interpolant that augments the state with conditional noise. They then introduce Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), which factor the map between timesteps into an expand operator (augments state space with new coordinates/tokens conditioned on current state) and a transport map (pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant). The framework extends to the discrete simplex for graph and sequence generation.

Result: EFlows and EFMs provide a principled framework for variable-size generation across continuous and discrete modalities, with existing fixed-canvas flows recovered as a special case where the expand operator is identity.

Conclusion: EFlows and EFMs establish a principled framework where output size is a learned, controllable degree of freedom, broadening the applicability of flow-based generative models beyond fixed-dimensional settings.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

</details>
