### [324] [PhantomSeal: Proactive Deepfakes Defense with Identity/Context Protection and Forensic Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20564)
*Liangqin Ren,Zeyan Liu,Ye Wang,Yuxin Chen,Fengjun Li,Bo Luo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PhantomSeal is a proactive defense that embeds a stealthy "cloak identity" into images to simultaneously prevent face-swapping deepfakes and enable forensic tracing, reducing the attack success rate of SimSwap to 0.30% and achieving 97.97% manipulated-content identification accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deepfake defenses are predominantly post-hoc (detecting fakes after generation), while proactive defenses that intervene before generation remain limited in real-world effectiveness. Moreover, no prior proactive approach simultaneously protects both user identity and image context from face-swapping attacks while also supporting forensic tracing.

Method: PhantomSeal introduces a novel cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier into users' images. This identifier steers the deepfake generation process to produce content resembling the chosen cloak identity rather than the intended target, thus disrupting successful face-swapping. The embedded signal also enables feature-based forensic analysis to trace manipulated content.

Result: PhantomSeal reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap (an advanced face-swapping model) to 0.30% and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content. Extensive experiments across different face-swapping architectures and models demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness.

Conclusion: PhantomSeal is the first proactive defense achieving simultaneous identity and context protection against face-swapping attacks with forensic tracing capability, demonstrating strong real-world potential across multiple deepfake models.

Abstract: Deepfakes, especially face-swapping attacks, pose significant challenges to authenticity, security, and ethics across science, engineering, and society. While most existing detection/tracing approaches operate post hoc, proactive defenses that aim to intervene before deepfake generation remain limited in terms of real-world effectiveness. In this paper, we present PhantomSeal, the first proactive defense to simultaneously protect both the identity and the context of users' images from being used in face-swapping attacks, while supporting forensic tracing. We present a novel cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier. This mechanism steers the deepfake generation process toward producing content that resembles the chosen cloak identity, thereby preventing successful face-swapping while enabling effective feature-based forensic analysis. The effectiveness and robustness of PhantomSeal is demonstrated in extensive experiments across different face-swapping architectures and models. For example, it reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap, an advanced deepfake model, to 0.30%, and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content. Codes can be found at https://github.com/LiangqinRen/PhantomSeal

</details>


### [325] [AuthProbe: Specification-Driven, Multi-Identity Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Recruitment API](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20574)
*Jay Barach*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AuthProbe is a black-box scanner that detects BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities in HTTP APIs by using multiple controlled identities, OpenAPI specifications, and ground-truth response comparison to identify unauthorized cross-identity object access with high precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BOLA/IDOR has been the top-ranked OWASP API security risk since 2019 and has caused major data exposures in recruitment technology. Existing defenses like WAFs and single-identity scanners fail because malicious BOLA requests are byte-for-byte identical to legitimate ones — making detection fundamentally dependent on multi-identity analysis.

Method: AuthProbe operates by (1) ingesting an OpenAPI specification to drive test generation, (2) discovering objects owned by each controlled identity, (3) attempting cross-identity reads (accessing one identity's objects while authenticated as another), (4) comparing responses against ground-truth fetches by the true owner to confirm leaks, (5) walking predictable identifiers to detect enumeration vulnerabilities, and (6) reporting missing authentication and existence oracles. It outputs a severity-thresholded exit code and machine-readable reports suitable for CI gating.

Result: On a synthetic recruitment API replicating the McHire failure class, AuthProbe detected every planted cross-identity read with zero false positives on a hardened counterpart. Runtime scales linearly with the number of objects under test.

Conclusion: AuthProbe provides an effective, practical, and precise black-box solution for detecting BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities, filling a gap left by WAFs and single-identity scanners. Its open-source release under Apache 2.0 with an authorized-use guardrail enables integration into CI/CD pipelines for continuous API security validation.

Abstract: Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA), also known as Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR), has topped the OWASP API Security ranking since 2019 and is the root cause of some of the largest exposures of applicant data in recruitment technology. The defining feature of this flaw class is that a malicious request is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a legitimate one, which is precisely why web application firewalls and single identity scanners fail to catch it. We present AuthProbe, an open-source, black-box scanner that detects BOLA and IDOR in HTTP APIs by driving its tests from an OpenAPI specification and by acting under two or more identities that the operator controls. AuthProbe discovers, for each identity, the objects that identity legitimately owns, then attempts to read one identity's objects while authenticated as another and confirms a leak by comparing the response against a ground-truth fetch by the true owner. It also walks predictable identifiers to expose enumeration and reports missing authentication and existence oracles. The tool returns a severity-thresholded exit code and machine-readable reports so that it can gate a continuous integration build. On a synthetic recruitment API in which the McHire failure class is reproduced, AuthProbe detects every planted cross-identity read with no false positives on a hardened counterpart, and its running time grows linearly with the number of objects under test. AuthProbe is released under the Apache 2.0 license with an authorized-use guardrail.

</details>


### [326] [ChannelGuard: Safe Models Do Not Compose into Safe Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19430)
*Elias Hossain,Md Mehedi Hasan Nipu,Fatema Tuj Johora Faria,Tasfia Nuzhat Ornee,Maleeha Sheikh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ChannelGuard is a training-free, defense-in-depth framework that places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel in multi-agent LLM systems, using embedding similarity against adversarial phrase banks to block or compress malicious content without additional LLM calls. It blocks Tool Poisoning entirely across all tested backends and reduces Prompt Injection success by half, while a white-box adaptive paraphrase attack evades all embedding gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM applications route messages through unmonitored inter-agent channels (planner→worker→verifier→synthesizer), creating attack surfaces that existing defenses miss by guarding only input boundaries or operating as opaque server-side filters. Current evaluation practices using outcome-only reporting conceal how safety depends on provider-side filters rather than application-layer defenses, leading to a false sense of security when backends change.

Method: ChannelGuard places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel. Each gate scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank using embedding similarity, then deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks the content. No additional LLM calls are incurred. An attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. The approach is evaluated on 2,100 traces across 8 attack families, 5 defenses, and 3 model backends (Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5), with GSM8K benign-preservation testing and a judge audit (κ=0.900).

Result: Undefended pipelines achieved 0.000 attack success on tool/memory poisoning but owed safety almost entirely to Azure's server-side filter (54/60 blocks), silently shifting alignment responsibility when the backend changed. ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocked Tool Poisoning 30/30 at the application layer identically across all three backends, reduced Prompt Injection success from 0.333 to 0.167 (half), and preserved GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase attacks evaded all embedding gates; a perturb-and-vote baseline performed better against such attacks.

Conclusion: Outcome-only safety reporting in multi-agent LLM systems is misleading, as it masks backend dependence. Defense-in-depth with inter-agent channel gating provides backend-agnostic protection at negligible cost (training-free, no extra LLM calls), but embedding-similarity gates remain vulnerable to white-box adaptive paraphrasing, suggesting hybrid approaches (e.g., perturb-and-vote) are needed for robustness.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM applications chain a planner, worker agents, a verifier, and a synthesizer, and every hop between agents is an unmonitored channel through which an adversary can smuggle instructions. Existing defenses guard only the input boundary (IBProtector, Llama Guard, perplexity filters, SmoothLLM) or run outside the application as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters. We show this gap carries a consequence rarely measured: on a 2,100-trace evaluation across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends, an undefended pipeline that appears fully safe under standard reporting (attack success 0.000 on tool- and memory-poisoning) owes that safety almost entirely to the cloud provider's server-side filter (54 of 60 blocks on Azure GPT-5), and silently shifts to the agent model's own alignment on a backend without such a filter. Outcome-only reporting hides this dependence. We present ChannelGuard, a training-free defense-in-depth framework placing information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel; each scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank by embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks it, adding no LLM call, while an attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30 of 30 at the application layer, identically across Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, and Anthropic Haiku 4.5, whereas the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends; it also lowers Prompt Injection attack success by half (0.333 to 0.167) and preserves GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase evades every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline does better. An extended appendix adds baselines, ablations, sweeps, a benign-preservation analysis, and a judge audit (kappa = 0.900), at a total cost of 47.36 USD.

</details>


### [327] [Deepfake News Detection: A Multimodal Framework Integrating LipNet, DeepSpeech and ResNET for Enhanced Audio-Visual Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20579)
*Ameena Khan,Muhammad Ahsan Aziz,Muhammad Junaid Asif,Naeem Akhter,Rana Fayyaz Ahmad*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A multi-modal framework for deepfake news detection that jointly analyzes lip movements, audio, and facial features, achieving 94% accuracy on FakeAVCeleb using an ensemble of RF, MLP, and LSTM classifiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid advancement of generative AI has made realistic deepfake videos and cloned voices widely accessible, threatening the authenticity of digital news media. There is a pressing need for robust detection methods that can effectively discern AI-manipulated multimedia content.

Method: A multi-modal framework that extracts features from three modalities: (1) lip movements encoded via LipNet, (2) speech content encoded via DeepSpeech2, and (3) facial features extracted using BlazeFace and represented with ResNet18. These feature vectors are concatenated into a holistic representation and classified using an ensemble of Random Forest, MLP, and LSTM networks. Audio augmentation is also applied to enhance performance.

Result: The proposed approach achieves 94% accuracy on the FakeAVCeleb dataset when using augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline.

Conclusion: The results confirm the robustness and practical potential of the proposed multi-modal framework for deepfake news detection, demonstrating that joint exploitation of audio and visual cues yields strong discriminative performance.

Abstract: Deepfake news refers to AI-generated (or AI ma-nipulated) multimedia content intentionally generated to deceive audiences by manipulating the facial expressions, or speech while maintaining the realistic appearance. The rapid progress of generative AI has made the synthesis of highly realistic fake videos and cloned voices widely accessible, posing a serious threat to the authenticity of digital news media. This paper presents a multi-modal framework that discerns the authenticity of video content by jointly exploiting audio and visual cues, thereby addressing the challenge of detecting the deepfake videos. We proposed a framework that involves features extraction from lip movements, audio content and video frames. Lip movements and speech content are encoded using the LipNet and DeepSpeech2 models, while facial features are extracted by leveraging the use of BlazeFace and represented with ResNet18. The extracted feature vectors are concatenated into a holistic video representation and classified with an ensemble of machine learning and deep learning models, including Random Forest (RF), Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Exten-sive experiments performed on the FakeAVCeleb dataset shows that the proposed approach attains an accuracy of 94% using augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline. The results confirm the robustness and practical potential of the proposed framework for deepfake news detection.

</details>


### [328] [Geometric Configurations of Perturbed Jailbreak Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20581)
*Lynn Delcon,Andres Algaba,Vincent Ginis*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Analyzes internal representations of perturbed jailbreak prompts in small Qwen and Llama models, finding no clear behavioral hyperplane separating compliant vs. refusal responses, with only a few specific tokens ("Sure", ",", "ĊĊ") showing significant association with compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: String-level perturbation techniques that transform unsuccessful jailbreak prompts into successful ones pose a major security threat to LLM safety. Understanding how these perturbed inputs are internally represented could reveal vulnerabilities and inform defense mechanisms.

Method: The authors examine two representation spaces — (1) last-layer-last-token embeddings and (2) top-50 next-token probability space — across small-weight models from Qwen-2.5-Instruct (1.5B, 3B, 7B) and Llama-3.2-Instruct (1B, 3B, 3.1-8B) families. They analyze whether these spaces contain a behavioral hyperplane separating compliant from refusal answers.

Result: The last-layer-last-token embedding space separates prompts by spelling/format. The top-50 next-token probability space is effectively one-dimensional but harder to cluster. No behavioral hyperplane was found in either space within the refusal-dominated answer set. Only the token "Sure" in Qwen-1.5B and tokens "," and "ĊĊ" in Llama-1B showed significant association with compliant-labeled answers.

Conclusion: The internal representations of perturbed jailbreak inputs do not exhibit a clear, linearly separable behavioral hyperplane for compliance vs. refusal, suggesting that safety-relevant signals may be encoded in more distributed or non-linear ways. The sparse token-level associations hint at model-specific and scale-dependent encoding of compliance.

Abstract: Perturbation techniques that turn unsuccessful jailbreak prompts into successful ones are continuously evolving, constituting a major security threat to LLM safety. In this paper, we investigate the internal representations of such string-level perturbed jailbreak inputs in the small weight models of the Qwen-2.5-1.5B/-3B/-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-1B/-3B/-3.1-8B-Instruct families. We select two representation spaces: the last-layer-last-token embedding space and the top-50 next-token probability space. The former space separates prompts based on their spelling and format, while the latter space is effectively one-dimensional but appears more complex to cluster. Within our refusal-dominated answer set we find no behavioral hyperplane in either space. Only the next token "Sure" in the 1.5B Qwen model, and both tokens "," and "ĊĊ" in the 1$ Llama model, display a significant association with a compliant-labeled answer.

</details>


### [329] [Enhancing Attack Detection Capabilities in BACnet/IP Networks Using Machine-Learning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20686)
*Derek Manzella,John D. Hastings*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of tooling and labeled datasets for detecting BACnet/IP attacks on Building Automation Systems by: (1) modifying CISA's Zeek BACnet parser for unified logging, (2) building a simulated HVAC testbed with physics-based behavior and attack labeling, and (3) evaluating five unsupervised anomaly detection models against six attack types. One-Class SVM performed best (avg F1=0.864), with near-perfect detection of high-volume DoS/reconnaissance but weaker performance (~77% F1) on stealthy tampering and false data injection attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Defenders lack adequate tooling and labeled datasets for detecting BACnet/IP-specific attacks on Building Automation Systems. Existing network monitoring tools produce fragmented logs that complicate feature engineering, and no realistic, labeled BACnet attack dataset with physics-based device behavior exists for training and evaluating ML-based intrusion detection.

Method: The authors make three contributions: (1) modify CISA's Zeek BACnet parser to generate unified per-packet logs for streamlined feature engineering; (2) develop a simulated BACnet/IP testbed using bacpypes3, modeling a small commercial HVAC system with physics-based device behavior, schedule-aware controllers, and per-packet attack labeling; (3) evaluate five unsupervised anomaly detection models (including One-Class SVM) on baseline traffic plus six attack types: denial of service, reconnaissance, property tampering, and false data injection.

Result: One-Class SVM achieved the best overall performance with an average F1 score of 0.864 across all six attack types. High-volume attacks (DoS, reconnaissance) achieved F1 scores above 0.99, while stealthier attacks (property tampering, false data injection) scored around 77% F1.

Conclusion: Unsupervised anomaly detection, particularly One-Class SVM, is highly effective for detecting high-volume BACnet/IP attacks like DoS and reconnaissance. However, detection remains substantially weaker for low-volume, stealthy attacks such as property tampering and false data injection, indicating a need for further research on detecting subtle manipulation in BAS networks.

Abstract: Building Automation Systems (BAS) manage critical building functions using protocols such as BACnet/IP, yet defenders have limited tooling and few labeled datasets for detecting BACnet-specific attacks. This work addresses these gaps through three contributions. First, CISA's Zeek BACnet parser is modified to produce a unified per-packet log, simplifying feature engineering for machine-learning (ML) pipelines. Second, a simulated BACnet/IP testbed is developed using bacpypes3 to model a small commercial HVAC system with physics-based device behavior, schedule-aware controller logic, and per-packet attack labeling. Third, five unsupervised anomaly detection models are evaluated using baseline traffic and six BACnet attack types, including denial of service, reconnaissance, property tampering, and false data injection. Results show that One-Class SVM achieved the strongest overall performance, with an average F1 score of 0.864 across all attacks and F1 scores above 0.99 for high-volume denial-of-service and reconnaissance attacks. Detection is much stronger for high-volume attacks, such as DoS attacks and reconnaissance, than stealthier techniques such as tampering and false data injection, which scored around 77%.

</details>


### [330] [Buzz to Boom: Detecting Message Progression Vulnerabilities in Electron Applications via Segmented Directed Fuzzing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20698)
*Jianjia Yu,Zhengyu Liu,Ziyang Li,Yu Sun,Yinzhi Cao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Proton is a segmented directed fuzzing framework that detects Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs) in Electron applications by decomposing cross-process fuzzing along message-passing boundaries. Evaluated on 589 real-world apps, it found 23 zero-day MPVs (22 leading to OS command execution), resulting in 11 CVEs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Electron security research only addresses unsafe configurations and malicious DOM content, but cannot detect or exploit Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs) — multi-step, cross-process attacks where attacker-controlled inputs propagate across processes via message passing to reach privileged APIs like command execution. No prior work tackles this complex, cross-process exploit chain detection.

Method: Proton decomposes end-to-end fuzzing into per-process segments along message-passing boundaries. Each segment is fuzzed with one of two goals: (i) reaching a sink in the current process, or (ii) propagating a payload to the next process to enable further exploration. Payloads that cross process boundaries seed the corpus of the subsequent segment. Finally, Proton synthesizes crash inputs across processes to validate complete end-to-end exploits.

Result: Evaluation on 589 real-world Electron applications yielded 23 zero-day MPVs. Of these, 22 enabled OS command execution, including in projects with over 50k GitHub stars. Responsible disclosure resulted in 13 acknowledgments, 11 fixes, 11 CVEs, and a bug bounty from Vercel.

Conclusion: Proton demonstrates that segmented directed fuzzing across message-passing boundaries is an effective approach for discovering complex, multi-step MPVs in Electron applications, exposing a previously unaddressed class of vulnerabilities with significant real-world impact.

Abstract: Electron is a popular framework for building cross-platform desktop applications using web technologies. Such applications consist of multiple processes with different privilege levels that communicate via message passing. When inter-process messages carry attacker-controlled inputs, they can propagate across processes and reach privileged APIs, e.g., command execution. Such a message propagation behavior is characterized as Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs). The exploitation of MPVs is challenging because it often requires multiple steps, e.g., first arbitrary code execution in one process via message passing, and then command injection in another process using another message crafted in the first process. To our knowledge, existing works on Electron security only study unsafe configurations and malicious Document Object Model (DOM) content, i.e., they cannot detect or exploit these vulnerabilities that need to be triggered by complex cross-process exploits via message passing. We present Proton, a segmented directed fuzzing framework for detecting MPVs. Our key insight is to decompose end-to-end fuzzing into per-process segments along message-passing boundaries, where the goals of fuzzing each segment are either: (i) reaching a sink in the current process or (ii) propagating the payload to the next process, to enable the exploration of another process. In the second case, the messages seed the corpus of the next segment. Finally, Proton synthesizes crash inputs from each process to validate end-to-end exploits. We evaluate Proton against 589 real-world Electron applications, resulting in 23 zero-day MPVs. Among them, 22 lead to OS command execution, including projects with over 50k GitHub stars. We responsibly disclosed all findings. To date, we have received 13 acknowledgments, 11 fixes, and 11 CVEs, including a bug bounty from Vercel.

</details>


### [331] [Evaluating Large Language Models for Symbolic Security Protocol Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20712)
*Paolo Modesti,Syed Ahmed,Ioannis Sfyrakis,Derek Enodolomwanyi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks LLMs (GPT and DeepSeek, in chat and reasoning modes) on security protocol verification across 130 obfuscated protocols with 388 security goals. LLMs achieve modest recall/precision trade-offs, with reasoning models improving precision but missing many attacks, particularly on authentication goals. LLMs do not match formal verifiers (ProVerif/OFMC) but may serve as pre-screening filters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formal verification tools like ProVerif and OFMC are the gold standard for security protocol analysis, but are computationally expensive and require expertise. The authors investigate whether LLMs can provide comparable, more accessible analysis as a potential complement or lightweight alternative.

Method: The study evaluates GPT and DeepSeek in both chat and reasoning modes over three runs on 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols covering 388 security goals. Performance is scored against ground truth from ProVerif and OFMC, measuring recall, precision, F1, and verdict stability across runs. DeepSeek's two modes share a single underlying model, isolating the effect of reasoning; GPT's modes span a model-version change, making its comparison only suggestive.

Result: Chat models achieve 69–81% recall but precision below 31%. Reasoning models reverse this: GPT reaches 66.5% precision, DeepSeek 45.4%, but both detect just over half of attacks. DeepSeek's reasoning mode raises precision from 27.2% to 45.4% compared to chat. All models perform worst on authentication goals (well under half of injective/non-injective agreement attacks detected by reasoning models; chat models over-flag at low precision). Confidentiality is the exception: F1 up to 95.7% in reasoning mode. Verdict stability varies (89.7% identical for GPT, 74.0% for DeepSeek). Self-reported confidence is uniformly high but uncorrelated with correctness.

Conclusion: LLMs do not match formal verification tools on this benchmark. Their best potential use is as pre-screening filters, not as replacements for rigorous formal analysis.

Abstract: Security protocol verification relies on formal tools such as ProVerif and OFMC. This study evaluates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform comparable analysis. We test GPT and DeepSeek in chat and reasoning modes over three runs on 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols covering 388 security goals, scored against ProVerif and OFMC. Chat models reach 69 to 81% recall at precision below 31%. Reasoning models reverse this trade-off, reaching 66.5% precision for GPT and 45.4% for DeepSeek, but detect just over half the attacks. DeepSeek's two modes share one underlying model, so the comparison isolates reasoning itself, which raises precision from 27.2% to 45.4%. The GPT contrast spans a model-version change and is only suggestive. All models perform worst on authentication goals: reasoning models detect well under half of injective and non-injective agreement attacks, whereas chat models over-flag them at low precision. Confidentiality is the exception, with F1 up to 95.7% in reasoning mode. Verdicts are unstable across runs, identical on 89.7% of goals for GPT but 74.0% for DeepSeek. Self-reported confidence is uniformly high yet shows no meaningful correlation with correctness. On this benchmark LLMs do not match formal verification, but may serve, at best, as pre-screening filters.

</details>


### [332] [Security Vulnerability Patterns in AI-Generated Code: A Cross-Model Comparative Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20713)
*Shanna M. Kahn,John D. Hastings*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LLM-generated automation scripts from ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini were analyzed for security vulnerabilities. Every script contained exploitable flaws; 9 of 17 vulnerability classes appeared across all three models, and weighted CVSS scores differed by less than 10% across platforms, indicating the risk is task-inherent rather than model-specific.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based coding tools increasingly empower non-expert users to produce automation scripts that may enter enterprise workflows without adequate security review. The authors aim to quantify the security risk posed by such LLM-generated code across multiple models and task domains.

Method: Identical prompts across three automation domains were issued to ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini. The resulting code was subjected to a standardized vulnerability review using Claude Code. Each identified vulnerability was scored via CVSS v3.1 and mapped to both the OWASP Top 10:2021 and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks.

Result: Every generated script contained exploitable vulnerabilities. Nine of 17 vulnerability classes were present in code from all three models; 14 of 17 appeared in at least two models. Weighted CVSS scores across platforms differed by less than 10%, demonstrating that vulnerability prevalence and severity are consistent across LLM providers and tied to the automation task category rather than the specific model.

Conclusion: The security risk of LLM-generated automation code is not attributable to any particular model but is inherent to the task domain. Organizations should therefore focus not on selecting a "safer" LLM tool, but on whether such code should ever be deployed without human security review.

Abstract: LLM-based coding tools enable non-expert users to generate routine automation scripts that may enter enterprise workflows without meaningful security review. This study examines that risk directly. Code was collected from ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini using identical prompts across three automation domains. Claude Code performed a standardized vulnerability review. Each identified vulnerability was scored using CVSS v3.1 and mapped to the OWASP Top 10:2021 and the MITRE ATT&CK frameworks. Every script contained exploitable vulnerabilities. Nine of the 17 identified vulnerability classes appeared in code from all three models, while 14 of the 17 vulnerability classes appeared in at least two models. The weighted CVSS scores across platforms differed by less than 10%. The risk is not tied to any particular model but rather to the task category. Organizations should therefore ask not which tool to trust, but instead whether LLM-generated automation code should be deployed without review.

</details>


### [333] [Leaky Language Models: Stealing Architecture and Inference Optimizations via Per-Token Timing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20723)
*Sadegh Majidi,Niloofar Mireshghallah,Kazem Taram*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LeakyLMs is a side-channel attack that infers proprietary model architecture and deployment configurations from production LLMs solely through token-generation timing. It detects speculative decoding usage and draft model context length (e.g., Gemini Flash 2.5 uses ~128K tokens), and recovers architectural properties (layers, hidden dimensions, attention heads) by modeling token-generation latency on NVIDIA GPUs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production LLM providers expose models only through APIs, concealing critical architectural and deployment details. Prior attacks required intrusive access. The authors address the gap of inferring this proprietary information non-intrusively using only remote timing signals, motivated by both security implications and the need for transparency in black-box LLM services.

Method: LeakyLMs comprises two core attacks: (1) A deployment inference attack that detects inference-time optimizations (speculative decoding) and infers draft model context length by analyzing timing patterns in token generation; (2) An architecture recovery attack that constructs a detailed timing model of token generation on NVIDIA GPUs, characterizing how latency scales with model configuration and hardware parameters, then performs a search over the architecture space by matching observed timings to the model.

Result: The deployment attack revealed that Google Gemini Flash 2.5 uses speculative decoding with a draft context window of approximately 128K tokens. The architecture recovery attack, when tested on Llama models, placed the near-correct architectural configuration in the top-10 guesses more than 90% of the time.

Conclusion: Token generation timing alone constitutes a significant information leakage vector for black-box LLMs. Providers should be aware that deployment strategies and model architectures are inferable through timing side channels, raising both competitive and security concerns for proprietary LLM services.

Abstract: This work presents LeakyLMs, a set of attacks that leak proprietary model, architecture, and deployment information from production language models. LeakyLMs is the first to demonstrate that key model and deployment details can be inferred using only token generation timing, even when interacting through remote APIs. LeakyLMs introduces two core attacks. The first attack targets inference optimizations and deployment strategies. For example, our attack detects whether a provider uses speculative decoding, a widely deployed inference-time optimization, and further identifies the context length of the draft model used in the pipeline. Our measurements show that Google Gemini Flash 2.5 uses speculative decoding with a draft context window of approximately 128K tokens. The second attack recovers key architectural properties, including the number of transformer layers, hidden dimension size, and number of attention heads. To achieve this, LeakyLMs builds a detailed and accurate model of token-generation timing on modern NVIDIA GPUs, characterizing how latency scales with model configuration and hardware parameters. The attack then performs a search over the architecture space using this timing model. In experiments with Llama models, the near-correct architectural configuration appears in the top-10 guesses more than 90% of the time.

</details>


### [334] [IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20759)
*Ankur Singh,Jinqiu Yang,Tse-Hsun Chen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic security evaluation of AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex Desktop) reveals that 66.5% of malicious issue requests from a novel benchmark (IssueTrojanBench) bypass all guardrails. The study finds that rejection relies almost entirely on LLM-level defenses rather than agent frameworks, with GPT models broadly vulnerable and Sonnet 4.6 showing selective, risk-aware blocking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents are increasingly deployed in real-world development with autonomous access to files and tools, inheriting dual security risks: LLM-level threats (adversarial prompts, poisoned training data, backdoors) and agent-level threats (tool misuse, data exfiltration, environment compromise). The paper aims to systematically evaluate how these combined vulnerabilities manifest in state-of-the-art deployed coding agents.

Method: The authors construct IssueTrojanBench, a novel benchmark containing malicious issue requests organized around four attack categories (malicious instructions embedded in issues), six delivery vectors (e.g., PDF, issue comment), and perturbation-based augmentations. They systematically test these attacks against three state-of-the-art coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex Desktop) powered by two model families (OpenAI GPT-5.3 Codex/GPT-5.4 and Anthropic Sonnet 4.6), measuring penetration rates through both agent-level and LLM-level guardrails.

Result: 66.5% of malicious issues from IssueTrojanBench successfully penetrate all guardrails. Rejection is almost entirely attributable to LLM-level defenses rather than agent frameworks. GPT models are broadly vulnerable across attack types, while Sonnet 4.6 demonstrates more selective, risk-aware blocking—particularly against high-impact actions. Current agent-level defense strategies provide limited additional protection.

Conclusion: The findings underscore an urgent need for stronger safety mechanisms at both the agent and model levels. Agent frameworks currently offer negligible incremental protection beyond the LLM itself, and the high penetration rate across deployed systems indicates that existing safeguards are insufficient for the autonomy and tool access granted to modern coding agents.

Abstract: AI coding agents powered by LLMs are increasingly integrated into real-world software development, where they generate, edit, and execute code with autonomous access to local files and tools. Coding agents inherit security risks from both the LLM backbone, where adversarial prompts, poisoned training data, and backdoor triggers can cause models to emit insecure or attacker-chosen code, and their agentic architecture, where tool-using autonomy enables induced misuse of external APIs, data exfiltration, and persistent compromise of development environments. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of malicious issue requests against state-of-the-art coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex Desktop), powered by two major model families (OpenAI GPT-5.3 Codex/GPT-5.4 and Anthropic Sonnet 4.6). Our novel benchmark IssueTrojanBench contains malicious issues that are constructed based on four novel attack categories (i.e., embedded as malicious instructions in issues), six delivery vectors (e.g., PDF, or issue comment), and further augmented by perturbations. Our results reveal critical vulnerabilities in the as-deployed modern coding agents, i.e., 66.5% of the malicious issues from IssueTrojanBench penetrate all the guardrails (agent- and LLM-level) of coding agents. Our further analysis shows that rejection is almost entirely from LLMs rather than the agent frameworks, with GPT models broadly vulnerable and Sonnet 4.6 exhibiting more selective, risk-aware blocking of high-impact actions. Our evaluation also highlights that the current agent-level defense strategy offers limited additional protection for coding agents. Our findings highlight the urgent need for stronger agent- and model-level safety mechanisms to protect AI coding agents.

</details>


### [335] [GPE: Evaluating Robust Evidence Aggregation for Fact Verification under Controllable GEO-Style Poisoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20730)
*Zhaoqi Wang,Zijian Zhang,Xiaomei Yuan,Pengtao Kou,Jiamou Liu,Zhen Li,Liehuang Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces GPE, a benchmark and evaluation framework for testing fact-verification systems under adversarial evidence conditions, where retrieved documents may be poisoned via generative engine optimization (GEO). It reveals robustness failures invisible under clean evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly rely on search tool-retrieved documents, creating an attack surface where adversaries can manipulate retrieved content via generative engine optimization (GEO). Existing fact-verification benchmarks lack controlled adversarial evidence environments, making it impossible to assess model robustness against such poisoning attacks.

Method: The authors propose GPE, comprising (1) a multi-domain fact-verification benchmark and (2) an evaluation framework that enables controlled manipulation of evidence sources and poisoning ratios. Experiments span multiple verification methods and poisoning attack types to systematically assess degradation and efficiency trade-offs.

Result: GPE exposes significant robustness degradation and efficiency trade-offs under adversarial evidence that remain hidden in clean evaluations, confirming the inadequacy of standard benchmarks for security-sensitive deployment.

Conclusion: Evaluating fact verification under adversarial evidence environments is essential; clean benchmarks alone are insufficient. GPE provides the necessary controlled setting for such robustness assessment.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly use search tools to retrieve up-to-date information, introducing a new attack surface in which retrieved documents can be manipulated. This risk is amplified by the development of generative engine optimization, which can make selected content more likely to be retrieved, cited, and adopted by models. Existing fact-verification benchmarks and evaluation frameworks do not provide the controlled evidence environments needed to assess robustness against GEO poisoning. We therefore propose GPE, which consists of a multi-domain fact-verification benchmark and an evaluation framework for controlling evidence sources and poisoning ratios. Experiments across multiple verification methods and poisoning attacks demonstrate that GPE exposes robustness degradation and efficiency trade-offs that cannot be observed through clean evaluation alone, confirming the need to evaluate fact verification under adversarial evidence environments.

</details>


### [336] [Classical Acceptance Is Not Hybrid Authentication: Measuring X.509 Verifier Semantics in Post-Quantum Migration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20800)
*Taesung Kim,Boheung Chung,Keonwoo Kim,Yousung Kang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Hybrid X.509 certificate validation is structurally broken: in separable designs, post-quantum evidence can be silently ignored, allowing classical-only validation to masquerade as a hybrid result. The authors demonstrate this across seven codebases and six certificate schemes, showing that even when post-quantum signatures verify, the binding between classical and post-quantum credentials is not enforced by default. A revocation desynchronization attack realizes this downgrade in practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid X.509 certificates aim to ease post-quantum migration by carrying both classical and post-quantum credentials. The separable design places post-quantum evidence where classical-only validators can ignore it for backward compatibility. The authors investigate whether this structural separation creates a gap wherein a verifier accepts a certificate as "hybrid-validated" while only the classical path actually determined the outcome — a silent downgrade attack that undermines the purpose of hybrid security.

Method: The authors construct a specification-derived formal verifier model and an executable, policy-parametric reference contract specifying what a verifier must recognize, verify, make outcome-bearing, and check before reporting hybrid validation. They then empirically measure validation behavior across eight path-validation stacks (seven independent codebases), nine validation modes, and six certificate schemes. They test under hybrid-required policies and lifecycle desynchronization scenarios (e.g., post-quantum credential revoked while classical remains valid).

Result: (1) Under hybrid-required policy, nearly every stack parsing a separable hybrid certificate accepts on the classical path without making the post-quantum evidence outcome-bearing. (2) One enforcing mode fractures interoperability over a signature-input encoding not yet interoperably profiled. (3) Stacks that verify post-quantum signatures still do not enforce the binding by default — the gap is structural, not due to missing primitive capability. (4) Under lifecycle desynchronization, when a bound post-quantum credential is revoked while the classical certificate stays valid, the default path still accepts because the bound credential lies outside the decision's scope. Binding success ≠ authentication success.

Conclusion: Current standards do not require that post-quantum evidence be outcome-bearing in hybrid X.509 validation. The structural gap allows silent downgrade to classical-only security, realized in practice across all major stacks. The authors contribute a diagnosis of why standards fail here and a reference contract for correct hybrid validation.

Abstract: A relying party validating a hybrid X.509 certificate --- carrying both a classical and a post-quantum credential --- must distinguish whether its accepting judgment rests on the post-quantum evidence or only on the classical path. To preserve compatibility, the separable designs place that evidence where classical path validation may ignore it. A verifier can then validate the classical path and accept while the post-quantum evidence never bears on the decision --- a valid classical result silently promoted to a hybrid conclusion it did not establish. We measure this across eight path-validation stacks (seven independent codebases), in nine validation modes, over six certificate schemes. Under a hybrid-required policy, nearly every stack parsing a separable hybrid certificate accepts on the classical path without making the post-quantum evidence outcome-bearing; one enforcing mode instead fractures interoperability over a signature-input encoding not yet interoperably profiled; and stacks that verify post-quantum signatures still do not enforce the binding by default: the gap is structural, not explained by missing primitive capability alone. Under lifecycle desynchronization the downgrade is realized: when a bound post-quantum credential is revoked while the classical certificate stays valid, the default path still accepts, because the bound credential lies outside the decision's scope. Binding success is not authentication success. We contribute a specification-derived verifier model and an executable, policy-parametric reference contract --- what a verifier must recognize, verify, make outcome-bearing, and check before reporting a validation as hybrid --- with a diagnosis of why standards do not require it.

</details>


### [337] [Which Model Is Actually Serving You? IRIS: Budgeted Black-Box Auditing of Model Substitution and Routing Dilution in LLM Gateways](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20860)
*Yuewei Zhang,Zhi-Hai Zhang,Hanzhang Qin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: IRIS is a black-box audit for commercial LLM gateways that uses only generated text (random numbers/strings) to detect model substitution (dilution) and fractional routing, attribute the actual backend, estimate the routing fraction ε, and dynamically size its own query budget — all without needing log-probabilities, token ranks, or reference samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial LLM gateways may deceptively substitute cheaper models or route only a fraction of requests to the advertised model. Existing black-box audits require privileged signals (log-probs, token ranks, reference samples), use fixed query budgets, and only return binary verdicts. A text-only audit that handles whole-stream substitution and fractional dilution with self-sizing budgets is needed.

Method: IRIS prompts endpoints to generate random numbers or strings (digit/n-gram fingerprints). A cheap pilot phase fits an exponential query-error decay curve to determine the required budget before suspect queries are issued. It performs three tasks: (1) detection — distinguishing substitution/dilution via hypothesis testing on error-rate convergence; (2) attribution — matching the fingerprint pattern to known backends; (3) ε-estimation — recovering the routing fraction using the observed error-rate asymptote. Adaptive allocation further improves query efficiency.

Result: On Qwen3 intra-family tests: 0.99 AUROC for backend verification, with attribution sharpening as queries accumulate. On OpenRouter: 0.85 mean power at 0.017 FPR for detecting ε=0.3 dilution, recovering ε within 0.04. Live cross-provider audit flags 14/15 same-model provider pairs via quantization/kernel deviations (corroborated by MET traces). Matches or beats comparable black-box auditors; adaptive allocation lifts matched-budget target-hit rate from 73% to 87%.

Conclusion: IRIS demonstrates that text-only audits can effectively and efficiently detect LLM gateway fraud, attribute backends, and estimate routing fractions with self-sizing budgets, matching or exceeding prior methods that required privileged signals.

Abstract: Commercial LLM gateways mediate access to hosted models, but the served backend may not match the advertised one: it may substitute a cheaper model on every request or route only a fraction $ε$ of requests to it. Prior black-box auditors often need a privileged signal (log-probabilities, token ranks, or reference samples) or a target-specific probe, fix the query budget in advance, and return a yes/no verdict. We present $\mathrm{IRIS}$, an audit that needs only the returned text: it asks endpoints to generate random numbers or strings, fingerprints the backend, and is the first to combine, in one text-only audit, detection of whole-stream substitution and fractional dilution, attribution of the served backend, routing-fraction ($ε$) estimation, and a query budget it sizes itself. A cheap pilot fits the exponential query-error decay and freezes that budget before any suspect query is issued. On an intra-family Qwen3 ladder $\mathrm{IRIS}$ verifies the backend at $0.99$ AUROC and sharpens attribution as queries accumulate; across a commercial OpenRouter library it catches $ε{=}0.3$ dilution on margin-qualified pairs at $0.85$ mean power ($0.017$ false-positive rate) and recovers $ε$ to within $0.04$ for enrolled diluents; and a live cross-provider audit flags $14$ of $15$ same-model provider pairs by genuine quantization and kernel deviations, corroborated on third-party MET traces. Against comparable black-box auditors, $\mathrm{IRIS}$ matches or beats detection on shared tasks, and adaptive allocation lifts the matched-budget target-hit rate from $73$% to $87$%. Further experiments cover adversarial gateways, knob identifiability, unseen diluents, and false-positive control.

</details>


### [338] [Toward cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: A security hypothesis, preliminary formal model, and proof-of-concept implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21325)
*M. Llambí-Morillas,D. Fernández-Fernández*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Presents a formal framework for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), binding agent identity, requests, context, and policy satisfaction into a single verifiable relation using zk-SNARKs, while identifying the structural separation of identity, request, and execution binding as an open problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current authentication/authorization for autonomous AI agents lacks cryptographic proof that a specific agent's request satisfies policy within a given execution context. This gap is critical as agents increasingly operate autonomously on protected resources with minimal human oversight.

Method: Formalizes CVA as a relation R_CVA binding agent principal, request, execution context, and policy satisfaction with selective confidentiality. Defines security properties (authorization soundness, principal/request/policy binding, replay resistance). Provides an executable proof-of-concept using Groth16 zk-SNARKs.

Result: Identifies the tripartite structural separation of identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem not addressed by existing agentic security frameworks. Presents a falsifiable research agenda for resolution.

Conclusion: Cryptographically verifiable agent authorization is feasible and necessary. The key open challenge lies in structurally decoupling and recomposing identity, request, and execution binding — a gap unaddressed by current frameworks — requiring further formal and empirical work.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority, but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This paper hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted $R_{CVA}$, that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems (a distinction {not explicitly addressed by} current agentic security frameworks) and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.

</details>


### [339] [Themis Consensus Extension v1: MEV Mitigation by Randomized Delayed Execution and Intent-Hiding Transactions in Application-Specific Blockchains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21406)
*Shoeb Siddiqui,Mateusz Nowakowski,Stanislav Vozarik,Gleb Urvanov,Peter Kris*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper analyzes Themis, a consensus extension separating MEV into reordering-based (VER) and denial-based (VED) extraction. VER uses multi-producer sequential commitment and deterministic shuffling; VED uses layered encryption with delayed decryption. Under specific adversary assumptions, it limits post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent, though it explicitly disclaims fairness, full censorship resistance, and builder-executor collusion resistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MEV arises when privileged consensus participants manipulate transaction ordering, insertion, or exclusion for profit. Themis aims to mitigate unilateral ordering control and information leakage without requiring a trusted third party, by architecturally separating the problems of value extraction by reordering (VER) and value extraction by denial (VED).

Method: The protocol splits VER across two consecutive block producers: the first commits a transaction set, and the second derives a publicly verifiable, deterministic, unpredictable seed to generate a dependency-preserving permutation (using Fisher-Yates shuffling with Xoshiro256++). For VED, users submit layered-encrypted transactions: a builder strips the outer layer and commits the opaque inner ciphertext, and a designated executor later reveals and executes the plaintext. The analysis assumes selfish but non-colluding validators, an adversary below the consensus fault threshold, secure cryptography, and accountable role performance. It also covers probabilistic extraction, spam, dependent transactions, decryption liveness, session boundaries, total denial, and threshold coalitions. An Aura-based Substrate implementation was later migrated to BABE with sr25519/VRF seed paths.

Result: Under the stated assumptions, the construction limits unilateral post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent from relays and the builder. However, it does not guarantee send-order or receive-order fairness, complete censorship resistance, resistance to builder-executor collusion, or per-transaction price guarantees. The analysis formally bounds probabilistic extraction and characterizes vulnerabilities under threshold coalitions and denial scenarios.

Conclusion: Themis provides a principled separation of VER and VED with bounded guarantees under explicit assumptions. The work narrows the original 2021 Mangata proposal's claims, grounding them in rigorous analysis, and documents the evolution from an Aura-based to a BABE-based implementation. Its main limitations — no fairness, no full censorship resistance, and collusion vulnerability — define its applicable deployment contexts.

Abstract: Maximal extractable value (MEV) arises when privileged participants select, exclude, insert, or reorder pending transactions for private gain. We specify and analyze the Themis Consensus Extension v1, first published by Mangata in 2021. The design separates value extraction by reordering (VER) from value extraction by denial (VED). For VER, block construction and execution occur across consecutive producers: one producer commits a transaction set, and the next derives a publicly verifiable, deterministic, previously un- predictable seed and executes a seed-determined, dependency-preserving permutation. For selective VED, a user may encrypt a transaction for a designated builder and executor. The builder removes an outer layer and commits the opaque inner ciphertext; the executor reveals and executes the plaintext only after commitment. Under selfish but non-colluding validators, an adversary below the underlying consensus fault threshold, secure cryptography, and accountable role performance, the construction limits unilateral post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent from relays and the builder. It does not provide send-order or receive-order fairness, complete censorship resistance, resistance to builder-executor collusion, or per-transaction price guarantees. We analyze probabilistic extraction, spam, dependent transactions, decryption liveness, session boundaries, total denial, and threshold coalitions. We also document the initial Aura-based Substrate implementation and its subsequent transition to a BABE-based sr25519/VRF seed path, together with delayed execution, Fisher-Yates shuffling, and Xoshiro256++. The result preserves the original proposal while narrowing its claims to explicit assumptions.

</details>


### [340] [Where You Tap Matters: A Probe-and-Model Benchmark for Open-Set RF Fingerprinting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21564)
*Gabriele Oligeri,Savio Sciancalepore,Ingrid Huso,Fatima Al-Mousawi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates how the probe point in the receiver chain affects Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification (RFFI) performance. Across five probe points in a BPSK receiver, the authors show that timing recovery and carrier recovery stages are critical for effective open-set RFFI, while other stages degrade performance. LLM-designed autoencoders confirm probe-dependence and do not outperform a simple baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature on RFFI is inconsistent about where in the receiver chain signal samples should be collected for fingerprinting. Different receiver operations (carrier recovery, gain normalization, pulse shaping, timing recovery) apply distinct transformations that may either tighten within-transmitter variability or suppress discriminative features. No prior work has systematically quantified how probe-point selection impacts open-set RFFI performance.

Method: The authors collect real-world BPSK signals at five distinct probe points along a standard receiver chain. They evaluate open-set, reconstruction-error-based RFFI using a controlled pipeline with fixed preprocessing and MSE scoring. Additionally, they benchmark several autoencoder architectures designed by LLMs to test whether probe-point dependence persists across model selection and whether more complex architectures can compensate for suboptimal probe points.

Result: RFFI performance is strongly probe-dependent. Timing recovery and carrier recovery stages enable low false-acceptance operation with limited in-distribution/out-of-distribution overlap. Other stages require a false-acceptance ratio above 0.1 to achieve a true-acceptance ratio of 0.9. LLM-designed autoencoders confirm probe-dependence and fail to outperform the baseline autoencoder, while typically increasing training time. Probe selection dominates performance more than autoencoder complexity.

Conclusion: Probe-point selection is the dominant factor in reconstruction-based open-set RFFI, outweighing model complexity. Researchers and practitioners should prioritize careful receiver-chain probe placement — specifically at or after timing/carrier recovery — rather than pursuing increasingly complex neural architectures for RFFI.

Abstract: Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification (RFFI) enables transmitter identification at the physical layer by learning device-specific impairments from received signals, yet the literature is inconsistent about where in the receiver chain those samples should be collected. Since distinct transformations are applied to the signal by the different receiver operations, i.e., carrier recovery, gain normalization, pulse shaping, and timing recovery, they can either tighten within-transmitter variability or suppress the features RFFI requires for classification. We present a systematic real-world evaluation of open-set, reconstruction-error RFFI using data collected at five probe points along a standard BPSK receiver chain. Our results show that RFFI is strongly probe-dependent: timing recovery and, to a lesser extent, carrier recovery enable low false-acceptance operation with limited in-distribution-out-of-distribution overlap, whereas other stages often require a false-acceptance ratio above 0.1 to achieve a true-acceptance ratio of 0.9. To test the validity of our findings across model selection, we benchmark several LLM-designed autoencoders using a controlled pipeline that holds preprocessing and MSE scoring fixed. These architectures confirm that RFFI is probe-dependent. Moreover, they do not outperform the baseline at the chosen operating point and typically increase training time. Overall, probe selection dominates reconstruction-based open-set RFFI performance, more than the autoencoder complexity.

</details>
