### [341] [Verifier-First Evaluation of Agentic LLMs for Infrastructure-as-Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20478)
*Mohamed Jouini*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Comprehensive empirical study comparing seven agentic strategies for generating Terraform IaC from natural language, using a modernized benchmark (IaC-Eval v2). Key findings show verifier-guided iterative refinement achieves 84.4% pass@1 with GPT-4o, active retrieval significantly boosts small models, and 79% of policy failures stem from information gaps resolvable by exposing policy text.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IaC generation from natural language is not just a syntax problem — it must satisfy provider schemas, plan dependencies, and organizational policy constraints. Existing work lacks rigorous, verifier-first empirical comparison of agentic strategies under these multi-stage correctness criteria.

Method: Evaluated seven agentic strategies on IaC-Eval v2 (186 AWS/Terraform tasks with Rego v1 intent policies). Strategies include: Active RAG (ReAct agents with MCP/ChromaDB), iterative refinement with verifier feedback, GEPA reflective instruction optimization, and SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection. All pairwise comparisons used McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals (n=186, α=0.05). Failures categorized across three verifier stages: terraform validate, terraform plan, and opa eval.

Result: (1) Active RAG raised Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001). (2) Iterative refinement achieved 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o), with binary convergence. (3) GEPA instruction optimization added +7.5 pp over Active RAG (p=0.026). (4) SIMBA matched Active RAG (p=1.0) without retrieval but missed SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY errors. (5) 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are resolvable when policy text is visible (p=0.016).

Conclusion: Verifier-first evaluation reveals that the dominant remaining bottleneck in agentic IaC generation is policy-awareness information gaps, not syntax or planning failures. Future work should focus on policy-grounded generation rather than retrieval or refinement alone.

Abstract: Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) generation from natural language requires satisfying provider schemas, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints, not merely producing syntactically plausible configurations. We present a verifier-first empirical study of seven agentic strategies for Terraform generation evaluated on IaC-Eval v2, a modernized 186-task AWS/Terraform benchmark with Rego v1 intent policies. Our evaluation separates failures into three verifier stages (terraform validate, terraform plan, opa eval) and applies McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals on all pairwise comparisons (n=186, alpha=0.05).
  We report five principal findings. (1) Active retrieval via ReAct agents with MCP or ChromaDB-backed RAG raises Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001), primarily by reducing VALIDATE_FAIL from 144 to 66 tasks. (2) Iterative refinement with verifier feedback achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1, exhibiting binary convergence -- tasks either resolve in one retry or exhaust the budget. (3) GEPA reflective instruction optimization raises the Active RAG baseline by +7.5 pp (p=0.026) using only 80 verifier-guided rollouts, providing evidence that prompt optimizers can improve verifiable IaC generation without weight updates. (4) SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection achieves performance equivalent to Active RAG (p=1.0) without retrieval infrastructure, but fails to address the dominant SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY error class (50% of failures). (5) A diagnostic Rego-injection experiment shows that 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap failures resolvable when policy text is visible (p=0.016), motivating policy

</details>


### [342] [Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation: to Enable More Secure Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20933)
*Jesse Phillips,Tracy Hall,Paul Rayson,Mo El-Haj*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes combining task-specific Transformer models with LLMs via prompt engineering for source code summarization, achieving 7.8% improvement in BLEU-4 and 5% in other NLG metrics over LLM-only approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Source code summaries are critical for software maintenance in the SSDLC but are often missing, incomplete, or outdated. Task-specific Transformers score well on NLG metrics but prioritize lexical overlap over quality, while LLMs produce semantically rich summaries that diverge lexically from human-written ones, yielding low metric scores. The gap between semantic quality and metric performance motivates a hybrid approach.

Method: The authors propose "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation," which uses a task-specific Transformer model's output as part of prompt engineering to guide LLMs. Four LLMs are prompted with four different prompt designs, each incorporating Transformer-generated summaries to assist the LLM in producing higher-quality summaries.

Result: The proposed method yields a 7.8% improvement in BLEU-4 and a 5% improvement across other NLG metrics compared to using LLMs alone.

Conclusion: Combining task-specific Transformer outputs with LLMs through prompt engineering effectively bridges the gap between lexical alignment (metric scores) and semantic quality, enabling better source code summaries that support secure software maintenance.

Abstract: Neural Source Code Summarisation (NSCS) aims to generate natural language summaries of source code to improve developers' and maintainers' understanding of code. Source code summaries are vital during the maintenance phase of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC), as they improve maintainers' understanding of code and help reduce the number of bugs and vulnerabilities in a software system. However, summaries are often missing, incomplete, or outdated in many software systems. Solutions to this problem use small, task-specific Transformer models or code-aware Large Language Models (LLMs). Task-specific Transformer-generated summaries often score well across many natural language generation (NLG) metrics, but these metrics reward lexical overlap rather than summary quality. Conversely, the ability of LLMs to capture semantics and produce high-quality summaries presents an exciting solution to this problem. This is especially relevant given the increased availability of LLMs and improvements in workstation hardware in recent years, which mean that some LLMs can now be run on developers' workstations. However, because of their abstractive nature, LLM-generated code summaries often differ greatly from developer-written summaries in the words and phrases they use, resulting in low scores across NLG metrics. We show how combining these two methods, by using Transformer-generated summaries in prompt engineering, may enable LLMs to create better source code summaries and help software practitioners maintain secure systems. We prompt four LLMs using four different prompts, with a task-specific Transformer used to assist the LLMs within the prompts. We present "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation", a method through which we observe an improvement of 7.8% in BLEU-4 and 5%.

</details>


### [343] [Maintenance Signals in AI-Assisted GitHub Repositories: Evidence from GenAI Adopters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21079)
*Rikuto Tsuchida,Youmei Fan,Kazumasa Shimari,Raula Gaikovina Kula,Gema Rodríguez-Pérez,Kenichi Matsumoto*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Analysis of 622 GitHub users and 179 AI-assisted repositories reveals that while GenAI reduces code generation effort, it shifts maintenance burden toward documentation (longer READMEs with more headers/code blocks), managing external AI dependencies (API rate limits, provider APIs), and validating AI-generated content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically investigate whether and how the adoption of generative AI in software development shifts maintenance costs—specifically toward documentation, validation, debugging, and dependency management—rather than simply reducing overall effort.

Method: The authors conducted a comparative empirical study on GitHub, analyzing: (1) 622 users who publicly signal GenAI adoption, (2) 179 repositories containing visible AI-assistance configuration files, (3) 179 matched traditional (non-AI) repositories as a control group, and (4) 248 issues created within AI-assisted repositories. Metrics include README structure (headers, code blocks, external URLs), issue categories, and dependency patterns.

Result: AI-assisted repositories span diverse project types and feature longer README files with significantly more headers and code blocks compared to traditional repositories. Conversely, traditional repositories contain more external URLs. Issues in AI-assisted repos frequently involve external GenAI dependencies, such as API rate limits and reliance on provider APIs, indicating novel maintenance friction points.

Conclusion: GenAI adoption demonstrably shifts maintenance costs toward content verification, external AI dependency management, and AI-specific behavioral validation. These represent emergent categories of technical debt that organizations and tooling should anticipate when integrating GenAI into development workflows.

Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce code-generation effort, but it may shift work to documentation, validation, debugging, and maintenance. We study observable maintenance-cost signals among GenAI adopters on GitHub by analyzing 622 users who publicly signal adoption, 179 repositories with visible AI-assistance configuration files, 179 matched traditional repositories, and 248 issues created in AI-assisted repositories. AI-assisted repositories span diverse project types and contain longer README files with more headers and code blocks, while traditional repositories contain more external URLs. Issues concerning GenAI technology often involve external dependencies, such as API rate limits and reliance on GenAI provider APIs. These findings suggest that AI assistance shifts maintenance costs toward verifying generated content, managing external AI dependencies, and validating AI-specific behavior.

</details>


### [344] [Improving Communication of Changes in Model-Based Engineering with Model-Independent Change Descriptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21084)
*Philip Ochs,Lars Gesmann,Tobias Pett,Ina Schaefer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a method to automatically translate formally specified model changes (delta modelling) into human-readable, model-independent natural language descriptions, bridging the gap between formal rigour and inter-disciplinary communication in model-based engineering. A mixed-methods evaluation combining quantitative (implementation, case study) and qualitative (user study) assessments demonstrates feasibility and practical potential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In model-based engineering, changes made by one discipline are hard for other disciplines to understand. Formal change descriptions are precise but lack human interpretability; informal descriptions are readable but lack objectivity and standardisation. Neither supports effective inter-disciplinary communication, creating a need for an automated approach that combines the semantic precision of formal methods with the accessibility of natural language.

Method: The authors define mapping functions that transform formally specified changes — represented using delta modelling — into model-independent natural language change descriptions. The approach is evaluated through a mixed-methods design: (1) quantitative assessment of technical feasibility via an implementation framework and technical applicability via a case study, and (2) qualitative assessment of plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility via a user study.

Result: The implementation framework confirms technical feasibility, the case study demonstrates technical applicability on a realistic scenario, and the user study provides positive qualitative evidence for plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility of the approach.

Conclusion: The work establishes a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects, effectively bridging formal change specification and human-interpretable communication across disciplines.

Abstract: In model-based engineering, inter-disciplinary teams collaborate through models, which change over time for purposes of system development, what makes the proper description of such changes crucial for engineers. However, any change made by the engineer of one discipline will be difficult to understand by the engineers of other disciplines. To overcome this limitation, model-independent change descriptions can be derived instead, which preserve semantics of the changes and do not require model-specific knowledge. The two opposing approaches here are to describe changes using either informal language or formal notions of change. While informal language lacks objectivity and standardisation, formal notions of change lack human interpretability, and thus offering no support for inter-disciplinary communication. In this paper, we propose functions to map formally specified changes, represented in the approach of delta modelling, to change descriptions in model-independent language. In an exhaustive mixed-methods evaluation, we bridge the gap between the theoretical and the practical representation of changes. We quantitatively assess technical feasibility, with an implementation framework, and technical applicability, along a case study; and we qualitatively assess plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility, in a user study. Our work shows a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects.

</details>


### [345] [Information is all you need: Requirements Engineering Quality Reframed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21319)
*Henning Femmer,Julian Frattini*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Proposes a holistic theory of RE quality based on information particles transferring between roles and artifacts, modeling RE as information flow to unify artifact- and process-based quality perspectives. A simulation demonstrates actionable insights, e.g., why high-quality specs get bypassed in agile contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing appeals to "context" in RE quality are too vague. There is a need for a coherent, unified theoretical framework that bridges artifact-based and process-based views of RE quality to explain why RE processes and artifacts succeed or fail.

Method: Develops a holistic theory modeling RE as information transfer, where discrete "information particles" of domain knowledge flow between roles (stakeholders, developers, testers) and artifacts. An exemplary simulation is used to illustrate and validate the theory's explanatory power.

Result: The simulation demonstrates that even a high-quality specification can get bypassed in an agile context due to properties of information flow, providing actionable insights for calibrating RE processes to optimize information transfer.

Conclusion: The proposed theory offers both organizational utility—enabling calibration of RE processes—and a coherent theoretical framework for systematically understanding success and failure in RE processes and artifacts.

Abstract: To move beyond this vague appeal to context, this vision proposes a novel holistic theory of requirements engineering (RE) quality. This theory models how information particles, i.e., discrete pieces of domain knowledge, are transferred between roles and artifacts. Since the RE process is ultimately an information transfer, holistic RE quality depends on the properties of information flow, i.e., how effectively and efficiently information is transferred from sources (like stakeholders) to targets (like developers and testers), uniting both artifact- and process-based perspectives on RE quality. In an exemplary simulation of the theory we illustrate why a high-quality specification gets bypassed in an agile context, thereby demonstrating that a simulation can provide actionable insights into calibrating the RE process to optimize the information flow. Beyond organizational applications, we envision that the theory can serve as a coherent theoretical framework for understanding the success or failure of RE processes and artifacts.

</details>


### [346] [Teaching Business Process Modeling to Leverage Soft Skills of Computing Students](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21344)
*Maria Istela Cagnin,Rick Kazman,Elisa Yumi Nakagawa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Teaching business process modeling to computing students through industry-driven, project-based learning effectively develops soft skills—professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork—that are critical for future professionals in an AI-augmented software development landscape.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations rely on software to achieve business goals, yet computing professionals often lack understanding of business processes. Simultaneously, AI is reshaping productivity in software development, intensifying job market competition. Soft skills are therefore essential for career resilience, but evidence on how to systematically develop them in computing education is lacking.

Method: An industry-driven, project-based pedagogical intervention was conducted with 53 computing students. Students directly interacted with organizational stakeholders to model real-world business processes. Feedback was systematically collected to assess which soft skills were practiced and developed during the experience.

Result: The study demonstrated that teaching business process modeling can leverage key soft skills, specifically: professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork. Student feedback confirmed these skills were actively practiced and strengthened through the intervention.

Conclusion: Teaching business process modeling provides dual benefits: domain-relevant technical knowledge and soft skill development. For the Computer Science Education community, this offers evidence-based support for integrating such subjects into curricula to better prepare students for the era of AI-assisted software development.

Abstract: Background and Context: Organizations have highly depended on software systems to realize their business processes and achieve strategic business goals and competitive advantage; hence, computing professionals who can understand these processes could more effectively build such systems. At the same time, while Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increased the productivity in developing these and other systems, professionals should be better prepared due to the competitiveness of the job market; thus, soft skills could be an important factor to ensure their position in this market. Objective: This paper aims to analyze and present the impact of teaching business process modeling to leverage key soft skills of future computing professionals. Method and Findings: Our method involved an industry-driven, project-based approach with 53 computing students who actively interacted with stakeholders and modeled the organization's business process. We systematically collected the students' feedback, including the soft skills practiced and demonstrating that professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork can be leveraged. Implications: The main implication of this work for the Computer Science Education research community is to provide evidence that teaching business process modeling subjects is particularly beneficial for future professionals, as it could contribute to preparing them regarding their soft skills for the era of AI-assisted software development.

</details>


### [347] [Toward Federated Cognitive Digital Twins over the Edge-to-Cloud Continuum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21357)
*Alessandra Somma,Alessio Bucaioni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that merges federation and cognition, distributing intelligence across edge-to-cloud via local twins (real-time monitoring, lightweight cognition) and global twins (system-level reasoning, coordination) to improve scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in distributed CPSs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Digital Twin architectures suffer from two main limitations: (1) centralized/monolithic designs cause scalability, latency, and resilience problems in distributed environments like smart cities; and (2) insufficient semantic integration and high-level reasoning capabilities weaken DT-based decision-making. While Federated Digital Twins address scalability through decomposition and Cognitive Digital Twins add semantic reasoning and explainability, neither approach alone successfully combines distributed intelligence with cognitive capabilities in a unified architecture.

Method: The authors propose a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that spans the edge-to-cloud continuum. It employs two tiers of twins: local twins deployed at the edge for real-time monitoring and lightweight cognitive processing, and global twins operating at higher layers (cloud) for system-level reasoning, simulation, and cross-twin coordination. This design unifies federation (distributed autonomy) with cognition (semantic reasoning, explainability, AI-driven decision support) within a single architectural framework.

Result: The abstract does not report empirical results or quantitative evaluations; it focuses on presenting the architectural proposal and its claimed benefits — improved scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed CPSs.

Conclusion: The FCDT architecture, by distributing intelligence across edge and cloud while embedding cognitive capabilities, overcomes the individual limitations of Federated DTs and Cognitive DTs, offering a more scalable, responsive, and intelligent solution for complex distributed Cyber-Physical Systems.

Abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly adopted to monitor, analyze, and optimize Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) through continuous interaction between physical assets and their digital counterparts. However, current DT architectures often rely on centralized and monolithic designs, leading to scalability, latency, and resilience issues in distributed environment such as smart cities. Moreover, they provide limited support for semantic integration and high-level reasoning, reducing the effectiveness of DT-based decision-making. Recent studies on Federated Digital Twins (FDTs) have addressed scalability by decomposing complex systems into interacting twins, but they still largely centralize intelligence in cloud components. In parallel, Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) enhance DTs with semantic reasoning, explainability, and AI-driven decision support, yet they are typically difficult to integrate into distributed architectures. This paper proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that combines federation and cognition within a unified approach. The architecture distributes intelligence across the edge-to-cloud continuum through local twins, which provide real-time monitoring and lightweight cognitive capabilities, and global twins, which perform system-level reasoning, simulation, and coordination. By integrating distributed autonomy with cognitive reasoning, the proposed approach improves scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed CPSs

</details>


### [348] [From Resource Flow to Executable Tests: Petri-Net-Guided LLM Test Generation for Concurrent Stateful Rust APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21530)
*Kaiwen Zhang,Guanjun Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A Petri-net-guided methodology generates concurrent stateful Rust API tests by bridging formal scenario design with LLM-based code synthesis. Colored Petri nets model resources, lifecycles, and causal dependencies; derived scenarios (legal, near-legal, partial-order) serve as constrained intermediate representations. A local-faithfulness contract with structural repair preserves intent during concretization, while Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons and a layered semantic oracle distinguishes synthesis failures from true API violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated concurrent tests for stateful Rust APIs often violate preconditions, lack depth, or accidentally sequentialize. Model-based and systematic testing offer semantic rigor but demand substantial manual code to concretize abstract scenarios. The gap between formal scenario design and low-cost test concretization remains unaddressed.

Method: A Petri-net-based approach where API resources, lifecycle conditions, and causal dependencies are modeled as colored tokens and transitions. Three scenario classes are derived: legal deep-state, near-legal, and partial-order concurrent scenarios. These scenarios serve as a constrained intermediate representation for LLM-based code synthesis. A local-faithfulness contract and structural repair loop preserve modeled intent during concretization. Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons, and a layered semantic oracle separates synthesis failures from API behavioral violations.

Result: The paper presents the methodology and its components (Petri-net modeling, scenario derivation, LLM-based concretization with repair, schedule shaping, layered oracle) as a coherent framework. Quantitative evaluation metrics are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: The proposed Petri-net-guided methodology effectively bridges formal scenario design and low-cost LLM-based test concretization for concurrent stateful Rust APIs, addressing the key limitations of both purely LLM-driven and purely model-based approaches.

Abstract: Concurrent stateful library APIs expose behavior through evolving resource ownership, lifecycle states, and competing interleavings. Large language models can synthesize executable Rust tests, but their outputs often violate API preconditions, remain shallow, or reduce concurrency to accidental sequential traces. Conversely, model-based and systematic testing techniques provide semantic control but commonly require substantial handwritten code to turn abstract scenarios into executable tests. This paper addresses the gap between formal scenario design and low-cost test concretization. We present a Petri-net-guided methodology for test generation over concurrent stateful Rust APIs. The method represents API resources, lifecycle conditions, and causal dependencies as colored tokens and transitions; derives legal deep-state, near-legal, and partial-order concurrent scenarios; and uses these scenarios as a constrained intermediate representation for LLM-based code synthesis. A local-faithfulness contract and structural repair loop preserve the modeled intent during concretization, while Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons for systematic exploration. A layered semantic oracle then distinguishes synthesis failures from violations of the target API's expected behavior.

</details>


<div id='cs.IR'></div>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [349] [Probabilistic Residual Learning for Online Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20863)
*Wenyuan Wang,Yusong Zhao,Zihao Xu,Hengyi Wang,Qi Xu,Zhigang Hua,Yan Xie,Yi Wang,Zihao Zhao,Bo Long,Chengzhi Mao,Shuang Yang,Hengguan Huang,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: PRL is a plug-and-play causal Bayesian framework that improves existing DL recommender systems by learning residuals between ground-truth and base predictions, using probabilistic user clustering and do-calculus to control for domain-level confounders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern DL-based recommender systems suffer from black-box opacity and high computational complexity, which hinders systematic performance improvement. Existing enhancement methods lack principled ways to identify and correct specific sources of prediction error.

Method: PRL employs three key mechanisms: (1) probabilistic clustering of users into groups for localized residual modeling; (2) modeling domain-level confounders that affect both user and item representations; and (3) aggregating cluster-specific residual predictions over confounders via do-calculus for causal intervention. The approach is model-agnostic and operates as a plug-and-play module on top of any base DL recommender.

Result: Experiments show that PRL is compatible with various base DL recommender systems and consistently improves their recommendation performance. Additionally, PRL automatically discovers meaningful user clusters as a byproduct.

Conclusion: PRL offers an effective, causally grounded, and interpretable method for refining black-box recommender systems, combining probabilistic user segmentation with causal adjustment to deliver targeted performance gains without modifying the underlying base model.

Abstract: Modern recommender systems are typically based on deep learning (DL) models, where a dense encoder learns representations of users and items. As a result, these systems often suffer from the black-box nature and computational complexity of the underlying models, making it difficult to systematically enhance their recommendation capabilities. To address this problem, we propose Probabilistic Residual Learning (PRL), a causal Bayesian recommendation model that models the residual between ground-truth and base predictions, enabling targeted refinement of existing systems. Specifically, PRL (1) probabilistically groups users for localized residual modeling, (2) models domain-level confounders that influence user and item representations, and (3) aggregates cluster-specific residual predictions over the confounders using do-calculus. Experiments demonstrate that our plug-and-play PRL is compatible with various base deep learning recommender systems, improving their performance while automatically discovering meaningful user clusters.

</details>


### [350] [LO-FAR: A Cost-Aware Local Filter for Sparse Feature Ranking in Industrial Ad Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20873)
*Egemen Erbayat,Luis Duque,Sohini Roychowdhury,Mohammad Amin,Srihari Reddy*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LO-FAR is a lightweight, CPU-only sparse feature ranking method for industrial recommendation models. It ranks features using standalone held-out predictive signals from local estimators, avoiding GPU-intensive retraining. On a production dataset with 475 sparse ID features and 1M+ interactions, it completes ranking in ~2 CPU-hours while matching the downstream CTR/CVR performance of heavier alternatives like shuffle-based importance and Binary Stochastic Neurons across retention budgets of 100–400 features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial ad recommendation models depend on high-cardinality sparse ID features (user histories, contextual IDs), each requiring dedicated embedding tables that dominate storage, training, and serving costs. As traffic and models evolve, these features must be repeatedly re-evaluated. Existing ranking methods (permutation importance, stochastic gates) require GPU-bound retraining loops, making them too slow and expensive under tight compute budgets and iteration cadences. A practical, cost-effective feature ranking workflow is needed.

Method: LO-FAR (Localized Feature Ranking) is a model-agnostic, CPU-only workflow. Each candidate sparse feature is evaluated using a lightweight local estimator that measures its stand-alone held-out predictive signal — no full model retraining or GPU is required. Features are ranked purely by this local predictive quality, enabling rapid iteration under compute constraints.

Result: On a production dataset with over 1 million logged interactions and 475 sparse ID-list features, LO-FAR completes full ranking in approximately 2 CPU-hours. Across retention budgets of 100–400 features, LO-FAR preserves downstream Normalized Entropy gains on both CTR and CVR tasks that are competitive with shuffle-based importance, Binary Stochastic Neurons, and a coverage-based heuristic.

Conclusion: When cost and turnaround constraints are binding, a simple local filter like LO-FAR is a practical, deployable alternative to heavier interaction-aware feature ranking methods, delivering comparable downstream model quality at a fraction of the computational cost.

Abstract: Industrial ad recommendation models rely heavily on sparse, high-cardinality ID-list features that encode user histories and contextual identifiers. Each is backed by a dedicated embedding table, so these features dominate storage, training, and serving cost and must be revisited as traffic and downstream models evolve. Therefore, sparse feature ranking is not just an offline modeling problem but also a recurrent systems decision limited by compute budgets and iteration cadence. We present Localized Feature Ranking (LO-FAR), a CPU-only, model-agnostic workflow that ranks each candidate feature from its stand-alone held-out predictive signal using lightweight local estimators rather than the GPU-bound retraining loops of permutation- and stochastic-gate-based methods. On a production dataset of more than one million logged interactions and 475 sparse ID-list features, LO-FAR completes ranking in approximately two CPU-hours and preserves downstream Normalized Entropy gains on CTR and CVR tasks that are competitive with shuffle-based importance, Binary Stochastic Neurons, and a coverage-based heuristic across budgets of 100--400 retained features. The contribution is a deployable workflow showing that, when cost and turnaround constraints are binding, a simple local filter can be a practical production choice over heavier interaction-aware alternatives.

</details>


### [351] [Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20938)
*Fırat Öncel,Jihoon Jeong,Emiliano Penaloza,Mirco Ravanelli,Laurent Charlin,Cem Subakan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: CCBR is a controllable recommendation framework that uses textual user profiles derived from item content (images, audio, video) as bottlenecks, enabling interpretable, user-steerable recommendations while maintaining competitive performance with latent-representation models and outperforming the TEARS baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional recommendation systems use latent (dense) representations that are black-box and difficult to interpret or control. Users have no mechanism to steer recommendations toward their preferences. The authors aim to bridge this gap by introducing controllability and interpretability through explicit textual representations inferred directly from multimodal item content.

Method: The CCBR framework plugs into collaborative filtering models and introduces a text bottleneck: user profiles are represented as textual summaries inferred directly from item contents (images, audio, video) rather than from user-provided text. This enables text-based and multimodal interventions, allowing users to steer recommendations by manipulating the textual profile.

Result: CCBR achieves competitive performance with standard latent-representation models across image-, audio-, and video-based datasets. It outperforms TEARS, a recent controllable recommendation baseline. Systematic intervention experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the user steering mechanism.

Conclusion: CCBR successfully combines competitive recommendation performance with interpretability and user controllability via content-derived textual bottlenecks, offering a practical and transparent alternative to traditional latent-representation recommender systems across multiple modalities.

Abstract: Traditional recommendation systems rely on latent (dense) representations, making them difficult to interpret and control. We propose the Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations (CCBR) framework, which builds its recommendations from textual user profile representations. CCBR plugs into collaborative filtering models and introduces controllability via text bottlenecks. We show that CCBR enables text-based and multimodal interventions, allowing users to steer the model towards the directions they prefer. Different from existing controllable recommendation systems, CCBR infers the text summaries directly from item contents (images, audio or video). Across image-, audio-, and video-based datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed framework obtains competitive model performance with standard (latent-representation) models while providing controllable model summaries via text. The model also outperforms TEARS, a recent baseline for controllable recommendation systems. Through systematic interventions, we demonstrate the efficacy of the user steering mechanism.

</details>


### [352] [Fast and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for High-Dimensional LLM Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20957)
*Nico Hezel,Kai Uwe Barthel,Bruno Schilling,Konstantin Schall,Andre Moelle,Klaus Jung*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper describes two submissions to the SISAP 2026 Indexing Challenge: (1) fast kNNG construction on 1024-dim BGE-M3 embeddings using Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) quantization with reranking, and (2) MIPS on Llama-3.2-8B features via dimensionality augmentation and a novel 1D presorting method (FLAS) to improve cache efficiency during graph traversal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The SISAP Indexing Challenge imposes strict constraints on ANNS algorithm performance. The authors aim to optimize two distinct tasks: accelerating k-Nearest Neighbor Graph construction speed without sacrificing recall, and reducing query latency in Maximum Inner Product Search through better memory access patterns and spatial locality.

Method: For Task 1 (kNNG construction), the authors employ Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) for efficient vector quantization, combined with targeted reranking strategies to preserve recall. For Task 2 (MIPS), they transform the asymmetric inner product problem into a Euclidean search space using dimensionality augmentation. A key innovation is Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS), a 1D presorting mechanism applied before graph construction that reorders data points to improve spatial locality and cache hit rates during graph traversal.

Result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results (e.g., recall@k, QPS, or construction time). It states the methods were submitted to the 2026 SISAP challenge and notes the source code is publicly available, implying competitive performance under challenge constraints.

Conclusion: EVP-based quantization with reranking enables fast, high-recall kNNG construction, while dimensionality augmentation plus FLAS-based 1D presorting effectively addresses the MIPS problem with improved cache efficiency. Both techniques are practical for large-scale ANNS under strict resource constraints.

Abstract: The annual SISAP Indexing Challenge benchmarks Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) algorithms under rigorous constraints. This paper presents our submissions for the 2026 edition, addressing both $k$-Nearest Neighbor Graph (kNNG) construction on 1024-dimensional BGE-M3 embeddings (Task 1) and Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) on unnormalized Llama-3.2-8B features (Task 2). To optimize construction speed, we utilize Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) for efficient quantization, supplemented by targeted reranking strategies to maintain high recall. For MIPS, we transform the asymmetric inner product problem into a Euclidean search space via dimensionality augmentation. To reduce query latency and optimize memory access, we introduce a 1D presorting mechanism via Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) prior to graph construction. This significantly improves spatial locality and cache hit rates during subsequent graph traversal.
  Source Code: https://github.com/Visual-Computing/sisap26-deglib

</details>


### [353] [Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21028)
*Junchao Zeng,Junzhang Zhu,Junyang Chen,Yudong Li,Wei Liu,Chengxiang Zhuo,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: BARGE addresses structural gaps in Generative Recommendation by introducing Item Context-Aware Attention to preserve item-level structure and Hierarchical Path Reranking with Dual-Path Decoding to mitigate semantic drift, achieving significant gains in both offline benchmarks and online A/B tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Generative Recommendation methods encode items as hierarchical semantic IDs via residual quantization and generate them token-by-token. This approach suffers from two structural gaps: (1) flattening multi-token IDs destroys item-level structure, and (2) inconsistency between training and inference over hierarchical codebooks causes semantic drift, degrading recommendation quality.

Method: BARGE introduces three components: (1) Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA), which restores item-level structure during encoding by attending to context within each item's token group; (2) Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR), which reranks candidate paths across codebook levels to correct semantic drift during decoding; and (3) Dual-Path Decoding (DPD), a complementary decoding strategy that further suppresses drift from an alternative angle.

Result: Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and large-scale offline tests show BARGE achieves superior recommendation performance. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform demonstrates practical impact: +0.60% CTR, +1.34% click unique visitors, and +1.70% total reading time.

Conclusion: BARGE effectively bridges the item-level structure and semantic drift gaps in generative sequential recommendation, delivering both academic and industrial-scale improvements validated through offline benchmarks and real-world online deployment.

Abstract: Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a new paradigm for sequential recommendation, in which a representative line of work encodes items into hierarchical semantic IDs via residual quantization and predicts the IDs token by token. However, this generative formulation still exhibits structural gaps with respect to the recommendation task: flattening multi-token IDs into a single sequence destroys item-level structure, and the inconsistency between training and inference over a hierarchical codebook gives rise to semantic drift. To bridge these two gaps, we propose BARGE, which employs Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) to restore item-level structure during encoding, and Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) together with Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) to suppress semantic drift from two complementary angles during decoding. Extensive experiments and analytical studies on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test demonstrate that BARGE achieves superior recommendation performance. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform yields improvements of 0.60% in click-through rate, 1.34% in click unique visitors, and 1.70% in total reading time, confirming the practical value of BARGE in industrial-scale recommendation.

</details>


### [354] [SHIFT: Self-reconstruction Harnesses Implicit Fine-grained Thinking for Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21333)
*Yuxiao Luo,Da Li,Mingjie Zhang,Zhentao He,Shikun Zhang,Wei Ye*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SHIFT is an LLM-based retrieval training framework that combines implicit reasoning in latent space with fine-grained next-token-prediction reconstruction to address the mismatch between contrastive learning objectives and reasoning, outperforming existing retrievers on reasoning-intensive benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reasoning-enhanced retrievers face a fundamental mismatch: contrastive retrieval objectives are not aligned with generation-based reasoning objectives. "Rewrite-then-retrieve" methods are computationally expensive due to explicit reasoning, while implicit-reasoning retrievers (GIRCSE, LaSER) use soft tokens for efficiency but still suffer from this objective mismatch. The authors aim to resolve this tension by unifying retrieval training with generation-aligned reasoning.

Method: SHIFT has two core components: (1) LLMs are converted into reasoning-efficient retrievers using residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in latent space, enabling implicit reasoning without explicit text generation; (2) A fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction objective is introduced to bridge the gap between contrastive learning (standard for retrieval) and implicit reasoning, ensuring the latent representations retain generation-compatible semantics.

Result: Extensive experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that SHIFT consistently outperforms other widely used retrievers. Detailed ablation analysis illustrates the mechanism and contribution of each component.

Conclusion: SHIFT effectively harmonizes implicit reasoning with retrieval training by aligning contrastive and generative objectives, yielding state-of-the-art performance on reasoning-intensive retrieval tasks while maintaining efficiency.

Abstract: LLM-based retrievers have become a fundamental component of modern information retrieval systems. The paradigm of "rewrite-then-retriev" introduces explicit reasoning before retrieval. In addition, implicit-reasoning retrievers such as GIRCSE and LaSER improve efficiency by replacing explicit reasoning with soft tokens. Although these methods demonstrated competitive performance on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, they struggle to address the mismatch between the objectives of retrieval and generation. In this work, we propose SHIFT ($\textbf{S}$elf-reconstruction $\textbf{H}$arnesses $\textbf{I}$mplicit $\textbf{F}$ine-grained $\textbf{T}$hinking for Retrieval), a retrieval training framework based on LLMs. Firstly, we transfer LLMs into reasoning-efficient retrievers with residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in the latent space. Secondly, we alleviate the mismatch between contrastive learning and implicit reasoning using fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction. Extensive experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks show that SHIFT consistently outperforms other widely used retrievers. We also carried out a detailed analysis to illustrate how our method works.

</details>


### [355] [Diffusion Language Model for Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21519)
*Chengyi Liu,Yongqi Zhou,Junwei Pan,Zhixiang Feng,Chengguo Yin,Haijie Gu,Jie Jiang,Yinghao Liu,Yujuan Ding,Qing Li,Wenqi Fan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: DLMRec proposes a discrete diffusion language model for recommendation, replacing autoregressive generation with a diffusion-based paradigm that better captures structural item dependencies, incorporates collaborative signals via a stochastic tokenizer, and improves generation stability through curriculum training and voting aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive generation in LLM-based recommenders suffers from two key limitations: (1) the next-token objective prioritizes sequential order over structural inter-item dependencies that reflect genuine user preferences, and (2) prefix-constrained left-to-right decoding prevents bidirectional context and allows early errors to accumulate without correction. Diffusion language models offer a natural alternative that addresses these shortcomings.

Method: DLMRec integrates three components: (1) a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer that encodes multi-hop collaborative signals into discrete tokens suitable for diffusion modeling; (2) a curriculum-driven training strategy that progressively aligns the denoising process with preference recovery at both item and token levels; (3) a stability-aware voting mechanism that aggregates iterative predictions to enhance generation consistency and robustness.

Result: Not specified in the abstract.

Conclusion: Not specified in the abstract.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-empowered recommender systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for generative recommendation, leveraging their strong semantic reasoning and generative capacity to model complex, diverse user preferences. However, most existing approaches rely on an autoregressive paradigm that is suboptimal for recommendation. The next-token objective emphasizes sequential order rather than the structural inter-item dependencies underlying user preferences. In addition, prefix-constrained generation restricts bidirectional context and commits to left-to-right decoding, causing early errors to accumulate without correction. Inspired by the success of diffusion language models, we propose \textbf{DLMRec}, a discrete diffusion language model tailored for recommendation that offers a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation. Specifically, DLMRec introduces three key components to bridge diffusion language modeling with recommendation. First, a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer encodes multi-hop collaborative signals into expressive discrete tokens compatible with diffusion modeling. Second, a curriculum-driven training strategy aligns the denoising process with preference recovery through progressive item- and token-level learning. Third, a stability-aware voting mechanism aggregates iterative predictions to improve generation consistency and robustness.

</details>

### [356] [pAI-Econ-claude: A Gated Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Architecture for AI-Assisted Economic Theory Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21268)
*Chen Zhu,Xiaolu Wang,Weilong Zhang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: pAI-Econ-claude introduces a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development, where specialized gates diagnose failures and human checkpoints retain authority over irreversible decisions. Evaluated against an ungated baseline on five economic-theory tasks, the gated architecture was preferred in 4/5 rankings, reducing failure severity from 1.58 to 1.16 and increasing usefulness from 2.60 to 3.10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents in social-science tasks like economics produce outputs lacking cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signals. This creates a reliability problem for multi-agent systems: no component can certify the final result, making it unclear how to organize generation, critique, coordination, and human judgment.

Method: The authors propose pAI-Econ-claude, a gated architecture where agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records. Specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without certifying correctness. Human checkpoints retain authority over decisions costly to reverse. The system is evaluated against an ungated baseline across five matched economic-theory tasks, with two blinded evaluators providing pairwise rankings.

Result: Blinded evaluators agreed on all five pairwise rankings, preferring the gated architecture in 4/5 tasks. Mean failure severity dropped from 1.58 (baseline) to 1.16 (gated); overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest gain came from a reality check rejecting a false market-structure premise and a proof review prompting revision of a false welfare claim. The one negative case showed scaffolding can overly compress an economically important mechanism.

Conclusion: Gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification. The allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy.

Abstract: In many social-science research tasks, such as economics, LLM-based agents must produce outputs for which no cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signal exists. This creates a distinctive reliability problem for multi-agent systems: how should generation, critique, coordination, and human judgment be organized when no component can certify the final result? We address this problem through pAI-Econ-claude, a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development. Agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records; specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without certifying correctness; and human checkpoints retain authority over decisions that are costly to reverse. We evaluate the architecture on five matched economic-theory tasks against an ungated baseline. Two evaluators blinded to configuration agreed on all five pairwise rankings, preferring the gated architecture in four tasks and the baseline in one. Mean failure severity fell from 1.58 to 1.16, while overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest observed gain occurred when a reality check rejected a false market-structure premise and a proof review prompted revision of a false welfare claim. The negative case shows that scaffolding can also compress an economically important mechanism too aggressively. The results support a bounded claim: gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification, and the allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy. The workflow is publicly available at https://github.com/maxwell2732/pAI-Econ-claude.

</details>


### [357] [FedAgentKE: Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution for Heterogeneous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21361)
*Weihao Li,Jun Bai,Ziyang Song*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: FedAgentKE is a lightweight federated framework that enables heterogeneous LLM-based agent systems to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning knowledge through semantic distillation and aggregation, without sharing raw data, improving cross-framework and cross-task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent frameworks operate in isolation, with local experiences fragmented across systems. Even memory-based agents that reuse workflows remain confined to individual frameworks, preventing cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative evolution of reasoning capabilities.

Method: FedAgentKE employs federated semantic knowledge evolution with three core mechanisms: (1) iterative semantic knowledge distillation from local agent reasoning, (2) privacy-preserving aggregation of semantic abstractions across distributed frameworks, and (3) adaptation of the aggregated knowledge back into individual agents — all without sharing raw reasoning trajectories.

Result: Consistent performance improvements were demonstrated under both cross-framework and cross-task evaluation settings, validating the effectiveness of federated semantic knowledge evolution.

Conclusion: Federated semantic knowledge evolution presents a promising direction for building collaborative agent ecosystems where heterogeneous agents can benefit from collective reasoning experience while preserving privacy.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on reasoning, tool use, and iterative execution, yet existing agent frameworks still operate largely in isolation. While recent memory-based agent systems improve individual agents through local retrieval and workflow reuse, local experiences remain fragmented across isolated agent frameworks, limiting cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative reasoning evolution. We propose FedAgentKE, a lightweight framework for Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution across heterogeneous agents. FedAgentKE enables distributed agent frameworks to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning abstractions through iterative semantic knowledge distillation, aggregation, and adaptation without sharing raw reasoning trajectories. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements under both cross-framework and cross-task settings, highlighting the potential of federated semantic knowledge evolution for future collaborative agent ecosystems.

</details>
